resumo: Missing covariate data is a feature common to most epidemiologic and clinical studies. It is now widely recognized that the routinely used complete-case analysis—which excludes subjects with any missing variable—can (i) yield highly inefficient estimators in regression analysis, and (ii) be severely biased when the data are not a completely random sample of the full data (thus not missing completely at random). In the simplest and most familiar setting where the observed data arise from simple random sampling (ie, independent and identically distributed data), weighted estimating equations provide a powerful framework to perform regression analysis, while appropriately accounting for covariate data missing at random but not necessarily missing completely at random. In this issue of Epidemiology, Moore et al1 use 2-stage weighted estimating equations or re-weighted estimating equations to perform logistic regression of Y, the indicator of “trying to loose weight in the last 12 months” on Z, the indicator of high cholesterol that is missing by happenstance, controlling for a subset of fully observed covariates X collected in the third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES III). NHANES III used stratified, multistage sampling and thus does not follow a simple random sampling design. The authors use all sampled participants with complete observations, but propose to jointly account for individuals' differential propensity both to be selected into the survey sample and to have an observed cholesterol indicator. They note that this can be achieved by multiplying participants' respective contribution to the complete-case logistic score equation by the product of the (known) inverse probability of being selected and the (unknown) inverse probability of having an observed cholesterol indicator (see equation (3) of their paper). The missingness mechanism, which stochastically determines which of the sampled participants have complete data, is unknown to the analyst and therefore must be estimated. Fortunately, missingness at random implies that an individual's probability of having an observed cholesterol indicator (R = 1) does not depend on whether or not she has high cholesterol, but may depend on other fully observed variables Y, X, and S. Here, S includes covariates that might not be of primary scientific interest, but are necessary with Y and X, to explain any association between R and Z. Under this assumption, one can therefore proceed by substituting the unknown weights with estimated weights,2 constructed with an estimate ˆπ = π (X, Y, S; ˆα) of Pr(R = 1|X, Y, S), where ˆα denotes the observed data maximum likelihood estimator of the coefficients of the logistic regression of R on (X, Y, S). Moore et al essentially adapt this approach to their two-stage procedure, but require the stronger assumption that S can be dropped from π. In this commentary, special consideration is given to issues of statistical efficiency and modeling robustness. First, even in the absence of model mis-specification, inverse-probability weighting can be highly inefficient. This is because, even when (as suggested by Moore et al), one fits a highly parameterized model for π (of course within limits of the data), inverse-probability weighting still fails to make optimal use of data (Y, X, S) observed among all individuals including those missing Z. Second, an incorrect working regression model for the missingness mechanism, π, will invariably result in a biased re-weighted estimator of the parameter β = (β0, βx′, βz) indexing the main logistic regression model of interest logit(Pr(Y = 1|X, Z; β)) = β0 + βx′X + βzZ. In this short commentary, we briefly address these 2 issues by describing a straightforward implementation of an estimator that (a) partially protects against model mis-specification of the weights by remaining consistent for β when the model for π is incorrect, provided that a working parametric model g (Z|Y, X, S; η), with unknown parameter η, for the conditional density of the covariate Z given (Y, X, S), is correct, (b) remains consistent for β when π is correctly modeled, irrespective of the correctness of the posited model for the conditional density of Z, and (c) is in large sample and in the absence of model mis-specification, guaranteed to be more efficient than inverse-probability weighting. By virtue of satisfying (a) and (b), this estimator is an example of a so-called doubly robust estimator. Because we rarely know which if any of (a) or (b) holds, double robustness is a desirable property as it effectively provides the analyst with 2 separate chances of obtaining a consistent estimator of the logistic regression parameter β, instead of the single chance conferred by inverse-probability weighting and conventional likelihood or Bayesian solutions to this problem.3–8 When compared with existing implementations of doubly robust estimators,8 the main appeal of the proposed approach is that it is easily performed using Proc NLMIXED in SAS and thus can be used in routine data analyses without much additional effort. The accompanying technical report9 provides an extension of the method to regression analysis with outcome missing at random, and to the estimation of a marginal structural mean model for point exposure under the assumption of no unmeasured confounding. A Simple Doubly Robust Estimator To simplify this presentation, I depart from the survey sampling framework of the paper; however, as I will later discuss, the described methodology equally applies to the survey setting. Thus, I assume that the observed data consists of n samples of independent and identically distributed data O = (R, ZR, X, S, Y) obtained from a common statistical distribution function. Then, under the missing at random assumption, and assuming that an individual's probability of having complete data is bounded away from 0, ˆβdr satisfies (a), (b), and (c), where ˆβdr is obtained as followed: First, obtain the estimator ˆη that maximizes the complete-case working log-likelihood function σni=1Ri × log (g (Zi|Yi, Xi, Si; η)). For Zi categorical, continuous or a count, conventional models from the exponential family as well as any other user-supplied parametric model can be implemented in Proc NLMIXED of SAS. If Zi is binary, go to the next step; otherwise, for observation i = 1, … n, and user-supplied integer K, generate pseudo data Zi,k*, k = 1,…, K, from ĝ = g(Zi,k*|Yi, Xi, Si; ˆη). Then go to the next step. For binary Zi, find ˆβdr that maximizes the weighted-pseudo-log-likelihood function ll (β*) = σi=1n[ˆωi log(f (Yi|Xi, Zi; β*)) + (1 − ˆωi) × (σz=01g(z|Yi, Xi, Si; ˆη) × log (f (Yi|Xi,z; β*)))] where log (f (Yi|Xi, z; β*)) = (Yi log (Pr (Y = 1|Xi, Zi; β*)) + (1 − Yi) log (Pr(Y = 0|Xi, Zi; β*)) is the log-likelihood for logistic regression, and Categorical Zi can generally be handled in a fashion similar to the binary case, provided the number of categories is not excessive. For other types of variable Zi, let ˆβdr = ˆβdr (K) be the maximizer of llK (β*) = σi=1n[ˆωif (Yi|Xi, Zi; β*) + (1 − ˆωi) × (σk=1Kf (Yi|Xi, Zi,k*; β*))], where Zi,k* k = 1, . . ., K are obtained in step 2. Maximizing either ll(β*) or llK(β*) can be done in SAS Proc NLMIXED with the “model y∼ general (·)” statement, where · stands for an individual's contribution to either ll (β*) or llK (β*) whose functional form can be specified by the user. See the example of programming code provided in the Appendix. An informal argument as to the correctness of the approach comes from noting that the first derivative of say ll (β*) gives the estimating function where u (Y, Z, X; β*) = [1, Xi′, Zi]′ (Yi − Pr(Y = 1|Xi, Zi; β*)) is the logistic regression score function evaluated at β*, and ˆE (·|Yi, Zi, Si) stands for the conditional expectation with respect to ĝ, the estimated density function of Z given Y, X, and S; this estimating function is exactly an empirical version of the estimating function previously derived and used for efficiency purposes2,10 and subsequently shown to be doubly robust.6,7,8 The first term of the equation corresponds to inverse-probability weighting for logistic regression, and only uses complete cases. The role of the second term is to make optimal use of all of the observed data. It serves to recover information by leveraging any existing correlation between Zi and (Yi, Xi, Si) to “impute ” expected contributions to the estimating function for both complete and incomplete observations. When both models for π and g are correct, one can show that ˆβdr is generally asymptotically more efficient than the inverse-probability weighting estimator2 used by Moore et al,1 which solves σi=1nˆωiu(Yi, Zi, Xi; β*) = 0. A similar result holds for llK (β*), although ˆE (·|Yi, Zi, Si) is then replaced by a summation over the pseudo-observations Zi,k*, k = 1, . . . K. When Z is continuous, this summation is in effect evaluating an integral by Monte Carlo simulation, thus avoiding the need for numerical integration. The choice of K can only affect the efficiency of the resulting estimator and not its consistency. When all models are correct, smaller values of K will invariably lead to less efficiency than large ones; however, values of K between 5 and 15 should probably suffice in most applications. The estimator ˆβdr is asymptotically normal, therefore formal inferences on β can be based on Wald-type confidence intervals constructed with the nonparametric bootstrap estimator of variance. It is important to note that ll (β*) (equivalently llK (β*)) cannot be viewed as a proper log- likelihood function, but rather serves as a device to obtain an estimator with properties (a), (b), and (c). Finally, the proposed method can be applied to vector-valued Z with components consisting of continuous, discrete or covariates of mixed type, and is thus very general. A Simulation Study In a small simulation study aimed at illustrating the finite sample behavior of this estimator compared with inverse-probability weighting, I simulated 1000 random samples of size n = 500, of independent and identically distributed data under a generating mechanism which does the following: samples S and X from independent standard normal densities; generates dichotomous Z and Y from the joint probability mass function where I impose and so that logit (f(1|Z, X; β)) = β0 + βzZ + βxzZX + βxX and logit (g(1|Y, X, S; η)) = η0+ ηyY + ηyxYX + ηxX + ηsS, where ηY = βz and ηyx = βxz; and finally obtains R from Bernoulli sampling with success probability given by logit (π(X, Y, S; α)) = α0 + αyY + αsS + αxX + αyx2YX2 + αsySY + αs2xS2X, thus imposing MAR. The Table 1 reports results from fitting ˆβdr and ˆβipw (the inverse-probability–weighted estimator) to the observed data (RZ, R, X, Y, S) under 4 different model specifications; first, in estimating ˆβdr and ˆβipw I consistently estimate both π and g in the scenario corresponding to the “all true” row of results in the Table, next I mis-specify π by setting αyx2=αsy=αs2x = 0 under the setting which is reported in the “wrong π” row of results of the Table, then I mis-specify g by setting ηyz = 0 under the setting which is reported in the “wrong g” row of results of the Table, and finally both g and π are incorrectly specified as above, in the final row labeled “all wrong” results.TABLE 1: Simulation ResultsUnder the correct model specification of both π and g (corresponding to the first 2 rows of results in the Table), both estimators have finite sample bias of comparable size across parameter estimates. As predicted by theory, ˆβdr is more efficient than ˆβipw, with ranging between 87% and 92% for different parameters. Under mis-specification of g, both estimators maintain small finite sample bias, while neither appears to clearly dominate with respect to efficiency across all parameters. Next, I find that in agreement with theory, ˆβipw is severely biased under mis-specification of π relative to ˆβdr which again maintains negligible bias. Under mis-specification of both π and g, the bias of all estimators is also larger as expected. Survey Sampling I have briefly demonstrated a simple implementation of a doubly robust estimator of the parameters of a logistic regression model with covariates missing at random. Although this method is described under random sampling, it is easily adapted to the survey sampling setting. In fact, this is achieved by simply weighting each person's contribution to the pseudo-log-likelihood by the inverse of their probability of being selected into the sample. I revisited the NHANES III data used by Moore et al1 and obtained a doubly robust estimate of β using my approach. Remarkably, out of 14 logistic regression coefficients, my estimated effects agreed for all but 3 parameters; education: 12 = 0.282 (instead of 0.134 reported by Moore et al), >12 = 0.572 instead of (0.356); routine health care visit <2 years = 0.493 (instead of 0.703 reported by Moore et al); and history of premature heart disease = 0.202 (instead of 0.002). However, I did not obtain confidence intervals for these estimates, as the nonparametric bootstrap in this setting requires taking into account the design of the study, a task beyond the scope of this commentary. With very few changes, the approach proposed herein equally applies to linear and log-linear regression with missing covariates, most commonly used for continuous and count data respectively; details are omitted but are easily deduced from the accompanying technical report.9

titulo: Mechanical Bowel Preparation: Are We Ready for a Paradigm Shift?
instituicoes: Banaras Hindu University | Institute of Medical Sciences
palavras_openalex: mechanical bowel preparation | colorectal surgery | postoperative complications | anastomotic leakage | wound infection | intra-abdominal abscess | colonic mucosal damage | randomized controlled trials | methodological quality of trials | bowel preparation | evidence-based medicine | colonic bacteria | relaparotomy | postoperative ileus
resumo: Colorectal surgery is still a challenge to the surgeon with respect to wound infection, intra-abdominal abscess and anastomotic leak. Since these complications are mainly caused by endogenous colonic bacteria, it was always thought logical that reducing the fecal load and bacterial count would reduce the rate of complications. This led to the concept of bowel antisepsis and cleansing in the 1940s and was accepted as a dogma in the 1970s. Since then various techniques of bowel preparation, the agents used and the modus operandi have changed many times. Such rapid changes indicate that either the surgeons are not uniformly happy with the procedure or are still looking for an ideal agent.Although traditionally mechanical bowel preparation (MBP) had its proposed advantages and shortcomings which were matter of some debate, its true role was never assessed through the eyes of evidence-based medicine. Hughes [1] (1972) was the first to challenge its long-claimed beneficial role when MBP was an incontestable routine. It was followed by a flurry of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in the last two decades scrutinizing the role of MBP in elective colorectal surgery. Interestingly, all had concluded that MBP does not have any significant advantage in decreasing complications of colorectal surgery. Researchers went on further to prove that MBP actually increases infectious complications and anastomotic leaks and causes significant morphological and inflammatory changes in the colonic mucosa [2]. These were evidence enough to abandon it as a routine, which however actually did not happen. On the contrary, serious questions were raised on the accuracy of these RCTs. Unfortunately, none of these actually met the CONSORT guidelines completely.A historic meta-analysis by Bucher et al. [3] evaluating seven RCTs concluded that there was no evidence to support the use of MBP in patients undergoing elective colorectal surgery. Though it was the highest form of evidence, it was not devoid of technical errors and the outcome analysis was conflicting and incongruent. More recent multicentric randomized trials are better structured, however, and statistically robust. To name a few, a multicentric trial from Sweden which accrued 1,505 patients to give the study almost the desired power failed to demonstrate any significant benefit of MBP in reducing wound infection, overall infection and relaparotomy rate [4]. A systematic review by Guenaga et al. [5] done with meticulous selection of studies to prevent bias and type II error concluded that prophylactic MBP was not beneficial for the patients and controversially the bowel preparation might lead to more anastomotic leakage. Though it was not a part of consensus statement, the authors recommended such procedure should be omitted. In a multicenter randomized trial by Contant et al. [6], the rate of anastomotic leakage did not differ significantly between with and without MBP groups (p < 0.69). Although other septic complications, fascial dehiscence and mortality did not differ, those with MBP had fewer abscesses after anastomotic leakage (p < 0.001). In another novel study, questionnaires evaluating multiple subjective symptoms arising from MBP were assessed among patients [7]. Interestingly, though the time to postoperative oral intake did not differ, bowel emptying occurred earlier in the no-MBP group. Overall, the patients expressed significant distress to MBP. Thus, as more and more evidence has accrued, the role of MBP has faced a big challenge with some authorities saying it is unnecessary, while others think it may actually harm.In the midst of these newer observations, one pertinent query remains. Polyethylene glycol (PEG) has been used for bowel preparation in most of these RCTs/multicenter trials. The outcome of using other agents like sodium phosphate or picosulfate in bowel preparation is not adequately known in comparison to PEG. This makes one ask ‘is it the procedure which is at fault or the agent?’ This is reflected in a meta-analysis by Slim et al. [8], which included 11 trials and focused on the methodological qualities and congruent outcome measures like anastomotic leak and septic complications. They observed significantly higher anastomotic leakage after MBP. All other endpoint analyses also favored a no-preparation approach without a significant difference. Interestingly, subgroup analysis showed that anastomotic leakage was significantly greater after bowel preparation with PEG compared to no preparation but not after other types of preparation. Although the authors conclude with evidence in favor of omitting MBP, they also make a point regarding comparison of other bowel preparations with PEG. A recent trial by Itani et al. [9] comparing PEG with sodium phosphate concluded that bowel preparation with sodium phosphate is superior. Another recent review by Nichols et al. [10] (2005) concluded that MBP has still a high potential of decreasing infective complication rate, and it works best when combined with preoperative oral and perioperative parenteral prophylactic antibiotics. These observations indicate that surgeons are still not ready to forego bowel preparation, which has been practiced as a dogma for more than half a century and continue to search for the ideal agent.The role of MBP in rectal surgeries has not been adequately addressed to. As most of the studies involve colonic resections and few studies have focused only on rectal resections, the body of evidence is inadequate for decision-making. Traditionally, rectal washouts were common and are still widely practiced. Bretagnol et al. [11], in a nonrandomized study, compared 51 consecutive patients with rectal resection without MBP to a matched group of 61 controls with MBP. Although the overall morbidity was higher in the MBP group, the rate of anastomotic leakage was similar (8 vs. 10%; p = 1.000). Interestingly, peritonitis occurred more, though not significantly, in the no-MBP group, and a trend toward higher infectious complications was noted in the MBP group. Another nonrandomized retrospective study (n = 144) from the Netherlands, which included low anterior resections without MBP, reported a less than 5% anastomotic leakage rate as compared to a leakage rate of up to 18% in studies using MBP [12]. Though this study is weak and noncomparative, it is worth mentioning that surgeons from different corners are trying to evaluate the outcome of rectal resections without MBP. At present, it is too premature to comment anything in this regard. More evidence in the form of multicenter trials is required for evaluation of role of MBP in rectal surgery.With the rise of laparoscopic resection for colon cancers, the role of MBP needs to be defined in this arena. Although data are inadequate, attempts have been made to evaluate this complex situation. In a retrospective study by Zmora et al.[ 13], patients with and without MBP, who underwent laparoscopic colectomy, were compared. There was no statistical difference between the two groups with regard to postoperative infective complications and anastomotic leak rate, indicating that laparoscopic colectomy can safely be performed without MBP. Larger prospective trials, however, are required to come to safe conclusions. Since, depending on situation, the laparoscopic technique may vary, e.g. a purely laparoscopic approach or a laparoscopic-assisted approach or even a laparoscopic hand-assisted surgery especially when the tumor needs intraoperative palpation and localization, it is difficult to make comparisons on equal grounds as the studies tend to be lengthy and time-consuming particularly when conversion rate is high.It is intriguing that despite adequate evidence, recommendation to abandon MBP as a routine still fails to find place in the guidelines of various surgical societies (Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland, 2001 [14], The guidelines of the Clinical Standards Board of Scotland in 2003 [15]). In 1997, it was observed that 100% of American colorectal surgeons used MBP prior to colorectal surgery [16]. A survey of the American colorectal surgeons in 2001 revealed that 46% used sodium phosphate, 32% used PEG and 15% selectively alternated between the two [17]. Another survey of five northern European countries (2005) showed that 75% surgeons used MBP [18]. These practices among surgeons globally indicate that preoperative bowel preparation is still very much in vogue, in spite of recent data accumulating against it. This is probably because irrespective of geographical distribution surgeons are mostly dogmatic in their habits and are reluctant to change. Absence of a strong recommendation is thus reflected in their continued practice of MBP.Thus, it seems the surgical fraternity is not yet unanimously ready to abandon bowel preparation in elective colorectal surgery. Though most surgeons world over still practice bowel preparation of some form and believe in its beneficial role, recent good evidence points otherwise and is still accumulating. As of now, we stand on the crossroad and are uncertain whether we are slowly facing a paradigm shift as far as MBP is concerned. Despite evidence gathering momentum, it is restricted to a few centers or authorities or academic institutes, and is yet to become a universal phenomenon. For this to happen, recommendation for abandoning MBP needs to find a place in the guidelines of various surgical societies. We have to wait some more time to know whether it continues to hold its place or is abandoned as a practice of the past. As of now, we can only hope for consensus statements backed by good level of evidence in future so that morbidity of the patients undergoing colorectal surgery is not unduly increased.Nil.

titulo: A Call to Arms: The Credibility Gap in Interventional Pain Medicine and Recommendations for Future Research
autores: Steven Paul Cohen | Richard A. Deyo
instituicoes: Johns Hopkins Hospital | Johns Hopkins Medicine | Johns Hopkins University | Kaiser Permanente | Oregon Health & Science University | Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences
palavras_openalex: interventional pain management | credibility gap | epidural steroid injection | confirmation bias | publication bias | evidence-based medicine | radiofrequency denervation | sacroiliac joint pain | clinical trial design | research recommendations | pain clinic
resumo: There is a credibility gap in interventional pain medicine. Our evaluations of the interventions we perform differ significantly from those of our colleagues in other specialties. This has significant ramifications that affect our patients, training programs, and reimbursement schedules. A similar difference of perception exists for some procedures in other specialties (e.g., radiology, interventional cardiology, and spine surgery), but it is particularly conspicuous for pain interventionalists. Even noninterventionalist pain specialists perceive the procedures we perform to be less effective than we do . For epidural steroid injections (ESI), the most commonly performed procedures in pain clinics across the United States , clinical trials performed by interventionalists are nearly three times more likely to yield positive results than those performed by noninterventionalist physicians, such as surgeons, rheumatologists, or neurologists . For evidence-based and systematic reviews on ESI, the conclusions reached by authors who are interventionalists are more than three times as likely to be favorable than those done by noninterventionalists . These reviews examine the same articles, using the same grading schemes, yet reach dramatically different conclusions. Similar discrepancies exist for other interventions as well, including radiofrequency denervation, sacroiliac joint pain, and intradiscal treatments . There are several potential explanations for these discrepancies. First and perhaps most obvious is confirmation bias, which is the tendency to seek out or interpret information in a way that confirms one's preconceptions and discounts conflicting evidence. This is a natural human trait. For individual studies, we might invoke a better ability of specialists to design and evaluate clinical trials (e.g., better selection) to account for some of the disparities. As an example, investigators studying ESI should not include individuals with nonspecific axial back pain and should aim to separate leg pain (which is more likely to respond to treatment than back pain) from back pain for their primary outcome measure. However, whereas better study design may partially account for differences in clinical study outcomes, it fails to explain differences in the conclusions of systematic reviews. Publication bias refers to the fact that positive trials are more likely to be published than negative trials. This may bias the literature overall, but again fails to explain discrepancies in interpreting published evidence. Aside from published studies, some of the skepticism of our clinical colleagues may result from the difference in results often observed between fastidious clinical trials (efficacy) and routine care (effectiveness). Clinical trials typically include stringent lists of inclusion and exclusion criteria, often eliminating patients with advanced age, comorbid disease, or complex medication regimens. In clinical practice, we typically treat patients who are receiving opioid therapy, have psychopathology, are receiving disability compensation, and have unresolved secondary gain issues, all of which dampen treatment effects. In trials, techniques are highly standardized and follow-up is brief, which may maximize the observed treatment effect, and in some cases reduce the placebo response rate . In practice, techniques vary more widely, and follow-up is for a lifetime. Structural and methodological limitations can also magnify apparent treatment effects in clinical trials. Studies evaluating pain interventions are notoriously difficult to blind for doctors and patients (e.g., subjects who undergo radiofrequency denervation often feel the heating, or experience postprocedure neuritis, and those who receive ESI may experience pain shooting into their leg or elevated glucose levels). Inadequately blinded studies are more likely to yield exaggerated results, especially for subjective outcome measures such as pain . For all these reasons, it is no surprise that real-world results often fail to match those observed in clinical trials. This could explain why our noninterventional colleagues are less impressed with our practice results than some clinical trials might suggest. But it does little to explain the differences between trial results or interpretations by different specialty groups. One contributing factor to the credibility crisis is that as we train more physicians to perform these procedures, we may become more lax in selecting patients for interventions. There is a correlation between the number of procedures done for pain (e.g., spine surgery, injections, and imaging) and the number of doctors who perform these procedures . As a result, more patients with “weak indications” may receive injections (e.g., an ESI done in a patient with long-standing axial back pain). The most likely reason for this phenomenon is that our reimbursement scale is skewed toward procedures and away from conservative management. There also appears to be a tacit or even explicit understanding in some practices, in which doctors agree to prescribe opioids only if patients agree to undergo regular injections. On multiple occasions, patients whose pain physician retired, lost their medical license, or discharged the patient from the clinic openly approached me with this offer of a “quid pro quo” during our initial consultation. A desire to continue opioids is hardly an indication for interventional therapy. Approximately 85% of published medical studies are positive, with even higher percentages noted in disciplines such as psychology and social sciences , which play integral roles in pain therapy . There are over a dozen medical journals devoted to pain, publishing hundreds of articles per month. If we consider all the positive trial results, and compound the benefit of increasingly effective treatments each month going back to the 1970's, then pain should be vanishingly rare in the 21st century. Yet the reported prevalence of chronic pain has soared to epidemic proportions . Even considering the magnification of treatment results in fastidious efficacy studies, the numbers do not add up. The publication of mutually exclusive or implausible findings also poses a credibility problem. For example, medial branch (facet joint nerve) blocks are sometimes claimed to provide long-term benefit in a majority of individuals . Yet, in trials evaluating radiofrequency denervation, only a small percentage of those who respond to medial branch blocks sustain long-term relief that obviates the need for radiofrequency treatment . Furthermore, prolonged pain relief from blockade of the nerves supplying a painful structure is inconsistent with what we observe in the operating room: nerve blocks done as anesthesia for surgery do not generally alleviate pain for long time periods. The notion of prolonged relief is also irreconcilable with the conceptual basis for “comparative controlled blocks” to diagnose facet joint pain. The concept behind comparative controlled blocks is that a “true” diagnosis is only rendered if a patient responds with pain relief commensurate with the expected duration of action of a short- and a long-acting local anesthetic, administered blindly . Experiencing several months of relief after receiving a drug whose duration of action is 2 hours (e.g., lidocaine) is more consistent with a placebo response than a true pharmacological response. Either one of these concepts must be false or both are only partially true (and partially false), but they both cannot be correct. A similar concern applies to regional injection therapies that claim to work for a wide assortment of pain conditions characterized by different mechanisms (e.g., botulinum toxin for plantar fasciitis, myofascial pain, neuropathic pain, headaches, and interstitial cystitis.) . Finally, skepticism is appropriate regarding reports of astounding long-term results with a one-time treatment that lacks a solid preclinical foundation (e.g., intradiscal methylene blue) . Controversies such as the ones noted earlier typically arise when there is a paucity of rigorous science. We believe a stronger evidence base for our practice is essential. In designing research, we should not set out to prove that we are right, assuming that we know the answer. That strategy leads to weak science, and an ethical assumption of randomized trials is that we have equipoise: we genuinely do not know the answer. Here are a few suggestions for improving the evidence base, although these are certainly not exhaustive. Interventionalists should not shrink from the responsibility of conducting randomized controlled trials, which remain our best protection from mistaken inferences due to natural history, regression to the mean, placebo effects, and selection biases. The history of vertebroplasty offers an instructive example of this need. Carragee noted that early uncontrolled case series touted 90% success rates with very rare complications. And yet, “with each increase in the quality of evidence, the apparent quantity of effect has diminished and diminished. …” He notes that the same story has played out many times in clinical medicine . In designing clinical trials, researchers should consider enrolling a wider range of subjects from multiple venues (i.e., multicenter studies) to better reflect those who will receive the treatment in actual practice. This is one of the principles being enunciated in the new language of “comparative effectiveness” research. Do you worry that some patient groups predictably will not respond? Then stratify the analysis (e.g., comparing patients receiving opioids with those not receiving opioids, or employed patients vs those receiving disability compensation) or perform appropriate multivariate adjustment. Simply excluding patients who may respond poorly means that we will never learn the truth. Be skeptical: what makes perfect intuitive sense sometimes proves wrong. Many centuries ago, the greatest scientific minds believed that it was intuitive that the earth was the center of the universe. Rather than reflexively defending the status quo, we need to listen to critiques, consider which ones may have some validity, and seek to address them. This is how the greatest leaders operate. A greater focus should be placed on studying who benefits most from having a procedure at all. Although technical details also require investigation, they should not be the exclusive domain of inquiry. Among the different causes of treatment failure, poor patient selection is far more common than either technical failure or misdiagnosis. For example, the composition of injectate and orientation of the needle are likely to have much smaller effects on ESI outcomes than proper patient selection. In developing clinical guidelines, greater attention is needed to reducing and/or resolving conflicts of interest and to multidisciplinary participation. The Institute of Medicine recently proposed standards for writing clinical guidelines that call for clinicians who benefit from a particular clinical service to be excluded from guideline panels, or to comprise a small minority. Inclusion of methodologists such as biostatisticians and epidemiologists, clinicians from other specialties, and patient representatives was a key recommendation . A recent study suggested that the quality of guidelines posted in the online National Guideline Clearinghouse was generally poor and that those developed by subspecialty societies were of lower quality than those developed by government agencies or outside the United States . Start training a cadre of fellows in clinical research methods. Strong clinical research is not a hobby to be indulged on nights and weekends. The concepts and body of relevant knowledge required to evaluate clinical studies are quite different from those needed to master pharmacokinetics or physiology. Clinical trials are expensive, time consuming, and a test of any sane person's patience and persistence. Well-trained clinical investigators will be essential to compete for funding from National Institutes of Health or the newly created Patient Centered Outcomes Research Institute, which is focused on comparative effectiveness research. These investigators likely will not get rich. In conclusion, we are at a crossroads in pain medicine. We can continue to tread the path of least resistance, embellishing evidence and exploiting loopholes in the remuneration system, or we can invest in performing rigorous studies that examine efficacy and cost-utility, with the expectation that our investment now will pay long-term dividends for ourselves, our patients, and our successors. We need a knowledge base that becomes cumulative, rather than self-contradictory. The medicine of the 21st century has inexorably changed from the medicine of our predecessors, in that there is greater accountability, a greater emphasis on clinical trial outcomes, and a compelling need to contain costs. As a specialty, we can choose now to preemptively address these concerns by greater transparency and more meticulous research, or continue to ignore the irrevocable transformations that are occurring, at our own peril.

resumo: Tactical Citizenship: Domestic Workers, the Remainders of Home, and Undocumented Citizen Participation in the Third Space of Mimicry Charles T. Lee (bio) The sociologist Saskia Sassen has written of the global cities as the concentrated command points and central strategic sites for global capitalist market production. In the midst of the popular phantasmic aspiration for global cities, Sassen points to the grim development of economic polarization where the increasing number of high-income white-collar jobs breeds a great number of low-paying dead-end jobs. Not only does the high-income sector (both residential and commercial) have a huge demand for low-wage service labor (e.g. cleaning, serving, ornamenting), the manufacturing sector is also going through a downgrading process “in which the share of unionized shops declines and wages deteriorate while sweatshops and industrial homework proliferate.”1 It is in these low-wage service and manufacturing sectors with loose labor-protection enforcements in the hyper-capital cities that we encounter the most prominent presence of immigrant workers. Writing in Los Angles, the sociologist Pierrette Hondagneu-Sotelo asks us to imagine “a day without a Mexican”: When you arrive at many a Southern California hotel or restaurant, you are likely to be first greeted by a Latino car valet. The janitors, cooks, busboys, painters, carpet cleaners, and landscape workers who keep the office buildings, restaurants, and malls running are also likely to be Mexican or Central American immigrants, as are many of those who work behind the scenes in dry cleaners, convalescent homes, hospitals, resorts, and apartment complexes. . .. Along the boulevards, at car washes promising “100% hand wash” for prices as low as $4.99, teams of Latino workers furiously scrub, wipe, and polish automobiles. Supermarket shelves boast bags of “prewashed” mesclun or baby greens (sometimes labeled “Euro salad”), thanks to the efforts of the Latino immigrants who wash and package the greens.2 Taking out the Latino immigrant workers will shut down an overwhelming proportion of the capitalist operation of Los Angeles and, increasingly, many other metropolitan cities that rely on immigrants’ laboring bodies. Those who proudly wear the label of “citizens” and who conspicuously benefit from the low-expense arrangement in their everyday life, however, are often incensed at the invasion by the “illegal aliens,” their stealing of “our” jobs, tax dollars and social benefits, and their diluting of “our” cultural heritage. Unaccounted for is the larger globalization process that places these undocumented subjects in a condition where neither secure dwelling nor legitimate traveling is possible. On one hand, neo-liberal policies such as the Structural Adjustment Programs (SAPs) pursued by the U.S.-based financial institutions (i.e. the World Bank and the IMF) through blatant privatization and massive cutting of social subsidies in the Third World regions have collapsed those local economies and shattered their denizens’ sense of secure dwelling, forcing a huge wave of migration outward in search of better job opportunities and a more humane living standard.3 On the other, the system of nation-state citizenship delimits these subjects’ chances of migration through official channels, forcing them to go underground and travel without legitimate documents — whether by overstaying their visas, crossing borders in the desert on foot, or traveling along with smugglers.4 But even such predicament does not readily translate into passive victimization of a mystical “Third World.” Rather, while discrimination and exploitation abound in the globalization of undocumented workers, a resistant agency of the subordinate class also surges forth strongly, courageously, and creatively. Hence, while global cities are the conspicuous sites of flexible capitalist operation that takes advantage of “cheap” and expendable immigrant labor, they are also sites of what social theorist Michel de Certeau calls “secondary production” — a hidden and intricate process bred by the weak in their daily negotiations and struggles against the rich, strong and powerful.5 In the context of globalization, this hidden resistance is often performed by the laboring immigrant workers in both the service sector (e.g. domestics, janitors, hotel maids) and the manufacturing sector (e.g. garment sweatshops), many of who are undocumented and without the official state endowment to act out citizenship. resumo: Blurring the Color Line: The New Chance for a More Integrated America . Richard Alba . Cambridge, MA : Harvard University Press , 2009 . Blurring the Color Line is an important book. Richard Alba describes the decisive mass-scale assimilation of Irish Catholics and the descents of southern and eastern European, as well as the rise of Asian Americans after World War II and, in the process, demonstrates that “ethno-racial hierarchies, at least in democratic, economically dynamic societies, are less rigid than they’re sometimes thought to be” (p. 21). The fundamental question addressed in this insightful study is whether we could see a similar development in the twenty-first century that would effectively erode the rigid racial boundaries disadvantaging African Americans and Hispanics. Alba’s answer, with certain contingencies, is basically affirmative. I will discuss the contingencies shortly. Let me first focus on why he feels it is a mistake “to view our current ethno-racial inequalities as enduring” (p. 7). Alba argues that three conditions led to the relaxation of ethnic boundaries in the mid-twentieth century. The first is what he calls “non-zero-sum mobility,” which occurs when the gains of lower-status disadvantaged groups do not come at the expense of more advantaged groups. Following World War II, non-zero-sum mobility existed for the descendants of Irish Catholic, Jewish, and Orthodox Christian immigrants because economic expansion enabled these groups to obtain more education and better jobs than their parents before them had achieved without sacrifices by native white Protestants. Indeed, many of the children of white Protestants surpassed their parents as well. Under such conditions, the mobility of the disadvantaged groups is less likely “to raise the specter of threat to established privilege and an intensification of competition along racial and ethnic lines” (p. 74). The second condition, which must work in tandem with non-zero-sum mobility, is the ability of less privileged groups to convert their socioeconomic advancement into social proximity with the dominant group, mainly through residential integration. Under such conditions, the children of less privileged groups are more able to gain access to spatially based resources—such as good schools—and develop the social skills and interracial and/or interethnic friendships that contribute to success in mainstream settings when they reach adulthood. Finally, a third condition, which enhances the effectiveness of the first two conditions, is a revision of the ideology that reinforces racial or ethnic boundaries to acknowledge that members of the minority group “have the same moral worth” as members of the dominant group (p. 75). “Those with enlightened views may take on the role of moral entrepreneur,” states Alba, “and act in ways to spur change—by reminding their recalcitrant co-ethnics of the moral imperatives implied by the democratic ideals they hold sacrosanct, facilitating the entry of minority individuals into spheres from which they were previously excluded and protecting them when their presence in such sites is challenged” (p. 75). It is true, according to Alba, that significant boundary changes can be brought about by other means, such as those generated by the civil rights and women’s movements. However, the three conditions in concert are sufficient to account for the striking boundary changes in the decades following World War II, a period that saw the increased entry of white ethnics into the mainstream and the decreased salience of the boundaries that had excluded them previously. The most significant contribution of Blurring the Color Line is the compelling argument that African Americans and Hispanics could also experience the most important condition to bring about boundary changes over the next 25 years—non-zero-sum mobility. Why? Mainly because of the retirement of members of the massive baby-boom generation—who are heavily white, well educated, and hold a disproportionate number of the best-paying occupations. Indeed, argues Alba, the baby-boom generation’s “departure could open up the labor market in a way that has not been true since the middle of the twentieth century” (p. 16). Alba points out that when we look across cohorts today we see a greater penetration of African Americans and Hispanics entering the labor market into top decile and other top quartile positions. Because of this increased ethno-racial diversity near the top, many whites now interact with minorities who are their peers in these positions. And because the percentage of minorities is increasing in the United States, it is reasonable to assume, he argues, that the recruitment into the best jobs will continue to reflect the racial and ethnic demography of birth cohorts. However, despite the special significance of non-zero-sum mobility for ethno-racial boundary change, there are certain contingencies that could change this scenario for African Americans and Hispanics in the next several decades, contingencies that Alba carefully assesses in reaching his ultimate conclusions about the possibility of a more integrated United States. First, there is the possibility that structural economic changes, or a deep and prolonged economic slump, could alter the need to replace the retiring baby boomers with a new cadre of highly trained workers. However, Alba notes that current occupational forecasts “suggest that the long-term prospects for the expansion of jobs in the top half of the workforce are good” (p. 168). Second, large-scale postponement of retirement by the baby boomers could also change the prospects for a period of considerable non-zero-sum mobility. However, Alba feels that this too is unlikely to reach a scale “that would substantially reduce the need for new workers” (p. 168). Third, the United States could resort to recruiting trained immigrants from other countries to fill jobs requiring higher levels of qualification. However, Alba proclaims that the United States will increasingly have to compete with other countries around the world for highly skilled immigrants—countries like Germany, Italy, and Spain whose fertility levels have been well below job replacement levels in recent years. Additionally, the source of highly trained workers from foreign-student populations will be limited in the United States due to the difficulties in obtaining student visas in the post 9/11 era, as well as the aggressive and increasingly successful recruitment of international students by European universities. Moreover, it is reasonable to expect that India and China could take steps to retain their highly skilled nationals if and when they reach certain points of economic development and demographic shift. Fourth, although non-zero-sum mobility would open up higher-paying positions that could be filled by minorities, the expansion of opportunity would enable white women and working-class white males to move into these positions in significantly higher numbers. However, Alba believes neither can satisfy the demand for highly skilled workers in the next several decades. The cohort of whites “that will come of age during the next twenty-five years are notably smaller than are the white baby boomers they will replace” (p. 172), and “it would take something close to a revolution in the arrangements currently governing domestic life and the raising of children to unleash fully the working power of women” (p. 179). Alba does a good job of showing why each of these demographic factors would not satisfy the demand for new workers, but he fails to address their combined impact. Indeed, it is conceivable that the combination of a large-scale postponement of retirement by the baby-boom generation, the hiring of highly trained foreign immigrants, however limited by international competition, and the upward movement of women and working-class whites would provide a sufficient number of workers to replace those baby boomers who actually choose to retire. Nonetheless, even if these factors in tandem would still fail to satisfy the demand for new positions, the most serious threat to the potential for ethno-racial change in the next quarter-century, and the severest challenge to Alba’s thesis remains—namely, the extent to which African Americans and Hispanics are able to take advantage of the opportunities for non-zero-sum mobility, given their lagging postsecondary educational attainments. In addressing this problem, we should be reminded of the two other conditions that led to the relaxation of ethnic boundaries in the mid-twentieth century, and consider the likelihood that each, along with non-zero-sum mobility, could be reproduced in the next quarter-century for less privileged groups of color—gaining access to spatially based resources, such as good schools, through residential integration; and the emergence of a progressive ideology that effectively promotes equality of opportunity. If non-zero-sum mobility does emerge in the next quarter-century, the conditions associated with the removal of racial/ethnic group competition would be favorable for the emergence and acceptance of a more progressive ideology of equality of opportunity as applied to Hispanics, African Americans, and other groups of color. However, there is little reason to assume that African Americans will experience residential integration on a mass scale in the next few decades. Alba is fully aware of the magnitude of the enduring problems stemming from racial segregation. He therefore calls for a greater national investment in education, as well as an effective program of affirmative action. Let me first focus on the need for affirmative action in a period of non-zero-sum mobility. Research suggests that the white backlash against racial entitlements, such as affirmative action, contributed to the government’s retreat from antidiscrimination policies during the 1980s, a retreat that may have influenced hiring and promotion decisions in the corporate sector as well.3 It should not be surprising that waning support for affirmative action programs would have an adverse effect on African Americans in particular. For example, a number of empirical studies have revealed significant differences in the family environment and neighborhood environment of blacks and whites that are understated when standard measures of socioeconomic status (SES) are employed.4 Take, for example, the question of family background. Even when white parents and black parents report the same average income, white parents have substantially more assets than do black parents.5 Whites with the same amount of schooling as blacks usually attend better high schools and colleges. Furthermore, children’s test scores are associated not only with the social and economic status of their parents, but also with the social and economic status of their grandparents. This means that it could take several generations before adjustments in socioeconomic inequality produce their full benefits. Thus, if we were to rely solely on the standard criteria for college admission, like SAT scores, even many children from black middle-income families would be denied admission in favor of middle-income whites, who are not weighed down by the accumulation of disadvantages that stem from racial restrictions and who, therefore, tend to score higher on these conventional tests. For all these reasons, the success of younger educated blacks remains heavily dependent on affirmative action programs, whereby more flexible criteria of evaluation is used to gauge potential to succeed. Alba is absolutely on the mark when he emphasizes the important role of affirmative action. Considering the fact that under conditions of non-zero-sum mobility, the advancement of trained and educated minorities is less threatening to the members of the dominant group because such mobility does not adversely affect their life chances, affirmative action programs, especially those that emphasize flexible criteria of evaluation to gauge a person’s potential to succeed, will be more readily accepted. The policy implications are obvious—race-specific policies like affirmative action will be required for the foreseeable future, even under conditions of non-zero-sum mobility, to ensure the continued mobility of educated minorities. But affirmative action programs are not really designed to address the problems of the most disadvantaged and poorest minorities, especially those who live in impoverished inner-city ghettos. This is where we have to seriously consider Alba’s call for a greater national investment in education, in lieu of an effective long-range program of residential integration, that could lift up those minorities who reside in poor segregated neighborhoods and attend the poorest schools. In other words, we are talking about creating conditions that would enable disadvantage minorities to take advantage of non-zero-sum mobility in the next quarter-century. I say this is more difficult to achieve than promoting programs of affirmative action because it would call for an enormous expenditure that would have to be approved and allocated by Congress. Given the current economic crisis—with, at the time of this writing, an annual deficit of a $1.4 trillion and a debt of $13 trillion—and the nation’s political polarization, it would be naïve to assume that such an expenditure would be readily approved in the next several years. Accordingly, if we are beginning a period of non-zero-sum mobility, the minority individuals who are most likely to benefit will be those who are trained and educated, those who have the qualifications to enter the higher echelons of the labor market, whether directly or via affirmative action programs. Alba recognizes that “the scenario of ethno-racial change coupled to non-zero-sum mobility will not help the minority poor very much” (p. 239). That is why he has called for greater investment in educational institutions and for programs that provide greater opportunity for occupational mobility so that more youngsters who have been raised in poor families and grown up in poor neighborhoods will improve their chances in life. To his credit, he also recognizes that a reduction of such impoverishment will call for “income redistribution through tax and welfare policies and with greater public investment to improve communities where the poor reside and the institutions that serve them” (p. 240). But, to repeat, for the seeable future, especially given the present economic and political climate, only the most optimistic observers would anticipate that such a program would receive the necessary public and political support. Thus, if Alba’s compelling arguments are indeed correct, the new chance for a more integrated United States will largely apply to the more privileged people of color, not the minority poor.

resumo: Rotational atherectomy was developed as a second-generation vascular interventional device specifically to address lesions known to be difficult to manage with balloon angioplasty. Commercialized as the Rotablator, this device utilizes a high-speed rotating elliptical burr coated with a fine diamond abrasive to achieve plaque ablation [1]. The very fine diamond abrasive and flexible drive shaft were incorporated into the design to allow normal soft elastic components of the vessel wall to deflect away from the device so that tissue ablation occurs preferentially against the relatively hard and inelastic components of atheromatous plaque [2-6]. This unique property of differential plaque ablation makes the rotational atherectomy ideally suited for treatment of lesions that are unfavorable for balloon angioplasty, especially calcified lesions, bifurcation lesions, ostial stenoses, chronic total occlusions, and diffuse disease [7-14]. Since its introduction in 1990, the Rotablator has undergone a number of design modifications and changes in recommended technique. The device has been used for both lesion modification and plaque debulking on virtually all types of lesions. Its role in the stent era has also been evaluated. The present article summarizes what we have learned over the past decade about the use of the device to treat obstructive atherosclerosis in the coronary circulation. Although much emphasis is placed on lesion selection in the application of rotational atherectomy, patient selection and clinical characteristics require special emphasis. The diamond abrasive of the Rotablator ablates atheromatous plaque into microparticles, which are not retrieved but rather washed out through the distal coronary circulation. Most ablated microparticles are ≤ 10 μm in diameter, but larger particles are also produced, which can obstruct microcirculation and cause ischemic complications or patchy microinfarctions [4, 15]. High-speed rotation of the burr also produces microcavitations as a result of the Bernoulli effect. The microcavitations are in a size range of 60–90 μm, which can also temporarily obstruct the microcirculation for 20–30 sec [16]. Microparticulate embolization and microcavitation contribute to the slow flow and no-reflow, which occurs more frequently with this device than with others [16-19]. Transient ischemic complications thus may be more frequent than with other devices, even though the incidence of non–Q-wave and Q-wave myocardial infarction are not necessarily increased [20]. Patients with compromised ventricular function, poor distal run-off, multivessel disease with contralateral coronary occlusions, and large plaque burdens (lesion lengths ≥ 25 mm) are at greater risk for ischemic complications [21]. Use of this device in these settings, and in the last remaining conduit and with severely compromised LV function, is discouraged unless appropriate measures are taken to protect the patient from ischemic complications, including placement of an intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation pump (IABP) or use of transfemoral cardiopulmonary support (CPS) [22]. Female gender is also a negative predictor, not only of procedural success, but also of ischemic complications [18]. Careful attention to technique and adjunctive pharmacology is crucial to the outcome in these situations. Downsizing to smaller burrs initially with stepwise increments and size is advised [23-25], as is limitation of the runs to ≤ 30 sec each [26-28] and careful attention to rpm drops to keep them to a minimum and preferably ≤ 5,000 rpm [26]. The Rotablator is FDA-indicated for use in single-vessel native atherosclerotic coronary artery disease with stenoses ≤ 25 mm in length that can be crossed with a guidewire, multivessel coronary artery disease that does not pose undue risk to the patient as outlined above, and native coronary artery restenosis lesions following prior percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty. Rotational ablation is contraindicated for occlusions through which a guidewire cannot be passed in the true lumen, for treatment of the last remaining vessel in patients with compromised LV function, and in the treatment of saphenous bypass graft stenoses. Rotational atherectomy is also contraindicated in vessels with visible thrombus or dissections. The device is particularly suited for heavily calcified lesions [13, 18, 29] and hard recoiling stenoses, such as aorto-ostial, branch ostial, or bifurcation lesions [30, 31]. The “undilatable” stenosis is also a signature lesion for the Rotablator and is well treated with this device (Fig. 1) [32]. Procedural outcomes in these situations is uniformly high and exceeds 90% for each of these lesion subsets. Complex B2 and C lesions are also more effectively treated with rotational atherectomy than with PTCA or excimer laser angioplasty, provided that there is no outflow obstruction, poor distal run-off, or visible thrombus [18]. Highly angulated stenoses ≥ 60°, or eccentric lesions on bends, especially those where the eccentric lesion is opposite a ≥ 45° bend, are not effectively treated with this device and are at increased risk for dissection and perforation and so should be avoided [18, 33]. [Color figure can be viewed in the online issue, which is available at www.interscience.wiley.com]. The Rotablator system consists of the burr, drive shaft, advancer, and console (Fig. 2). The original system consisted of an integrated single-use burr, drive shaft, and advancer. The more recent version of the device incorporates a separate advancer and detachable burrs that allows use of multiple burrs with a single advancer. Both the dedicated and exchangeable advancers incorporate a compressed gas (air or nitrogen) turbine to produce high rotational shaft speeds at low torque. The advancer also has a brake to keep the guidewire from moving or rotating during use. As the drive shaft is advanced and spins around the guidewire, there is a fiber optic cable to provide turbine rpm data to the console and a saline flush port to connect to pressurize saline flush for the drive shaft. The compressed air advancer hose also connects to the console so that activation of the air turbine and adjustment of turbine rpm is regulated by the console. The console also has an elapsed timer to record individual run times and cumulative advancer activation times. A low-speed (70,000 rpm) Dynaglide setting is also selectable from the console for purposes of burr exchange and removal. Rotablator console, advancer, burr, and wire clip. [Color figure can be viewed in the online issue, which is available at www.interscience.wiley.com]. It is crucial that the wire clip be attached to the guidewire at all times when the advancer is activated to keep the wire from spinning when the advancer is activated and the brake is released. It is also essential to provide continuous saline flush to the drive shaft to reduce friction or else the device may stall or lock up from excessive friction and heat. Careful attention must also be paid to the compressed gas tanks to ensure adequate and consistent gas pressures for the entire procedure or else platform rpm speeds may drop or the burr may stall during use. Minimum tank pressures of ≥ 1,000 psi are recommended before each procedure. Placement of a venous sheath is advised for administration of fluids and vasopressors as needed as well as for placement of temporary transvenous pacing electrodes. Microcavitation may lead to transient obstruction of the microcirculation and induce bradycardia and/or AV block. Vibration produced with rotational ablation can also heighten vagal tone and precipitate or aggravate bradycardia and AV block. Placement of a temporary transvenous pacemaker is thus advisable, especially for circumflex or right coronary artery interventions, or when the left anterior descending coronary artery is treated with a contralateral right coronary artery occlusion. Care to avoid right ventricular perforation with temporary pacing electrode placement is emphasized, as cardiac tamponade from RV perforation is more common with rotational atherectomy (0.67%) than with any other device [34, 35]. When tamponade occurs from RV perforation, it is usually also somewhat delayed, occurring frequently 2 hr after the procedure and so may not be apparent while the procedure is being performed [34]. Prophylactic placement of an intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation pump is also advisable when several adverse patient and lesion characteristics are present as outlined above [22]. Because of the high incidence of bradycardia and AV block with rotablator procedures, atropine 0.6–1.0 mg intravenously is advised before rotablation begins except in patients with a history of glaucoma. Aminophylline has also been used with success to prevent brady arrhythmias and reduce the need for temporary transvenous pacing [36], although its use has not been widely adopted. Coronary vasospasm, both epicardial and microvascular, is frequent in the treated vessel with rotational atherectomy. A cocktail consisting of verapamil (10 mg/L), nitroglycerin (4 mg/L), and heparin (2,000 units/L) was developed to prevent spasm and in situ thrombosis with rotational atherectomy [37]. This cocktail appears to reduce the incidence of spasm as compared with historical controls and has since become the standard mix added to the saline flush. Adenosine has also been employed to prevent or treat microvascular spasm and no-reflow phenomenon. In one case-control series, intracoronary adenosine (24–48 μg) before and after each rotablator run reduced the incidence of no-reflow from 11.6% to 1.4% as compared with the standard cocktail [38]. Both the cocktail and adenosine are often used in concert. Rotaglide is an emulsion of egg yoke phospholipids, olive oil, and EDTA, designed to reduce friction of the drive shaft on the guidewire during rotational ablation. It is added to the saline flush and has been demonstrated to reduce rpm drops and decrease heat generation. Rotaglide has been demonstrated to decrease the incidence of non–Q-wave myocardial infarction (MI) and vessel dissection and is recommended for routine use with rotational atherectomy [39]. It can be mixed directly with the rotablator cocktail in the saline flush and is compatible with adenosine. The anticoagulation regimen for rotational atherectomy has evolved with the advent of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonists. Standard heparinization to activated clotting times (ACT) of ≥ 300 sec is advisable without or 200–300 sec with the use of GP IIb/IIIa receptor antagonists. Abciximab (ReoPro) has been documented to reduce the incidence of non–Q-wave CK elevations and abrupt closure during rotational atherectomy [40, 41]. The use of GP IIb/IIIa receptor antagonist has since been widely adopted [26]. The use of low-molecular-weight heparins or bivalirudin during rotational atherectomy has not been systematically studied. The size of the guiding catheter should be chosen according to the largest burr anticipated to be used to treat the target lesion. A 6 Fr guiding catheter can accommodate up to a 1.5 mm rotablator burr. Contemporary large-lumen 8 Fr guiding catheter (inner diameter of ≥ 0.089″) can accommodate up to a 2.25 mm burr, although generally only a 2.15 mm burr at maximum is recommended. Large-lumen 9 Fr guiding catheters (inner diameter of ≥ 0.97″) can accommodate up to a 2.38 mm burr. A 10 Fr guide is generally needed to use the largest 2.5 mm coronary burr. Guiding catheter trauma or damage may occur if too large a burr is used. Side-hole guiding catheters are generally preferred to provide some coronary perfusion during times of slow flow and no-reflow, and the shape selection should be chosen for one that will provide the most axial intubation of the coronary ostium to avoid an angulated entry of the burr into the artery and the potential complications thereof. Only dedicated rotablator guidewires can be used for rotational atherectomy. The A-wire has a 0.009″ core and a 0.017″ intermediate radiopaque 2 cm tip. The C-wire also has a 0.009″ core, but a floppy radiopaque 3 cm tip. More recently, the rotafloppy and rotafloppy gold guidewires have been produced, which incorporate a 0.005″ core and a 0.014″ floppy radiopaque 2.2 cm tip. The 0.009″ A&C wires are stiffer than the rotafloppy guidewire and so provide more support, but also straighten arteries more and cut corners in angulated segments to a greater degree. This may bias the burr to the inner curve of angulated bends and at times cause spasm or pseudostenoses [42]. Caution needs to be observed in advancing burrs biased against bends, and into areas where wire-induced vasospasm and pseudostenoses have developed as perforations and intimal dissections may result [43]. Advancement of the burr at lower speeds (100,000–120,000 rpm) in these situations may reduce the risk of complications [24, 43]. The 0.007″ rotafloppy guidewire is more flexible and has eliminated many of these problems and has the added benefit of being more maneuverable so that the wire can be more actively biased into lesions and away from proximal bend segments as needed to maximize burr-to-plaque contact and minimize burr-to-normal vessel wall contact when treating eccentric lesions or vessels with substantial proximal vessel tortuosity [24, 26, 43]. The rotafloppy guidewire is thus the most popular guidewire used today for rotational atherectomy. Application of a small burr first to create a pilot channel, followed by gradual stepwise increase in burr size, has been demonstrated to be associated with higher procedural success rate and fewer major angiographic and clinical complications than starting with larger burrs or a single large burr [18, 19, 24, 44]. The duration of each run and total spin time correlate with the development of slow flow and no-reflow, ischemic complications, and procedural success [18, 28]. Short individual runs of ≤ 30 sec are recommended, with total spin times not recommended to exceed 5 min [18, 26-28]. Before initiating plaque ablation at the lesion site, the burr should be activated proximal to the lesion within the coronary artery to establish a platform speed and eliminate any frictional motion of the burr before making lesion contact. Recommended platform speeds have decreased with time and now are 180,000 rpm for ≤ 2 mm burrs and 160,000 rpm for > 2 mm burrs. More recent experimental and clinical data suggest that even lower platforms speeds of 140,000–160,000 rpm may result in less distal microembolization and platelet aggregation, reducing ischemic complications [45]. Long-term restenosis also appears to be favorable with lower-speed ablation [29], but the use of lower platform speeds in this range has not been subject to a prospective randomized trial and has not been universally adopted. The method of lesion contact for ablation has also evolved with time. Short-contact to-and-fro pecking motions are preferred over prolonged periods of continuous contact. Short pecking motions only with brief periods of lesion contact minimize rpm drops as well as the chances that the burr will stall. It also minimizes heat generation at the lesion site by allowing blood to pass and dissipate heat more frequently. The risk of ischemic complications and late restenosis also correlates with prolonged rpm drops ≥ 5,000 rpm lasting 5 sec or more and can be largely aborted with careful attention to using the brief-contact pecking technique and with continuous feedback of rpm using a strip chart recorder (Fig. 3) [28]. Example of abrupt deceleration captured with a strip chart recorder of Rotablator advancer rpm. [Color figure can be viewed in the online issue, which is available at www.interscience.wiley.com]. The maximum burr size has been a topic of much debate and study with recent evaluation in a prospective randomized fashion. Use of larger burrs with an aggressive atherectomy strategy employing final burr to artery ratios of > 0.70 does not yield an acute higher angiographic success rate or a larger postprocedural minimal luminal diameter (MLD) and is associated with a greater risk of slow flow and no-reflow as well as high-level CPK-MB elevations of ≥ five times normal [28, 46]. There is also a trend toward a higher restenosis rate, especially when prolonged rpm drops of greater than 5,000 rpm occur, which occur more frequently with larger burrs [28]. For this reason, a final burr-to-artery ratio of ≤ 0.70 is recommended [28, 46]. Plaque modification and alteration of lesion compliance appear to be adequate at this level of plaque ablation, making adjunctive PTCA safe and effective, even in heavily calcified lesions [47], without taking the additional risk of acute ischemic complications. Adjunctive directional coronary atherectomy and stenting have also been documented to be successful with burr-to-artery ratios in this range. Rotational atherectomy has been subjected to three prospective randomized trials comparing it to balloon angioplasty: one trial in simpler A and B1 lesions (DART), and two trials in more complex B2 and C lesions (ERBAC) and (COBRA). For simple lesion subsets, rotational atherectomy offers no advantage over balloon angioplasty in terms of either acute procedural success or freedom from acute complications or late restenosis [48] and so generally is not recommended.
