titulo: Not If, but How? Using Technology and Task-Sharing to Strengthen the Global Anesthesia Workforce
autores: Elizabeth T. Drum | Matthew Dylan Bould
instituicoes: Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario
palavras_openalex: task sharing | mobile technology | online learning | point-of-care ultrasound | telemedicine | teleconsultation | access to surgical care | low-income settings | rural Nepal | digital health | anesthesiology education | point-of-care testing
resumo: In our daily lives, the pace of technological development continues at a seemingly ever-increasing rate. Moore’s1 law, the observation that the number of transistors you can fit on an integrated circuit board increases exponentially, explains why almost all of us carry a computer in our pocket, which is orders of magnitude more powerful than desktop computers 20 years ago. It is easier than ever to connect to the Internet, with ubiquitous fast data or Wi-Fi. This technology transforms how we live. Most children growing up today cannot imagine a world without constant connectedness and the new normal of entertainment, social media, online shopping, and peer-to-peer based sharing of transport and accommodation. And the Internet is everywhere—even online educational platforms are available for all levels of learners. Mobile technology is also transforming the developing world. The uptake of this technology is far faster than the development of safe surgical and anesthesia care. While there are 5 billion people in the world that lack access to safe, timely, and affordable surgical care,2 there are fewer than 2.5 billion that lack access to 3G or 4G mobile broadband Internet. The Internet is as transformative in low-income settings as it is in high-income settings, with varied effects such as increasing access to banking, improving compliance with antiretrovirals, and helping farmers understand crop markets.3 Medicine, science, and technology have joined forces in the past half-century to radically change the face of diagnostic care. In the 1960s, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory developed digital image-processing technology for the Apollo Lunar Landing program; that technology is now routinely used in computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging.4 The microbial check valve, used in dental offices to prevent contamination and reduce bacterial exposure to patients and staff, was originally designed for use on the International Space Station.5 Point-of-care ultrasound has allowed ultrasound to move from out of the traditional radiology suite into emergency departments and even anesthesiology departments for diagnosis and treatment of potentially life-threatening intraoperative conditions.6 Bearing in mind this rate of change, with ever expanding technological advances, and our ability to apply technology to uses other than what it was developed for, what will the future of technological development bring across countries as diverse as the United States and Nepal? Shah et al7 have used mobile technology for a novel educational program for nondoctor anesthesia providers in rural Nepal. They used tablets, e-learning modules, an electronic log book, e-mail, SMS messaging, and phone calls to upgrade nonphysician anesthesia providers who had had 6 months training to the level of those in a newer, 12-month training program. The electronic log book allowed data to be collected on surgical operations, patient characteristics, anesthesia techniques, available equipment, and patient-level outcomes for over 4000 cases. This kind of data could not come at a better time. It is clear that the global neglect of the delivery of surgical and anesthesia care has failed health systems in the developing world, that remedying this situation is an essential and cost-effective measure, and that the situation cannot be fixed without guidance from robust data.8 It is also clear that to strengthen the global anesthesia workforce, we also need to close an education gap. Although complications were noted in almost 8% of cases, there was no anesthesia-related mortality recorded. Perhaps this should not be too surprising, the anesthetic contributory mortality has been found to be 467 per million anesthetics (95% confidence interval, 391–559) even in developing countries in studies from the 1990s to 2000s9; at this rate, you would not expect >2 cases in a sample of 4143. Overall, 24-hour mortality was also low at 0.1% (95% confidence interval, 0.03%–0.27%),10 which is comparable to the 0.24% total perioperative mortality found in developing countries in the 1990s and 2000s.9 Although the data collected in Nepal were only an incomplete snapshot of the anesthesia care rendered at each hospital and throughout the country, they were supportive of the quality of training of these anesthesia providers. It is also possible that these numbers were underreported in a data set that relied entirely on self-reporting of adverse events or that there was selection bias regarding where or by whom patients received anesthesia care. It would be valuable for future research to use corroborating data to establish the accuracy of this method of data collection and to identify whether it could be expanded to allow more robust data collection on surgical volume, anesthesia type, perioperative mortality rate, and other key indicators. As the authors note, next steps should include determining whether this kind of data collection will be successful outside the context of an educational course and whether it can be scaled up across larger numbers of anesthesia providers. It would also be useful to have more detailed, qualitative information about the more challenging cases with significant complications, which may allow more learning about potential improvements in training, equipment, and systems of care. This technology could also be used to continue mentoring and for continuous professional medical education and collaborative relationships between physician and nonphysician anesthesia providers after the term of the course. Shah et al7 used a novel form of distance blended learning, combining 3 weeks of contact time with e-learning and distance mentoring over 12 months. It was relatively inexpensive at a cost of $2342 per person and would be a little less expensive now that the software is designed, although the largest parts of the costs were for logistics and mentor payment. This serves as a reminder that, although technological tools can be transformative, they cannot replace our trainers and training programs: it was the blend of expert educators and technology that was successful. Their program was based on the sound educational principles of competency-based medical education and seems to be an exemplary model for technology-enhanced learning in global anesthesia. Elsewhere, other technology is changing the face of medical education globally. WhatsApp Messenger, a cross-platform instant messaging software, is now the default forum for large groups such as Surgical Society of Zambia and for anesthesia teams on call in Lusaka to communicate about scarce resources or to ask for advice about an electrocardiogram. This tool has been described as an essential tool for global surgeons11 and has also been used for medical education in high-resource settings,12 something all of this technology has in common. Cloud computing allows the sharing of electronic learning resources. Voice over Internet Protocol providers such as Skype and other videoconferencing solutions allow anesthesiologists in Nairobi, Kampala, London, and Boston to come together and discuss the management of challenging pediatric cases across these very different contexts. It is difficult to predict what the future will hold for technology-enhanced learning in global anesthesia. However, it seems likely that these tools will become increasingly important in strengthening the workforce in low-resource settings, where the world’s highest burden of surgical disease is mismatched with the fewest perioperative health care professionals. What was once disruptive technology often becomes standard of care.13 Lifebox has done much to close the “oximeter gap”—and oximetry was used in 98% of cases in the Shah et al7 study. What does it say that 100% of the cases had an anesthetist with a tablet and Internet, but only 89% had noninvasive blood pressure measurement and 0.02% end-tidal capnography? It should also be noted that all these electronic Internet-based education and learning technologies and communication strategies rely on the availability and reliability of high-speed Internet service. Shah et al7 noted that one of the limitations was the lack of availability of fast Internet service. Broadband Internet and e-learning are powerful tools to help strengthen the global anesthesia workforce and should be available to all anesthesia providers. Is the Internet “the new oximetry” when it comes to advancing education and learning in global anesthesia? Shah et al7 also note that task sharing in anesthesia remains controversial. They cite a recent meta-analysis that found that perioperative maternal death was twice as high when the patient was anesthetized by a nonphysician as compared to a physician anesthesia provider.14 However, this meta-analysis looked at mortality in anesthesia administered by a physician in 6 studies and by nonphysicians in 8 separate studies, with no studies directly comparing physician versus nonphysician care. There are many possible confounders, not least that studies included in the analysis with nonphysicians tended to be from sub-Saharan Africa, whereas studies with physician anesthesia providers were more likely to be from Asia, and there are many national and geographical differences, including social determinants of health, comorbidities, systems of health care, and health care professional density. In contrast, a recent Cochrane review and meta-analysis, which included comparative studies from the United States and Haiti, was unable to find a difference in outcomes between physician and nonphysician anesthesia providers.15 The mathematical argument for task sharing with nonphysician anesthesia providers is compelling. It is estimated that 2.2 million more anesthesia providers, surgeons, and obstetricians are required to achieve the Lancet Commission’s goal of 80% coverage of safe, affordable, and timely surgery by 20302; this is more than double the current numbers of providers. Realistically, there is no capacity to train this number of physicians in this period of time. The lack is especially felt in rural areas, because the few physicians in low- and middle-income countries tend to be concentrated in the big cities. Global anesthesia success stories, like the Nepal-Canadian Anesthesiologists’ Society International Education Foundation (CASIEF) partnership, have changed the landscape of anesthesia in that country—from 7 physician anesthesiologists in 1985 to the establishment of a training program, which has trained 62 anesthesiologists over 20 years with good retention of staff and development of the Society of Anesthesiologists of Nepal with annual anesthesia symposia.16,17 However, the article by Shah et al7 makes it clear that there is still a huge reliance on nonphysician anesthetists who provide all anesthesia care at the district level. Sixty percent of district hospitals do not even conduct any operations, and it is unlikely that this is due to a lack of need for surgical procedures.18 The reality in many low- and middle-income countries is not if we should be task sharing with nonphysicians, but how. The Nepal model as described by Shah et al,7 of physician anesthesiologists mentoring and training nonphysicians and supervising their practice where possible shows the value of a system where both physician and nonphysician anesthesia providers are developed to work together. Lipnick et al19 recently eloquently described how important these collaborations are and issued a call-to-action for the global anesthesia community to embrace the concept of task sharing. They argue for a team-based approach to patient care that begins at the time of training. As a global anesthesia community, we need to find ways to work together to improve the training, clinical care, and education of all anesthesia providers. We need to make sure to provide education for anesthesia for the bellwether procedures and for the most vulnerable populations: pediatrics, obstetrics, the elderly, and other fragile patients. Shah et al7 are off to a good start. We have much work to do. What are we waiting for? DISCLOSURES Name: Elizabeth T. Drum, MD, FAAP, FCPP. Contribution: This author helped write the manuscript. resumo: 1 The discourse about poverty  Germany For a long time, poverty was a matter of material resources. Of course, living  poverty means struggling to meet basic needs and is closely related to lack of money and an inability into guarantee basic subsistence. This remains unchanged. However, since the late 1990s the discourse about poverty  Germany, inspired by EU  policy thinking, goes beyond this monetary focus. Today, being poor represents more than having little money, because poor people are likely to withdraw from social, cultural and political participation. They face a high risk of    non--monetary terms as well, which  turn is likely to diminish a society's capacity to ensure  cohesion  general (Silver 1994, Barnes et al 2002). Two main axes shape the German poverty debate. One emphasizes the risk that society might suffer from polarization as the gap between rich and poor people is widening. This is related to the debate of a rising underclass: About eight percent of the total population belongs to this group according to a study conducted by the Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung. Their main characteristics are long-term unemployment and lack of prospects, political inactivity or extremist orientation concentrating to a large extent  the Eastern part of Germany (Neugebauer 2007). The other position is dominated by the opinion that downward mobility is no longer a class related risk. Poverty is supposed to gradually increase, eventually becoming an every--day risk, and is supposed to become especially widespread among the middle class (Bude 2008, Castel and Dorre 2009). Policy debates throughout Europe make frequent reference to the term social exclusion even though there is little consensus on how to define its substance. Poverty, unemployment and the multidimensionality of  disadvantages are commonly understood as bases or even synonyms for  exclusion, taking it for granted that they impede  integration and that a decent standard of living decides who is in or out  society. The consequences of  disadvantages for individual participation chances as well as for overall  cohesion move to the forefront. This is reflected  theoretical developments which emphasize the capacity of individuals to live a decent life and draw attention to the political circumstances, institutional structures and welfare state arrangements that enable people to live respectable, affluent and secure lives (Sen 1993, 1999). Due to this change  perspective, EU  policy thinking focused more and more combating unemployment to diminish poverty risks. Access to the labor market is regarded as most important for enabling participation chances, because employment not only significantly increases a household's income but also its  integration. Germany, like other European countries, experienced growing unemployment rates and demographical changes during the recession period, which resulted  a need to diminish  security expenditures and to raise employment rates. Therefore, the activation policy which has been launched during the last decade is surely inspired by the European  policy discourse to ensure  cohesion, but primarily reflects governmental needs to decrease unemployment and  security expenditures. Moreover, the change  perspective on poverty as such (from distribution to integration) was accompanied by a change  attitude with regard to the question of individual responsibility for the experience of and escape from poverty. The key phrase  und Fordern (rights and duties) paraphrases the general approach that institutional as well as individual efforts have to be strengthened  order to improve the labor market situation and diminish poverty rates. On the one hand, labor market agencies have been reformed and supportive measures have been extended. On the other hand, access to unemployment benefits and the level of  assistance have been restricted with regard to the period of entitlement and its eligibility  order to increase effort to return to the labor market as soon as possible and accept work for lower pay. …

autores: Todd Gabe | Jaison R. Abel | Richard L. Florida
instituicoes: Federal Reserve Bank of New York | University of Maine | University of Toronto
topico_primario: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality
palavras_openalex: job ladder | occupational mobility | economic inequality | middle class decline | educational attainment | labour market transitions | Great Recession recovery | unemployment | labor force exit
resumo: There is growing concern over rising economic inequality, the decline of the middle class, and a polarization of the U.S. workforce. This study examines the extent to which workers in the United States transition from low-end to higher-quality occupations, and explores the factors associated with such a move up the job ladder. Using data covering the expansion following the Great Recession (2011-2017) and focusing on short-term (i.e., less than 1 year) labor market transitions, the authors find that just slightly more than 5% of workers in low-end occupations moved into a higher-quality occupation. Instead, around 70% of workers in low-end occupations stayed in the same occupation, 11% exited the labor force, 7% became unemployed, and 6% switched to a different low-end occupation. Study results point to the importance of educational attainment in helping workers successfully climb the job ladder.

titulo: The wicked interplay of hate rhetoric, politics and the internet: what can health promotion do to counter right-wing extremism?
palavras_openalex: right-wing extremism | health promotion | alt-right | Christchurch mosque shootings | far-right terrorism | online hate speech | social media | populism | Islamophobia | antisemitism | xenophobia | homophobia | misogyny | inclusive society | counter-extremism
resumo: On 15 March 2019, a gunman self-identifying as a member of the alt-right movement committed two consecutive terrorist attacks at mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand. A sign of our digital era and social-mediatized gaze: he live-streamed the attacks on Facebook to share with his virtual community. This happened only a few weeks before the 23rd IUHPE World Conference on Health Promotion, that took place in Rotorua, New Zealand on 7–11th April, 2019. Interestingly, while the conference’s legacy paper largely emphasizes the importance of sustainable development and climate change adaptation strategies (International Union for Health Promotion and Education, 2019), it also identifies the development of inclusive habitats, governance, systems and processes as a significant goal for health promotion. To this end, health promotion should ‘[foster] peaceful, just and inclusive societies which are free from fear, racism, violation and other violence’ (International Union for Health Promotion and Education, 2019). The health promotion community seems to be particularly adept at agreeing on consensus Statements, Charters, Déclarations and Calls to Action––but what actual research and practice would we need to address right-wing extremism? The Christchurch tragedy can be considered an isolated event, but it is indicative of a rise in reactionary populism, hate crimes and extremism motivated by right-wing (e.g. alt-right, far-right) ideologies in Western societies. The annual Global Terrorism Index (Institute for Economics and Peace, 2018) shows that between 2002 and 2017 there was a steady rise in the number of far-right extremism incidents and related deaths in Western Europe and North America. In the United States, 73.3% of extremist-related fatalities in the last decade can be attributed to far-right extremists attacks, exceeding incidents attributed to Islamic extremists (ADL, 2019). In Europe, despite a larger number of deaths related to Islamic extremism, there is concern about the steady increase in the number of deaths from far-right terrorism (Institute for Economics and Peace, 2018). In the United Kingdom, following the Christchurch attacks, threat from ‘extreme right-wing terrorism’ was added to official threat-level warnings (Merrick, 2019). These extreme and visible events do not come out of nowhere. They are the manifestation of hate rhetoric and discourses espousing racial supremacy, islamophobia, anti-semitism, xenophobia, homophobia and misogyny (Eckermann, 2017; Roth, 2017; Institute for Economics and Peace, 2018). It is no coincidence that there is a resurgence in these beliefs that are now being globalized at a rapid pace. While the current wave of populism has been linked to inequalities brought by ‘unchecked economic globalization’ (Eckermann, 2017), right-wing extremism has similar roots, triggered by fear of ethnic and religious diversity ‘where concerns about cultural identity, economic opportunity and terrorism intersect’ (Roth, 2017). Immigration, which lies at the center of the public debate in many societies (Roth, 2017), is subject to polarization and instrumentalization of this issue by extremist ideologies and nationalist agenda (Davey and Ebner, 2019). At the same time, it has been hypothesized that acts of violence are triggered by threats––or perceived threats—to national pride in Western societies, as well as by structural violence induced by social inequalities (Wilkinson and Pickett, 2010). Similarly, the Global Terrorism Index (Institute for Economics and Peace, 2018) identifies poor social cohesion, alienation and perceived discrimination as societal factors associated with terrorism and radicalization in countries with high levels of economic development. Perceived discrimination, feelings of humiliation and social fragmentation are fueled by far-right conspiracy theories that are increasingly spread on social media, such as the ‘Great replacement theory’ (Davey and Ebner, 2019). This theory claims that white European populations are being deliberately replaced by people of other ethnicities and cultures (Davey and Ebner, 2019). Through this lens, immigration is perceived as an invasion that will result in a ‘white genocide’, powering the wrong perception that majority groups are being persecuted by oppressed minorities. In the current era of the information society, social media provides a powerful platform for all kind of extremist mindsets to form and develop (Müller and Schwarz, 2018), allowing lone hatemongers to collectivize their hatred, build support and broadcast their discourse. Online platforms have facilitated ‘(…) weaponizing propaganda and ideology, spreading extremist belief, facilitating recruitment and radicalization, but also galvanizing and directly prompting terrorist attacks’ (Institute for Economics and Peace, 2018). But if far-right extremism gathers in clusters of the dark corners of social media, it is also echoed in the nationalist speeches of politicians in many industrialized countries who use people’s pre-occupations (e.g. immigration and security) as well as twisted information to generate fear and ignite populism. A recent and vivid example would be Trump’s presidential campaign in the United States, which praised nationalism, launched attacks on refugees and accused undocumented migrants of stealing jobs (Giroux, 2017; Roth, 2017). Recent studies support the ‘Trump effect hypothesis’, showing that Trump’s election and anti-Muslim tweets are associated with a significant rise in reported hate crimes across the US (Müller and Schwarz, 2018). Recently, Davey and Ebner (2019) found a strong association between online campaigns of extremist groups disseminating the ‘Great replacement theory’, alternative media relays of these messages and anti-immigration messaging of political actors and commentators; highlighting the vicious interplay between the digital, societal and political spheres. Population health is closely tied to the quality of social contexts, their inclusivity and their capacity to nurture mental wellbeing, dignity and the empowerment of all members. Hate crimes and horrific terrorist events related to far-right extremism are a visible symptom of a deeper social and well-being malaise. Underlying these events are racism and discrimination, which are more subtle forms of violence that instill and reinforce social relationships of dominance and oppression (Krieger, 2014). Discrimination embedded at different levels in society (i.e. interpersonal, structural, institutional) is a threat to individual health and wellbeing and can lead to inequities in accessing important socio-economic resources, as well as healthcare and social services (World Health Organization, 2008; Krieger, 2014). According to Eco-social theory, experiences of discrimination or oppression become biologically embodied through different pathways, contributing to poor health outcomes among minorities groups, reinforcing existing health inequities (Krieger, 2014). Some of the pathways through which oppressive societal relations generate inequitable health outcomes include economic and social deprivation, higher rates of exposure to hazards and toxins, social trauma, health-harming responses to discrimination, targeted marketing of harmful commodities or inadequate medical care (Krieger, 2014). Along the same lines, the allostatic load concept proposes that the intensity and chronicity of exposure to perceived stressors such as discrimination or oppression impact mental and biological function (e.g. cardiovascular, immunological, mental and nervous system function) and increase the risk of subsequent health problems (Carlson and Chamberlain, 2005; Duru et al., 2012; Fuller-Rowell et al., 2012). As such allostatic load provides an explanation for differential morbidity patterns in majority and minority groups, where, in the case of the latter, ‘the accumulation of wear and tear on physiological systems’ (Carlson and Chamberlain, 2005) permanently affect individual capacity to adapt and to cope with social and contextual challenges. Social inequities are a fundamental element in the interplay between extremist mindset, bigotry, and discrimination and population health. Higher levels of inequity are associated with higher levels of social disintegration, violence and perceived ‘threat to pride’ (Wilkinson and Pickett, 2010), all of which are drivers of radicalization and extremism and in turn intensify unhealthy relationships of oppression. Promoting health involves ensuring a secure, inclusive, respectful and nurturing society for all. An evidence-based, intersectoral health promotion approach that moves beyond individual behaviorist action can help build capacity to tackle extremism. To tackle the roots of this problem, multipronged efforts, implemented in the digital, social and political spheres, need to be developed. For example, in response to the Christchurch terrorist attacks, a novel strategy, the Christchurch Call, was enacted. It is a joint commitment by governments and actors from the technological industry to eliminate terrorist and violent extremist content online (Government of New Zealand, 2019). This Call rests on the premise that ‘A free, open and secure internet is a powerful tool to promote connectivity, enhance social inclusiveness and foster economic growth’ (Government of New Zealand, 2019). Among many commitments, governments expressed a vow to strengthen resilience and inclusiveness of societies through education but also through the fight against inequality (Government of New Zealand, 2019). This is where health promotion comes into play. With the digital transformation, social media must be conceived as more than just a tool, but as an integral part of supportive environments for health (Kickbusch, 2019). As emphasized by Kickbusch (2019), the digital transformation makes it necessary for new governance models to emerge, involving different actors from the political, social, health and digital spheres who ensure that values of democracy, empowerment, common goods and public responsibility are respected. Health promotion can and should be a catalyst in bringing all these views together. As highlighted by Corbin (2018) who reflected on the role of health promotion in the context of the #MeToo movement, health promotion not only needs to focus on strategies to empower oppressed minorities, but also to meet potential oppressors and extremists where they are. Building on this view, and in accordance with the Christchurch Call, we need to develop and implement more educational programs that foster inclusion and prevent radicalization. These programs could aim to develop critical analytical and digital literacy skills to detect the weaknesses of one-sided discourses and the manipulation tactics used by extremists (Davey and Ebner, 2019). As Davey and Ebner (2019) pointed out, rhetoric such as the Great replacement theory conveys the idea that identity is necessarily tied to ethnicity, a misconception that needs to be deconstructed by education, but also by our political leaders, media and institutions. Another potential strategy involves changing norms or perceptions of norms. For example, based on results from multiple studies, Paluck and Chwe suggest that conflict prevention efforts should aim to change perceptions about community support for hate crimes, ‘because people’s actions depend on their awareness of the approval or disapproval of others around them’ (Paluck and Chwe, 2017). After all, lone hatemongers are not so alone; they are backed by their virtual community, which builds their motivation and fuels their grievances. To illustrate their point, these authors cite studies showing that peer-to-peer interventions are effective in changing social norms and discouraging bullying and racist discourses, particularly when peers are viewed as having an important status (Paluck et al., 2016; Munger, 2017). It appears that one of the first things to do is to stand collectively against hate rhetoric, bigotry and intolerance. To date, there has been little public health research on far-right extremism and its consequences for population health, and on the mediating role of web platforms and the implications for upstream health promotion strategies. The International Union for Health Promotion and Education, as well as our local health promotion associations and communities need to acknowledge this new threat to the wellbeing of our societies and to elevate this issue on their agenda. They need to develop our collective capacity to tackle right-wing extremism by sensitizing our leaders and institutions, raising awareness and educating about its societal and health impact and by advocating for public funding that will allow furthering intervention research on these topics. Health Promotion International can serve as an incubator, a forum for innovative ideas and research interested in inclusion, fairness, health and the association of these factors with the economic, political, social and cultural landscapes. The recent call by our Editor-in-Chief to investigate the social epidemiology of social media (de Leeuw, 2018) provides fertile ground to study the links between extremism, social media, inclusion and tolerance, health and wellbeing of the whole society. But more than investigating these relationships, as health promoters we need to stand publicly against right-wing extremism and hate rhetoric and to be positive leaders by fostering anti-oppressive, inclusive and culturally safe approaches to intervention and research. The author would like to acknowledge Selma Chipenda-Dansokho for her careful review of this manuscript.

titulo: Who Can Access the “Good” Jobs? Racial Disparities in Employment among Young Men Who Work in Paid Care
periodico: The Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science

palavras_openalex: paid care work | racial inequality in employment | young men | black-white wage gap | job polarization | low-wage employment | job security | labor market inequality | labour market precarity | university education | gender division of labor | National Longitudinal Survey of Youth
resumo: Men have slowly increased their presence in paid care jobs that have long been considered as “women’s jobs.” But job growth in the paid care sector is polarized between “good” jobs and “bad” jobs in terms of pay and job security, and racial minority men are more likely to enter low-paying care-work jobs. Using work history data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 and 1997, this study examines the patterns and mechanisms of racial disparity in young men’s access to jobs of varying pay levels in the care-work sector and how such patterns have changed as the labor market has become more precarious and unequal. Findings suggest that young black men—especially those without a college education—have been increasingly excluded from accessing “good” jobs in the paid care sector. Moreover, this black-white disparity cannot be fully explained by racial differences in individual-level characteristics.

resumo: Purpose A prominent labour market feature in recent decades has been the increase in abstract and service jobs, while the demand for routine work has declined. This article examines whether the components of Type A behaviour predict workers' selection into non-routine abstract, non-routine service and routine jobs. Design/methodology/approach Building on the work by Barrick et al. (2013), this article first presents how the theory of purposeful work behaviour can be used to explain how individuals with different levels of Type A components sort into abstract, service and routine jobs. Then, using longitudinal data, it examines whether the components of Type A behaviour predict occupational sorting. Estimations were performed based on the linear regression method. Findings The results show that the Type A dimension “leadership” was associated with a higher level of abstract and service job tasks in occupation. High eagerness-energy and responsibility were also positively linked with occupation's level of abstract tasks. These results suggest that workers sort into jobs that allow them to pursue higher-order implicit goals. Originality/value Job market polarisation towards low-routine jobs has had a pervasive influence on the labour market during the past few decades. Based on high-quality data that combine prime working-age register information on occupational attainment with information about personality characteristics, the findings contribute to our knowledge of how personality characteristics contribute to occupational sorting in terms of this important job aspect.

titulo: The labour market impact of robotisation in Europe
autores: José‐Ignacio Antón | David Klenert | Enrique Fernández‐Macías | Maria Cesira Urzì Brancati | Georgios Alaveras

resumo: This paper explores the impact of robot adoption on European regional labour markets between 1995 and 2015. Specifically, we look at the effect of the usage of industrial robots on jobs and employment structures across European regions. Our estimates suggest that the effect of robots on employment tends to be mostly small and negative during the period 1995–2005 and positive during the period 2005–2015 for the majority of model specifications. Regarding the effects on employment structures, we find some evidence of a mildly polarising effect in the first period, but this finding depends to some extent on the model specifications. In sum, this paper shows that the impact of robots on European labour markets in the last couple of decades has been ambiguous and is not robust. The strength and even the sign of this effect are sensitive to the specifications, as well as to the countries and periods analysed.

titulo: Complex-Task Biased Technological Change and the Labor Market
autores: Colin C. Caines | Florian Hoffmann | Gueorgui Kambourov

palavras_openalex: task complexity | wage growth | labor reallocation | higher-order thinking skills | O*NET | automation | skill heterogeneity | labor market effects of automation
resumo: In this paper we study the relationship between task complexity and the occupational wage- and employment structure. Complex tasks are defined as those requiring higher-order skills, such as the ability to abstract, solve problems, make decisions, or communicate effectively. We measure the task complexity of an occupation by performing Principal Component Analysis on a broad set of occupational descriptors in the Occupational Information Network (O*NET) data.We establish four main empirical facts for the U.S. over the 1980-2005 time period that are robust to the inclusion of a detailed set of controls, subsamples, and levels of aggregation: (1) There is a positive relationship across occupations between task complexity and wages and wage growth; (2) Conditional on task complexity, routine-intensity of an occupation is not a significant predictor of wage growth and wage levels; (3) Labor has reallocated from less complex to more complex occupations over time; (4) Within groups of occupations with similar task complexity labor has reallocated to non-routine occupations over time. We then formulate a model of Complex-Task Biased Technological Change with heterogeneous skills and show analytically that it can rationalize these facts. We conclude that workers in non-routine occupations with low ability of solving complex tasks are not shielded from the labor market effects of automatization.

instituicoes: Trakia University

resumo: The aim of the present article is to study and analyze the present state of agricultural farms in Bulgaria, and to provide directions for their development. The following tasks have been set in order to accomplish this goal: to establish the main difficulties in farm functioning; to discover the factors with an impact on their development; to offer adequate measures for sustainable growth. The study encompasses the period from the beginning of the transition to market economy in the 1990s to the end of the first programme period after Bulgaria’s accession to the EU. The sources of information used in the analysis include data from national statistics, agrarian reports from the Ministry of Healthcare and Food, literature by other authors, as well as our own research. Main conclusions: the agricultural reform in Bulgaria in the 1990s led to establishing a production structure of private agriculture farms; the latter is strongly polarized – with a large number of small size and few large size farms. Part of the small farms is maintained by people who have no other employment opportunities. Many of them start working with limited production resources and knowledge, they have an insufficient access to loans and professional training. These and several other factors obstruct successful farm functioning and decrease production results. Bulgaria’s accession to the EU deepened the polarization between small and big agricultural farms. This process was also affected by the EU Common Agriculture Policy, and most of all - the single payment scheme per unit of used land area. To stimulate the growth and development of family agriculture business in Bulgaria, the state needs to provide special conditions: young people will require professional entrepreneurship culture, they must acquire experience in developing successful agricultural farms at home and abroad; cooperation with research institutions is needed, as well as preferential crediting, introduction of “green” production technologies, etc.

resumo: We study changes in employment by occupations characterized by different degree of exposure to routinization in the six largest Latin American economies over the last two decades. We combine our own indicators of routine task content based on information from the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIACC) with labor market microdata from harmonized national household surveys. We find that the increase in jobs was decreasing in the automatability of the tasks typically performed in each occupation, and increasing in the initial wage, a pattern more consistent with the traditional skill-biased technological change than with the polarization hypothesis.

titulo: Labor Market, Distributive Gains and Cumulative Causation: Insights from the Brazilian Economy
autores: Esther Dweck | Carolina Troncoso Baltar | Marília Bassetti Marcato | Camila Unis Krepsky
instituicoes: Universidade Estadual de Campinas (UNICAMP) | Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro
palavras_openalex: cumulative causation | job polarization | employment structure | occupational structure | income distribution | wage inequality | government consumption | investment | low-wage employment | service sector | trade sector | Brazilian labor market
resumo: This paper investigates the impact of economic growth patterns on employment structure, highlighting the effects of the main final demand components' variations. Brazil is an interesting case study, as it has experienced a combination of sustained economic growth, an improvement in income distribution, and a notable increase in job formalization in the 2004-2013 period. We explore how the Brazilian growth pattern contributed to the employment growth and changes in the occupational structure (informal and formal jobs, and wage-level) and provide original insights into the Brazilian labor market in the long 2000s. We find no signs of typical job polarization, as changes in job structure relate to reductions in wage inequality. We develop a structural decomposition analysis to measure the demand components' role in explaining the Brazilian labor market's transformations based on an effective demand input-output model. Drawing on an analysis of cumulative causation between income distribution, household consumption, and occupational structure, we find that induced consumption significantly impacted service and trade industries, increasing the low-wage jobs growth rate. Our analysis suggests that the combination of cumulative causation with government consumption and investment growth is crucial to explain distributive gains and the absence of job polarization in the Brazilian labor market.

titulo: The heterogeneous impact of COVID-19 in a two-sided market: evidence from a live-streaming platform
autores: Qifan Huang | Saizi Xiao | Castiel Chen Zhuang
instituicoes: Malaysian Institute of Economic Research | Peking University | University of Nottingham | University of Nottingham Malaysia Campus | University of Washington
palavras_openalex: COVID-19 pandemic | two-sided markets | live streaming platforms | live streaming e-commerce | wage inequality | demand shocks | user participation | gender differences | labour market flexibility | digital platforms
resumo: Two-sided digital platforms play an increasingly important role in our economy. During the COVID-19 pandemic, our involvement with these platforms increases drastically, but little is known about how the behavior of consumers and the labor market performance of workers in a two-sided market are affected by an economy-wide shock. This article uses a unique real-time dataset from a live-streaming platform to investigate how virtual gifting of fans and live e-commerce decisions and sales of anchors are influenced by COVID-19. Our general quantile regression approach suggests that the pandemic severity on the fans side instead of the anchors side increases virtual gifting to low-paying anchors, consistent with our theoretical prediction. In addition to the prices adjusted by the platform, we also find user participation and gender potential mechanisms through which COVID-19 affects virtual gifting. Due to increased popularity caused by the pandemic, low-paying anchors conduct more live e-commerce and achieve higher sales. Our results document the de-polarization of a novel and emerging labor market with flexible workforce on a digital platform and emphasize the need to take market structures into account when studying the impact of demand shocks.

titulo: Environmental NMR
instituicoes: University of Toronto | University of Toronto Scarborough
palavras_openalex: soil organic matter | contaminant sequestration | contaminant fate | soil remediation | aqueous-organic interface | diffusion NMR | saturation transfer | cross-polarization | epitope mapping | soil heterogeneity | remediation strategies | contaminated sites
resumo: The environment is a complex and dynamic entity. Environmental reactivity often arises from a complex synergism between a wide array of organic and inorganic materials, with many key fundamentals such as physical conformation, aqueous accessibility, pH, temperature, and biota, playing critical roles. As such, studying complex materials such as air particles, soils, sediments, plants, complex aqueous chemistry, and living organisms is essential but far from trivial. For example, soil has been described in the journal Science as 'the most complex biomaterial on earth', yet scientific practice often dictates that researchers study soil in as close to its natural fully swollen state as possible, as drying, fractionation, and extraction may remove the aqueous–organo interface, negate biological activity, and alter conformation and structure. As such, environmental researchers are faced with a considerable challenge with a desperate need to extract detailed molecular-level information from some of the most complex and heterogeneous samples known. NMR spectroscopy is ideally suited for environmental analysis as it is highly versatile in terms of both the vast array of experiments available and the range of samples that can be studied. Solid-state, HR-MAS (gel-state), and solution-state approaches can be applied to study a wide range of phases and provide unprecedented levels of information regarding both structure and molecular interactions. A modern technological iteration termed Comprehensive Multiphase-NMR integrates solid-state circuitry, pulse field gradients, and spectrometer lock, which, when combined with spectral editing approaches, permits all components (liquids, gels, and solids) to be studied and differentiated in fully swollen natural samples in their native state. Such NMR tools are critically important for bridging a fundamental gap in our scientific knowledge as to how and why chemicals become sequestered in the environment, which in turn hampers the development of optimal remediation strategies. This is expressed well by Bertsch and Seaman in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences who stated 'a complete understanding of the chemistry of complex soil assemblages is prerequisite to accurately assessing environmental and human health risks of contaminants or in designing environmentally sound, cost-effective chemical and biological remediation strategies'. Cost estimates for the cleanup of contaminated sites in the European Union and the United States are in the order of magnitude of 1.4 trillion euro. It has been reported that 70% of soils from the contaminated sites in Germany are being stored in vast waste disposal facilities until better cleanup technologies can be developed. The range of modern NMR experiments exploiting, diffusion, saturation-transfer, epitope mapping, cross-polarization, rigidity, and dynamics have unrivaled the potential to explain complex processes such as contaminant fate and sequestration at the molecular level. Despite its vast potential, however, environmental NMR spectroscopy is still underutilized in the field. In part, this arises from a lack of exposure to key demographics early in their careers. This is summarized by Caroline Preston (a pioneer of Environmental NMR) who stated in a review 'students in environmental disciplines such as soil science are becoming increasingly divorced from modern organic chemistry (molecular-level analysis, pyrolysis mass spectrometry, isotopic tracers, NMR). This generates a vicious cycle, where students who have never experienced hands-on operation of large equipment or acquired the minimum theoretical background will be unlikely to generate a successful application during their subsequent careers'. As such, it is the responsibility of NMR researchers, educators, and instrument manufacturers alike to ensure that students with diverse backgrounds can utilize NMR spectroscopy to its full potential and in an accessible manner. Key information required to measure and explain bioavailability, bioaccumulation, biotransformation, and toxic mode of action of contaminants (and contaminant mixtures) can be directly assessed using NMR and is desperately needed to set more targeted and effective environmental policies. Mass spectrometry is currently the primary tool in the environmental research and, because of its excellent sensitivity, is ideal for targeted analysis (i.e. for a list of specific chemical pollutants); however, it is often the case that wide-range unknowns (either different chemicals or transformation products) are present, which can easily be missed by mass spectrometry-based tools. Conversely, while NMR detection is certainly less sensitive, it is generally a very non-selective detector that gives a comprehensive overview as to everything in a complex matrix. As such, it is often the key (and sometimes only) tool that can answer big questions such as 'what are air particles composed of?' and what is 'soil organic matter?'. Interestingly, even in the domain of contaminant detection, NMR could have had a critical role to play. One key example is of a researcher Donald Taves from the University of Rochester who performed 19F NMR of his own blood in 1976. Based on his finding, he speculated on 'widespread contamination of human tissues with trace amounts of organic fluorocompounds derived from commercial products'. Interestingly, it was decades later that these perfluorinated chemicals were 'rediscovered' using mass spectrometry and have reached ~50 ppb in the general population and up to ~500 ppb in wild polar bears. Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) are two of the most widely distributed and studied perfluorinated contaminants. A recent review by the National Collaborating Center for Environmental Health (Canada) summarized 'To date associations have been found between PFOS or PFOA levels in the general population and reduced female fertility and sperm quality, reduced birth weight, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), increased total and non-HDL (bad) cholesterol levels, and changes in thyroid hormone levels. In a highly exposed community living near a chemical plant, PFOS and PFOA have been associated with pre-eclampsia (pregnancy-induced hypertension), birth defects (PFOA only), and increased uric acid levels – a marker of heart disease. Occupationally-exposed workers may have increased risk of prostate and bladder cancer.' It is interesting to postulate that if NMR were used more rigorously and routinely in environmental research, such compounds would have been hard to miss by 19F NMR and would likely have been brought to the attention of regulators and policy makers decades sooner. Historically, NMR has been central in addressing structure and composition. This special issue contains an interesting and entertaining Historical by Dr Caroline Preston on the evolution of environmental NMR since its inceptions in the 1960s. Since then, NMR has played a key role in expanding the fundamental understanding as to the structure of plants, soil organic matter, and dissolved organic matter in rivers, lakes, and oceans. NMR has found a strong footing, arguably as the leading structural tool for organic mixtures and heterogeneous materials, in general. This special issue expands structural avenues with a review of NMR to understand air particulates and an in-depth look into organic matter from Michelson meteorite, phosphorous quantitation in soils, and the study of intact plants. Structural studies provide not only in-depth understanding but also accurate NMR assignments, which in turn provide the opportunity to better understand and explain reactivity and molecular interactions within complex samples using NMR. Hydrophobic contaminants and agrochemicals stick tightly to soil organic matter, reducing their effectiveness and leading to sequestration. Conversely, dissolved organic colloids in water tend to partition these otherwise aqueous-insoluble compounds, leading to their long-range transport. As such, there is great interest in how and why organic compounds and heavy metals bind to environmental matrices. This special issue contains an excellent review covering the interactions of natural organic matter and organic pollutants. Low field NMR is applied to understand processes, stability, and structure in biochar and soils. Low field NMR is of particular importance as it is likely the precursor to more widespread portable detectors that hold great promise for low-cost in-field monitoring, which is covered in a Perspective within this special issue. With the understanding as to 'what soil is?' and 'which chemical components?' bind contaminants, the key questions become 'what does it all mean?' and 'how are living systems impacted?' For example, if a herbicide is bound tightly to the protein fraction of soil, is it still bioavailable? Would this still hold true with climate change or change in land use? An even more challenging but important question is 'out of the 100s or 1000s chemicals we are exposed everyday, which ones truly impact our health?' Indeed, similar questions are asked everyday by policy makers. NMR has great potential to address such challenges when employed as the 'molecular interpreter' of living systems under environmental stress. NMR provides a molecular fingerprint and, when combined with appropriate statistical methods, can be used to identify stress in general and the biochemical pathways influenced by a stressor. As the field develops, if different stressors or categories of stressors produce unique stress signatures in organisms, then these signatures can be exploited to diagnose the cause of stress in the wider environment. In this special issue, NMR on extracts is used to better understand the stress in soils and water fleas. Other research demonstrates the viability of the approach in vivo with aquatic organisms. Finally, large-scale NMR or statistical studies are used to unravel and understand the molecular processes occurring during waste water treatment. In summary, the special issue contains a brief but diverse snapshot into the potential of NMR spectroscopy in environmental research. The field is as interesting as it is challenging. Considering the plethora of samples and diversity of studies, along with the versatility of NMR and the desperately needed unique molecular information it provides, it is clear NMR is critical to the future of the field. The rate of growth of Environmental NMR will depend on the following: the willingness of scientists with diverse backgrounds to embrace cutting edge NMR technology, the readiness of NMR experts to work across pedagogical boundaries and make the field accessible, and the continued investment of NMR manufacturers to push for new frontiers (especially sensitivity) to improve the tools available. Finally, I would like to thank everyone who contributed to the special issue and gave their time, energy, and enthusiasm to make it possible. On a personal note, I would like to thank Bruker Biospin (Germany, US, and Canada) and Mark Krembil of the Krembil Foundation for his continued and ongoing assistance. In particular, from Bruker, I would like to thank Dr Manfred Spraul, Dr Werner Maas, Dr Michael Fey, and Dr Henry Stronks, whose willingness to push the frontiers helped to foster my own interest in NMR and whose kind donations and support have made my research possible.

resumo: During laser material processing with ultrashort laser pulses an unwanted emission of X-rays in the regime of keV can occur, when a critical intensity is exceeded. The resulting emission per pulse is negligible but can rapidly accumulate to a significant value for the occupational safety, when high repetition rates (kHz) are used. In the present work, the characteristics of the resulting X-ray emission by means of the radiation dose, is investigated for various irradiation and process parameters. The varied parameters are inter alia material (steel and bismuth), intensity (max. 3*1014 W/cm²), polarization, surface roughness (0.1 µm < Ra < 13 µm) and pulse duration (0.95 ps – 10 ps). The results show a significant dependence of the tested parameters, are mostly in good agreement with present publications and complement them for various influencing factors. Furthermore, they confirm the potential health risk by laser induced X-ray emission during laser material processing with high intensities.

resumo: The COVID-19 pandemic dramatically reshaped the labor market, especially for service sector workers. Frontline service sector workers, already coping with precarious working conditions, faced proximate risks of COVID-19 transmission on the job and navigated new workplace safety measures, including masking, social distancing, and staying home while sick, all in a polarized political environment. We examine polarization in the effects of COVID-19 workplace safety measures on workers' feelings of safety and well-being. Specifically, we examine how support for former President Trump moderates the relationship between COVID-19 safety practices (masking, social distancing, staying home while sick) and workers' feelings of safety and well-being. To do so, we draw on novel data collected by The Shift Project from 2,039 service sector workers at 89 large firms during the COVID-19 pandemic. We find that workplace safety measures are positively associated with workers' self-assessments of feeling safe and with mental health, but only for Biden voters.

resumo: Abstract This article investigates how mothers’ and fathers’ daily time use changed across social classes from 1990 to 2013 in Germany. In the 2000s, Germany’s adherence to the male breadwinner model was eroded by labor and family policy reforms typical of the adult worker model, which assumes individual self-sufficiency. The implications for gender and class inequality have been heatedly discussed. Drawing on the German Time Use Survey, I find that gender equality in the division of labor is greatest among full-time dual-earner couples with standard schedules. The prevalence of this pattern increased among the middle- and upper-class in historically conservative western Germany, but declined across classes in formerly socialist eastern Germany. In parallel, nonstandard work patterns and dual-joblessness gained in importance among lower-class couples, particularly in eastern Germany. I conclude that the adult worker model benefited mothers with access to standard full-time jobs but at the cost of greater class polarization.

titulo: Time to reimagine diagnosis in the acute care setting
autores: Michael S. Pulia | Dimitrios Papanagnou | Lekshmi Santhosh
instituicoes: Thomas Jefferson University | University of California San Francisco Medical Center | University of California, San Francisco | University of Wisconsin–Madison
palavras_openalex: diagnostic errors | emergency department | diagnostic process | dual-process theory | clinical judgment | cognitive errors | symptom-based diagnosis | diagnostic decision-making | diagnostic excellence | patient harm | diagnostic testing limitations | altered mental status
resumo: Diagnostic error is a significant cause of preventable patient harm across health care settings, yet progress has proven elusive. This was recently brought into sharp focus by an Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)-sponsored systematic review examining diagnostic errors in the emergency department (ED). Based on only three small studies conducted outside of the United States, the authors extrapolated that diagnostic errors in U.S. EDs are prevalent (7.4 million cases annually) and result in 350,000 cases of permanent disability or death.1 Although the authors did point out that these rates are similar to those observed in other health care settings, a group of U.S. emergency medicine professional societies issued a joint statement outlining concerns over flawed methodology and overreaching conclusions. As acute care providers who are also National Academy of Medicine (NAM) Scholars in Diagnostic Excellence, we aim to provide context related to diagnosis in acute care that is critical to the interpretation of the report's findings as well as highlight innovative and forward-thinking opportunities to improve the diagnostic process. Acute care settings, particularly the ED, present unique challenges to the diagnostic process, including, but not limited to, high decision-making density, crowding/boarding, frequent interruptions, limitations in available diagnostic testing, and electronic health record (EHR) usability issues. When combined with high patient acuity, incomplete patient information (i.e., secondary to altered mental states), atypical disease presentations, and rapidly evolving clinical trajectories, the ED becomes a challenging diagnostic milieu. In response, diagnosis in the ED primarily focuses on ruling-out diagnoses with high risk of morbidity and mortality and identifying patients in need of additional evaluation (e.g., admission or specialist referral). The lack of emphasis of establishing a definitive diagnosis is demonstrated by the frequent use of symptom-based diagnoses; many patients treated in the ED are discharged without a definitive pathologic diagnosis. While the findings of the recent review are not based on solid evidence, there should be universal agreement that the ED is a priority area for diagnostic inquiry given that it functions as a rapid diagnostic hub for the health care system and the inherent, system-level challenges to accurate and definitive diagnosis in this setting. It is well established that ED providers utilize a variety of heuristics or cognitive shortcuts as a strategy to maintain efficiency. According to dual-processing theory, these heuristics involve type 1 thinking, which is characterized as rapid, nonconscious, and contextualized. This contrasts with type 2 thinking, which is slow, deliberate, and decontextualized. A natural consequence of type 1 guided decision making is an increased risk of cognition-related diagnostic errors (i.e., clinical judgment). Cognitive errors are the most commonly identified cause of diagnostic errors with some well-defined examples including premature closure (e.g., attributing delirium to asymptomatic bacteriuria and missing an intracranial hemorrhage), availability bias (e.g., ordering nonindicated chest imaging because of a recent pulmonary embolism case), and anchoring bias (e.g., delayed recognition of sepsis in older adults without fever). Interventions capable of mitigating the downsides of type 1 thinking to improve diagnostic calibration (intersection of accuracy and confidence) are critical to reducing diagnostic errors in acute care. By design all ED encounters conclude with a transition of care. These transitions (e.g., admission to an inpatient service, discharge, transfer to long-term care facility) are subject to diagnostic and therapeutic momentum and thus may perpetuate or amplify errors. Despite the highlighted challenges to diagnosis in the ED, clinicians must navigate expectations of patients and downstream providers. For instance, patients may be unsatisfied without an identified etiology of their symptoms and providers may request the ED assign a definitive diagnosis prior to accepting the patient for admission. While these may be reasonable requests, they fail to adequately consider barriers to definitive diagnosis in the ED, encourage the use of type 1 thinking, and discourage acknowledgment of diagnostic uncertainty. Despite the frequency of diagnostic uncertainty, there remains minimal guidance on how to safely transition patients in the context of ongoing uncertainty. Approaches that encourage clinicians to communicate the presence and degree of diagnostic uncertainty are paramount to improve the safety of care transitions. To address the significant challenges to diagnostic safety in acute care, it is imperative to consider multimodal approaches. System-level interventions can provide added layers of safety to mitigate cognitive errors by individual providers. When optimized from a usability perspective, the EHR represents a powerful potential tool to improve the diagnostic process. Some successful examples are EHR-embedded decision support tools that guide providers to consistently apply evidence-based algorithms and checklists for utilization of CT scans in patients with suspected pulmonary embolism or children with head trauma. A less technical tool to mitigate cognitive errors may be to encourage diagnostic cross-checking. One randomized trial examined systematic cross-checking of cases between emergency physicians on shift and reported a 40% relative reduction in adverse events in the intervention group.2 While this finding can be summed up by "two heads are better than one," there are clearly major barriers to universal implementation of this approach. A selective application of cross-checking to high acuity or cases involving perceived diagnostic uncertainty, however, could potentially achieve similar benefits without compromising efficiency. Future EHR-embedded artificial intelligence algorithms could provide similar cross-checking at scale through the collective intelligence of diagnostic evaluations observed in large EHR data sets. The EHR could also automatically flag cases involving potential diagnostic errors (e.g., ED diagnosis discordant from the hospital discharge diagnosis) to improve awareness and facilitate structured feedback. As diagnostic error risk is increased during transitions of care, leveraging the EHR to routinize these care transitions could help, for example, by explicitly requiring documentation of diagnostic confidence. While systems interventions are necessary components, it is also essential to address cognition to improve diagnostic judgment. Starting at the earliest stages of medical education, physicians should be introduced to the concept of metacognition, including type 1 and type 2 thinking and common cognitive biases, and receive training in mindfulness, critical thinking, and team cognition.3 In addition, culture change is needed around both communication and documentation of diagnostic uncertainty with downstream providers and patients alike. Rather than framing this as a deficiency in clinical skills and something that should never been acknowledged, diagnostic uncertainty of varying degrees should be normalized as an expected occurrence during emergency care.4 Education and training through the use of validated instruments to scaffold provider conversations with their patients, for example, through the uncertainty communication checklist, has been demonstrated to increase mastery in physicians successfully communicating diagnostic uncertainty to ED patients.5 In conclusion, the AHRQ report should not be read as an indictment of EM providers but, rather, raise awareness about the need for more effective solutions to address diagnostic error in this unique and high-risk clinical environment that provides acute and unscheduled care. The resulting controversy is best met with a redoubling of efforts and increased support for research examining how we can more effectively identify and reduce diagnostic error across all health care settings and mitigate the associated waste and patient harm. titulo: The feminisation of the notary profession in France: end of a patriarchal bastion or sedimentation of a gender stratification?

resumo: The legal professions have been largely gendered. Their feminisation raises questions about the progressive disappearance of gender-based inequalities. While some, such as lawyers, were feminised early and spectacularly, others, which were for a long time very male, also seem to be moving towards parity. This is particularly true of the profession of notary, whose closure has been particularly remarkable in France; for a long time exclusively male, the profession was opened to women in 1948. However, this closed profession has recently experienced a reversal: more than half of its members are now women. This feminisation is all the more remarkable because it is very recent; facilitated by the rise of the diploma and the diversification of access to the profession, it has undergone several phases of acceleration, in the 1990s with the introduction of salaried employment, and since 2015, with the Loi croissance which increases the number of notaries and liberalises the profession. While this so-called “Macron” reform has accelerated its feminisation, it has also contributed to the reinforcement of gender stratifications and segmentations within the profession, and can potentially lead to a polarization of the market, which is, after all, very gendered.

titulo: The hybrid outcome of urban change: global city, polarized city?
instituicoes: Vrije Universiteit Brussel
periodico: Glocalism Journal of Culture Politics and Innovation
palavras_openalex: global cities | socio-spatial polarization | urban segregation | deindustrialization | welfare state decline | urban restructuring | hybridity | local urban policy | housing market
resumo: A wide range of studies supports the assumption that levels of socio-spatial polarization, segregation, and exclusion are rising in global cities over the past decades as a direct outcome of certain global processes, such as the deindustrialization process, its associated changes in division of labor, and declined redistributive power of the welfare state. However, that assumption – known as the polarization thesis – is criticized based on several contentions, including the oversimplification of the global/local interplay by overlooking the role of local contingent factors that may modify, intensify, or reverse the expected socio-spatial outcome in individual cities. This study aims to capture the hybrid nature of the socio-spatial outcomes of global cities by proving that the complex process of restructuring of cities is a form of structural and chronological hybridity. Through providing a solid empirical ground for investigating the general applicability of the socio-spatial polarization thesis, as well as evaluating the influence of local contexts of cities on the outcomes of urban change. The research offers a theoretical review of the multifaceted restructuring of global cities. Then, the macro trends of global economy are linked to their micro outcomes (segregation patterns within cities), through understanding the implications of cities’ economic functions on local urban policies and housing markets. Finally, the changes in socioeconomic segregation over the past decades are calculated for a large dataset of 66 global cities. The collective result of the analysis shows the downfalls of the generalized hypothesis. While the discussion of individual cities highlights certain contextual particularities, that are contributing to the production of unique socio-spatial configurations in different global cities.
