titulo: La economía mexicana: De la recesión a la depresión ante la pandemia de la Covid-19 / The Mexican economy: from recession to depression in the face of the Covid-19 pandemic
autores: María Elena Tavera Cortés | Edmar Salinas Callejas
instituicoes: Instituto Politécnico Nacional | Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana
palavras_openalex: Mexican economy | COVID-19 pandemic | economic recession | economic depression | gross domestic product | business cycles | fiscal policy | monetary policy | government change | structural polarization | business elites | political elites | recovery policy | 1929 Great Depression | countercyclical policy
resumo:
Los ciclos economicos pueden ser de diversos tipos, de produccion, consumo, inversion, ocupacion, precios; aqui se usara para el analisis de la economia mexicana el ciclo de produccion o del producto, de manera que el comportamiento del PIB es el eje del analisis. Los ciclos economicos han transitado de un comportamiento espontaneo a un comportamiento regulado, este cambio se dio a raiz de la gran depresion de 1929, sea con una estrategia anticiclica o con una estrategia prociclica, que son las estrategias que se han aplicado desde el fin de la Segunda Guerra Mundial. El objetivo de este trabajo es analizar como se da la recesion de la economia mexicana en 2019 y como se transita a la depresion de 2020, la primera coyuntura economica determinada por el cambio de gobierno y sus efectos inmediatos, y la segunda coyuntura determinada por la pandemia de Covid-19 y la estrategia de politica economica aplicada en el corto plazo. Los instrumentos de politica fiscal y monetaria para manejar las coyunturas de recesion y depresion economica se instrumentan desde un corte normativo, estableciendo medidas de respuesta fiscal y monetaria para controlar los impactos negativos de la desaceleracion economica en un caso, y de la aguda contraccion economica en el otro caso. Las medidas de politica economica aplicadas en Mexico y la posible salida de la depresion, presentan diversas dificultades, que se expresan en la polarizacion entre una fraccion de la clase empresarial y la elite politica desplazada con el cambio de gobierno, y el nuevo gobierno, las politicas de recuperacion planteadas por uno y otro bando, con la polarizacion estructural, son la forma y el fondo del conflicto. El 1% de las empresas genera 69.7% de la riqueza y 47.5% del empleo, y 99% de las empresas generan 30.3% de la riqueza y 52.5% del empleo.
Abstract
Economic cycles can be of various types, production, consumption, investment, occupation, prices; the production or product cycles will be used here for analysis of the Mexican economy, so that GDP behavior is the focus of the analysis. Economic cycles have shifted from spontaneous behavior to regulated behavior, this changed originated in the great depression of 1929, either with an anticyclical or procyclical economic policy, which are the strategics that have been implemented after de Second World War. The objective of this trial is to analyze the 2019 recession occurs and how it is transitioned to the 2020 depression, the first economic situation determined by the change of government and its immediate effects, and the second situation determined by the Covid-19 pandemic and the economic policy strategy implemented in the short term. Fiscal and monetary policy instruments to manage economicus downturns and economic depression are implemented from a regulatory cut, establishing fiscal and monetary response measures to control the negative impacts of economic slowdown in one case and acute economic contraction in the other case. The economic policy measures implemented in Mexico and the possible departure from the depression present various difficulties, which are expressed in the polarization of a fraction of the business class and the fraction of the political elite displaced by the change of government. Recovery policies raised on both sides and the polarized structural condition are the form and substance of the conflict. As 1% of companies generated 69.3% of wealth and 47.5% of employment, while 99% of companies generate 30.3% of wealth and 52.2% of employment

titulo: Ten Observations: The 2021 ICA Presidential Address
instituicoes: University of Amsterdam
palavras_openalex: International Communication Association | COVID-19 pandemic | communication scholarship | gender and caregiving | North-South inequality | democratic backsliding | media and journalism | racism | virtual conference | professional society governance
resumo: Members of the International Communication Association, colleagues, friends. This is not a standard presidential address. There is nothing normal about the situation the world is currently in. Despite vaccinations being rolled out, and my sincere congratulations to those of you who have received or have had loved ones being vaccinated, the pandemic is still raging in many places on the planet. And many social and economic costs are still to come. The pandemic has challenged the members of our association. And the association itself. The ICA is built upon a community that meets and interacts. From the moment in March 2020 where we flipped the Australia conference to an online conference, and all the way to today, where we supposed to meet in Denver, Colorado. It is just 15 months. It seems like forever. In the past period, we have seen that the struggles are real. And ongoing: the precarious role of young scholars, the imbalance with which the pandemic has affected female colleagues and caregivers as Grace Ahn and other articulated recently in Communication, Culture & Critique. The sense of disconnect, the exhaustion, the loneliness, and the worries. They are all real. The global north-south divides have become even clearer. Existing inequalities even more apparent. And it is not over yet. It is my sincere wish that the coming months, will be months that offer hope. ‘What doesn’t kill you, makes you stronger’. These words, appropriated by many, including Kelly Clarkson, seem almost appropriate to describe the resilience and ability to move forward that has characterized our field in the past period. In my address today, I make 10 observations about our field and association. Ten things that made me think in the past year, 10 things that I saw, wondered about, feel passionate about. They are 10 observations about where communication scholarship, and the ICA, can and should play a role. Ideas for an IDEA agenda. 2020 was a year characterized by the pandemic, but also by democratic backsliding, democratic resilience, injustice, and racism. We represent a field, Communication, that can both help understand the impact of and role of media and journalism in these societal dynamics. How media and communication can contribute to not only sustaining power, but also to change. We can and do contribute to discussions about Inclusion, Diversity, Equity, and Access. We need to do that not only in our work, but also in how we organize our field. In the past year, we have made important steps towards making the ICA and our community a space that offers more commitment to IDEA. But we need to do more. We can turn to inspiration from our students, our early career community, and our IDEA committee members, to learn how we can bring about organizational change. But we also need to ask ourselves how we can contribute to this agenda in society at large. How we ask our questions, the parts of the world we study, how we listen, and share our knowledge, matter. We are generating a wealth of knowledge that we can put to use. Scholarly values matter. As Alondra Nelson, the newly appointed Deputy Director for science and society for the White House and former president of the U.S. Social Science Research Council, recently said when taking office: ‘we need to situate and ground our science in values of quality, trust and accountability.’ I believe this is a powerful and fundamental statement. Quality, trust, accountability. These are guiding values, they are empowering values, and they are binding values. To be a relevant voice, we need to strive for quality in our research, we need rigor and self-reflection. We need to continuously earn trust in our work. And we need to be accountable for our work, to our colleagues and society at large. These are values we should pursue, values we should teach, and values that should guide the ICA. Scholarship should be open. In the run up to and after last year’s conference, we launched several Open scholarship initiatives: sessions, roundtables, tutorials, an open scholarship section of the website, and open scholarship opportunities in the conference and journals. A lot has happened in this space since and I hope the ICA and the communication field can lead by example. We were perhaps late to the open scholarship movement, but I believe we have much to offer when thinking about open communication scholarship. We can offer respectful and critical ideas about different types of scholarship, from ethnographic to digital, and how to square that with openness, transparency, and reflection. And as communication scholars we can help getting the communication about open scholarship right: New research is often just a small pieces of a puzzle, and most often not a big, sensational headline from a pre-print manuscript. Democratic backsliding is also about communication. In many countries, in many democracies, across the world, we are experiencing not only the questioning of authority and trust in information, but also actual threats to journalists and to scholars and undermining of democratic institutions. The work by Barbie Zelizer and colleagues in this space is so important. Do we study enough countries and contexts? How can our communication scholarship be part of this conversation? What knowledge can we leverage? We have a rich body of work speaking to the importance of communication, journalism, and the free press vis-à-vis populist movements. We can show how media and communication, including on tech platforms, have ignited and fueled processes of democratic backsliding. But how can we, as individuals, and as a field and an association, do more to put this knowledge into action and be guardians of freedom of communication and the press? Big tech has become too powerful. The past years have shown that big tech companies are central features of our information infrastructure. They operate in a free market, often in lieu of regulation. Or taxes for that matter. They are at the eye of the storm when we discuss democracy. They have shortsighted, often ad hoc, mostly U.S. driven policies and community rules, and no systematic, accountable, public facing system of governance. Being a central part of the societal, economic, democratic, and regulatory conversation of getting this right, is a major task for our field. We look to guiding voices like Joan Donovan and Marietje Schaake for this. And we work on being a vocal advocate for ensuring scholarly access to for example social media platform data. Turning away from democratic debate? In recent years, we have paid a lot of attention, in our research and in societal debates, to information sharing, politically driven ideological bubbles, and processes of polarization and radicalization. This remains of utmost importance. But the past year has perhaps also highlighted another important cleavage. An inequality and a cleavage in whom it is that turn in, and importantly out, and away from the public and democratic debate. Ideological and identity driven media and information choices matter, but perhaps we need to pay more attention to those tuning away from, and out of, the public and political debate all together. Our information ecology offers rich opportunity to engage with media and communication and yet avoid the political and the democratic debate. Perhaps a large part of the citizenry being absent from the democratic debate is as worrying as the polarization of that debate? Health and science communication at the core. The Covid19 pandemic has overwhelmingly been addressed as merely a public health concern. Too little attention, in most countries, has been paid to the pandemic as a challenge in terms of effective health communication, interventions, and behavioral campaigns. Too little attention has been paid to the mental well-being, too little attention has been paid to insights from science communication on how to discuss misinformation and vaccines. We have colleagues in our field and ICA who have been trailblazers and who have had real policy impact. But we need to make communication insights matter more in this space, which starts with politics and public administrators looking more broadly at what a pandemic and a health challenge is. Digital competences are basic competences. The past year has thrown the globe into the ultimate digital and online experiment. This period has highlighted and amplified the importance of digital competences. Add to this, citizens’ competences when it comes to the roll out of artificial intelligence and hybrid human–machine interactions in all corners of society. Many of our colleagues looking at media literacy and different life stages have a lot to offer, as do those studying platforms and human–machine interactions, and AI systems. I take inspiration from great colleagues like Kate Crawford or Gina Neff. As communication scholars we can leverage that knowledge to provide robust education, understanding of the full ecology, and insights on how to develop digital competences. Is “small” the new “big”? As we ride the wave of big data, network analyses, digital trace data, we are also challenged as communication scholars to apply many of our current designs. How to effectively study the impact of social media platforms? We do not have the right data access; we have a hard time reliably assessing usage and exposure. We need to enrich this with smaller scale studies; ethnographies, observations, in-situ studies, and repeated measures within individuals. New and exciting work is going on this space, and communication scholars are actually really well poised to combine methods and designs from humanities, social sciences, and computational and digital research. Beyond single discipline answers? The questions our societies are faced with today when it comes to communication are not simple. The world looks to us for answers about the impact of gaming, the impact of social media, and the role of communication in the climate crisis. Not small, or easy questions. I very much believe that a combination of solid, small, and focused contributions in combination with larger, interdisciplinary teams. Combining questions of governance, communication, data, and ethics, require not only insights from beyond our own field, but also a key role for the communication field. Colleagues, ICA friends. My 10 observations have come to an end. They were eclectic. They have been prompted by developments in the past year, in response to what is happening in our field and in our association. It is my hope and conviction that our ICA is a place to address many of these questions. The in many ways horrible year 2020 has perhaps made the ICA stronger. Despite the inability to meet and interact, as we usually do, we have found new ways to connect and be helpful colleagues, mentors, and educators. And maybe we have also reached out to scholars, met colleagues, and found new collaborators that we would have missed on the floors of the conference hotel or our own institutions. The pandemic worsened inequalities but also offered opportunities. The last year has been humbling. Out of all comfort zones. I was born in the 70s, I am child of 80s (with a lasting love for the music and the pop culture), a teenager of 90s. The world was unfair, but in many ways seemed to be moving to better place. I was 16 when Berlin wall came down. 18 when Denmark won the European football championship. I am white, male, from Denmark, and I work at ASCoR. Like many of my generation, my descent, and yes, also my gender, I have been given a lot of privileges. Today, at 46, I look at the world and worry that we are now in a time where the world becoming better, is far from clear. And many people around the globe rightfully ask for it to become better for them. There are immense democratic, social, environmental challenges ahead. No matter whether thinking about communicating big political ideas, changing our behavior, engaging with family, expressing ourselves online, communication and media are at the very core of change. Communication can, should, and I believe will be at the center of findings answers to these challenges. It has been a privilege to serve as your President. It was humbling to give a year to the ICA: Student Hardship fund, going virtual, IDEA support fund, mentorships, regional hubs. These were all topics we did not expect to be as prominent as they have become. Being an ICA President is a transitory and really a teamwork job. I want to thank the EC colleagues, our ICA headquarters, Laura, the Board of Directors, and everyone engaged in committees, divisions, and interest groups. The ICA and the membership that I have come to know better has shown viability and resilience, amidst the huge challenges. This bodes well for the future.

titulo: Graduate Plastic Surgery Education and Seventy-Five Years of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery
palavras_openalex: plastic surgery residency | history of plastic surgery | residency training | academic medical centers | preceptorship | American Board of Plastic Surgery
resumo: The flagship of the media fleet of education for plastic surgery is Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery and has been so since inception 75 years ago. Under the stewardship of but four editors (Ivy, McDowell, Goldwyn, and Rohrich), the Journal (note the capitalization) has provided education in the arenas of clinical practice, research, socioeconomic topics, and graduate medical education. The last, graduate plastic surgery education, has been serviced by Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery in two modes: one, as the storehouse of information available to the resident for access; and two, as a forum for discussion and exchange of thoughts and concepts about the requisite elements and structure of plastic surgery resident education. Although on occasion opinion pieces have appeared about undergraduate education, the remainder of this essay is focused on the former (Fig. 1).Fig. 1.: For 75 years the Journal has been the vehicle for discussion, debate, and documentation of the evolution of graduate plastic surgery education.Review of the early volumes of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery yielded the first article directed toward resident education, a 23-page opus1 in an era when a single issue was but 110 pages, authored by the quadrumvirate of plastic surgery at Barnes Hospital in St. Louis, headed by James Barrett Brown. The entire piece is devoted to specific dictates to “house officers” about weighty topics such as appropriate preoperative orders and the correct method of preparing the operative site. The alpha article that embraced some nettlesome issues in plastic surgery resident education was authored by S. M. Dupertuis.2 Dupertuis advocated for the deletion of preceptorships that permitted those who completed same to become American Board of Plastic Surgery–certified. He also broached the question of whether perhaps 3 years of residency was required, amazingly prophetic of a requirement adopted nearly 60 years later. The issue of resident education is inextricably linked to the role and status of plastic surgery as a unit within an academic medical center. The decade following Dupertuis’s prescient piece, a discussion of the role of a plastic surgery unit and the relationship with general surgery and the academic setting ensued. Milton Edgerton of Johns Hopkins opined, “To this, I would add that in a medical school he should be a member of the general surgery department and serve the interests of that department....”3 Edwin Ellison, the chief of surgery at Marquette, later renamed Medical College of Wisconsin, invited to speak at the 1960 Association, American Association of Plastic Surgeons, meeting, engaged in a semantic twist of titles, designating surgery as a division and the surgical specialties as departments.4 Nevertheless, the drawing (Fig. 2) depicted the functioning hierarchy, with plastic surgery and the other units administratively subservient to general surgery. In most respects, this posture did not permit plastic surgery to prosper. Bradford Cannon, a founding member of the American Board of Plastic Surgery, deplored the absence of a single training program in plastic surgery in the six New England states.5Fig. 2.: Membership of the components of the Marquette surgery unit. From Ellison EH. The inter-relationship of the department of plastic and reconstructive surgery and the division of surgery in the medical school. Plast Reconstr Surg. 1960;26:312–320.The responsibility of a plastic surgery unit administratively and financially autonomous and on an equal footing with other specialties was defined by Hoopes in his American Association of Plastic Surgeons presidential address,6 but he did not explicitly incorporate that definition in departmental status. At the same meeting of the Association, Zook was substantially more explicit: “The solution … we plastic surgeons must present a united front in acquiring departmental status.”7 The clarion call, though, was from Rohrich, who iterated the inescapable logic that plastic surgery justifiably deserved the status as an independent—independent from general surgery—department.8 A follow-up publication outlined the necessary steps to achieve departmental status.9 Despite the iteration of a unified stance by American Council of Academic Plastic Surgery in a white paper,10 progress as measured by the trajectory of conversion from division to department has been measured.11 As described above, the two issues of the role of the plastic surgery unit within the academic medical center and the structure of resident education, prerequisite and requisite requirements, are intertwined. Yet, discussions published in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery often pursued parallel but separate tracks. The discourse in the arena of graduate medical education for plastic surgery has centered on three issues: first, the optimal track or curriculum of a plastic surgery residency; second, and much more recently, the advent of competency-based assessment of resident performance; and third, the recognition of the necessity for greater diversity within academia and our residencies. Essentially, the discourse about the prerequisite education, the experience prior to the requisite plastic surgery education and training, revolved about the extent of exposure to general surgery, presumably an extension of our roots in that specialty. Peacock perhaps embodied the established or orthodox position: “in most instances, the completion of a chief residency in general surgery is mandatory for competence of that degree.”12 Others did not share that degree of certitude. Perhaps a minority, but individuals in plastic surgery leadership, such as Dingman,13 Robinson,14 and even the chair of surgery at Case-Western Reserve University, Holden,15 opined publicly for a “judicious integration” of training of the plastic surgery resident. Weeks,16 in a prophetic presidential address to the Association, proposed a restructure that included 1 year, the first, of general surgery. The sentinel paper by Chase,17 perhaps as a “voice in the wilderness,” established a broad framework that would serve as the initial building blocks or perhaps seeds that germinated into the Stanford University Plastic Surgery pioneering venture into the domain of integrated training. That venture represented a considerable modification of the traditional and set prerequisite general surgery, followed by the required plastic surgery residency. Nevertheless, a substantial hiatus ensued before the pages of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery reflected an active dialogue between those who adopted a posture of status quo and the advocates of a necessary change in our curriculum of plastic surgery resident education and training. The former hinged the argument on the necessity of a core preparation in the general principles of surgery, the latter that resident education should be specialty-specific, specific to plastic surgery. Although debate on the issue was conducted in several forums, including the Association of Academic Chairmen in Plastic Surgery (now the American Council of Academic Plastic Surgery), at the time the organization of plastic surgery training program directors and the American Association of Plastic Surgeons, the pages of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery initially reflected the discourse when this writer outlined that the general surgery training background had historical roots but not the appropriate prerequisite education and that substantial modification was required (Fig. 3).18 At this juncture, the debate focused less on the necessity for full general surgery residency as prerequisite but rather coalesced on the number of years of same.Fig. 3.: The relationship of plastic and general surgery in 1940 and 1990. (Above) Areas of clinical responsibilities for general surgery (left), plastic surgery (right), and the overlap between the two specialties in the year 1940. Titles outside the boxes represent areas of subspecialization yet to be developed and incorporated. (Below) The evolution of areas of clinical responsibility for general and plastic surgery over 50 years. The overlap has narrowed to include essentially management of burns and surgery of the breast only. Titles outside the two boxes represent entities of clinical responsibility that, for the most part, lie in other specialty domains. Reprinted from Luce EA. Integrated training in plastic surgery: Concept, implementation, benefits, and liabilities. Plast Reconstr Surg. 1995;95:119–123.Two models or tracks emerged, sanctioned by the Residency Review Committee and the American Board of Plastic Surgery, one termed independent, with a variable duration of prior general surgery (eventually full general surgery residency required), and the other termed integrated, of 5 or 6 (eventually 6) years of plastic surgery education. The back door of the variable general surgery years required permitted a subsequent aberration to occur, the “combined” or “coordinated” program—an aberration that demanded “the [Residency Review Committee] … delete the combined or coordinated program and eradicate the fatally flawed mutant strain that has emerged in our natural evolution from the traditional, if anachronistic program, to a truly contemporary method of plastic surgery resident education.”19 Not until nearly 15 years later was such a genetic deletion accomplished. Within the next 2 years, retreats were organized by the short-lived Congress of Plastic Surgery Organizations in 1990 and 1991 that included the American Association of Plastic Surgeons, the Residency Review Committee, and the residency directors group.20 At that meeting an “integrated” pathway was presented amid a robust discussion.21 Conversion of a tradition-bound but an anachronistic method of resident education to a radically altered model driven by plastic surgery from day one of graduate medical education mandated consideration of methods of implementation, benefits, and liabilities.22 Nevertheless, as espoused by Rohrich, a revolution was underway.23 One of the building blocks of a logic structure that concluded that departmental status was essential was the link to implementation of a new conceptual model of plastic surgery education. Proponents of the integrated model understood that a true integration of training and education would establish rotations with a progressive increase in responsibility, all within the framework of the specialty (plastic surgery differentiation) and yet with sufficient exposure to general surgery to ensure education in basic surgical principles. Publications have addressed another challenge, selection of a future plastic surgeon from a cadre of senior medical students,24 and have attempted to compare with a variety of metrics traditional versus the integrated programs25–28 and implications. Others have focused on the lack of standardization of curriculum29 or rotations.30 The conceptual model of the integrated residency was not completely embraced across the landscape of academic plastic surgery.31,32 The late Dr. Jurkiewicz’s admonition that we, the specialty, have failed to establish the metrics and the data to determine the hypothesis that the integrated track is superior to the independent model, to educate residents, as Hunter33 reiterated in discussion of Schneider et al.29 The complexity of graduate medical education in general and plastic surgery resident education in particular was rendered yet more complex by the advent of a competency-based system by the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education. Viewed through the lens of a medical educator, the emphasis is one of assessment, an assessment to determine completion of residency education and training by the attainment of competence rather than time spent. Although attention (and criticism) has been unduly focused on the logistics and practicality of a time-variable system of residency completion,34 the elements of periodic performance evaluation, initiated in the junior years, attended by frequent formative feedback are the attributes of a system built on the foundation of adult learning principles. In addition, residents highly value detailed and granular feedback rather than the two- or three-word end-of-rotation global assessment. If frequent and credible assessment is the core of the competency-based system, then the mandate is the use of validated, practical, and economically feasible assessment tools.35 Another division of clinical competency besides the six components listed above (can we dismember competency into six parts?) is technical and nontechnical skills. An instrument for the evaluation of procedural capabilities specific to plastic surgery has been developed, tested, and published.36 Tools for the assessment of nontechnical skills, other than the objective structured clinical examination, are at best in the embryonic phase of gestation.37 Central to the development of a competency-based system was implementation of the plastic surgery milestones.38 The milestones, as the name implies, are interval points on the path or journey toward the attainment of independent practice. If the goal of incorporation of the integrated residency into the fabric of academic plastic surgery hinged on achievement of departmental status, then the success of a competency-based approach assuredly dictates an acceptance of the milestones as the yardstick for resident performance evaluation. Publications in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery that have examined the programmatic experience with use of the milestones have been scarce and limited to a comparison of resident and attending evaluation of said resident,39 a catalog of possible milestone assessment tools,40,41 and a survey conducted of training program directors shortly after inauguration of the plastic surgery milestones in 2014 to determine preparation and readiness of programs to implement the mandated system.38 The authors concluded, based on the results, that two-thirds of the respondents opined that the milestones would improve neither the depth nor the quality of resident training. Perhaps to no surprise, less than one-fourth were satisfied with their respective preparation for the new system. Inherent is the inertia of change, a conversion from an established, if inadequate, routine to one that is substantially more complex and entails considerably more data, with the attendant documentation. Despite the passage of 7 years, some evidence exists that the transformation is substantially less than complete. Gosain and coauthors42 also canvassed plastic surgery training programs quite recently, in particular the chairs of the clinical competency committee, to ascertain the individual programmatic mechanics of competency-based assessment. The results are not encouraging and of some concern, particularly since milestones 2.0 lie on the near horizon and hope springs eternal.43 The central focus of the milestones is one of assessment and, although inarguably important, depicts a necessarily limited view of the panorama of the current status of plastic surgery resident education. A broader and more comprehensive view44 delivers some reassurance. Currently, resident programs employ a number of diverse methods of provision of education at the graduate level and have a broad range of didactic activities as well as protected educational time, as mandated by the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education. Can we improve? Certainly. Innovative technology, compelled and propelled in utilization by the pandemic, offers opportunities to become more efficient and yet inclusive. The capacity to archive electronically (digitally) education material as tutorials, lectures, and scientific publications can provide the foundation for “self-directed” learning, learning initiated by the learner, functioning autonomously. The hazard implicit by incorporation of self-directed learning into the fabric of programmatic resident education is the potential gravitation toward loss of accountability and structure in the absence of interactive teaching45 (Fig. 4). The second element in a process of successful improvement is a concerted embrace of a conceptual conversion of our conference structure from one of a pedagogic (“to lead the child”) learning format, dominated by lectures and talks (essentially lectures), to one based on the principles of adult learning45: experientially derived learning including the capacity to commit mistakes, problem-oriented rather than teacher-centered, immediate relevance and feedback, ability to apply the information shortly after learning, and participation by the learners in the establishment of their educational goals.Fig. 4.: (Left) Self-directed learning lends autonomy to the learner but no balance. (Right) An element of structure and accountability achieves a balance between autonomous self-directed learning and teacher-centered learning. Reprinted from Luce EA. The future of plastic surgery resident education. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2016;137:1063–1070.A number of topics relevant to graduate medical education and plastic surgery, such as the education-service conundrum46–48 and aesthetic surgery,49 that have appeared in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery will be left without comment. The final topic or issue is the dedication of the Journal and the editor, Rod Rohrich, in particular, to address the necessity of diversity and the presence of implicit gender bias in academic plastic surgery. The pertinent and seminal articles have appeared in the recently instituted section of the Journal entitled Plastic Surgery Focus.49,50 Earlier, Mackinnon sounded the note of dissent of the perception of plastic surgery as a traditional male specialty and inaugurated the matter of awareness of the experience of the woman plastic surgery resident.50 As senior author, she then broached the concerns of discrimination, harassment, and the unequal promotion and recommendation of women.51 Recent contributions have followed with evidence that women are underrepresented in leadership positions in academic plastic surgery, including departmental chairs and program directors, and the importance of gender diversity to our specialty.52,53 Others54 have re-emphasized that gender bias still persists in plastic surgery residency programs. The 75 years of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery as the vehicle for debate, discourse, and scientific investigations in the arena of graduate medical education and plastic surgery has consisted of publications of the principal deliberations and issues that impact resident education and training. Beginning with James Barrett Brown’s detailed descriptions of the conduct of preoperative and postoperative care to the considerations of installing an entirely novel method of resident assessment, these publications are a documentation of the ascending trajectory of a vital and dynamic specialty.

titulo: Supporters and dependants: the concept of economic dependency ratio as an indicator of changes in regional structures in Finland in 1989-1997
autores: Toivo Muilu | Jarmo Rusanen | Arvo Naukkarinen
instituicoes: University of Oulu
palavras_openalex: economic dependency ratio | regional structural change | unemployment | spatial polarization | population density | georeferenced records | 1 km grid cells | rural areas | urban-rural disparities | economic recovery | Finland | spatial planning
resumo: An examination is made of the concept of economic dependency ratio and its applicability as a tool for analysing changes in regional structures in Finland against the background of the unprecendented rise in unemployment from 4.4 % to 22.2 % that took place in 1989‑1993, when Finland moved from the middle rank in the European employment statistics to become one of the countries with the worst unemployment. The traditional statistical approach based on administrative areas is fired out with georeferenced data for 1 x 1 km grid cells. The principal empirical observation at the municipality (local government district) level is that the small, predominantly rural districts of East­ern, Central and Northern Finland had poor economic dependency ratios that showed no appreciable improvement during the subsequent general econom­ic recovery. GIS analyses based on deciles of population density confirmed this polarization of the differences in regional structure, since although unem­ployment and the economic dependency ratio deteriorated most markedly in the densely populated urban areas during 1989‑1993, the most sparsely pop­ulated areas lagged well behind these in development during the recovery years of 1993‑1997. The results suggest that the use of georeferenced data can pro­vide additional information for planning and decision‑making purposes in the form of more accurate identification of problem areas.

resumo: Although the COVID-19 pandemic has undoubtedly disrupted the scientific enterprise, spine surgeons remained committed to improving the science of our discipline. We present a review of high-quality, peer-reviewed articles over the past year, revealing advances in our understanding of cervical myelopathy and trauma, deformity, spinal cord injury, and other degenerative spinal conditions. These articles were chosen for their originality, insightfulness, methodology, and potential impact on the field of spine surgery. COVID-19 and Spine Surgery The coronavirus has resulted in a global pandemic, with 120 million infected people around the world and over 2.6 million lives lost by March 2021. This disease results in pulmonary compromise and the need for inpatient hospitalizations in a subset of patients. An estimated 3% to 32% of patients required intensive care support and artificial ventilation. Hospitals in the United States and across the world responded swiftly and in similar ways. Travel bans were rapidly initiated to limit the spread of the virus and to preserve the physician workforce, non-urgent surgical procedures were cancelled in order to increase hospital capacity for patients infected with the virus, and in-person clinics were cancelled and were replaced by telemedicine visits to slow down the rate of community spread. The economic impact on health care was staggering. In the initial weeks of the pandemic, 60,000 health-care jobs were lost1, and almost all interventional spine procedures were postponed or cancelled. Over 60% of spine surgeons reported reductions in their salary or benefits, and 17% reported that they, or other spine surgery providers, were involuntarily reassigned to cover non-neurosurgical services during the COVID-19 pandemic. Sixty-nine percent received no financial compensation for these work efforts, and 31% of respondents were compensated at a rate equal to or lower than their established salary rate. Cervical Pathologies Cervical Spondylosis and Cervical Spondylotic Myelopathy Degenerative cervical myelopathy remains the most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction. In a Level-I multicenter study, Fehlings et al. investigated whether riluzole enhances outcomes in patients undergoing a decompression and fusion procedure for degenerative cervical myelopathy. This was a multicenter, double-blinded, placebo-controlled, randomized, phase-3 trial of patients undergoing a surgical procedure across 16 university-affiliated hospitals in the United States and Canada. Patients were randomized to either riluzole or placebo. The primary end point was a change in modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) scores at 6 months after the surgical procedure. Secondary outcomes were changes from baseline in functional status (Nurick grade), disability (Neck Disability Index), American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) score, grip strength, Numeric Rating Scale scores, and quality of life (Short Form-36 [SF-36] and EuroQol-5 Dimensions [EQ-5D]). Of the 408 patients who were screened, 300 were eligible and 290 were randomly assigned to the intervention group (n = 141) or the placebo group (n = 149), and 108 patients were excluded. The mean patient age was 58 years. Baseline characteristics were balanced between both groups. At 6 months after the surgical procedure, both patient groups showed improvement in mJOA scores; however, there were no between-group differences in the extent of improvement. Similarly, the extent of improvement from baseline in all secondary outcomes was not significantly different between both groups. At 1 year after the surgical procedure, the riluzole group demonstrated a greater reduction in neck pain, although pain was not a prespecified primary end point. Riluzole does not provide an additional benefit with respect to functional outcome scores in patients undergoing decompression and fusion for cervical myelopathy2. In a Level-I study investigating the effectiveness of local intraoperative corticosteroids at decreasing dysphagia after multilevel anterior discectomy and fusion surgical procedures3, Kim et al. demonstrated a significant decrease in the severity of postoperative dysphagia with local intraoperative corticosteroids. This was a prospective, double-blinded, randomized controlled trial of patients undergoing multilevel anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF). Patients were randomized to receive the treatment (local corticosteroids) or placebo. Additionally, patients received 10 mL of intravenous dexamethasone, regardless of group allocation (institutional protocol). The primary outcome was change in swallowing assessed with the Eating Assessment Tool-10 (EAT-10) and the Swallowing Quality of Life (SWAL-QOL) Questionnaire. There were 128 patients who were eligible and were randomized, and 109 patients (56 in the treatment group and 53 in the control group) were used in the analysis. At baseline, both groups were balanced; however, the treatment group had a lower frequency of drain placement and shorter operative time. The EAT-10 scores were significantly lower in the corticosteroid group on postoperative day 2, and this difference was durable through 1 month after the surgical procedure. The findings of this study suggest that the local administration of corticosteroids after multilevel ACDF is associated with decreased severity of postoperative dysphagia3. Cervical Trauma In a Level-II study4, Buchanan et al. investigated whether the addition of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) adds value for patients presenting with acute traumatic cervical spinal cord injury. This was a vignette-based study of patients presenting with acute spinal cord injury to a level-1 trauma center between 2010 and 2019. Patients included in the study presented to the emergency department with signs of quadriplegia, and underwent computed tomography (CT), MRI, and subsequently a surgical procedure within 48 hours of arrival. The clinical vignettes were presented to the surgeons in 2 phases. In phase I, the clinical vignettes were presented with only the corresponding CT scans, and in phase II, the vignettes were presented with both CT and MRI scans. A minimum washout period of 2 weeks was included between phases I and II to prevent recall bias. Twenty-nine patient vignettes were utilized for this study (a total of 174 surgical plans). The researchers found that surgical timing was changed in 55% of cases, approach was changed in 44% of cases, and targeted vertebral levels were changed in 63% of cases. Combined, 93% of surgical plans changed after the MRI. Collision sports have inherent risk of injuries, such as cervical spinal injuries. Up to 10% of injuries in the National Football League (NFL) are head, neck, and spine injuries. Return to play after cervical injuries is controversial, given the paucity of data on this topic. Using a modified Delphi methodology, Schroeder et al.5 attempted to establish return-to-play recommendations. They conducted a 3-round survey with fellowship-trained spinal surgeons and physicians from the NFL. The first-round survey was sent to all Cervical Spine Research Society (CSRS) members and consisted of 14 clinical scenarios and 38 questions related to cervical spine injuries in football. The results for this survey informed the development of 13 consensus statements, which were subsequently sent to CSRS members (second round). The feedback from the second survey was used to develop return-to-play recommendations for professional athletes who sustained cervical spine injuries. The researchers reported strong consensus among respondents that athletes with cervical spine injuries who undergo 1 or 2-level ACDF without increased T2 signal intensity may return to play. There was low consensus for returning to play for athletes who undergo a 3-level ACDF. For asymptomatic athletes without radiographic evidence of spinal cord injury (increased T2 signal intensity) and spinal canal diameter of >10 mm, there was strong consensus for returning to play. There was no consensus on retuning to play for cases with pseudarthrosis after ACDF. For athletes with a history of cervical spine injury, there was strong consensus for screening MRI scans before sports participation5. Cervical Deformity Adult cervical deformity is a common cause of disability in elderly patients. A surgical procedure for deformity correction is technically challenging and is associated with high complication rates and prolonged recovery. Kim et al.6 investigated the incidence, patient-level risk factors, and recovery rate of neurological complications in patients undergoing a corrective surgical procedure for adult cervical deformity. There were 106 patients enrolled in this multicenter study. The mean age was 60.8 years and the mean duration of follow-up was 18.2 months. Neurological complications occurred in 18.9% of patients, of which 68.1% were major complications. The majority (91%) of complications resolved within 6 months, with only 2% of patients with delayed neurological recovery. In a Level-III study, Lau et al. reported outcomes and complications profiles after a Smith-Petersen osteotomy compared with a 3-column osteotomy for the correction of adult cervical deformity. This was a retrospective, single-institution study of patients with adult, non-oncologic cervical deformity. Ninety-five patients with a diagnosis of cervical or cervicothoracic deformity were included. The mean patient age was 63.2 years, and 60% of patients were female. With regard to the mean preoperative values, the cervical sagittal vertical axis was 6.2 cm, the lordosis was 6.8°, the T1 slope was 40.9°, and the coronal Cobb angle was 6.7°. Forty-six patients underwent Smith-Petersen osteotomy and 49 patients underwent 3-column osteotomy. Three-column osteotomies were most commonly performed at T3 (26.5%), followed by T2 (20.4%). Overall, compared with baseline, there was a significant improvement in all cervical radiographic parameters. The combined complication rate (major and minor) was 37.9%. Neurological complications occurred in 16.8% of patients, surgical complications were seen in 17.9%, and medical complications were seen in 23.2% of patients. When comparing complication profiles, the overall complication rate was 32.6% in the Smith-Petersen osteotomy group and 42.9% in the 3-column osteotomy group. This difference was not significant. Complication rates were highest when osteotomies were performed at C7 (37.5%) and T1 (37.5%)7. Lumbar Stenosis, Spondylolisthesis, and Clinical Outcomes Endoscopic spinal surgery has grown in popularity over the past decade. Compared with traditional minimally invasive or open approaches, the use of endoscopy is associated with minimal tissue disruption and pain. To date, the preponderance of these studies focused on endoscopic discectomy, with few studies investigating the effectiveness of this approach for lumbar laminectomy. Salim et al. investigated the effectiveness of a unilateral endoscopic approach for bilateral decompression in patients with lumbar stenosis. The primary outcomes were changes in the visual analog scale, Oswestry Disability Index, MacNab criteria, Medical Research Council (MRC) grading for leg strength, and ASIA score for sensation. Sixty patients (97 levels decompressed) with degenerative spinal stenosis were enrolled in the study. The mean age was 61 years and 38% of patients were male. The mean follow-up period was 30 months. Postoperatively, there was a significant improvement in back and leg pain and disability across all outcome measures assessed. Using the MacNab criteria, 88.4% showed excellent to good outcomes. A unilateral percutaneous endoscopic approach to perform bilateral decompression for patients with lumbar stenosis is both safe and effective8. Lumbar epidural steroid injections are commonly used for nonoperative management of lumbar radiculopathy. In patients who undergo failed conservative management and require a surgical procedure, it is unclear whether preoperative epidural steroid injections may increase risk of postoperative infection. In a retrospective study of 15,011 patients who underwent elective lumbar spine surgical procedures for radiculopathy and/or spinal stenosis at a single institution, Kreitz et al.9 investigated the temporal relationship between preoperative epidural steroid injection, patient demographic characteristics, and comorbidities on postoperative infection. Of the 15,011 patients enrolled, 5,108 underwent fusion procedures and 9,903 underwent decompression only. Patients were categorized as having no preoperative epidural steroid injection or a preoperative epidural steroid injection <30 days, 30 to 90 days, and >90 days prior to the surgical procedure. titulo: Health and health care disparities related to rehabilitation and COVID ‐19
autores: Jeannie K. Harden | Cheri A Blauwet | Julie K. Silver | Maurice G. Sholas | Zainab Rasheed | Monica Verduzco‐Gutierrez
instituicoes: Brigham and Women's Hospital | Central Michigan University | Harvard University | Massachusetts General Hospital | Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital | The University of Texas at San Antonio Health Science Center
