resumo: We are in the middle of one of the more devastating pandemics of the last hundred years, surrounded by illness, suffering, and death due to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection and the resultant coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). Fundamental to this human suffering is the disproportionate impact it is having on marginalized communities. The pandemic has offered us a closer look into health and health care disparities that underpin this trend, inclusive of the impact of structural racism and structural ableism. As the pandemic rages on, we are seeing the evolution of a new population of persons with disabilities secondary to clinical manifestations of COVID-19 that are marked by long-term symptoms, impairments, and the psychological impact of the stigma and misunderstanding surrounding the infection.1 This emerging disabled population only underscores patients' limited access to care because of the shortage of physiatrists and the curtailing of physiatric services deemed nonessential during a response to overwhelming surges of COVID patients in critically stressed health care systems. Telemedicine has been widely used in efforts to improve access to care, including in rehabilitation medicine,2, 3 while mitigating the spread of the pandemic, but it is far from being a panacea. A step in the right direction would be a balanced response that is inclusive of people with disabilities, taking into account physical, cognitive, and socioeconomic barriers in access to care for routine medical and more urgent COVID-related issues, with provisions for tailored strategies that promote more equitable access to services and resources. Suggestions for improving health care for persons with a disability in a pandemic follow. Another special consideration is women physicians and scientists, including physiatrists, as the pandemic has exacerbated many preexisting disparities in the health care workforce. Reducing the attrition of women physiatrists would have an impact on the community, the workplace, and academic medicine as a whole—realms in which women comprise a large proportion of integral roles. It would be no exaggeration to describe it as a mammoth undertaking to address the many complicated layers of health disparities, as the authors claim to be in no way exhaustive in discussing these issues. Nonetheless, physiatrists are in a unique position to advocate for marginalized populations negatively affected by a global pandemic4 by increasing our own awareness of such issues and doing our part to promote more equitable care. The aim of this article is to highlight some health and health care disparities in the United States specifically involving physical medicine and rehabilitation (PM&R) that are brought to light by the COVID-19 crisis. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) define health disparities as “preventable differences in the burden of disease, injury, violence, or opportunities to achieve optimal health that are experienced by socially disadvantaged populations.” It is clear that disparities existed in health and health care before the onset of the current global pandemic caused by COVID-19.5 As the pandemic developed through 2021, the level of community spread, access to treatment, and individual outcomes accentuated disparities that exist in the United States. People from racial and/or ethnic minority groups have experienced higher nationwide cumulative age-adjusted rates of hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, and death rates due to COVID-19 in the first year of the pandemic compared to white Americans.6 American Indian or Alaska Native, African American/Black, Asian or Pacific Islanders, and Latino populations have experienced disproportionately higher rates of SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19 related mortality. The differences in health care access and exposure to risk may be driving infection and mortality rates disproportionately higher, as many individuals who identify with historically, socially, or economically marginalized communities live in poverty and work as essential workers.7 This disparity may be related to increased rates of comorbid health conditions in minority groups. It is also known that individuals from racial and ethnic minority groups face inequity due to historical and societal racism, which leads to poor access to health care and economic instability. Americans who are of lower socioeconomic status have greater challenges sheltering in place and maintaining proper social distancing due to living in crowded places, being classified as essential workers, continuing to live and work in crowded spaces without proper personal protective equipment (PPE), and having to rely on public transportation. Conversely, individuals living in higher socioeconomic conditions have more extensive resources, higher health literacy, and access to the newest information that assist them in implementing plans that limit the spread of COVID-19.8 Equitable access to preventive measures including vaccination and accessible and free testing and masks is necessary to help bridge current gaps. In addition, more work will need to be done to study the impact of socioeconomic inequities and structural racism on COVID-19 outcomes. Physiatrists work with patients who experience health and health care disparities due to an intersection of race/ethnicity, gender, socioeconomic class, and physical and cognitive disabilities. The CDC estimates that one in four Americans are living with some type of disability. Historically, people with disabilities, especially those needing assistance and living in care facilities, are at increased risks during pandemics because of disruption of routine and long-term care. Additionally, during emergent situations, people with disabilities are often forgotten in the planning and response processes, which lead to poor outcomes.9 And although children are less severely symptomatic from COVID-19, systemic efforts to mitigate the pandemic with school closures and social distancing guidelines affect children with disabilities who rely on in-person schooling to derive the benefits of supportive services provided by their schools.10, 11 There are barriers to provision of physiatric care and long-term care for those from minority racial and ethnic groups, and these are especially exacerbated during the COVID-19 pandemic. The World Health Organization has recommended the use of rehabilitation as a key to improve health outcomes of patients with COVID-19.12 However, some social determinants of health (eg, lack of health insurance) will preclude access to rehabilitation services and physicians, negatively affecting outcomes. Existing literature demonstrates that Hispanic and Black patients are at risk for worse outcomes following strokes, hip fractures, spinal cord injuries, and traumatic brain injuries because of low access to rehabilitation education and services and disparities in the referral process.13, 14 Even when long-term services and supports are used by people of racial and/or ethnic minority groups, there is evidence of lower quality of care, poorer outcomes, and higher vulnerabilities of these individuals that are expected to be exacerbated during a global pandemic.15 These systemic disparities for racial/ethnic minority groups need urgent attention during the COVID-19 pandemic. The American Academy of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation has implemented a national crisis management plan that has called for timely and equitable access to multidisciplinary care for patients.16 Significant long-term disability with multisystem involvement has now been seen in a growing population of patients who have survived COVID-19. Although there is a wide spectrum of clinical responses to the novel coronavirus, some have developed more chronic symptoms now referred to as postacute COVID-19 syndrome. This population of survivors continue to suffer for weeks or months with fatigue, postexertional malaise, and cognitive dysfunction,17 along with many other symptoms across multiple organs. In addition to patients with more traditional postintensive care syndrome, there is an even larger number of patients with ongoing symptoms and functional deficits who did not spend any time in the intensive care unit or hospital.17 There is much stigma and misunderstanding for patients with postacute COVID-19. Many of those who suffer describe difficulties with access to care for fear of transmission and did not receive any treatment if they were not hospitalized. Additionally, many physicians do not know how to adequately treat postacute COVID-19 syndrome as it is a new disease state that has little to no research. At this time, most of the research and treatment options are prioritized for patients with acute COVID in the hospital setting. Being that SARS-CoV-2 is a novel virus, there is still much that the medical community does not know. Many patients have taken to social media groups to share stories, compare symptoms, and discuss alternative treatments.18 These survivors with long COVID are a new population of persons with disabilities who physiatrists will have to treat long term. Along with the stigma and issues with access to care after COVID-19, patients with more chronic postacute COVID-19 syndrome may not be able to work or work reduced hours because of residual symptoms.19 Without a job, they can lose health care coverage and may not be able to see clinicians or receive needed therapy. Given a known disproportionate effect on persons from underserved communities who are already underinsured, it will also be more difficult to get rehabilitation services—from pain management to electrodiagnostic studies to therapy—within their current system of care. We must be ready as the PM&R community to serve this vulnerable patient population with the tools we have. Our experience in helping patients with a plan to return to work especially those with deficits in cognition and endurance is crucial to their recovery.20 Physiatrists are leaders in disability management and need to actively direct care for survivors of COVID-19. The coronavirus pandemic is stressing the health care system. Aside from the direct illness caused by COVID-19, and the disparate effect that the virus has had on minoritized communities, the global pandemic has overstretched health care resources in many regions of the country. As health care systems focus on treating those with COVID-19 infection, there are fewer assets to provide care for other chronic and acute conditions. Governors were motivated to use the power of executive orders to limit medical interventions deemed nonessential. Between March 2020 and May 2020, 34 states and the District of Columbia limited the abilities of health systems to provide elective or nonurgent care services.21 Those prohibitions specifically curtailed many of the services provided by physiatrists, particularly ones unrelated to COVID-19. As such, the demand for functional assessments and interventions built steadily during this period of diversion. Physiatrists were challenged to evolve and find new ways to provide care, many transitioning to telemedicine or maintaining in-person appointments, although with significant volume limitations. In the end, we were left with patients requiring services but unable to access them for an indefinite period of time. Unfortunately, given current worsening trends related to community spread of COVID-19, these restrictions may again go into effect and affect physiatrists, and the patients we serve, in many regions of the country. Physiatry is undersized to deliver services to everyone in the United States who needs this care. This remains a tremendous problem for patients recovering from insults to their central nervous system and/or those requiring complex musculoskeletal interventions against the backdrop of COVID-19. The most recent comprehensive survey of physician prevalence by specialty was in 2017.22 That study found that there were 9316 physiatrists practicing in the United States for a population of 325.1 million. By comparison, there were 113,346 family practice physicians, 42,315 emergency medicine physicians, and 13,703 neurologists. Currently, the American Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation notes 13,830 Diplomates, and the U.S. population has increased to 331 million. There continues to be a significant mismatch between the need for PM&R services and what can be provided by the specialty. That shortage will be further exacerbated by the reality that rehab services are not uniformly distributed across the country. In a modeling study of the physiatry workforce, the South region had the lowest numbers of full-time equivalent physiatrists per million people, with the fewest in the state of Mississippi.23 This region of the United States, often referred to as the stroke belt, has a large population of marginalized persons from minority racial/ethnic groups who have more disease burden and disparities of care. Additionally, given that physiatrists are concentrated at tertiary care academic centers, patients currently living beyond the reach of accessible transportation to these centers and thus marginalized in their access to physiatry services will find more barriers to care. Those previously able to access services may also find difficulty attaining care. Proverbially, this rising tide is flooding those in the valley and those on higher ground. The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the need for physiatry services while simultaneously restricting patient access to specialists in the field. In the future, the growth in the physiatry workforce should be concentrated in underserved regions. During the time of the novel coronavirus pandemic, clinicians have rapidly adopted telemedicine in their practices.24 Telemedicine was previously used only intermittently as an alternative to in-person care; however, because of pandemic restrictions this has now become a boon for accessibility and a common means of health care access, including for persons with disabilities.13, 14 Beyond not exposing patients to communicable diseases, there are known benefits to telemedicine including less cost of care, increased patient satisfaction, decreased costs related to transportation and paid personal assistance services, improved communication on medication reconciliation, and an ability to see patients in their own environment, which may uncover more about their social determinants of health. Despite these numerous benefits, there are still many barriers to address regarding persons with disabilities and use of telemedicine.25 Although the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1991 protects the rights of people with disabilities to access electronic information technology, this is not broadly known and thus many health care systems do not account for full disability accommodations in their telehealth offerings. Furthermore, broadband is inaccessible in many rural and low-income areas where many persons with disabilities live. Health disparities may be accentuated when we consider the intersection of disability with race and ethnicity. Already noted are the trends across the country where minority populations had higher risk of COVID-19 infections and death.4 Another publication further described barriers of care via telemedicine for intersectional groups.26 Examples include non-English speakers who do not understand instructions to join an online electronic medical portal. Furthermore, popular applications for telemedicine do not have built in translators. Additionally, minoritized populations may be less likely to live in an area where broadband service allows a suitable telemedicine connection. With these considerations, telemedicine has improved access to health care for those who already have it but concomitantly adds yet further disadvantages to those who have limited access due to technological, regulatory, and infrastructural barriers. Long-term changes to break down these barriers need to be addressed during this new era of telehealth to ensure full participation for persons with disabilities. Leaders must consider the unique needs of the disability community throughout health equity efforts in the COVID response. An estimated 25% of adults in the United States self-report disability, and disability is highly correlated with age as well as socioeconomic disadvantages.27 Demonstrating the intersectionality of disability with race and ethnicity, figures from the CDC indicate that nearly one in four Black Americans as well as one in six Hispanic Americans report disability.28 In this context, universally accessible approaches when planning and implementing the COVID response will increase impact and ensure that leaders are reaching all underserved communities. Furthermore, the change that must be made to reduce disparities for persons who live at the intersection of disability and being from historically, socially, or economically marginalized racial and ethnic groups starts internally. Those of us in the physiatry community must produce and understand data, recognize our unconscious biases, and hold groups responsible for deficiencies in our health care systems. For health care institutions, disability equity must be emphasized in the development and implementation of COVID policies. All essential COVID-related communications (both patient facing and employee facing) should be available in accessible formats (eg, American Sign Language [ASL], large print, accessible to screen reading technology) and in different languages. Additionally, restrictive visitor policies must delineate the difference between a routine visitor versus an essential support person (eg, personal care attendant [PCA]). Given that a patient with a disability always has a right under the law to be accompanied by a designated support person, procedures must be developed to enable exceptions to the visitor policy when warranted.29 Universal mask policies, although necessary to reduce community spread, create additional communication barriers for individuals with disabilities who rely on lip reading or ASL.30 Although some health care systems have procured clear masks to mitigate this issue, these are in short supply in many places across the country and not ubiquitously available. As previously mentioned, the rapid expansion of virtual care has improved access to care for many individuals with mobility disability but exacerbated disparities for others such as those with vision, hearing, communication, or intellectual disability.25 Addressing this gap also requires tailored strategies such as live closed captioning or digital patient navigators. At the community level, COVID-19 has had a profound impact on many people with disabilities who rely on hands-on support to live independently.31 During the initial surges across the United States in 2020 and subsequent surges in 2021, many care partners who themselves come from at risk communities (eg, PCAs, extended family members) did not have adequate access to PPE—a situation that, although somewhat improved, continues to prove challenging.32 Reduced access to routine services for people with disabilities such as primary care and ambulatory specialty visits has further exacerbated health risks above and beyond the risks attributable to COVID in and of itself.33, 34 Related to COVID-19, persistent barriers in access to testing likely disproportionately affect people with mobility and other types of disability and furthermore for minoritized racial/ethnic groups, particularly given that options for public transportation have frequently been curtailed. All of these challenges must be taken into consideration in the planning of municipal response efforts. Regarding future pandemic planning, people with disabilities must be included in the response efforts to ensure that the needs of the community are represented and accounted for. The historic mantra of the disability movement “nothing about us, without us” has recently be revised to “nothing without us.” Simply put, representation matters and people with disabilities must be integral in the development of all health equity strategies during a pandemic. This concept should be inclusive of the acute phase incident command as well as efforts toward recovery and emergence out of crisis. Just as COVID-19 has shed light on the impact of structural racism on the health of racial and ethnic minority communities, it has also highlighted the impact of structural ableism on the long-term health of people with disabilities—for example, the unnecessary institutionalization of people with complex disabilities due to lack of coverage for in-home support. Crises such as a global pandemic allow us to reset our norms and reimagine a more equitable future for all, inclusive of people with disabilities and other intersectional identities. In addition to the strategies outlined here that reflect priorities for both the institutional and municipal response to a pandemic, it is important to highlight the need for better collection of disability data that can be used to identify inequities as well as monitor outcomes of treatment.35 Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, data on race/ethnicity clearly demonstrate that the virus has disproportionately affected the Black community, likely because of the long-term effects of structural racism.36 Although similar trends are affecting the disability community, these cannot be clearly described given that the collection of disability data has not been included in response efforts. Additionally, many people with disabilities have trepidation regarding receiving the COVID-19 vaccine because early trials—although likely inclusive of people with disabilities—did not report whether side effects or outcomes of treatment varied for people with disabilities or underlying chronic conditions. Into the future, all pandemic response efforts must include disability as part of data collection efforts. Given what we have learned regarding the cumulative impact of COVID-19 on the disability community, future pandemic response efforts must take into account the impact of disrupted routine care (eg, ambulatory visits and in-home care partners) and consider innovative strategies for community-based care delivery that accommodates people with complex needs. One example of such a model is the Commonwealth Care Alliance where individuals who are dually eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid are provided enhanced support and home-based care, demonstrating excellent patient satisfaction as well as improved outcomes.37 Assisting patients with navigating of their complex needs in the community avoids unnecessary hospitalizations and should be seen as imperative in the time of a pandemic. The pandemic has had and will continue to have a profound effect on the health care workforce, and the negative impact it has on women physicians and scientists may last throughout their careers. The pandemic has exacerbated preexisting disparities for many women in medicine, including physiatrists.38-40 For example, there were already pay and promotion inequities and during the pandemic many women took pay cuts or had a decrease in clinical revenue owing to budget cuts at work or increased childcare or eldercare responsibilities at home.41 Many  have  a marked increase in women  the U.S. workforce, and this  the health care  An article  by the  of American       the  of  in   many of the issues women in medicine are  For  there is the  of  or    in academic  that are disproportionately  by  Even if women do not  medicine, their  may be negatively affected by  in   and   that will affect future  along the academic   It is  that women with intersectional  (eg, racial/ethnic   women with a  will be disproportionately  For example, women who are racial or ethnic  may be  to do  work  at increasing vaccine  for  communities or to create   patient education  A recent study  that these types of   disproportionately  on the  of   physiatrists who identify with racial or ethnic minority groups may not only have low  but also    There is no way to   the  of physical,  and   on women in  however, the more leaders recognize the issues, the better  they will be to focus on additional layers of support that may reduce the attrition of women   in PM&R     access to  and equitable  of    at  COVID-19 has been a   of profound disparities in health and health care,  racism,   and  that continue to  in   these inequities and  the gap  requires  and   in  the   and after a systemic response to a pandemic.

titulo: Commerce, jobs and politics: the impact of the USA–China trade on USA domestic politics
instituicoes: University of Washington
palavras_openalex: US-China trade | political polarization | manufacturing employment | import penetration | election results | job displacement | regional economic restructuring | labor market disruption | trade policy | human capital policy | place-based policy
resumo: Purpose The purpose of the paper “Commerce, jobs and politics: the impact of the USA–China trade on USA domestic politics” is to examine the impact of Chinese trade with the USA to determine the consequences of the trade on manufacturing employment. The geographic and sectoral impacts of this trade are assessed. The conclusion is that the USA–China trade has affected political polarization in such a way as to affect electoral outcomes. Implications for policy are discussed in the paper. Design/methodology/approach The overall design is a focused case study in terms of its focus on the USA–China trade relations. There is also a statistical component due to the breakdown of the USA in economic commuting zones. Findings The major finding is that Chinese import penetration created substantial political polarization in the USA and that polarization affected electoral outcomes. Chinese import penetration also resulted in a shift of jobs from the eastern heartland to the coasts. Much of the transition was aided by the restructuring of jobs within firms from manufacturing to high-end services. Research limitations/implications Perhaps, the biggest limitation concerns how general and durable the findings are. The authors establish that the first decade after Chinese entry into the World Trade Organization (WTO) (2001) was characterized by economic disruption in the USA labor market. Whether the economic effects will have a longer duration is not known. Practical implications One practical limitation is that it is difficult to know what policy actions to take on the basis of the research: trade policy, human capital (education) policy or place-based policies which aid particular regions. Social implications The social implications in this paper are jobs and employment policy. Originality/value The author thinks this is very original work, though based on the work of several economists. But outside of a few articles, the author does not think much has appeared in political science journals.

titulo: Simulating Work-Family Conflict Impact on Performance among Language Teachers: System Dynamics Modelling
instituicoes: Alzahra University | Islamic Azad University, Science and Research Branch | Islamic Azad University, Tehran
palavras_openalex: work-family conflict | teacher performance | English teachers | burnout | job pressure | job satisfaction | system dynamics modeling | sensitivity analysis | teacher well-being
resumo: The subject of education has always been considered throughout history, and in the heart of education, a teacher has always been recognized as one of the most determinant and influential members. Many researchers have tried to pay attention to teachers and identify their personal and professional needs. This disquisition was designed and carried out to model the impact of job-family conflict factors on teachers’ performance, specifically in today’s global context where the role and responsibility of teachers is recognized as being more prominent than ever before. According to Young (2019), this conflict affects teachers’ performance and their satisfaction with the profession. The conflict between the job demands and requirements and individual’s roles in the family account for such polarization. The aim of our study was consequently to specify factors causing such conflict among 73 English teachers, to recognize their relationships, and to determine how they affected English teachers’ performance using system dynamics modelling and simulation technique. The sensitivity analysis performed in this study revealed that over a sixty-eight-month period, while teachers’ job burnout and job pressure increased exponentially, their job satisfaction followed an overshoot-and-collapse manner of behaviour. Moreover, during this period, their job performance decreased in a goal-seeking manner.

resumo: Using data from ENIGH 2000-2014, this paper aims, first, to describe what is happening in the Mexican labor market with regard to the relative demand and supply of workers defined by their occupation, when occupations are classified into non-routine and routine and, within these, into cognitive and manual, based on a thorough analysis of tasks. Second, this paper tries to understand how wages and formality are related to task-biased technological change (TBTC) in Mexico. The analysis differentiates the male and female labor markets.

instituicoes: Donald & Barbara Zucker School of Medicine at Hofstra/Northwell | Hofstra University
palavras_openalex: unexplained dyspnea | long COVID | empagliflozin | sildenafil | heart failure with preserved ejection fraction | pulmonary arterial hypertension | cardiopulmonary exercise testing | autonomic dysfunction | exercise intolerance | pharmacotherapy | SGLT2 inhibitors | phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors | differential diagnosis
resumo: A primary complaint of chronic dyspnea, often associated with exercise intolerance, is commonly attributed to a cardiac or respiratory system condition. Other frequent explanations include obesity, sleep apnea, malignancy, and anemia. Deconditioning, metabolic disorders, oxidative/mitochondrial myopathy, and neuromuscular pathology complete the differential diagnosis in patients reporting continuous or intermittent breathlessness lasting more than 1 month.1 The etiology is discoverable after a reasonable search conducted by primary care physicians in approximately 85% of the patients evaluated for chronic dyspnea/exercise intolerance. The remaining 15% of the patients are often referred to cardiologists or pulmonologists and undergo a variety of imaging and functional tests. These patients have symptoms out of proportion with the results of prior testing and lack of response to standard treatment for pre-existent or newly diagnosed conditions such as asthma or heart failure. The investigations with the highest diagnostic yield include the invasive cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET), which allows a breath-to-breath assessment of cardiac function; ventilation and pulmonary gas exchange, coupled with direct measurement of pulmonary and radial artery pressure; and blood gas parameters at rest and during exercise.1 In a large cohort of patients with unexplained dyspnea (n = 530) evaluated at the Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston with invasive CPET and careful review of previous testing, the most common causes were oxidative myopathy (24.5%), dysautonomia or preload failure (21.1%), heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) apparent only with exercise (17.7%), and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) present during exercise (16.6%).1 Evidence-based effective pharmacological interventions exist only for HFpEF2 and PAH.3 PAH is often present in HFpEF as a passive consequence of increased left atrial and pulmonary capillary pressures and impaired lung diffusing capacity.4 Unexplained dyspnea and exertional intolerance are common in patients with post–coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) fatigue syndrome and contribute, together with persistent fatigue, “brain fog,” memory loss, executive function deficits, and depressive psychopathology, to a significant decrease in quality of life and to occupational disability.5–7 A recent systematic review which assessed 9 studies and a total of 1816 survivors of hospital admission for acute COVID-19 infection identified fatigue in 52% and dyspnea in 37% of the patients examined 3 weeks–3 months after hospital discharge.8 Across the studies, the prevalence of dyspnea was not uniformly greater among patients who had required admission to an intensive care unit but was around 50% in persons with a pre–COVID-19 history of asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. A careful study of a small sample of patients with unexplained dyspnea post–COVID-19 who underwent CPET 9 months after the acute illness found excessive ventilatory response to exercise and circulatory impairment in most of the cases.9 Another small sample study compared unexplained dyspnea cases with versus without post–COVID-19 syndrome matched by age, sex, and subjective severity of breathlessness and found no significant CPET differences between groups.10 A reasonable approach to the diagnosis of unexplained dyspnea after a thorough internal medicine and pulmonary evaluation should focus on treatable condition, that is, HFpEF and PAH. Therefore, the diagnostic workup must include at last CPET to confirm the functional impairment and a rest/exercise echocardiogram11 to determine the presence of HFpEF and PAH. Measuring the plasma level of the N-terminal proB–type natriuretic peptide will provide additional support for the diagnosis of HFpEF.11 Clinical examination may be unrevealing because the pulmonary congestion in HFpEF is often subclinical.12 Empagliflozin, a sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT-2), marketed as an antidiabetic drug, which enhances renal glucose excretion, has been recently shown to improve the outcome of HFpEF in persons with and without diabetes.2 The study compared 2997 patients treated with 10 mg once daily off empagliflozin with 2991 patients receiving placebo. The participants had class II–IV heart failure with ejection fraction >40%. The empagliflozin group had a significantly lower rate of hospitalizations for heart failure over a median of 26 months of treatment (6.9 vs. 8.7 events/100 patient-years). By contrast, the effectiveness of other drugs tried for HFpEF, such as candesartan, spironolactone, and sacubitril–valsartan, had only marginal significance when compared with placebo.2 In pairwise comparisons, SGLT-2 inhibitors were shown to be superior to other antidiabetic drug classes, such as glucagon-like peptide-1 agonists or dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors and metformin, in improving left ventricular dysfunction.13 For the treatment of post–COVID-19 symptoms, it is important to note that emerging evidence indicates that SGLT-2 inhibitors have anti-inflammatory14 effects including M2 macrophage polarization and decreased proinflammatory cytokines.15 Empagliflozin is lipid soluble and may reach a serum/brain ratio of up to 0.5 and have been shown to inhibit acetylcholinesterase, reduce the oxidative stress, and modulate favorably neurotransmission and plasticity of neurons,15 with a demonstrable neuroprotective effect.16 Sildenafil blocks phosphodiesterase 5 and promotes vasodilation in the lungs. The drug has been used by patients with PAH for the past 2 decades. A systematic review of trials involving 545 patients indicated that a 12-week course improved exercise tolerance on the 6-minute walk distance time and health-related quality of life.3 Long-term treatment of up to 3 years was generally well tolerated and the patients maintained the progress regarding functional status.17 The drug crosses the blood–brain barrier, and animal experimental models have provided evidence of increased cerebral blood flow and of alleviate ischemia-induced neuroinflammation.18 The pleiotropic features of empagliflozin and sildenafil should encourage clinical trials of these drugs in post–COVID-19 patients with persistent dyspnea/exercise intolerance.

resumo: Two decades ago, I received my baptism of fire in public archaeology as a neophyte archaeologist in the Greek Archaeological Service. While this term was not used at the time to describe any aspect of archaeological work in Greece, working in the Service frequently entails immersion in classic dilemmas of public archaeology: for instance, how to parse one's enthusiasm about the archaeological process—excavation, analysis, and interpretation of the material remains of the past—to the public; how to marry an arguably esoteric, dry discipline, with inquiry pertaining to contemporary issues in society and genuinely interesting to lay audiences; how to balance the need to protect, preserve, and curate the non-renewable resource of the past, with the complex needs, desires and visions of various stakeholders in the community.Nevertheless, the notion of public archaeology remains somewhat alien to archaeology in Greece. This is hardly surprising given that: (a) most archaeological work (putting aside projects run by domestic and foreign academic institutions) is in the form of rescue excavations, which are oriented primarily towards preservation as part of the government's heritage management programs; and (b) archaeology is seen as inherently linked to both national education and national identity. Both these characteristics seemingly eliminate the need to argue for the relevance of archaeology in present-day communities, let alone consider multiple or ignored stakeholders within a given community, and to identify the unique purpose, value and flavor of the qualifier ‘public’ in archaeology.Since the advent of public archaeology in the 1970s in Anglo-American scholarship, thinking on this topic has evolved significantly. As discussed in more detail below, public archaeologies vary considerably in approach and objectives. A common direction is that of public education as effective heritage management and protection. Other approaches include public relations or fundraiser efforts in support of continuing projects, educating the public on the methods, benefits and uses of archaeology, and community service learning. Recent paradigms place emphasis on ‘democratizing’ the archaeological process by involving the public in all stages of knowledge production (e.g., constructivist, experiential, hands-on, inclusive, informationally open, crowdsourced archaeologies). The very meaning of ‘publics’ and ‘communities’ to be served by archaeology, the role of archaeology in shaping community identities, and the inherently political nature (intentional or not) of archaeological work in society have also been intensely scrutinized as part of the public-archaeology debate.Despite extensive writing and debate along these lines in the broader realms of archaeological thought, especially from the late 1990s onward, community-friendly or ‘engaged’ archaeologies of the ancient Mediterranean have been comparatively rare, little publicized, or very recent. A colloquium entitled “Public Archaeologies of the Ancient Mediterranean” (116th Annual Meeting of the Archaeological Institute of America, New Orleans, 8-11 January 2015), organized by the author, sought to take the pulse of public-archaeology thinking in the Mediterranean, with the geographic determination broadly applied (community-oriented activities undertaken in contemporary Mediterranean countries or those closely associated with the Mediterranean world historically, or work related to the ancient Mediterranean without necessarily having taken place in that region). While the colloquium did not aim at comprehensive geographic ‘coverage’ and a Greek predisposition was necessitated by the specific forum where the colloquium was held, an effort was made to include contributions representing a variety of regional perspectives as much as possible. The stated goals of this colloquium, and the resulting volume, are: (a) exploring the emerging roles of archaeologists in the Mediterranean as educators, mediators, and facilitators in the interpretation of the past; (b) gauging the local resonances (as opposed to a priori-determined benefits) and nuances of archaeological work in the daily lives of inhabitants; and (c) showcasing projects that engage a variety of stakeholders (including disenfranchised ‘others’) through excavations, site-based initiatives, community-embedded efforts, media, virtual, online projects, and so forth.A vibrant interest in the topic of public archaeology as a significant component of the discipline manifests itself in an enormous number of publications spanning five decades but culminating from 2000 onward, with titles such as Public Archaeology (McGimsey 1972), Community Archaeology (Liddle 1985), The Presented Past (Stone and Molyneaux 1994), Presenting Archaeology to the Public (Jameson 1997), Communicating Archaeology (Beavis and Hunt 1999), Public Archaeology (Merriman 2004c), Places in Mind (Shackel and Chambers 2004), Past Meets Present (Jameson Jr. and Baugher 2007a), Heritage, Communities and Archaeology (Smith and Waterton 2009), New Perspectives in Global Public Archaeology (Okamura and Matsuda 2011), The Oxford Handbook of Public Archaeology (Skeates, McDavid, and Carman 2012), Community Archaeology (Moshenska and Dhanjal 2012), Archaeology, the Public, and the Recent Past (Dalglish 2013); most recently, Archaeology, Heritage, and Civic Engagement (Little and Shackel 2014), Key Concepts in Public Archaeology (Moshenska 2017b, an ongoing ‘live’ book), and Public Archaeology (Gursu forthcoming). A number of dedicated journals have been established in the same timeframe, for instance Public Archaeology (2000–), AP: Online Journal in Public Archaeology (2010–), Journal of Community Archaeology & Heritage (2014–), Archaeostorie: Journal of Public Archaeology (2017–). Special issues of World Archaeology have appeared on the themes of community and public archaeology (October 2002, May 2015), in addition to an editorial in the European Journal of Archaeology (Schadla-Hall 1999). In tandem, there is growing interest in applications of the ethnographic method in archaeological work as it relates to the public (Edgeworth 2003, 2006; Colwell-Chanthaphonh and Ferguson 2008; Castañeda and Matthews 2008; Mortensen and Hollowell 2009). Likewise, taking into account the experiences of local communities (Stroulia and Buck Sutton 2010), harnessing innovative/digital technologies for public engagement (Tsipopoulou 2008; Bonacchi 2012), debating the broader relevance of archaeology to society (Holtorf 2007; Rockman 2011), and grappling with alternative viewpoints about the past (Simandiraki-Grimshaw and Stefanou 2012; Cherry and Rojas 2015) are all themes explored within this framework.If blooming interest in public and community archaeology is evident, the terms ‘public’ and ‘community’ are not transparent or unchallenged. To begin with, the term ‘community’—usually taken to mean a contemporary group of people local to an archaeological site or their descendants—is inherent in the discipline, since archaeology tends to take place at locales meaningful to present-day inhabitants (Marshall 2002: 211). However, it can be misleading in that it assumes the existence of monolithic, static, unchanging communities associated with a place. Not only can communities change over time (Little 2012: 403), but the very assumption that present-day stakeholders constitute a single community disregards the overlapping nature of group membership and identities (Marshall 2002: 216; Tully 2007: 158–59; Carman 2016: 143), to the point that a ‘community’ can be an archaeological construct of little resonance with the people involved (Pyburn 2011: 29, 31). It is crucial, therefore, to understand the nature of ‘community’ and the nuanced and complex dynamics of local groups as they relate to a place of archaeological interest before the latter can be ‘reached’ and ‘engaged.’While the term ‘public’ in this context is less problematic and usually refers to non-professional groups of people who are interested in or interact with archaeological sites, public archaeology carries different meanings (see Holtorf 2007; Moshenska 2017a, fig. 1.1, for detailed discussion). Some of these meanings include: a.Archaeology for the public, either state or CRM work undertaken for the public good: ‘the good’ defined as protecting and recording significant aspects of the past, producing information that matters beyond academia (Nassaney 2012: 415–16; see Little and Shackel 2014), and raising awareness about/promoting engagement with issues affecting sites, for instance urban development, climate change, or maritime heritage (Scott-Ireton 2013; Dawson et al. 2017). Usually such archaeologies are funded by the public in some way and are therefore accountable to it, not just in terms of compliance with legal requirements, but also putting funds to good use with an eye to public interest (Merriman 2004a: 2). Enrichment of K–12 school education and curricula, promoting archaeological literacy for preservation purposes, helping non-professional audiences understand the methods and usefulness of the discipline from an outside perspective (techniques, skills, concepts, etc.), delivering content as ‘outreach’ (lectures, presentations, museum exhibits, etc.) also can be seen to serve this general purpose (Stone 1994: 15, 20; Franklin and Moe 2012; Little 2012: 395).b.Archaeology with the public, which is usually taken to include community archaeology, emphasizing hands-on involvement of the public and collaborations with various stakeholders in the communities at hand (Moshenska and Dhanjal 2012; Little 2012: 395). The community service learning (CSL, Baugher 2007) or ‘citizenship’ model is another common variant of community archaeology, espousing the embeddedness of formal learning in the real world. The key premise of CSL is that students training to become heritage professionals learn best by exploring problems in genuine settings and cultivate a mindset of sustainable, ongoing civic participation, while providing service to community stakeholders and meeting the needs of the latter (Nassaney 2012: 417–18). In a similar but decidedly more activist direction, ‘engaged archaeologies’ seek to contribute actively to society's most key and pressing questions: for example, human rights, social justice, gender, race, class inequities, and environmental issues, rather than just conservation, tourism, and land management (Little 2011, 2012: 283, 285). According to this line of thinking, archaeologists are neither teachers of facts nor neutral mediators, but carry the ethical responsibility to engage public stakeholders in dialog with archaeology and with each other on the topics that really matter to them (Scham 2010; Hodder 2013: 26–27).c.Archaeology by the public represents a spectrum of practices connected with the previously discussed ones, and looking beyond educating or including the public in professional activities. Such archaeologies extend the notion of public engagement with the discipline and archaeological engagement with communities by grassrooting/‘democratizing’ every step of archaeological inquiry and research (Holtorf 2007: 107; Atalay 2012), including fundraising and publication. Such ‘archaeologies from below’ are meant to be open, community-driven, unafraid of the popular and ‘unauthoritative,’ non-exclusive, and non-hierarchical (Faulkner 2000; Moshenska 2017a, fig. 1.1). They are in full acknowledgment of and relinquishing power structures, disciplinary interests and hierarchies, and their effect on archaeological discourse. The main criticism of archaeology for the public revolves around the threefold question of how professional archaeologists understand their relationship with the public, how they understand the public's abilities to understand the past, and their own self-perception as producers, keepers, and disseminators of knowledge. A top-down, positivistic, and didactic archaeology tells people what they need to see, what to know, and what to think about the past, on the assumption that knowledge is objective, final, and inscrutable to the uninitiated, and that the public is knowledge-deficient, can only consume, and cannot handle too much (cf. Merriman 2004a: 5; 2004b: 87). Although it would be fair to say that not all work within this tradition reflects these attitudes, one-size-fits-all representations of the past can be static, illustration-heavy, overly dramatized, and essentialistic. resumo: consequences of globalization: upgrading or polarization?In both the academic and political debate on globalization, inequality is undoubtedly the most disputed theme (cf.Dicken, 2003; Held & McGrew, 2000).This is also true in the field of urban studies, especially in the debate on global cities, where much attention has been paid to the local social effects of globalization.Two opposing views have been brought forward.One states that the globalization of urban economies results in increasing local inequality and even social polarization (cf.Sassen, 1991(cf.Sassen, , 2001;; Friedmann & Wolff, 1982; Friedmann, 1986).The other states that globalization of urban economies leads to an upgrading of metropolitan labor-markets (cf.Hamnett, 1994; 1996;Waldinger, 1996).The debate on this issue has been going on for some time now and is still not brought to a conclusion.Empirical data has been presented that, allegedly, corroborates either one of both theoretical positions.This paper is based on the argument that the main reason for this empirical deadlock is the result of interrelated theoretical and operational ambiguities.The first ambiguity concerns the role of international competition.In the economic literature on globalization, in which countries and not cities are the units of analysis, the dominant argument is that globalization leads to upgrading labor-markets in the advanced economies (Dicken, 2003).The main line of reasoning here is that in order to maintain their competitive edge, advanced economies have to cut on labor costs by automation or else increase the quality of their products.Either way, globalization -in the sense of increasing international economic exposure -leads to upgrading national labor-markets.This is in line with what some authors have argued as to how urban labor-markets are developing (Hamnett, 1994; 1996;Waldinger, 1996).But global cities might be an exception here because one of the key characteristics of global cities is that global cities do not compete so much with other cities but, rather, form a limited set of strategically cooperating cities (Sassen, 1991; 2001).So, at least theoretically, polarization in global cities is not necessarily incompatible with the general argument of increasing international competition leading to upgrading labor-markets.Before assessing social inequality, one should therefore analyze the international exposure of urban economies.The second ambiguity concerns the conceptualization of the global character of an urban economy.In many cases -prominently so in the work of Sassen (1991Sassen ( , 2001) ) globalization is operationally conceived of as, or at least directly related to 'economic restructuring': the increasing employment in services and the decreasing employment in manufacturing industries.For global cities, economic restructuring to a large degree may

resumo: Curriculum Management and Governance Structure ♦ The Executive Curriculum Committee is the standing committee of the Emory University School of Medicine (EUSOM) responsible for oversight, content, and delivery of the curriculum (Figure 1).FIGURE 1:: Curriculum Management Organization The committee is traditionally chaired by a senior faculty member. Membership comprises faculty members selected by the Dean based on their knowledge of and interest in undergraduate medical education. The ECC has four subcommittees: Competency and Assessment, Clerkships, Electives, and Foundations. ♦ The Competencies and Assessment Subcommittee: This subcommittee manages the curriculum's focus on the nine competencies for undergraduate medical education adopted by the EUSOM. Their work results in recommendations that link the methods of competency assessment with the outcomes needed to evaluate our progress in attaining our curriculum objectives. Membership is determined by the Executive Associate Dean and chair of the ECC and may include ECC and non-ECC faculty members. ♦ Clerkship Directors: The directors of the required clerkships, the ECC chairman, and the Executive Associate Dean for Medical Education and Student Affairs are members of this Subcommittee. The chair of the subcommittee (currently the Director of the Application Phase Internal Medicine Clerkship) is also an ECC member. This committee serves to facilitate additional communication between the clerkships and the ECC. Issues discussed are wide ranging and include clerkship content (identifying areas of duplication), methods of teaching, commonalities of student evaluation, strategies for responding to student issues, and clerkship-specific practices that can serve as best practices across specialties. ♦ Clinical Electives Subcommittee: This subcommittee monitors and approves clinical electives offered to Emory and non-Emory medical students. Monitoring involves review of the electives' learning objectives, methods of teaching, faculty supervision, clinical experience, methods used to assess students and student assessment of the elective. Membership is determined by the Executive Associate Dean for Medical Education and Student Affairs and chair of the ECC and may include ECC and non-ECC members. The current subcommittee members include the Associate Dean for Clinical Education. ♦ Foundations Subcommittee: The directors of the Foundations Phase of the curriculum, select block directors, the ECC chair, and the Executive Associate Dean for Medical Education and Student Affairs are members of this subcommittee. This committee reviews the content, methods of teaching, and methods of evaluation related to the Foundations Phase of the curriculum. Membership is determined by the Executive Associate Dean and the ECC chair. Office of Education ♦ The Office of Medical Education and Student Affairs (OMESA) staff are responsible for the day-to-day operations of the undergraduate medical education program. ♦ OMESA's efforts focus on three principal areas: medical education (which includes support for overall curriculum management), support for interdepartmental courses, and those areas that traditionally fall into student affairs. ♦ OMESA staff support the following specific medical-education-related activities: the ECC, the electronic evaluation system, the Clinical Skills Center, NBME subject examinations, administration of the School of Medicine teaching spaces, and coordination of the information technology and media needs of medical education (in conjunction with the School of Medicine's Information Technology Services). ♦ The new curriculum requires the integration of the activities that were formerly the responsibility of many individual departments. This has resulted in an expansion of the staff within OMESA to provide the resources necessary to effectively support these responsibilities. ♦ OMESA has a staff of 16 (two with education-related master's degrees) for its medical education and student affairs missions. ♦ The Director of OMESA reports to the Executive Associate Dean of Medical Education and Student Affairs. ♦ The Office of Admissions, with four staff members, also reports to the EAD for Medical Education and Student Affairs through the Associate Dean for Admissions. ♦ One MD/PhD with a doctoral degree in medical education serves as 0.5 FTE advisor and research catalyst in curriculum-related endeavors. Financial Management of Educational Programs ♦ The current economic downturn occurred in the midst of a complete curriculum change at Emory. ♦ The implementation of the curriculum has continued with full funding. Faculty and staff salaries have remained level; however, funds dedicated to nonessential spending such as student and faculty travel and food associated with orientation and training activities have been reduced. Valuing Teaching ♦ Although Emory does not have an academy or institute for educators, our new curriculum relies heavily on a system of Societies. Each student is assigned to one of four societies. Within each society are four faculty advisors, each assigned eight or nine students for a given class. These faculty advisors, totaling 32, receive support such that 30% of their time is devoted to medical education. ♦ The society advisor roles include small-group teaching, academic counseling, and career counseling. ♦ The society advisors supervise regular meetings of eight to nine medical students throughout the four-year curriculum. ♦ The advisors are given weekly faculty development sessions regarding curricular content, teaching skills, and medical education. ♦ Two of the society mentors have attended Careers in Medicine workshops and lead faculty development in career counseling for the other society advisors. ♦ Teaching is a valued mission within EUSOM. ♦ All faculty members regardless of track are expected to participate in teaching, and promotion guidelines state that accomplishments as a teacher are a requirement for promotion. ♦ To assist in evaluating accomplishments for promotion, a required teaching portfolio was instituted to track qualitative and quantitative assessments. ♦ Criteria for the assessment of teaching are included in the faculty policies and each faculty promotion package is assessed for teaching accomplishments as part of the appointment and promotion process. Curriculum Renewal Process ♦ After completion of the Strategic Plan for Teaching and Education in 2003, the deans in OMESA, under the leadership of the previous Executive Associate Dean for Medical Education and Student Affairs, held several formal discussions regarding the need for a major curriculum revision. ♦ Significant changes in biomedical knowledge, the social and financial environment of health care, health care delivery, population demographics, and information technology, coupled with globalization and new methods of teaching, suggested the need for an unprecedented overhaul of the curriculum. ♦ These discussions resulted in the new curriculum planning. ♦ In the summer of 2004, the previous Executive Associate Dean planned a weekend retreat, inviting leaders from the medical school, Emory Healthcare, and Emory University to consider new curricular options for the school of medicine. ♦ Results of a pre-retreat survey once more indicated a commitment to moving forward. Survey responders responded emphatically that we should embark on a new curricular plan. ♦ The results of the survey compelled the planners to revise the retreat agenda, converting from contemplation of curriculum change to planning for change. ♦ During the weekend retreat, the attendees composed the characteristics desired of our graduates. ♦ We aspired to graduate physicians who would be passionate about medicine and making a difference in the lives of patients and society committed to the highest tenets of professional behavior highly competent in foundational medical knowledge and skill curious and creative thinkers lifelong learners committed to understanding the sociological, psychological, and economic issues affecting patient, family, and community health imbued with the desire and skills necessary to become leaders in their clinics, hospitals, and communities ♦ Subsequently, the retreat committee proposed the attributes of a curriculum that would be aligned with the desired characteristics of our graduates. The curriculum should be competency based increase student and faculty interaction integrate basic and clinical science, creating a curriculum of medical science provide an early introduction to clinical medicine increase education in the ambulatory setting provide flexibility include an extended experience in intellectual discovery or scholarship reduce lecture time and decrease reliance on rote memorization include methods of assessment that would effectively determine student achievement of our desired competencies ♦ At the completion of the retreat, an outline of the new curriculum emerged. ♦ There would be four phases: (1) Foundations (the underlying knowledge and skills required to assume the role of patient caregiver); (2) Applications (application of the newly acquired knowledge and skills to the care of patients); (3) Discovery (time spent with a mentor addressing an issue of importance and resulting in new knowledge); and (4) Translation (the transition of the student from primarily a learner to practitioner/learner). ♦ Empowered by the results of the faculty interviews and the retreat, the Dean and Executive Associate Dean for Medical Education and Student Affairs returned committed to moving forward to create a new curriculum. ♦ An organizational structure was formulated, led by a Steering Committee with a small Executive Committee. ♦ Eight subcommittees were formed: Foundations, Applications, Discovery, Translation, Advising/Mentorship, Institutional Relationships, Simulation/Information Technology, and Competencies/Assessment. ♦ Subcommittee Reports were submitted and approved by the steering committee and an overall report was received and ultimately approved by the Dean. ♦ In 2005, implementation committees were formed for the Foundations Phase of the curriculum and the Becoming a Doctor curricular “thread.” ♦ A Competencies and Assessment subcommittee was added to the Executive Curriculum Committee. ♦ In subsequent years, implementation committees have been formed for Applications/Translation and Discovery. The new curriculum began for the class entering in 2007 and has now enrolled the first members of that class in the five-month Discovery Phase. Learning Outcomes/Competencies Communicating effectively: Well-developed communication skills are critical to the successful achievement of every other competency. The competent graduate demonstrates interpersonal and communication skills that result in effective information exchange with patients, their families, professional colleagues, and team members. At the end of medical school, students should be able to use listening and observational skills effectively in doctor–patient interactions, communication with families, and interactions with professional associates be sensitive to the differences in background or culture (in self and others) that may influence or interfere with effective listening and communication use language effectively in doctor–patient interactions, communication with families, and interactions with professional associates use nonverbal communication skills effectively in doctor–patient interactions, communication with families, and interactions with professional associates use written language effectively for health-care-related activities Personal awareness, growth, and care: The competent graduate approaches the practice of medicine with awareness of his/her limits, biases, strengths, weaknesses, and personal vulnerabilities. He or she has assessed and understands the need to reassess personal values and priorities to balance personal and professional commitments. He or she is able to seek help and advice when needed and develops appropriate personal coping strategies. The competent graduate is able to accept constructive criticism and turn it into a growth experience. At the end of medical school, students should be able to identify personal, emotional, or health-related problems that might affect his or her well-being or ability to fulfill professional responsibilities recognize personal values and beliefs that may influence his or her practice of medicine cope adaptively with difficult emotions and stresses likely to occur during medical training and practice effectively deal with conflicts between self-interest and patient care know when and how to seek resources to improve one's own life Application of medical knowledge: The competent graduate demonstrates knowledge of health problems and their prevention based on current scientific understanding. At the end of medical school, students should be able to know and apply the following to the care of patients: normal human structure and function the life cycle the principles of human behavior the role of belief and culture in health and disease the genetic, biochemical, epidemiological, and pathophysiologic mechanisms of disease and their effect on structure and function the principles of therapeutic interventions the many contexts of medicine (social, economic, political, legal) predictive and preventive medicine public health apply knowledge of basic and clinical science to the care of individual patients and populations at large Critical analysis and contribution: The competent graduate is intellectually curious. The graduate has and is able to apply critical analysis and problem-solving skills to individual patient care; his or her own medical practice; patient and population care beyond his or her own practice; and to concerns of the medical community related to economics, politics, government, policy, religion, culture, and society. Furthermore, the graduate is able to apply these critical analysis and problem-solving skills to other areas of medical inquiry to contribute to the body of knowledge in the basic and clinical sciences, public health, community health, and medical education. At the completion of medical school students should demonstrate a commitment to and be able to describe the extent and severity of a medical/health care problem predict the sequelae of alternative courses of problem-solving strategies implement a problem-solving course of action optimize patient outcomes through the analysis of personal practices in the provision of medical care to individuals and groups of patients differentiate between research conducted using qualitative and quantitative evidence apply evidence from basic clinical research, population-based research, and statistical methods to the practice of medicine participate in the design, implementation, and dissemination of a study or intervention Lifelong learning: The competent graduate is aware of the limits of his or her personal knowledge and experience and is intellectually honest and curious. He or she continuously reviews their own knowledge and skill level, practices in the context of current medical knowledge, sets clear learning goals, pursues them, and applies the knowledge gained into his or her practice. At the end of medical school, students should be able to locate, appraise, and assimilate evidence from scientific studies evaluate changes in the academic or professional environment and develop adaptive strategies to meet these changes identify personally effective methods of learning to apply these methods to achieve their ongoing plan for lifelong learning develop a personal plan for ongoing maintenance of interest in general education and science identify, gather, analyze, and integrate information to support her or his own education and patient care practices. This includes the ability to use information technology to facilitate these tasks. Patient-centered care: The competent graduate follows the altruistic tradition of medicine, placing the welfare of their patients and society above self-interest. He or she views medicine as a socially responsible profession and patient care as a holistic endeavor, encompassing an awareness of individual illness in the context of the patient's social circumstances. At the end of medical school, students should be able to understand the critical importance of sensitivity and responsiveness to diversity understand how one's own background and circumstances may influence or interfere with one's ability to be sensitive to, responsive to, and respectful of differences in our patients link patients to needed community resources advocate for the health care needs of patients and communities Clinical practice: The competent graduate must demonstrate data gathering and procedural and clinical reasoning skills. resumo: This study aims to explore the future labour market, which faces significant changes, using Q methodology. The Ken-Q Analysis program was used to analyse the result. The results found that elderly workers' perceptions about the future labour market can be divided into four categories: 'positive future acceptance', 'pessimistic human-machine collaboration', 'pessimistic job polarisation', and 'ultra-pessimistic frustrated job seeker'. Based on the study results, the study seeks to suggest directions for Korea's employment policies to brace for the future labour market and suggest implications for international countries to develop for new employment policy.
