titulo: Educational inequalities
instituicoes: Institute for Fiscal Studies
palavras_openalex: educational inequality | social class | parental income | free school meals | GCSE attainment | educational attainment gap | educational reform | educational services | earnings | cognitive development | educational disadvantage | England education system | educational standards
resumo: There is a strong and persistent correlation between children’s educational outcomes and the social and economic circumstances of their parents. Children start school with very unequal levels of cognitive development, closely associated with their parents’ social class and income, and those inequalities persist through the school and post-school education systems. Christine Farquharson, Imran Tahir and Sandra McNally map the scale of inequality, show how inequality in performance develops as people move through the education system, relate these outcomes to the structure of educational provision in England and show how much educational attainment matters for earnings later in life. They show how there has been virtually no change in the ‘disadvantage gap’ in GCSE attainment over the past 20 years. Whilst GCSE attainment has been increasing over time, 16-year-olds who are eligible for free school meals are still ~27 percentage points less likely to earn good GCSEs than their less disadvantaged peers. Children from disadvantaged backgrounds also make slower progress through secondary school: in the 2019 GCSE cohort, just 40% of disadvantaged children who achieved the expected level at age 11 went on to earn good GCSEs in English and maths, compared with 60% of their non-disadvantaged peers. Whilst the fraction of poor pupils meeting minimum expected benchmarks has increased over time, gaps between poor and the rest are especially wide when looking at more rigorous benchmarks for attainment. Pupils who were not eligible for free school meals are around three times as likely as their more disadvantaged peers to achieve above the expected level at age 11 and at GCSE. They were also three times more likely to attend one of the most selective higher education institutions. In his commentary, Richard Breen takes up the issue of the persistence of these inequalities and the difficulties inherent in closing them, even in the context of efforts, or at least expressed concern, over many years. One of the issues is simply that better-off parents will respond to initiatives by trying to ensure that their offspring remain at the top of the pile. To quote Breen: ‘As Goldthorpe (2016, p. 105) has pointed out, advantaged parents, “will not […] simply be passive in relation to the expansion or reform of the educational system”; they will use their resources to maximize the benefits and minimize the perceived harm to their children from educational reforms. It is only in this light that it is possible to understand the persistent failure of educational reform to reduce class inequalities in attainment and, perhaps, to gain some insight into how best to proceed.’ One consequence is that it may be easier to raise absolute standards than to close gaps. This is not just a question of differences between the poorest and the rest. Performance rises every step of the way up the household income ladder. Whilst ~40% of young people who just miss out on free school meals achieve good GCSEs, that rises to 70% of 16-year-olds in the richest third of families. Children in the 10% richest families are more than twice as likely as those in the seventh decile to earn at least one A or A* grade at GCSE. And whilst 71% of private school students had earned a degree by age 26, just 17% of those from the poorest fifth of families had reached that milestone. More than half of the latter group had not progressed beyond GCSE level. The role of private schools is the focus of the commentary by Francis Green. Just >6% of all English school pupils attend private schools, but he calculates that ~15% of the resources devoted to schooling flows to that group. Work by Luke Sibieta at the Institute for Fiscal Studies has shown that the gap in spending per pupil between private and state schools has doubled in the period since 2010. Green goes on to show how this relatively small group of privately educated pupils are far more likely than others to enter the most prestigious universities and most powerful jobs, noting that ‘some 39% of the cabinet, 34% of the chairs of companies listed in the FTSE index and 44% of media columnists are privately educated’. The dominance of the privately educated at the top of politics, the judiciary and the civil service is even more marked. The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly worsened overall outcomes as well as widening inequalities. The share of pupils leaving primary school who meet literacy and numeracy benchmarks fell from 65% in 2018–19 to 59% in 2021–22. (The government’s levelling-up agenda aims to see this reach 90% by 2030.) Children from more disadvantaged backgrounds were much worse affected. Disadvantaged children had less access to resources to learn at home. They were less likely to receive resources such as online classes during the first lockdown, and more likely to be absent more frequently and for longer than their better-off peers. The long-term consequences of this are likely to be big and worrying. Educational inequalities don’t just exist across the income distribution. Girls do consistently much better than boys, being ~10 percentage points more likely than boys to reach attainment benchmarks at various stages of the education system. There are big differences between different ethnic minorities, with most outperforming the White majority on most measures, and some such as students of Indian and Chinese origin doing far better than others (Both the gender and ethnic differences are, however, excellent examples of how educational attainment doesn’t necessarily affect later outcomes in the same way for everyone, as covered in the articles by Andrew et al. and Mirza and Warwick). There is also substantial geographical variation, with educational attainment in London outstripping that in the rest of England. All local authorities in London perform above the national average in the share of 11-year-olds meeting expectations in reading, writing and maths, whilst the disadvantage gap in GCSE performance in Inner London is less than half as wide as that in the rest of the country. All that said, a 16-year-old’s family income is more than four times as strong a predictor of GCSE attainment as their local authority of residence. As Diane Reay points out in her commentary, it is also important to focus not just on inequalities in attainment, but also on inequalities in well-being, which themselves contribute to inequalities in attainment. She argues that the current system leads disadvantaged children to feel like failures, and to feel they have been failed by the system, from an early age, and hence to disengage. Farquharson et al. are keen to point out that inequalities in outcomes that we see are not necessarily inequalities created by the school system. They relate very closely to inequalities that pre-date school, and reflect differences in household economic circumstances and parental behaviours. The unequally negative effects of school closures during the pandemic provide ample evidence of that. Educational inequalities, or the performance of those with the lowest attainment, are not just about the education system. The causal links between education and wider socio-economic inequalities go both ways. One of the defining characteristics of the English education system is the difficulties that exist for those who are not academically successful by age 16. It is perhaps not surprising that almost none of the lowest performers at GCSE go on to gain a degree, whilst almost all of the higher performers do so. The problem is that other routes post-16 are complex and often low-quality; there are few second chances for those who struggle academically at age 16. There are very big differences in outcomes between those who fail to meet the expected standard at age 16 by a single mark and those who just succeed by a single mark. England stands out for the remarkably low fraction of young people who progress into higher level vocational training. England is also unusual in how many young adults have very low literacy and numeracy skills. Naturally, all of these issues affecting pupils’ progress and experience in school feed in to the likelihood that they go on to gain additional qualifications and skills afterwards. As covered in detail in other parts of this volume—for example, in the work on labour markets and health—attainment of a university degree appears to act, for many, as a passport to a very different kind of life. A thought-provoking commentary by McNeil and Soskice highlights the range of ways in which this is true. Graduates earn more, for sure, but they are also more likely to marry other graduates, work with other graduates, have more autonomy at work, live in places that mostly consist of other graduates, form friendships with other graduates, and think and vote like other graduates. McNeil and Soskice worry about the combined effect of these multiple forms of polarization and segregation on the quality of social relations (a key reason for potential concern over inequality, as discussed in Satz and White). In these authors’ view, the only option for redressing this is to continue to aggressively increase the number of graduates, requiring significant transformation of the higher education sector. Another line of tack is to strengthen the quality of the opportunities for skill development among those who do not go down the academic path. Deficiencies with our system of vocational education are the focus of Simon Field’s commentary. He points to the failure of the 16–19 system to ensure basic skills are embedded; the complexity, fragmentation and instability of the system of vocational qualifications; and the underfunding of further and adult education as amongst the key factors contributing to the relative failure of this part of the education system. The evidence that this is at the root of at least some of the persistent inequalities in lifetime incomes in the UK, as well as in poor economic performance, is longstanding and convincing. Farquharson et al. also show how important education is in determining earnings and labour market outcomes: ‘Around nine in ten graduates are in employment between their mid-20s and early 50s. Employment rates of people educated to GCSE level or below are far lower: amongst those in their 30s, for example, two in five women and one in five men are not in work. Graduates also enjoy higher earnings, with the median 40-year-old graduate earning twice as much as someone qualified to GCSE level or below. Despite a huge increase in the share of graduates, this “wage premium” has barely budged in the last five decades, at least for men. There is good evidence that at least some of this wage premium is due to the causal impact of education improving people’s outcomes, rather than just selecting and sorting people of differing ability.’ It is also the case, though, that social class has an independent effect on later earnings—the more affluent your background, the more you are likely to earn for any given level of education attained. This is particularly true for those who attended a private school. Farquharson et al. conclude by offering at least a framework for thinking about how to tackle this sticky issue: 1) Interventions need to look at the education system as a whole. Making changes at just one stage is unlikely to be highly effective. Each stage needs to fit together. 2) Related to this, early intervention is important but is not enough by itself and needs to be followed up. 3) Spending matters: if we want high levels of attainment and progress from those with more challenging backgrounds, we are likely to have to pay for it. 4) Decisions matter, over where to send children to school and what choices to make over courses, for example. Hence, parents and pupils need to be well informed. 5) Education is not just about test scores. Even beyond the immediate welfare of children, we know that broader ‘soft skills’ and experiences are very important for later life economic success and personal well-being. 6) Educational inequalities cannot be tackled by the education system alone. What happens within families and communities also matters hugely, as do wider societal inequalities. The education system is part of a wider system. This overview was written for the IFS Deaton Review of Inequalities, funded by the Nuffield Foundation (grant reference WEL/43603). The views expressed are those of the authors and not necessarily the Foundation.

resumo: Abstract Developed nations have experienced a longstanding trend of reshaping the labour market's occupational structure. This trend, named job market polarization, describes how middle‐level jobs have decreased their relative share of the labour market in favour of high‐ and low‐complexity jobs. The literature has pointed to technological change as the main factor in setting this configuration, which accompanied the transition to a knowledge economy as a source of competitive advantages. Still, the narratives of technological change are anchored to specific technologies and times that do not fit the emerging challenges of the fourth industrial revolution and the increasing relevance of the digital economy. In this paper, I explore how job polarization dynamics have interacted with active labour market policies' effectiveness by focusing on job training skill premiums. I use nationally representative data to evaluate cross‐sectionally and longitudinally the relationship between job training access, job polarization, and wages. The results show that polarization poses a wage penalty while it increases the relative value of training skill premium. I discuss how the setting of a polarized market could be considered for future skill‐based interventions concerning digital technologies.

resumo: In addition to overall dispersion, the distributional shape of economic status has attracted growing attention in the inequality literature. Economic polarization is a specific form of distributional change, characterized by a shrinking middle of the distribution and a growing top and bottom, with potentially important and unique social consequences. Building on relative distribution methods and drawing from the literature on job polarization, the authors develop an approach for analyzing economic polarization at the individual level. The method has three useful features. First, it offers intuitive and flexible measurement of economic polarization both between and within categories. Second, it helps disentangle two potential sources of economic polarization: compositional change, which involves changes to the allocation of workers across categories, and relative economic status change, which involves changes to the allocation of economic rewards between individuals. Third, it enables researchers to uncover and examine potential heterogeneity in economic polarization, for example, across occupations, geographic units, demographic and educational groups, and firms. The authors demonstrate the utility of this approach through two empirical applications: (1) an analysis of trends in wage polarization between and within occupations and (2) an examination of geographic variation in income polarization.

resumo: Since gaining independence in 1963, Kenya has navigated a complex interplay between ethnic fragmentation and economic development, marked by a myriad of challenges. This research article evaluated these dynamics, shedding light on the hurdles hindering progress and the avenues for advancement. Among the challenges analysed are: political instability and governance issues, resource allocation disparities leading to unequal development, pervasive corruption and rent-seeking behaviour, ethnic favouritism in employment and business, wavering investor confidence impacting economic stability, and the perpetuation of ethnic polarization in public discourse. The article reviews various literatures, gaps identified and field. Two theories Instrumental Marxist theory and Relative Deprivation theory complemented by pragmatism philosophy are utilised to enrich the findings herein. It employs historical research design since its qualitative in nature. The major finding is that the volatile political environment, characterized by contested elections, instances of violence, and power struggles, has created an aura of uncertainty that is detrimental to the economic stability. It concludes that, corruption and rent-seeking behaviour have posed formidable obstacles to Kenya's economic development, siphoning off resources meant for public welfare and distorting the allocation of opportunities.

titulo: Data Conscience: Algorithmic Siege on Our Humanity, by Brandeis Hill Marshall
topico_primario: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
palavras_openalex: algorithmic bias | data ethics | Black women | racial and gender inequality | algorithmic fairness | large language models | ChatGPT | data literacy | eugenics | Jim Crow | algorithmic accountability | algorithmic transparency | algorithmic literacy
resumo: In recent years, a proliferation of critiques of data and AI have addressed inequalities embedded in (and produced by) these technical systems as they are deployed in health care, the workplace, education, policing, social work, transportation, and more. And with the advent of ChatGPT and other systems trained on large language models (LLMs), we are in the midst of an explosion of public debate about AI. While often brilliantly argued, exposés and critical works can leave a pragmatic reader like myself wondering, OK, so how do we take action? And, as a former software developer, I also wonder, When does the path toward equity involve technical design and development and when does it require law, policy, advocacy, or other interventions outside of a tech and design space?Enter Data Conscience: Algorithmic Siege on Our Humanity by Brandeis Marshall. Marshall is a well-known public scholar who has a PhD in computer science. She runs the popular Rebel Tech Newsletter and holds more than two decades of experience as a data educator and data science consultant. Since Marshall is also a Black woman, Data Conscience joyfully and refreshingly centers on the experiences of Black women. I say “joyfully” because Marshall uses everyday examples from Black women's lives, such as her washing her locs, as a way of teaching the reader about writing effective algorithms. And I say “refreshingly” because the book avoids the supposedly “neutral” data examples that we all know are raced and gendered (e.g., the endless use of the mtcars data set to teach R—a good choice for making sure that car salesmen feel welcome in computer science).Written in a conversational and engaging tone, Data Conscience covers a lot of ground at multiple scales, moving adeptly between code snippets, data entity diagrams, historical context, and visionary policy proposals. Each of the book's eleven chapters opens with one of Marshall's tweets from the past several years. For example, the tweet “In tech, y'all are forever trying to do all the things at scale instead of quality” opens chapter 10 (231). These tweets set the scene for the discussion to come and also orient the tone around conversation and dialogue. In the first section of the book, Marshall opens with a discussion of the environmental constraints of trying to work toward equity with data and technology—for example, historic laws like Jim Crow that enshrined white supremacy, racist and ableist movements including eugenics, and the misconceptions that surround data ethics (spoiler alert—more data doesn't equate to better data and data ethics can't fix social problems). To try to tease out how technical systems interact with social inequities, Marshall introduces us to the bias wheel, her model for navigating four forms of bias: human bias, business bias, data bias, and algorithmic bias.These discussions—around history, laws, the nature of oppression, and the definitions of ethics—set the scene for the more technical chapters that follow. They also prepare readers for the idea that many of the most difficult challenges cannot be addressed by more data, transparent or interpretable models, or retrospective algorithmic audits. Some of our algorithmic ills simply need to be fixed politically, and Marshall helps practitioners understand both the opportunities and limitations of their trade for transformational social change. Chapters 5–8 are all about the data science process, from data acquisition to data analysis (“the rockstar and cash cow of the data industry,” (p. 164) in Marshall's memorable phrasing), and on to data visualization. These chapters dive into sample code, modeling data from Black Twitter about the Oscars, and critiques of top-k as a surefire measure of accuracy.The only chapter in this section that left me with unanswered questions was the eighth, “Double-Edged Visualization Sword.” Marshall critiques an easy reliance on “pretty pictures” and rightly points out that visualization can exclude disabled people, particularly those who are visually impaired. But this chapter could have gone further. For example, how might creative forms of visualization be used to connect with different audiences? How might visualization combat deficit narratives about minoritized populations instead of reinforcing them? Could visualization or other forms of data communication be leveraged for the purpose of equity? Additional visual and narrative analyses that I would have welcomed could have included Marshall's take on the proliferation of public health dashboards during COVID as well as counterpoints like COVID Black.The final section of Data Conscience (chapters 9–11) zooms back out from the data science pipeline to address data governance issues. Marshall takes the reader on a tour of legal and regulatory developments around AI, the role of algorithmic influencers (a term she coins for industry leaders who are injecting a tech-first perspective into governing AI), and a final chapter about possibilities for public and collective action. She demonstrates definitively how current laws are not sufficient to protect the civil rights of minoritized groups (and Black women in particular) in the digital sphere. And Marshall shows how algorithmic influencers routinely work to suppress, deplatform, and decenter Black women, perpetuating what (in a nod to Moya Bailey's work) she calls algorithmic misogynoir.These closing chapters offer some exciting and large-scale policy ideas. For example, Marshall advocates for a new federal agency modeled off the CDC called the Center for Technological Civility, whose mission would center on digital civil rights, misinformation, and safety. Such an agency could help advance data civics, a term she uses to describe public facing data activities and operations—practices of managing and disseminating data—that inform and enhance the lives of all members of society. There are many important ideas packed into this section that I hope that Marshall will continue to build on and make actionable in the form of policy proposals, research projects, and collective action networks. In particular, the ambitious nature of her proposals is quite thrilling when often what happens in the sphere of law and regulation is about retroactive redress rather than preventive informatic health and safety.Data Conscience is geared toward practitioners, and specifically toward data scientists and software developers working in industry. This is a great strength when many books and resources in the critical data studies field remain either mired in academic jargon or else so unyieldingly negative in their prognoses that there appears to be no way forward (technical, political, or otherwise). What is particularly helpful is how, without being preachy or pedantic, Marshall insists, over and over again, that tech and data people who care about equity need to expand their focus outside of tech and data. While she shows how some actions toward justice are indeed possible at the scale of the program, the app, or the database, Marshall brings us back home to the fact that social inequities cannot be solved through these tools alone. She consistently opens the possibility that “certain technologies need to be sidelined until their impact on society and its people can be determined” (227). This models an important and too-little-pursued political position for tech and data people—entertaining the possibility that a specific technology/tool/model/app simply should not exist.The final consistent throughline across Data Conscience is that working toward equity means prioritizing the most vulnerable people in society, and Marshall focuses her lens here on how tech has repeatedly failed to center Black people, and Black women specifically. As she writes, “Personhood status remains conditional throughout our society” (277), and tech is no exception to this, as we see in nearly all reports about algorithmic harms. She makes a powerful call to multiracial allyship: “Condemning the power structures enacted by history, social constructs, the law, economics and civic engagement is the burden of all of us, not just Black people navigating the original stain of enslavement in the United States” (279). And she urges the data science and technology community not to cop out and take a break when we face pushback to our anti-racist work because “Black women can't take a break from being a Black woman” (281).Ultimately, in place of “move fast and break things” Marshall proposes “move intentionally and make tech fairer for vulnerable communities” (245) as the slogan of an equity-first data science. This is an urgent message, and this reviewer, for one, hopes that the good humor, accessibility, and pragmatism of Data Conscience will help its message travel far and wide.

resumo: Abstract This study investigates how agents in contested occupations justify and legitimize their work. It examines Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) attorneys who prosecute immigrant removal cases on behalf of the federal government, delving into the narrative strategies that attorneys use to attain self-legitimacy within the agency. While existing literature suggests that self-legitimacy stems from either public support or an intrinsic belief in one’s deservingness of power, this study introduces a third pathway to self-legitimacy, agency entrenchment, in which government prosecutors draw on a highly internalized sense of patriotism and a duty to their organizational role, in the face of heightened public protest and changing administrative priorities. Analyzing forty in-depth interviews with ICE attorneys, this study identifies two primary approaches to agency entrenchment. The first is a bureaucratic approach, in which attorneys derive an internalized sense of duty from the existing law. The second is an enforcement approach, in which attorneys derive moral authority from what they see as their protector status. By deploying these narratives of self-legitimacy, ICE prosecutors attempt to resolve perceived conflicts between their legally mandated responsibilities and the ethical and reputational criticisms they encounter. The findings contribute to the broader understanding of the occupational dynamics between political polarization and law enforcement prosecution.

resumo: As a new form of social wealth, digital wealth is becoming an important force in the promotion of common prosperity. In the digital economy era, digital labor and data factors are important sources for creating digital wealth. The creation of digital commodity wealth is reflected in the process of value formation and value appreciation of digital goods, as well as in the expansion and reproduction process of data production factors. The creation of digital non-commodity wealth needs to rely on the coordination of multiple supply systems including government, enterprises, society and platforms. In the distribution of digital wealth in a socialist market economy, it is necessary to adhere to the basic distribution system with remuneration based on work as the main form and the coexistence of multiple distribution methods. It should fully reflect the value contribution of data factors while also addressing and resolving potential polarization effects caused by the distribution of digital wealth. On the basis of the new development stage, China should steadily advance the creation and accumulation of digital wealth on the basis of constantly strengthening, improving and expanding the digital economy, and should pay attention to standardizing the distribution of digital wealth in order to achieve a solid advance in the common prosperity of all the people.

resumo: Does technological change shape immigration policy in the United States? I argue that if technological change tilts the composition of workers towards manual employment, this leads to a more restrictive immigration policy. A theoretical model and empirical evidence analyzing voting on immigration bills in the House of Representatives supports this. Policy makers representing districts exposed to manual-biased technological change are more likely to support restricting low-skill immigration. Results are confirmed using specific automation technologies: IT capital and industrial robot adoption. The analysis is completed by (i) additional results on trade policy and political polarization, (ii) further stylized evidence on the mechanism.

resumo: As scholars of the American tradition, we know Charles Sanders Peirce as an original thinker with personal foibles and complex ideas, a primary source and yet an enigma in the main channel of the tradition. He is most profound in developing an architectonic system that rivals and proceeds beyond Kant in the interest of furthering the inquiry necessary for self-control and the development of the community of inquiry. The object of the Real consistently appears as a figure to Peirce's inquiry as its true home, and the community of self-and-other correcting minds sharing this goal of inquiry may bring themselves together in experience and work. This handbook is an example of such work that extends beyond this immediate occasion, as Peirce reminds us, because once alive within us, how could we conceive of such inquiry ever ending?The vision of Peirce that comes clear in this volume arises from the coherence of his philosophical, logical, and mathematical thought, drawn out by historical as well as recent applications. The significant advance of this handbook is the combination of US and international scholars drawing upon a wide circle of Peirce's influence and interest. The depth and breadth of analysis speaks to the power of Peirce's method of self-correction; it is the engine of his method. We can assess the changes, the principles, and the expressed sentiments, but the origin or character of Peirce's sentiments themselves or the full ground of the emergence of his ideas remains obscure. De Waal organizes the book in six parts. What follows is an interpretation of the content of these parts via summaries of the chapters and a brief concluding observation.Part I examines Peirce's personal life and interactions with organizations in order to qualify his successes and failures and perhaps explain why this genius had such a difficult life. Daniel L. Everett (chap. 1) represents Peirce as a special case of academic genius and faults the leadership of Johns Hopkins and Harvard for failing to accommodate his behavior and eccentricities and also includes touching narratives of children who knew and cared for the Peirces in Milford (17). Jaime Nubiola and Sara Barrena (chap. 2) examine Peirce's career through his five European trips and their importance for his collaborative scientific ventures, encounters with beauty (39), and as occasions of family drama with first wife Zina Fay and later with Juliette Froissy. Cheryl Misak (chap. 3) focuses on the difficult behavior of Peirce that finds its complement in the personal animus of Simon Newcomb, who assailed Peirce both at Johns Hopkins and at the US Coast Survey (51, 54). Despite these attacks, Peirce's genius was recognized by Venn, C. I. Lewis, and—through Lady Welby—by Ramsey and Wittgenstein. Pierce's uniqueness as a scientist, philosopher, and logician was mishandled by Charles Eliot and Daniel Gilman, who failed to recognize him as America's leading thinker (55). This beginning brings Peirce's personality forward as an angle of vision on his philosophical and scientific production, setting the ground for the technical evaluations of Peirce's philosophical and scientific career and the lasting impact of his logic and metaphysics after his death.Part II develops the topics of phenomenology and the normative sciences in six chapters. Richard Kenneth Atkins (chap. 4) provides a brilliantly clear description of the development of Peirce's categories and the phaneron that “needs no special tools and is open to all” to engage “whatever comes before the mind” (71). But this does not exhaust the “phaneron” due to the Real that remains beyond the representation by minds. Nathan Houser (chap. 5) develops Peirce's empiricism as the “rain of percepts” that is the inflow of phenomenal content: the “deeper levels of our bottomless lake of consciousness and subconscious mind consists mainly of conceptual or intellectual content based on our perceptual judgments” (88). This challenges Locke's and Dennett's attempts to articulate a completely materialist account of reality. Tiago da Costa e Silva (chap. 6) follows Peirce's phaneroscopic study and interactions with positive experience. Esthetics discovers, defines, and renders the admirable in itself more precise as the ideal that grounds conduct (103). Richard Shusterman (chap. 7) examines the aesthetic quality in moral action, noting that for Peirce, the “esthetic ideal is proposed as an ultimate end of action” (117). Self-control of feelings is possible through deliberate action guided by three sentiments; interest in an indefinite community, the possibility of this interest made supreme, and hope in the unlimited continuance of intellectual activity (124). James Jakób Liszka (chap. 8) also focuses on the significance of self-control that reflects design, an arrangement of parts reflecting the admirable and noble because that person has virtuous character and aims at higher goods. Peirce subjunctively identifies it as “What is it that we would deliberately pronounce to be kalon k'agathon?” (141). The end is not an action but the process of evolution of generals that are “destined” to become more and more “reasonable.” This is the character of “growth, a process by which new information is acquired and false beliefs discarded” (143). Juliana Acosta López de Mesa and Daniel G. Campos (chap. 9) turn their attention to agape love and the growth of justice that reflects the “cherishing love” of the Gospel of John (154). This account of self-control, drawing on Anderson and Trout, is more than fallibilistic self-regulation. What a good pragmaticist desires is power—“not the sham power,” Peirce says, “of brute force, which, even in its own specialty of spoiling things, secures such slight results; but the creative power of reasonableness, which subdues all other powers and rules over them with its scepter, knowledge, and its globe, love” (159).Part III, “Logic and Mathematics,” is the longest, comprising eight chapters. Mark Migotti (chap. 10) examines Peirce's claim that the study of logic challenges the characteristic defect of loose reasoning in philosophers. Peirce counters this with mathematical reasoning that infers from objects of observation a true continuity that cannot be directly observed (178). There is no point in separating logic from other sciences (183). Leila Haaparanta (chap. 11) develops Peirce's philosophy of logic through the model of overt action. “Logic is the theory of self-controlled and deliberate thought, and its principles are based on ethics” (195). Peirce's logic is a calculus of observation that we cannot step beyond, contra Frege's logic as universal language (199). Ilkka Niiniluoto (chap. 12) traces the history and interpretation of Peirce's abduction from his adoption of “an otherwise useless term” for his new account of hypothesis (211) to the development of plausible explanations by flashes of insight, those most likely to be verified by observation, or an “inference to the best explanation” (IBE). Even if not identical to abduction, IBE is abductive in explanatory virtues, that is, it reaches for novel possibilities necessary for explanation (222). Frederik Stjernfelt (chap. 13) examines Peirce's theory of generalized propositions and logic of relations. No sign is able to address the totality of its object, so it necessarily must select some way among many of indexically identifying it, and all signs require some knowledge of acquaintance grounding the proposition (234–35). Peirce's “universe of discourse” provides a rich alternative to the Frege-Russell-Wittgenstein positivists because “propositions are not limited to the linguistic form or to human beings” (237). Francesco Bellucci and Ahti-Veikko Pietarinen (chap. 14) develop Peirce's existential graphs that he claimed were his chief work in a general algebra of logic (GAL). Existential graphs proceed endoporeutically, from outside inward (251). These were unpublished in Peirce's lifetime, but there is growing evidence that the time is beginning to be ripe for Peirce's logical graphs to become “the twenty-first century's model for new kinds of logics” (257). Chiara Ambrosio (chap. 15) develops Peirce's diagrammatic thinking as an epistemic virtue that allows scientists to approach and use diagrams as “working objects” around which they negotiate their identities and commitments. Peirce follows Whewell's idea of a moral economy as a “web of affect-saturated values that stand and function well in relationship with each other” (268). Rather than innate ideas, Peirce's model is a process of reasoning that is transparent and rigorous, “communicable and publicly ascertainable” (270), which allows for truth to be perceived as “structural objectivity” (271). Louis H. Kauffman (chap. 16) explains Peirce's commitment to infinitesimals after the mathematical community had passed on (289). Peirce's denial of the law of excluded middle must be related to the connectivity/continuity of the line, a feature necessary for mapping topographical spaces. Peirce holds that a line is a continuity and not a collection of individual parts. In topological space, there is an option to “glue” two points together so that every open set containing one of them must contain the other (293). Thus, 0 is inexhaustibly tiny, an inexhaustible infinity. Peirce extends this to signs from representing an object to reach “a Sign of Itself, containing its own explanation” (295). A map must include a point on the map that coincides with a corresponding point on a territory. This interlocking relationship of the sign and object challenges the Godelian result that formal systems cannot express the full range of mathematical truth (296). Fernando Zalamea (chap. 17) argues that Peirce's most appreciated philosophical or semiotical work is connected to mathematics and logic (299). The pragmaticist maxim is that knowledge is pre-eminently contextual within some bounded mathematical definitions. Peirce's “proof of pragmatism” turns out to be fully mathematized, and conclusively proved, at least in the very broad context of category theory (303). Fransico Vargas provides a model for Peirce's continuum in which there are no more points whatsoever, only extended parts, and “a continuous weldedness governs the model, as predicted by Peirce” (306). Peirce's existential graphs were ignored for sixty years because of Quine's review but are now the focus of Arnold Oostra and students, “the first to extend Peirce's graphs to a nonclassical realm” (308). They are now exploring a “yet mysterious interdependence between the different shapes of the sheet of assertion and the different logics therein inscribed” (309).Part IV, “Pragmatism,” incorporates five chapters. Philip Kitcher (chap. 18) takes up the question of pragmatism as it emerges primarily in the work of Peirce and James and their divergences. The “world-formula” James tabs in his Baldwin Dictionary entry is “entirely different from Peirce's picture of the scientific community of philosophers, patiently revising their language” (320). Under this notion, Dewey “should no longer be counted part of the movement” because the application of the pragmatic maxim plays a “negligible role” in his program (322). Peirce's focus on the community ordered by the Inexorability of truth develops pragmatism as a way to improve methods of science (327). Peirce was the architect of a major philosophical movement, and James and Dewey owe debts to him (330). Cornelis de Waal (chap. 19) forcefully argues that “philosophers should be pragmatists” (325). Philosophy is a “positive science” to determine what our sentiments ought to be, informed by “the facts of everyday life” (337). Reasoning is an idea acting as a cause to create or confirm a belief, or to induce a voluntary action by developed self-control in the criticism of meaning (339). Conceptions are not mental states but general plans of action from a normative maxim—what we should do in order to avoid elements that are meaningless, and so “one cannot be truly engaged in philosophy without being a pragmatist” (345). Vincent Colapietro (chap. 20) examines theory, practice, and deliberation. For Peirce, reason is rooted in a classical conception of Logos, to discover reality, and the capacity of this discovery is limitless to human rationality (351–52). Theoretical employment of reason should be fallible and guided by phronesis (353). Peirce linked our capacity for radical deliberation and our capacity for theoretical discovery; “the machinery of logical self-control works on the same plane as does moral self-control” (355). This leads us to ask how we should comport ourselves as inquirers as we develop our deliberative agency. Mats Bergman (chap. 21) identifies the purpose of pragmatism as a response to the “routine recycling of the clear-and-distinct doctrine in logical treatises” (369). Pragmatic clarification takes over where “phaneroscopic analysis reaches its limits,” and becomes ampliative not just explanatory (377). The purpose of critical self-control is a continual amelioration of our own habits, and an “evolutionary pragmaticistic interpretation” serves to produce “a reconciliation or adjustment between reason and the facts of experience” (379). This Realism embraces ideals as organically generated by criticism of criticisms with no definite upper limits to the procedure recognizing pragmatic boundaries recommended by the purposes of inquiry (381). Aaron Bruce Wilson (chap. 22) follows Peirce's development of perception and empiricism. Peirce rejects foundationalist forms of empiricism but holds that perceptual judgments must (1) arise from uncontrollable response to a percept; (2) remain available for self-controlled levels of cognition; and (3) also describe something indexed by the percept that prompted it, which is a controversial step (389). Peirce's 1903 lectures claim that perceptual judgments are the first premises of all our reasonings, and they cannot be called into question (393). Peirce adopts the term percipuum to include both percept and perceptual judgment, which could be an illusion, but even a false judgment is “an index of reality” (400). Peirce's “nativism,” that there are beliefs that are of the general nature of instincts, does not “entirely abandon” his empiricism but shifts it from one that depends on perception to one that derives from perception (401).Part V, “Metaphysics,”  five chapters.
