resumo: The major problem in the current Korean labor market is not the decrease of labor flexibility caused by lack of contingent employees, but the dual structure and polarization of labor market caused by abuse of contingent employees. The basic direction in discussing contingent employment including dispatched employment should be ① improving employment practices causing segregation of employment status and abuse of contingent employees, ② coming up with an effective plan for employees not to be discriminated by reason of employment status, ③ preparing social safety net such as employment insurance which can do the role of ‘safety net’ practically.   Most of all the regulation direction of dispatched employment provided by Dispatch Law (whether to limit the categories of dispatch-allowed business and the terms of dispatch) will become a rudder of labor market policies of the government rather than a matter of expanding or reducing dispatched employment. The amendment of Dispatch law arranged by ruling party seems to be in direction expanding contingent employment and the amendment of Employment Insurance Act excludes temporary or unstable employees by tightening the eligibility requirements of unemployment benefits. The regulation direction arranged by the ruling party dose not correspond to 9.15 Agreement by Tripartite.

titulo: TRAÇOS-DE-UNIÃO DAS METRÓPOLES LATINO-AMERICANAS
palavras_openalex: Latin American cities | globalization | socio-spatial fragmentation | metropolitanization | urban development | urban economy | regional economy | regional development | late development | crisis of capitalism | deregulation | labor market segmentation | social polarization | local governance | economic concentration | Ibero-American cities
resumo: O trabalho tem o objetivo de tentar reconhecer os reflexos comuns da “globalização“ sobre as metrópoles iberoamericanas, escolhidas em função dos trabalhos de pesquisa realizados na Rede Iberoamericana de Investigadores. Inicialmente, procurou-se mostrar que dois aspectos, casados, tiveram importância fundamental sobre a formação e a atual reformulação das suas cidades e metrópoles: o desenvolvimento tardio e a atual crise sistêmica e estrutural da economia capitalista mundial. Compreendendo que a nova dinâmica econômica, regida pela desregulamentação e a flexibilização da relação salarial e a intensificação da segmentação do mercado de trabalho tem como conseqüência a tendência de polarização social, o trabalho identifica que a fragmentação sócioterritorial constitui um dos traços-comuns das metrópoles estudadas. À fragmentação sócio-territorial metropolitana, também corresponde uma fragmentação da gestão local e uma concentração do controle de grande parcela da economia mundial. Fazendo um corte transversal às questões comuns encontradas, buscou-se, como conclusão, a fixação de conceitos capazes de definir uma metrópole-tipo, geral, embora não se possa afirmar que tais conceitos sejam capazes de explicar o porte e a intensidade em que isso venha ocorrer em cada uma delas. Disso resultam metrópoles desagregadas socialmente, concentradas economicamente e fragmentadas espacialmente. PALAVRAS-CHAVE: Desenvolvimento urbano, metropolização, economia urbana, economia regional e desenvolvimento regional. COMMON ASPECTS BETWEEN LATIN AMERICAN METROPOLISES Edgard Porto Edmilson Carvalho The objective of this work is to try to recognize globalization’s common reflection over iberian-american metropolises, chosen by taking in consideration research works made by Rede Iberoamericana de Investidores. Initially, it was tried to demonstrate that the two following aspects, the late development and today’s structural and systemic crisis lived by world capitalistic economy, considered together, had fundamental importance over formation and actual reformulation of theses cities and metropolises. Considering that the new economic dynamics – ruled by disregulation, flexibilization of salarial relations and by the intensification of job market segmentation – leads to a social polarization tendency, this text considers that social-territorial fragmentation constitutes one of the common traces of the studied metropolises. To the social-territorial metropolitan fragmentation corresponds a local management fragmentation as well as the control concentration observed in a major part of world economy. Making a transversal cut on some found common questions, it was considered as a conclusion the fixation of concepts which are able to define a typical metropolis, in general, although it can not be affirmed that these concepts are able to explain the amount and the intensity that they may happen to occur in each one of them. As a result we find metropolises that are socially disaggregated, economically concentrated and spatially fragmented. KEY WORDS: Urban development; metropolization; urban economy; regional economy; regional development. TRAITS D’UNION DES MÉTROPOLES LATINO-AMÉRICAINES Edgard Porto Edmilson Carvalho L’objectif de cet essai est d’essayer de reconnaître les réflexes de la “mondialisation” sur les métropoles ibéro-américaines, choisies en fonction des recherches réalisées dans le cadre du Réseau Ibéro-américain de Chercheurs. Tout d’abord, on a voulu montrer que deux aspects associés eurent une importance fondamentale sur la formation et la reformulation actuelle des villes et des métropoles: le développement tardif et l’actuelle crise systémique et structurelle de l’économie capitaliste mondiale. Par le fait de comprendre que la nouvelle dynamique économique, régie aussi bien par la déréglementation et par la flexibilité de la relation salariale que par l’intensification de la segmentation du marché de travail, a comme conséquence la tendance à la polarisation sociale, cet essai identifie que la fragmentation socioterritoriale constitue l’un des traits communs des métropoles étudiées. À la fragmentation socio-territoriale métropolitaine correspondent également une fragmentation de la gestion locale et une concentration du contrôle d’une grande parcelle de l’économie mondiale. En faisant une coupe transversale aux questions communes rencontrées, en guise de conclusion, on a cherché la fixation de concepts capables de définir une métropole type, générale, bien que tels concepts ne soient pas capables d’expliquer la portée et l’intensité que cela arrive à chacune d’entre elles. De cela résultent des métropoles désagrégées socialement, concentrées économiquement et fragmentées dans l’espace. resumo: As the number of cochlear implant wearers continues to increase (see cover story), all three implant manufacturers are bringing an array of enhanced new products to market. These products are part of a rushing stream of innovations that is expanding cochlear implant candidacy, improving performance, and facilitating programming and follow-up care. “Back in the early 80s, we were thrilled when a cochlear implant patient heard a sound, even without understanding speech,” says Patricia Chute, AuD, associate professor of audiology at Mercy College, Dobbs Ferry, NY, who has worked with cochlear implants since 1979. “It's really exciting to see this technology evolve.” This article reports on today's new products and examines what's on the way. THE IMPLANT CENTERS' PERSPECTIVE In the late 1970s, the earliest cochlear implants were one-electrode, single-channel devices that gave recipients a “very basic perception of sound,” says Jon Shallop, PhD, who works in the Mayo Clinic cochlear implant program in Rochester, MN. Shallop is also a staff consultant and associate professor at the Mayo Clinic and Medical School, which contains one of approximately 300 centers in the U.S. specializing in cochlear implants. “With a single-channel cochlear implant, people could get some idea of loudness, tempo, and time patterns, but not pitch,” Shallop notes. Multichannel cochlear implants came to the U.S. market in the mid-1980s and it's been a fast ride since. By allowing multiple contacts per electrode, multichannels produce a range of frequencies for the cochlear implant user. “This is essential for achieving word recognition,” says Shallop. Technologic improvements have followed in “everything related to cochlear implants,” he adds. “With the first multichannel implants we were excited to see a sentence-recognition score of 30%. Today, that same type of patient is achieving 80% to 90% scores.” “We continue to get iterations of software that is smarter, more adaptable, and, in many cases, faster and more versatile than previous generations,” observes Noel L. Cohen, MD, professor and chair of the Department of Otolaryngology and director of the Cochlear Implantation Program at New York University Medical Center. SURGERY BECOMING SIMPLER AND SAFER While cochlear implants are becoming more complex, the implantation surgery has become simpler. Cohen, one of the nation's most respected cochlear implant surgeons, says, “Audiologists should know that the surgery today is mostly routine. The techniques are readily learned and, unless there is a complication, not terribly challenging.” He adds, “Implant surgery is not dangerous.” Complications remain a possibility, though. According to Cohen, a major problem in the past was a breakdown of the incision and flap, leading to infection. That threat has been greatly reduced by progressively smaller and less invasive incisions. A second complication was incorrect insertion of the electrode or damage to the electrode during surgery. “That was a matter of lack of experience,” says Cohen. Today, that complication rate has also diminished. Cohen continues, “Third is paralysis of the face, a frightening thing, especially to parents of a small child who goes into surgery looking perfectly okay but being deaf, and who comes back with half a face that's paralyzed. It's a horrible condition.” Here again, experience and improved surgical techniques have greatly reduced the incidence of facial paralysis to “something on the order of 0.05%,” says Cohen. (Another serious condition that has been suspected of being related to cochlear implantation in some cases is meningitis. For more on the topic, see the sidebar in this month's cover story.) HOW TO CHOOSE? As manufacturers compete in improving their technology, does one brand stand out as better than the others? “There are no indisputable data to say that one cochlear implant works better than another on any given population,” states Thomas Balkany, MD, another of the leading implant surgeons in the U.S. He is chairman of the Department of Otolaryngology at the University of Miami, where some 80 cochlear implantations are performed annually. “However,” says Balkany, “some design characteristics differ, so we educate patients about all three devices so they can make an informed decision. We insist that they have a good reason for their choice, to ensure there is no misunderstanding.” Esthetic appeal—the size, color, or shape of the BTE unit, for instance—is often a driving factor. So are a device's sound processing strategy, computing power, and battery options. Shallop adds that patients may have a bias toward a particular brand. “I don't mean that in a negative way,” he says. “They may think, ‘Aunt Mary has this particular device and is doing really well with it, so that's what I want to get, too.’” He adds, “We don't try to dissuade someone of their bias. Actually, a pre-set bias could be a positive factor. But we'll show patients demonstration units of all brands, with comparative information about battery life and what they can expect in terms of cost over the next several years.” Most patients will opt for a BTE processor rather than a body-worn model, says Shallop, “as long as the quality of sound is the same. But there are situations where a body processor might be more appropriate,” as with someone who is outside a lot and needs a very durable product. WHAT DO WEARERS HEAR? About a month after implantation, when the surgical incisions have healed, an audiologist “turns on” the implant sound. What exactly does the recipient hear? It's a learning experience, which varies among patients. “Typically, patients have no trouble recognizing speech as speech, but it may sound different from what they remember. Most patients adapt relatively quickly to the new sound,” says Chris van den Honert, PhD, director of research and development at Cochlear Americas. Electrical stimulation produces sound that is “qualitatively different from what the patient is accustomed to from hearing aids,” says Steve Staller, PhD, vice-president for quality, clinical, and regulatory affairs at Cochlear Americas. He explains, “Hearing aids amplify sound and they provide power, but not clarity, to a severe to profoundly deaf ear. Cochlear implants bypass damaged hair cells and stimulate the auditory nerve directly, providing a clearer signal to the brain.” Wearers can detect the subtleties of music, but generally, says van den Honert, “the stimulation strategy has been devised to deliver speech sensation. One thing implants don't do very well is represent harmonic relationships or musical intervals.” But they're working on it. Staller says, “Going forward, a lot of research is focused on clarifying sounds in the diverse set of environments that individuals live in, including music.” BUY NOW OR WAIT FOR NEW TECHNOLOGY? With all the improvements on the way, should a cochlear implant candidate wait for the next generation of technology before proceeding with surgery? That's a question that Douglas Lynch, director of corporate marketing at Advanced Bionics, hears often. As a cochlear implant user himself, Lynch says, “I respond that I was implanted in 1995 with the first generation of technology manufactured by Advanced Bionics. I could have waited, but you have to pick a moment in time and decide, ‘I want to hear better now.' If a cochlear implant is right for you, that's when you get one.” Yet how can Lynch, with his 8-year-old device, hear so well now, including without apparent difficulty during a telephone interview? His answer is external upgrades. “I used to wear a processor on my belt the size of a paperback book,” he says. “It was very, very heavy. But I would have worn a refrigerator on my back to be able to hear. “Now I'm on my fifth generation of external processors. While what's inside is here to stay, I still take advantage of advances in software.” In fact, what's inside can change, too. Lynch says there are times when his internal implant “doesn't have the horsepower to handle new technology.” So, within 5 to 7 years, he will likely get a fully implantable system for his other ear. ADVANCES THROUGH TELEMETRY While on-going research is improving sound quality for implant users, audiologists are benefiting, too. New technology is sharply cutting the time required to program new devices and to detect potential problems. One key to this progress is telemetry, the transmission of data electronically between the implant and the audiologist's computer. Shallop of the Mayo Clinic discusses how telemetry can help: “What if an electrode connection breaks somewhere or comes unhooked and creates an open circuit? How can you get a young child to tell you the electrode is acting intermittently? Well, through telemetry, which all the devices have. We can just hit a button and say, ‘Check electrodes.' If there's an open or short circuit, we'll learn that immediately.” At Cochlear Americas, van den Honert explains that such electronic signals are relayed back through the speech processor to the computer. “This lets you measure electrical discharges from the auditory nerve fibers, using the implant to stimulate and measure the response. It gives you an objective measure of the effectiveness of the stimulus.” This ability is especially important with young children and others who don't give the audiologist reliable feedback. In such cases, for instance, Cochlear's NRT (Neural Response Telemetry) system tells the audiologist if the patient is hearing a particular sound and approximately where that sound falls in the person's auditory dynamic range. Surgeons also use this clinical tool during implantation to check how the auditory nerve is responding to stimulation. Faster programming Telemetry speeds programming, too. Communicating directly with the implant to automatically set measurements on multiple channels simultaneously reduces the need to spend time getting feedback from patients. In addition, the new Advanced Bionics fitting tool, neural response imaging (NRI), evaluates the nerve's response to electrical stimulation. This may speed up programming with very young children. And the company's new SoundWave software sets measures for several channels at the same time, rather than one-by-one. Typically, programming can take about 2 hours, and sometimes longer, says Lynch. We're trying to get that down to an average of 30 minutes or less.” He adds, “Programming can be laborious, and when patients get fatigued, it's difficult to get good responses from them.” Cutting programming time also has financial implications. Lynch explains, “It's important for cochlear implant centers and audiologists [in getting] insurance reimbursement, because typically they can only bill for a session of 90 minutes or less within a 24-hour period.” In other words, if programming takes longer, the patient must return the next day, or the audiologist is not reimbursed for the full session. WHAT'S HAPPENING IN THE MARKET? Following is a summary of the latest developments by the three cochlear implant makers. Advanced Bionics New software is coming this year to program the new Advanced Bionics HiResolution sound processing strategy and to enhance the company's Clarion CII Bionic Ear platform. According to the company, HiResolution brings patients “the fine details of sound for significantly better speech understanding, music appreciation, and overall sound fidelity than is possible with hearing aids.” To do this, it generates greater sound detail—up to 90,000 nerve stimulation pulses per second, using up to 16 independent information channels. “Stimulating the nerves so rapidly kind of keeps them from going to sleep,” says Lynch. “That's closer to how the normal hearing nerve operates.” Also, says Advanced Bionics, sophisticated circuitry extracts fine temporal details of sound, and more numerous filter banks detail spectral information. The system has two styles of externally worn sound processors: the new Auria BTE and the pager-style Platinum Sound Processor. For audiologists, the HiResolution system is said to cut programming time by eliminating measurements that are no longer required. Cochlear Americas The Nucleus 3 system is the latest implant system from Cochlear Americas. The only implant offering a titanium case, it has 22 electrodes and 22 separate channels. The system features the patented Nucleus 24 Contour electrode array. The electrodes are pre-curved for better fit in the cochlea and to minimize pressure on delicate structures during surgery. The implant body has been reduced in size to require less drilling and less surgical time. Last year, Cochlear introduced the ESprit 3G third-generation BTE speech processor for Nucleus 24 recipients. Supporting three speech-coding strategies—SPEAK, CIS, and the ACE family—the 3G is available in many colors and is powered by three zinc-air batteries for 40 to 60 hours or more of operation. This year's “significant enhancements” include the ability to program the 3G processor for Nucleus 22 patients, says Sarah Harms, vice-president of marketing. This includes a “whisper setting” on the 3G, which lets users flip a switch for more gain on softer sounds. There is also a built-in telecoil allowing wireless access to telephones and assistive listening devices. For audiologists, the 3G enhancements include new NRT software to streamline programming. According to Staller, this stimulates nerves more quickly to make faster recordings. Cochlear's SPrint body-worn speech processor, meanwhile, features ADRO (adaptive dynamic range optimization), which continually adjusts sounds to the wearer's dynamic range over 22 channels. Cochlear calls ADRO “smart processing” for knowing when to increase gain for soft speech sounds without boosting background noise. Med-El Med-El introduced the COMBI 40/40+ cochlear implant to the U.S. market in mid-2001 and has seen “tremendous sales growth” here, particularly of its “Baby BTE,” says Chris Bertrand, president and CEO of Med-El Corporation, North America. Bertrand describes the Baby BTE as “something in between” an ear-level processor and one worn on the body. “It's about the size of a pencil, and can be attached to a child's clothing or hair,” he explains. As the child grows, the implant accommodates a variety of wearing options. Alternately, the company's CIS PRO+ body-worn speech processor is about the size of a small portable cassette recorder and fits in a pocket or a carrying pouch on the belt. Two rechargeable or standard AA batteries power the unit for about one full day, and the processor can connect to a telephone, television, and assistive listening devices. The standard electrode design features 24 widely spaced contacts arranged in 12 channels to stimulate more than two-thirds of the cochlea. “We're able to sample sound at 18,180 pulses per second and actually stimulate at the same high rate,” says Bertrand. He adds that the implant a patient receives as a baby is designed to last a lifetime. “But my guess is that as technology improves, patients will want to be implanted with something new every 10 to 15 years.” ON THE   all   to more    for cochlear implants.   will become faster and more  and the devices  says   of the University of   his  of  as a  he would  electrodes to continue their  so that their implantation  less  He continues,  time you  on the    cells you  may be  So we want to make  we are doing the  possible damage when we do cochlear  The  implantable device  more exciting    than the  implantable cochlear    that such devices could  clinical  in  from 2 to 5  and  to market within 5 to  The   have been   and rechargeable batteries that  through the   progress is being  in    it   implantable  will need a power  that  a  says van den   battery would   with the same  of  used to power the  generation of  which have a sound  about the size of a half  The  would be worn  a  for several   have been doing this for   Lynch. titulo: Chemotherapy Sensitivity — Resistance Assays
palavras_openalex: chemosensitivity testing | personalized chemotherapy | predictive biomarkers | evidence base | clinical decision-making | health care costs | patient selection for clinical trials | randomized controlled trials | health technology assessment | evidence-based practice | evidence-based policy
resumo: Cancer patients are traditionally treated empirically using agreed-upon protocols of chemotherapeutic agents based on results of randomized, controlled trials. Some experts have questioned this “one size fits all” approach to obtain the best possible outcomes, since some patients with the same characteristics as those enrolled in clinical trials respond to these protocols while others do not. The quest for improved selection of chemotherapy has led to the development of assays to determine whether an individual patient's tumor is likely to be sensitive to or resistant to routinely prescribed chemotherapy agents. Several types of such tests—chemotherapy sensitivity and resistance assays (CSRAs)—have been developed and are being used to varying degrees around the US to select optimal therapy for patients. Having reliable, standardized assays to determine chemosensitivity and chemoresistance of tumors is extremely attractive to both oncologists and patients. CSRAs have the potential to improve response and, it is hoped, long-term survival, spare patients from unnecessary treatments with deleterious side effects, and save millions of dollars in health care costs. Despite the availability of a variety of CSRAs for more than two decades, a recent study conducted by an American Society of Clinical Oncology Working Group determined that the evidence base for recommending CSRAs in routine clinical practice is lacking. The article, one of ASCO's periodic Technology Assessments, was published in the September 1 issue of the Journal of Clinical Oncology (2004;22: 3631–3638) and published a month earlier online ahead of print.Figure: Deborah Schrag, MD, MPH: “The ASCO Working Group did not find that there are any CSRAs that are ready for routine integration into the clinical setting. The reasons for this are multifactorial and include the technical success and yield of the assays, the lack of adequate prospective evaluation of CSRAs in clinical trials, and the tendency of CSRAs to recommend treatments that would be given empirically.”“Chemosensitivity and resistance testing is a fantastic idea!,” lead author Deborah Schrag, MD, MPH, said in an interview. “We can't wait for the day when we can have assays that help predict which chemotherapy drugs will be most helpful to a particular patient. The rationale for CSRAs is stronger than ever before, because of the wide range of therapies now available.” Dr. Schrag, an outcomes researcher at Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, where she is Assistant Attending Physician and the Elizabeth and Felix Rohatyn Chair for Junior Faculty, explained that the Working Group used specific and precise criteria for methodology to establish that the assays can improve clinical decision-making. “These were rigorous criteria applied to a comprehensive literature review. We found, for a whole host of reasons, that the evidence base for clinical use of these assays does not yet exist,” she said. The technology assessment was based partly on a comprehensive review conducted by the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association, which was also published in the same issue of JCO (Samson DJ et al 2004;22:3618–3630). Review Criteria The 17-member ASCO Working Group reviewed 1,139 abstracts identified by a comprehensive literature search and based their final assessment on 12 published studies that met prespecified criteria: eight identified by the Blue Cross and Blue Shield review, one provided by industry, and three identified by an ASCO updated literature search. The criteria for inclusion in the review stipulated that a study had to compare outcomes for patients whose chemotherapy was chosen empirically (based on clinical trial literature) versus patients whose chemotherapy was guided by results of CSRAs. The studies did not have to randomly assign patients to either assay-guided or empiric therapy, but had to include a total of 20 or more patients per group. Criteria Questioned The director of a company that offers the assays, however, Robert A. Nagourney, MD, questioned the criteria used by the ASCO Working Group, the composition of the Working Group itself, and the fundamental definition of a chemosensitivity and resistance assay that they employed. Dr. Nagourney is Medical and Laboratory Director of Rational Therapeutics, Inc. of Long Beach, CA, and Medical Director of the Malcolm C. Todd Cancer Institute of Long Beach Memorial Center. Rational Therapeutics, Inc. is one of a handful of centers throughout the country that offer assays based on cell death as a measure of apoptosis. “In this review, the authors affixed new, ‘invented’ criteria for CSRAs,” he said in an interview. “Tests should be gauged according to their ability to discriminate between positive and negative results— that is, their sensitivity and specificity. Criteria for tests should not require that patients live longer. Tests such as CAT scans, estrogen receptor tests, and PSA tests would fail those criteria. Tests do not prolong life.” Dr. Nagourney was not asked to be part of the ASCO Working Group, and he said that none of the investigators who have developed CSRAs that examine cell death as a measure of apoptosis were asked to participate. “The Working Group consisted of reviewers who are experts in clonogenic and proliferative assays. One of the deficiencies of the two reports in the Journal of Clinical Oncology was that the review process did not include investigators who work with assays that measure cell death [apoptosis',” Dr. Nagourney stated.Figure: Robert A. Nagourney, MD, of Rational Therapeutics, one of a handful of centers throughout the country that offers assays based on cell death as a measure of apoptosis, questioned the criteria used by the ASCO assessment, as well as the composition of the Working Group itself and the definition used for a chemosensitivity and resistance assay: “They affixed new, ‘invented’ criteria for CSRAs. Tests should be gauged according to their ability to discriminate between positive and negative results—their sensitivity and specificity. Criteria for tests should not require that patients live longer. CAT scans, ER tests, and PSA tests would fail those criteria.”No Planned Exclusion Asked for a comment, Daniel D. Von Hoff, MD, Co-Chair with Dr. Schrag of the ASCO Working Group and author of several published studies of clonogenic CSRAs, replied that there was no attempt at planned exclusion of experts in apoptotic assays or against any type of assay. “We all want the same thing—the right answer!,” said Dr. Von Hoff, Director of the Cancer Therapeutics Program at Arizona Cancer Center. He added that there had originally been one Working Group member who was working with apoptotic assays, but that person resigned due to a conflict of interest. Dr. Nagourney took issue with the definition of CSRAs that was used upfront in the article, which states: “A chemosensitivity assay refers to any in vitro laboratory analysis that is performed specifically to evaluate whether tumor growth is inhibited by a known chemotherapy drug, or more commonly, a panel of drugs.” In fact, Dr. Nagourney said, after years of effort, it is now known that what an assay should measure is whether a drug achieves apoptosis. “There is a fundamental difference between tests that measure cell proliferation and those that measure apoptosis,” he said. “The definition used in this article is incorrect. Both [JCO” papers obscure this difference, which compromises the credibility of these papers. The authors do not understand why some tests work better than others. Responding to this critique, Dr. Von Hoff said, “He [Dr. Nagourney” may well be right. We need a well-designed, prospective clinical trial to determine whether an apoptotic or a clonogenic assay is better than what a clinician can select for his patients. Variety of Tests, Variety of Methodologies Studies of sensitivity and resistance assays are complicated, Dr. Schrag noted. Several types of assays are used to study a variety of cancers using different methodologies. Also, the types of tumor tissue vary from fresh to frozen to metastatic. Some of the papers included in the review focused on technically challenging assays, such as the human tumor cloning assay and the subrenal capsule assay. The Working Group agreed that this technology is not easily exportable to non-research settings. Another critique of simpler assays was lack of a reference standard or clear cutoff, with no standardization among the various types of tests. Additionally, the time it takes to obtain test results can pose a problem in settings when rapid initiation of therapy is necessary. The members of the Working Group raised several questions about CSRAs that have not been addressed in studies. This includes whether sampling tumor from multiple sites in the same patients would yield a similar chemotherapy sensitivity and resistance profile. Also, it is not clear whether sampling primary tumor or metastatic tumor from the same patient would yield the same results. In addition, tumors that are readily obtained might lead to a selection bias in favor of patients with a greater tumor burden. Finally, the Working Group stated that it is important to ascertain how often assay results affect the choice of chemotherapy agent. This type of information is unavailable in the literature, Drs. Schrag and Von Hoff and their colleagues said. They noted that CSRA test results often lead to selection of the same chemotherapy combination that would have been chosen empirically, which suggests the utility of the tests is limited. “I believe that oncologists are hungry to do the right thing for their patients. We don't want to deprive them of therapy that has been proven to improve survival. The fear is that assay-guided therapy will deprive patients of potentially curative therapy,” Dr. Von Hoff commented. In support of the recommendations by the Working Group, Dr. Schrag et al. stated, “The Working Group did not find that there are any CSRAs that are ready for routine integration into the clinical setting. The reasons for this are multifactorial and include the technical success and yield of the assays, the lack of adequate prospective evaluation of CSRAs in clinical trials, and the tendency of CSRAs to recommend treatments that would be given empirically.” Clinical Trials Lacking Dr. Nagourney, too, laments the lack of clinical trials of CSRAs. He says that he has repeatedly offered to donate assays that measure cell death to various cooperative groups, as well as give his time and that of other experts experienced in these techniques, and to help seek industry support for such a trial. Yet his requests for a trial have repeatedly met with refusal. “The Cooperative Groups have been approached, but they haven't risen to the challenge to test cell death endpoints, so they can't say that these tests don't work. If you don't do the studies, then you can't claim the evidence is not there. This amounts to suppressing the opposition. I am confident that an appropriately conducted study would have favorable results,” he said. In Dr. Von Hoff's view, though, the Cooperative Groups have turned down many good ideas, and there are numerous investigators with study proposals that don't get off the ground: “I've got a drawerful of what I think are good ideas that have been turned down by Cooperative Groups, but maybe their judgment is correct,” Dr. Von Hoff said.Figure: Daniel D. Von Hoff, MD: Dr. Nagourney may well be right [in his criticism' We need a well-designed, prospective clinical trial to determine whether an apoptotic or a clonogenic assay is better than what a clinician can select for his patients….I believe that oncologists are hungry to do the right thing for their patients. We don't want to deprive them of therapy that has been proven to improve survival. The fear is that assay-guided therapy will deprive patients of potentially curative therapy.'Dr. Nagourney emphasized that his explanation for the refusal on the part of the Cooperative Groups he has approached does not rest on blaming individuals. Rather, he believes that the “culture” continues to rely on empiric therapy and to treat the same type of cancer with the same chemotherapy agents, even though this approach has not changed outcomes in over 50 years. “These two articles in Journal of Clinical Oncology represent an effort by proponents of a failing paradigm to protect themselves. Dozens of papers and numerous Phase II studies have been published. In the aggregate, these studies show that cell death based assays work,” Dr. Nagourney said. The Web site for Dr. Nagourney's company (www.rationaltherapeutics. com, under “Clinical Experiences”) displays, among other information about the predictive accuracy of cell death assays in various tumor types, survival curves purporting to show that patients treated with assay-guided therapy had improved survival if their tumors were sensitive to the chemotherapy regimens used compared with patients whose tumors were found to be resistant. These survival curves, however, were not from prospective clinical trials (i.e., the studies did not fit the criteria used by the Working Group). Response from Cooperative Group In another interview, Norman Wolmark, MD, Chair of the National Surgical Adjuvant Breast and Bowel Project (NSABP), said, “The Cooperative Groups are deeply engaged in research on avenues we consider promising. We have taken a different direction, based on where we feel the important gains will be made. We are heavily invested in finding molecular markers that are predictive.” Dr. Wolmark is also Chairman of the Department of Human Oncology at Allegheny General Hospital in Pittsburgh and a member of OT's Editorial Board. Among the studies is an NSABP study (B40) being specifically designed to determine molecular parameters that would be predictive of pathological complete response in the preoperative setting. This study will use fresh tissue. Dr. Wolmark noted that the NSABP is also continuing studies with the genomic health assay, which uses paraffin-embedded tissue. A study using this assay in node-negative, receptor-positive breast cancer patients was presented by Soon Paik, MD, at this year's ASCO Annual Meeting and was among those spotlighted in a “Best of ASCO” session. “NSABP is continuing research using the genetic health assay to predict response to tamoxifen and chemotherapy, and we hope to present results at the San Antonio Breast Cancer Symposium in December,” Dr. Wolmark said. Future Studies Although the ASCO Working Group called for future studies to establish the utility of chemosensitivity and resistance assays, they acknowledged that none are planned. They suggested that technology such as gene microarrays be evaluated as a competing strategy for selecting features based on tumor biology. The companion article led by David J. Samson, MD, of Blue Cross Blue Shield also called for future research comparing assay-guided and empiric therapy in well-designed randomized trails measuring outcomes and using contemporary regimens. Dr. Samson and his colleagues also stated that gene expression profiles might have greater potential than CSRAs to guide the choice of chemotherapy regimens. Dr. Nagourney said he believes that research efforts would be better directed at supporting studies of cell death based assays. CSRAs, he says, are a relatively low-tech option that are intuitively inherently attractive, while gene expression profiles represent a high-tech approach that will cost more money and take years to develop. “Every day 1500 patients in the US die of cancer. Why force patients to await the possible arrival of high-tech approaches like gene arrays when robust assays based on cell death are readily available, inexpensive, and have had a favorable impact on the lives of thousands of patients already?,” he asked. Persevere, Persevere, Persevere with Research The biggest need is for clinical trials, Dr. Von Hoff said. “We had a window of opportunity. For 20 years we have been studying CSRAs, and we couldn't show that they improved survival. Now we have more sophisticated technology, and a number of investigators are trying to tackle the problem of how best to individualize therapy and improve survival. God bless the people who are continuing with these efforts!”

All faculty and staff in a position to control the content of this CME activity have disclosed that they have no financial relationships with, or financial interests in, any commercial companies pertaining to this educational activity. Learning Objectives: After reading this article, the physician should be able to: Discuss the central nervous system (CNS) conditions that can be investigated by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Describe the value of MRI for the evaluation of early multiple sclerosis. Summarize the incidence of cerebrovascular accident (CVA) in the acutely vertiginous adult patient. Release Date: May 2008 Given concerns with radiation-induced malignancies from the excessive use of CT scans, intuitively an alternative method of evaluation that does not entail ionizing radiation would be invaluable. The MRI scan has emerged like a miracle, but this test is not without its downsides, including cost, availability, some contraindications, and the time needed to perform the scan. A spiral CT takes only a few seconds these days, but an MRI is still a big project. Exactly why this is such a logistical issue with radiology still eludes many an emergency physician, however. Patients, on the other hand, are well versed on MRI testing, often demand it (many times inappropriately), and don't give a hoot about our logistical issues. MRI technology has progressed at a dizzying speed, and newer modalities and techniques continue to improve the clinical information gleaned from MRI. The imaging is based on the magnetization properties of atomic nuclei and the strength and direction of the microscopic magnetic field that surrounds the nucleus. Powerful magnets change the orientation of the proton nuclei of the hydrogen atoms in water by temporarily aligning the nuclei and causing them to rotate within a strong magnetic field. The changes in the alignment of protons and the rate at which the magnetization change returns to equilibrium (relaxation) can be measured by the radiofrequency signal, or echo, emitted by the protons as they relax. This magically translates into an image on the computer. The MRI uses two different phases of longitudinal and transverse proton shifts/relaxation (the time constants are termed T-1 and T-2 images) to evaluate various tissues. Advancing technology now uses diffusion and perfusion components and terms such as “FLAIR” and fast spin echo. When a gadolinium-based contrast agent is injected intravenously, blood flow in arteries (MRA) and veins (MRV) and in tissue characteristic of tumors and inflamed tissue are enhanced. The concepts are mind-boggling (they won a Nobel Prize) and way beyond the scope of this discussion.Figure: Most review articles warn that tattoos may be problematic with MRI. Older tattoo pigments contained iron oxides (especially black and blue inks), but newer inks usually do not. Homemade tattoos, such as those obtained in prison, may contain bits of metal. There is no way to prospectively identify tattoos at risk. The literature is vague and unreferenced, but theoretically a tattoo containing metallic oxides (not titanium) could be irritated or heated in an MRI or produce some local image distortion. This issue appears to be overrated, but readers' personal experiences would be welcome.MRI does not use ionizing radiation, and has not been shown to be harmful to humans (yet). Gadolinium contrast is often used, but it adds minimal clinical information for ED purposes, and increases the cost of MRI by about $400. (CT iodinated contrast adds about $100.) Gadolinium aids in the evaluation of tumors, first-time seizures, infection and inflammation, and vascular structures. This agent is renally excreted, nonradioactive, noniodinated, nonallergenic, and does not cause renal insufficiency. The thorny problem of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis from gadolinium will be discussed in later columns. For the emergency physician, it is important to know that newer technologies now change the applicability of the MRI. When reading the literature related to MRI, it is necessary to know what technology was used and if your hospital has that technology. It was once stated that MRI could not detect acute bleeding very well, but it is excellent at detecting intracerebral hemorrhage and subdural and epidural blood and less reliable at detecting subarachnoid hemorrhage. Although a CT may be preferred to evaluate the bony skull in head trauma, MRI is the modality of choice to evaluate bones in occult scaphoid or hip fractures. If it were not for the time and logistics of obtaining an MRI and ever-improving CT technology (64-slice detectors are now the norm), MRI would likely supplant CT in almost all instances, except perhaps for skull fractures and acute cervical spine trauma. While CT is still the gold standard for the ED evaluation of suspected acute CVA, MRI can be quite helpful in evaluating many aspects of stroke. Indications for Emergent MRI of the Central Nervous System Quint DJ JAMA 2000;283(7):853 The author from the University of Michigan reviews indications for emergent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This review is eight years old, so even more indications have evolved with technological advances. MRI is superior to CT and myelography for the early identification of nontraumatic spinal cord compression due to its ease of performance and ability to detect multiple lesions with minimal patient manipulation. It may demonstrate such lesions before a patient loses the ability to walk and when intervention is most likely to preserve ambulatory function. MRI also can identify treatable lesions in traumatic cord compression, although plain x-rays and CT are superior for fully characterizing spinal fractures. Dural venous sinus thrombosis, which inhibits drainage of blood from the brain and can lead to multifocal infarction, is also considered an indication for emergent MRI. These patients commonly present with headache and visual disturbance, but also may exhibit symptoms of seizures or stroke. Carotid/vertebral arterial dissection, another indication for emergent MRI, is most commonly due to trauma, but other causes include hypertension, vasculopathy, and local infection. Possible indications for emergent MRI include suspicion of meningoencephalitis or vasculitis, for which findings on lumbar puncture and CT can be nonspecific. Potentially (although probably not at present), MRI may be better than CT to demonstrate acute or subacute subarachnoid hemorrhage. Perfusion MRI can show evidence of infarction as soon as 20 minutes after symptom onset, and in combination with the diffusion scan, perfusion MRI can identify areas of the brain at acute risk when there is decreased blood flow in the absence of established infarction. Comment: For CNS pathology, MRI is the imaging modality of choice for the evaluation of most CNS pathology, and is superior to CT and myelography for the early detection of spinal cord lesions. Emergent MRI can detect multiple lesions with minimal patient manipulation. The sensitivity of the MRI may demonstrate lesions before irreversible neurological injury occurs from spinal cord abnormalities. The table lists CNS conditions best evaluated by MRI. Our knowledge of acute stroke is still in the prehistoric area, and nascent theories have been discredited or enhanced with MRI technology. This test promises to revolutionize stroke evaluation and treatment, and someday we will be called naïve dinosaurs for relying on the CT scan, unless of course, the 2000-slice spiral scan is invented. Right now, though, an MRI is not used in the ED evaluation of acute CVA; it remains a backup test, usually for the inpatient, but stay tuned for further developments. Cranial artery dissection, vasculitis, and dural sinus thrombosis are rare clinical enigmas clarified with MRI. Even considering these unusual conditions is a clinical coup, so one could make an argument for doing MRI in all patients with headache, confusion, or unusual neurological findings. Our MRI is booked weeks in advance, and pandering to an obstreperous radiologist to get an emergent MRI is a distasteful yet ubiquitous endeavor. Why the MRI is not more available is a mystery to me and most patients. I do, however, remember when it also took an act of Congress to get a stat CT. Accuracy of Magnetic Resonance Imaging for the Diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis: Systematic Review Whiting P, et al Brit Med J 2006;332:875 A diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS) generally requires the occurrence of neurological dysfunction at different points in time involving different parts of the central nervous system (implying the presence of multiple lesions). Because these episodes are often separated by years, the diagnosis can be substantially delayed. Criteria purport to permit a diagnosis of MS after a single clinical attack if the patient also meets selected criteria on magnetic resonance imaging. These European authors reviewed the findings of 29 studies of MRI for an MS diagnosis (18 cohort studies and 11 studies with other design types). Methodological quality of the studies was generally considered to be poor, particularly with regard to blinding, use of an appropriate reference standard, duration of follow-up (which did not exceed three years in most studies), and availability of clinical information. Among the 15 studies with higher methodological quality, longer duration of follow-up was associated with lower sensitivity but higher specificity. The overall accuracy of MRI was substantially lower, however, in the higher quality studies. The presence of many lesions on MRI did not reliably rule in MS (positive likelihood ratios 2.0 for more than eight lesions and 3.0 for more than 10 lesions), and neither was MS reliably excluded by the absence of lesions on MRI (negative likelihood ratios 0.5 and 0.1). The author concludes that high-quality studies with longer duration of follow-up suggest that MRI is only somewhat accurate for the early diagnosis of MS after a single neurological episode. Comment: Most clinicians would intuit that the diagnosis of MS is rather easy with the use of MRI, but this article says that's not so. Early MS is a very difficult diagnosis because neurological dysfunction, often admittedly quite bizarre symptoms, occurs at different times and in various areas of the CNS due to multiple lesions. Waxing and waning of unusual symptoms (numbness all over, lost vision that returned) can delay the diagnosis for years. Advanced MS is readily detected by MRI, but following a single MS neurological event, MRI is only modestly accurate. It's easy to confuse MS with an evolving CVA, atypical migraine, numerous neuropathies, psychiatric conditions, and a plethora of metabolic abnormalities, but, the MRI is the diagnostic savior in evolved cases. Remember that MS is a disease of the young and of women who often may not be taken seriously, and it is punctuated with subjective symptoms that cannot be verified. I have seen MS present as only “numb from the neck down,” acute vertigo, “can't move my left arm,” urinary retention, eye pain/optic neuritis, and presentations that screamed conversion reaction to everyone in the ED. Isolated Acute Vertigo in the Elderly: Vestibular or Vascular Disease? Norrving B, et al Acta Neurol Scand 1995;91(1):43 In elderly patients, acute vertigo accompanied by nystagmus, nausea, and vomiting without other neurological abnormalities (representing “isolated vertigo”) is frequently considered to be a benign and self-limiting condition not requiring extensive diagnostic evaluation. In some patients, isolated vertigo also may be caused by potentially serious central pathology. This prospective Swedish study examined findings in 24 patients aged 50 to 75 with apparent acute “isolated vertigo” in the absence of previous vestibular symptoms or history of transient ischemic attack or stroke. The patients were evaluated with MRI (22 cases) or acute-phase CT scanning (two cases), in addition to electro-oculography and Doppler studies of the vertebral, basilar, carotid, and periorbital arteries. Infarcts of the caudal cerebellum were diagnosed in six patients (25%). Potential cardioembolic sources were identified in three of those six, and Doppler studies demonstrated ipsilateral vertebral artery occlusion in the remaining three. Cerebellar infarctions were characteristically associated with ataxic pursuit eye movements on electro-oculography (noted in four of six cases). On follow-up, which ranged from three to 33 months after initial presentation (median, 24.5 months), eight patients had been placed on either anticoagulants (two) or aspirin (six). One patient with an initially normal MRI but unilateral vertebral artery occlusion on Doppler sonography had experienced a stroke (representing an annual incidence of 2.5%). Cerebellar infarctions may be responsible for signs and symptoms in about one-fourth of patients presenting with apparent acute isolated vertigo. titulo: With Prehospital Intubation So Problematic, Experts Say It May Hurt Patients More than Help
palavras_openalex: out-of-hospital intubation | prehospital airway management | paramedics | rapid sequence intubation | laryngeal mask airway | Combitube | emergency medical services | airway management training
resumo: Is it time to turn back the clock on out-of-hospital intubation? Henry Wang, MD, an assistant professor of emergency medicine at the University of Pittsburgh, thinks maybe it is. And he is far from alone. This past year, Dr. Wang and five colleagues, published an analysis of the successes and failures of endotracheal intubation outside of hospital. The data paint a startling picture. Though they were careful to couch their findings in reasonable, even polite, language, there is no mistaking the implication. The portrait that emerges suggests over-reliance on field personnel who either have too few opportunities to maintain their skills or who are being called on to accomplish a procedure for which they have not been well prepared. “I think we are more pessimistic than other groups,” he conceded, acknowledging that his forecast for the situation is gloomier. Dr. Wang said the statistics are unlikely to change unless technical advances decrease the margin of error in field-related airway management. Already, that seems to be the case in some settings, he said. The situation, while still being debated in some circles of medicine, has garnered attention from some medical manufacturers busy developing and refining devices that strive to make airway management easier for all members of the rescue team. Two years ago, German investigators compared some of these devices in a formal study, finding that layngeal masks and combitubes proved a reliable form of technology for emergency airway management (Emerg Med J 2001;18:90). “I think we are more pessimistic than other groups.” Dr. Henry Wang When Dr. Wang and his co-investigators looked at what factors were likely to interfere with successful intubation, topping the list was the inability of emergency personnel to pass an endotracheal tube through the vocal cords and the difficulty in some cases of visualizing them enough to guide the procedure (Acad Emerg Med 2003;10:717). The findings came from an unusual multi-center database called the Prehospital Airway Collaborative Evaluation, which is being used to take periodic snapshots of the track record of out-of-hospital intubation. The data seem to affirm a situation some emergency physicians have long lamented, that conventionally trained rescuers such as paramedics often fail in their attempts to intubate patients successfully. Failure Rates Unlike those who suggest privately that paramedics aren't always effective in providing rapid-sequence intubation (RSI), Dr. Wang has put his moniker on a potentially powerful mouthpiece, the Annals of Emergency Medicine, where his editorial on the subject seems to lay out the issues in a critical, thought-provoking way. He and his colleague, Donald Yealy, MD, note that research on RSI shows a failure rate of 15 percent, and they state that field airway success rates have not changed substantially in 20 years (Ann Emerg Med 2002;40;168). They ask: “Can we accept this failure rate when performing RSI – or any other field procedure?” Now they are getting some answers to that question, though not the kind likely to end the debate. Daniel Davis, MD, an author of what is arguably the most compelling and the most controversial research on the topic and an assistant professor of emergency medicine at the University of California San Diego, has been part of the San Diego Paramedic RSI trial, which is tracking and analyzing out-of-hospital intubation data. He and lead author James Dunford, MD, along with three other investigators from the institution, have shown a relatively high rate of desaturation in patients with severe head injuries who undergo paramedic-administered RSI. The bottom line: Two years' worth of data indicate a higher mortality for patients undergoing RSI by paramedics. Perhaps most alarming, they also have found that RSI is described as easy by paramedics in a majority of cases in which desaturation has occurred (Ann Emerg Med 2003;42:721). “Here is a study on the issue, and it shows [patients] may actually do worse” with RSI, Dr. Davis said. But that shouldn't prompt anything but more research, he stressed. He said there is fairly definitive proof that out-of-hospital endotracheal intubation can, in fact, do more harm than good in some cases. But because his own study results seem to show that the greater degree of hyperventilation, the worse the outcome, that is a pretty good reason to keep on investigating RSI, Dr. Davis said.FigureThere are several possibilities that might explain the difference in outcome, but it remains unclear which one is the cause, or if the cause is multifactorial. Is it a function of the ability of technical support in the field? Overly broad patient selection for intubation? Lack of adequate training of personnel? Or is it the fact that head injury patients with hypoxia are intubated routinely, without seeking factors that might rule out some patients? All of these variables need to be taken into account, said Dr. Davis. “Here is a study on the issue, and it shows [patients] may actually do worse” with RSI. Dr. Daniel Davis In the future, there may be greater use of risk stratification for patients, refinements and improvements in training personnel who administer endotracheal intubation, and greater understanding of the role that CO2 monitoring can play in gauging when and how to remove the tube. Determining when RSI is most advantageous is the only way “the benefits of intubation will shine through,” Dr. Davis said. Inadequate Data In yet another editorial that appeared last year on the topic, Daniel Spaite, MD, and Elizabeth Criss, MD, both from the department of emergency medicine at the University of Arizona in Tucson, observe that there aren't good data on the utilization of intubation by paramedic teams (Ann Emerg Med 2003;42:729). Yet, “despite the absence of proof that out-of-hospital intubation is safe and effective, … there has been little controversy about the appropriateness of its use.” As many different articles on endotracheal intubation suggest, the procedure makes a lot of intuitive sense. When used properly, it enhances oxygenation and ventilation and maintains the flow of a compromised airway, unarguably a benefit to a patient with breathing difficulty. Drs. Spaite and Criss stress that the vast majority of positive findings have accrued from retrospective studies, which have relied largely on self-reports by emergency medical service personnel. The two note that essentially “no EMS intervention has been prospectively evaluated with robust methodologies that allow us to conclude that safety has been established, let alone effectiveness.” The pair dub this the Mount Everest approach, explaining, “When asked why we are implementing new therapies and procedures in the out-of-hospital setting, our answer is, in essence, ‘Because it is there.’” Does that mean throwing in the towel on intubation? Not according to some emergency physicians. By instituting protocols that avoid complications, these incidents can be severely curtailed, asserted Salvatore Silvestri, MD, who presented a study this past May at the annual meeting of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine on the effects of continuous CO2 monitoring, which showed the addition of this step makes a difference. In contrast to interpreting some findings as support for abandoning out-of-hospital intubation, his group's results show a way “to prevent unrecognized endotracheal tube misplacement,” said Dr. Silvestri, the medical director of the Orange County Florida EMS system. The solution? “More monitoring,” he said. In fact, the misplacement rate was 23 percent in a group of patients which was not monitored compared with less than one percent in a group that had continual CO2 monitoring, he said. Criticism of RSI In some ways, the debate over RSI is beginning to parallel the kinds of criticisms currently seen in other non-medical settings. Emergency medicine, at least in this case, may be taking a cue from corporate America in finding the answer. This past year, the Annals of Emergency Medicine had more than page count in common with the Harvard Business Review. Both journals delved into the ramifications that can occur during self-reporting outcomes. Neither had to look far to demonstrate how this process rolls along without garnering much suspicion. And it happens because a procedure — whether it is a marketing technique or a clot-busting drug — has been proven beneficial in one set of circumstances, so it is perceived to be of use in related situation. EMS may rely too heavily on field personnel who have too few opportunities to maintain their skills or who have not been well prepared to perform RSI Exporting a successful strategy in one setting may mean failure in another by not taking into account important variables, namely and perhaps most importantly, the different people involved in implementation. In late 2003, three Harvard professors looked at the biases that can influence bad, even unethical, business decision-making. Among them is “implicit prejudice,” in which associations that seem to go together receive acceptance of a successful hand-in-hand relationship, which they call the thunder and rain bias. Included in their countdown of inherent biases is the problem of in-group favoritism, in which credibility is assigned to those who already are part of the system or group. They also point out a silent bias known as overclaiming credit, in which people consider themselves to be better at things than they really are and to contribute more than they actually do (Harvard Business Review 2003;312D:56). Could the same sort of biases be playing a role in RSI? In interviews about the recent findings regarding out-of-hospital endotracheal intubation, some common criticisms emerge. The first is that EMS reviews on RSI, particularly when they are the basis for documenting success, may put such data on shaky ground. Secondly, because it has become widely reported that endotracheal intubation saves lives and protects morbidity, there hasn't been much research devoted to establishing whether that is true. The third is that, as the San Diego group seems to have found, EMS personnel seem to think they do a good job of endotracheal intubation even when their patients clearly are experiencing complications. All of the work that led to such perplexing findings really began more than five years ago when prospective researchers from the San Diego group approached the state and county EMS system for approval. Public officials responded that they needed to see data substantiating that early endotracheal intubation was appropriate. In 1997, the investigators established through retrospective study that there was a probable difference in outcome. A prospective study was approved and carried out from 1998 to 2002, and the results of that study showed reason for worry that RSI, at least in some cases, is associated with a worse outcome, when it was performed by paramedics. Then, a subset analysis suggested a difference in outcomes between field paramedics and aeromedical teams. The results also showed a high rate of hypoxia during the procedure and inadvertent hyperventilation, which was found more often in paramedic teams and was associated with worse outcomes, Dr. Davis said. Perhaps, as some authors in emergency medicine suggest, the answer lies not just with better training but with more standardized protocols. As Michele Blanda, MD, and Ugo Gallo, MD, observed in a comprehensive evaluation of the issue last year, a standard definition for airway management has yet to be identified, and so far, endotracheal intubation is generally regarded rather loosely as a clinical situation in which a health care provider experiences difficulty with ventiliation, laryngoscopy, or tracheal intubation. They observed: “There is strong evidence that specific strategies facilitate management of the difficult airway. Although the exact degree of benefit cannot be determined, there is strong agreement that a pre-formulated strategy will lead to improved outcomes.”

titulo: How James Wright Wasted His Life
palavras_openalex: James Wright | pastoral poetry | social criticism | poetics of failure | John Crowe Ransom
resumo: Intelligent reviewers have often found my books wanting, and so have I. I do not want to get revenge on the universe because I am not Dante or Shakespeare. I do believe that the labors of a minor poet have value.1 Despite what he says to Dave Smith in this letter of September 8, 1975, James Wright wasn’t a minor poet. But he was hard on himself. He criticized his old poems severely, stated his desire to “trim … away” his formerly “lush” language, and dismissed all of Two Citizens as a mistake.2 After translating the works of Trakl, Vallejo, and Neruda among others, Wright exchanged New Critical formalism for intuitive free verse. Many of the qualities that began to surface in 1963's The Branch Will Not Break (and in his suppressed collection, Amenities of Stone) were always present in his writing; Andrew Elkins describes Wright as a poet on a coherent quest, from the beginning of his career, for a type of spiritual wholeness antithetical to modern society.3 Yet it is clear both from his verse and his letters that Wright had a passion for the conversive. It was important to him to fail, dramatically, and then see things in a new light—his was a poetics of necessarily wasted endeavor. This article argues that Wright’s characterization of himself as a “minor” and intensely self-critical poet actually gave him the authority he required to write a type of pastoral which functions as social critique. As he insists that “the labors of a minor poet have value,” he playfully characterizes Dante and Shakespeare as the literary equivalents of Hercules while using, like his Kenyon tutor John Crowe Ransom, the language of labor to insist on forms of “value,” which are not those of the market and may in fact be opposed to economic priorities. Wright’s most famous poem, “Lying in a Hammock at William Duffy’s Farm in Pine Island, Minnesota,” crystallizes phrases we find scattered throughout his work. It is as if he were trying over and over to write this poem—even after he had already written, and published it. It has proved to be perhaps his most controversial lyric—even more so than “A Poem About George Doty in the Death House,” in which the immature poet suggests, with Larkinian perversity, that the Ohioan rapist-killer suffered more than the “homely girl” he killed. That poem fails to survive Wright’s own ethics in “At the Executed Murderer’s Grave”: “Doty, if I confess I do not love you, / Will you let me alone? I burn for my own lies.”4 Yet it is precisely this kind of self-criticism which has been objected to in the final line of “Lying in a Hammock”: Both his alcoholism and mental illness, and his shifting between formal verse and something more prosaic, link Wright to other mid-century American poets. Yet he depicts a certain type of crisis experience—and the subsequent return to the world—with a flayed surety unlike anyone else. In an interview of 1972 with Michael André, he defends the close of his poem, at the risk of shrinking its significance. “People have been outraged by this,” he says, because they think the last line of it is immoral. The last line is not immoral. The poem is only descriptive … All I did was describe what I felt and what I saw lying there in the hammock. Shouldn’t that be enough? … “I have wasted my life”—well, that’s the way I happened to feel at the moment. Actually, I haven’t wasted my life.6 We might in fact see Wright's agonized talk of morality as responsive to the hidden motivations of his critical opponents. Thom Gunn's scientific coolness, in his discussion of “Lying in a Hammock,” masks a rather macho disapproval of thought not finding its outlet in action. (How different is Wright’s refusal of striving, his nuanced acceptance of the present moment, to Gunn’s aphorism in “On the Move”: “One is always nearer by not keeping still.”)10 Gunn argues that the final line of Wright's poem is perhaps exciting because we are surprised to encounter something so different from the rest of the poem, but it is certainly meaningless. The more one searches for an explicit meaning in it, the vaguer it becomes. Other general statements of different import could well be substituted for it and the poem would neither gain nor lose strength.11 Wright cedes too much ground to Gunn when he defends his poem as simply a train of personal associations, and his last line as the thought of a moment. This leaves him vulnerable to the charge he himself makes in a letter of October 29, 1977 to Hayden Carruth: “I think that a fallacy pervades American verse these days, worse than a fallacy, a real curse; and it might be stated thus: I am a poet; and therefore anything which I happen to write is a poem.”15 Despite a taste for transcendence, and for consciously poetic language, Wright is more cautious than this, and has larger aims for his verse. The Branch Will Not Break and Shall We Gather At The River (1968) construct a contaminated pastoral which flirts with surrealism as it tries to imagine not an escape from, but an alternative to, the resumo: In recent years, Japan Drilling Co., Ltd. (JDC), the sole offshore drilling company in Japan, operates most of its rig fleets outside Japan. Competing against foreign drilling companies as the unique drilling company based in the resource-limited country like Japan, we would say that one of JDC's strengths on human resources aspect would come from the policy on the management of employees that (1) JDC deploys mainly Japanese employees under lifetime employment system for the prominent positions of the rigs such as a Drilling Superintendent, a Barge Superintendent, Chief Engineer/Electrician and so on and also that (2) JDC does utmost effort to minimize layoff of foreign employees as much as possible during the idol period of the rig unlike other foreign drilling companies which, it's just like they say, often do so, and we believe that such way of management eventually leads the drilling operations stable and also leads to receive recognitions from the clients in the world.On the other hand, in its medium-term management plan JDC also recognizes the polarization in the generation of rig employees as the one of most urgent and important issues to be tackled. JDC is therefore making its best effort (1) to recruit competent employees especially to secure talented new-graduates majored in the engineering faculty and (2) to train/foster and develop career of such fresh employees rapidly so that we can accelerate a generational change in proper timing.Securing workforce and career development are an important issues not only for Japanese employees but also for non-Japanese employees however due to limitations of space, it is focused on how JDC tackles such issues on young Japanese employees including new-graduates this time.

resumo: JOSEPH V. SIMONE, MD, President of Simone Consulting (Simone Consulting.com), has had leadership roles at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, Huntsman Cancer Institute, Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, the University of Florida Shands Cancer Center, the National Comprehensive Cancer Network, and the National Cancer Policy Board and has served on the NCI's Board of Scientific Advisors. He welcomes comments and suggestions for future topics for his column. E-mail him at [email protected]The mantras in health care today go something like this: The cost of healthcare is growing fast and is not sustainable. Doctors are responsible for this dilemma because they are paid and incentivized for doing more technical procedures, giving more medicine, and ordering more tests, which too often incur unnecessary costs. Patients, especially those with advanced solid cancers, and their families are responsible because they have unreasonable expectations for success. Pharmaceutical companies are responsible because they charge exorbitantly for new agents, some of which provide no benefit or marginal benefit. Patient advocates are responsible because they promote more therapy. Congress is responsible because it doesn't have the will to face this issue except with partisan demagoguery (“death panels”) to frighten people and stifle the search for and implementation of science-based cost reductions. President Obama is responsible because his health reform plan adds more patients to the insured ranks. One definition of mantra is, “a sacred verbal formula repeated in incantation, such as a magic spell, containing mystical potentialities.” That is what the verbal traffic about health care sounds like to me today. It is as if pointing the finger and shouting will somehow: (a) fix the problem; (b) put the blame on someone else, thus absolving the finger-pointer of any responsibility; or (c) add to the shouting chaos so that no change will take place, at least in that aspect involving the finger-pointer directly. One also may look at the op-ed pages of the New England Journal of Medicine each week and reliably find another article or two by economists or policy wonks that contain The Solution(s) to the problem. That solutions may contradict one other is a tribute to the Journal editors' lack of bias, but it doesn't help one understand what can be done practically to reduce costs without sacrificing the quality of care while reducing the quantity of care. But the 26 May 2011 issue of the Journal has a “Sounding Board” piece that I do understand: “Bending the Cost Curve in Cancer Care,” by Dr. Thomas Smith, an oncologist, and Dr. Bruce Hillner, a health services researcher. The authors offer recommendations for lowering the cost of cancer care that are feasible, practical, specific, and humane. To be sure, the recommendations would be difficult to carry out because of those who simply chant the mantras or see the issue only in political terms or personal financial terms. The authors offer 10 recommendations—five deal with changes in oncologists' behavior and five with changes in attitudes and practice more generally. I can provide only a brief summary here, so read the article for the detailed supporting evidence and rationale (http://healthpolicyandreform.nejm.org/?p=14541) Recommendations for Oncologists Recommendations for oncologists from the authors (“Unless otherwise stated, our recommendations are restricted to the care of patients with incurable solid tumors and not those with curable cancers”): Target [restrict] surveillance testing or imaging to situations in which a benefit has been shown. Limit second-line and third-line treatment for metastatic cancer to sequential monotherapies for most solid tumors. Limit chemotherapy to patients with good performance status, with an exception for highly responsive disease. Replace the use of white-cell stimulating factors with a reduction in the chemotherapy dose in metastatic solid cancers. For patients who are not responding to three consecutive regimens, limit further chemotherapy to clinical trials. Recommendations for Changing Attitudes & Practice: Oncologists need to recognize that the costs of care are driven by what we do and what we do not do. Both doctors and patients need to have more realistic expectations. Realign compensation to value cognitive services, rather than chemotherapy, more highly. Better integrate palliative care into usual oncology care (concurrent care). The need for cost-effectiveness analysis and for some limits on care must be accepted. Sounds good, but does this have a chance of going somewhere? After all, these measures are not new and not very radical. Each recommendation has been raised in some form at meetings, in practices, and in publications. So why might it be timely and how would it be implemented? I feel the same about this as I did when my colleagues and I started the Quality Oncology Practice Initiative (QOPI) through ASCO. Ten years ago one could see the push for quality measures growing after several reports from the Institute of Medicine decried the uneven and sometimes poor quality of cancer care and the lack of efforts to measure quality. We had two firm convictions from the start of QOPI that also apply to the cost/care conundrum today. First, we oncologists had to take the lead in this activity or risk government or industry imposing some form of “quality” system on us. That has proved to be the right decision, and both government and industry have shown respect for the QOPI effort. QOPI is a leader in developing a system for addressing the quality of cancer care. Second, since it seems inevitable that the cost of cancer care must decline or at least stop climbing, oncologists are the best advocates for patients and in the best position to know what is essential and what is not in cancer care since they have the experience and prompt, routine access to scientific publications that address these issues. It is my view, therefore, that oncologists should take the lead in building a structure and a plan for controlling the cost of cancer care. It won't be easy and there will be many naysayers among us. But as was true for QOPI, we have a responsibility for shaping a system of high-quality cancer care that is humane, scientifically based when possible, and free of the wasteful and excessively costly use of resources, both human and financial. If we don't do it, someone will impose a system on our patients and us. And there is a good chance that neither would like the result.

titulo: Remembering 1968, Professionally, Personally, & Historically
