resumo: In this European Public Health news, we present updates from EUPHA, the EUPHA working group on gender equality, WHO Europe and the upcoming European Public Health Conference. Zeegers and Nagyova reflect on the increase in polarization in the world which has been highlighted by the COVID-19 pandemic. Petelos et al. present the work EUPHA has been developing on gender equality. Something that should be totally obvious, but still needs specific attention, so that gender equality is accepted and implemented everywhere. Kluge et al. reflect on the future of digital public health, one of the priorities of WHO Europe. Digital health is no longer an option, it is essential. Barnhoorn and Staines highlight the excellent plenary programme of the 2021 European Public Health Conference, where digital health, communication, lessons learned from COVID-19 and climate change are all being addressed. In July, a famous Dutch crime reporter was killed in the streets of Amsterdam and a 14-year-old Dutch girl was beaten for not answering a question on her gender. Why? Because they were both—in their own way—outspoken and open, something that seems to be no longer accepted in this polarized society. In the society today, you are either from the North Pole or from the South Pole. The fact that 99.9% of people actually live between those two extremes seems no longer relevant. We learn from our world that a fragile balance between the two poles is essential to have a flourishing global society. Our world exists because the two poles make earth a liveable place for the population, but it is clear that living only on two poles will destroy this fragile balance. So why is society more and more polarizing? A first factor here is the media. If you are on Internet looking for ‘the lies on climate change’ (this would be a clear search for fake news), the search engines will mostly display articles and websites in that direction. But if you want to do another search on climate change, the Internet/Google will direct you back to the fake news sites. Which leaves individuals only a very limited choice while reconfirming their thoughts on climate change. Television channels (for those who still watch normal television) are also polarized, clearly shown by the fact that CNN was against Trump and Fox News was in favour. And this to an unprecedented extreme, clearly lacking any critical reflections and based solely on being a Trump supporter or not. This culminated in an unprecedented riot to take over congress. On social media, we see more and more polarization of messages. You are either in favour of vaccination or against, there no longer is a middle road. And those against vaccination seem to be discontented individuals who want to be heard. The fact that Martin McKee, public health expert by example, receives death threats via twitter should be unacceptable, but it still continues. It is true that Twitter has taken some measures to counter ‘fake news’, but it may be too little too late. A second factor is politics. In several countries, a bi-party political system is still in place (USA and UK) and this automatically leads to polarization. You are either for increased taxes for the rich or against, there is no political middle. Debates on important topics like health care for all are quickly reduced to yes or no. No alternatives. If we look at the US elections last year, it is clear that polarization of politics can easily spiral out of control. But even in countries as the Netherlands, with the famous polder model of compromise at political level, we can see a development towards increased polarization. And a third factor is the unbalance between individual’s rights and societal rules, which we are clearly seeing with COVID-19. Even though anyone you ask will have sympathy for the higher risk groups, a large majority is against restrictions on individual rights. The whole discussion whether to vaccinate the world (see our statement together with WEMOS on worldwide access to vaccines, https://eupha.org/repository/advocacy/EUPHA%20-%20Wemos%20statement.pdf, last accessed 10 August 2021) or whether the priority should be a third jab for ‘our’ citizens is a clear example of a preference for individual rights and nationalistic thinking. And this whole polarization is clearly visible in the field of public health as well. Public health is a field where already the description of public health as promoting and protecting the health of people and communities hints at polarization. You advise and you take protective measures. And these protective measures restrict the individual’s right to freedom and are therefore up for discussion in politics and in the media. Public health professionals are both criticized for proposing restrictive measures and ignored in the whole dealing with the COVID-19 pandemic. And this is a pity, as public health professionals are trained and thus have the competencies to be at the forefront of public health issues, including pandemics. The world needs to turn away from the North and South poles and the world’s population needs to use reasoning before reaching any conclusions. Reasoning is defined as ‘the act or process of drawing conclusions from facts, evidence, etc.’ (https://www.thefreedictionary.com/reasoning, last accessed 10 August 2021). It is the job of public health professionals to make sure that the media, the politicians and the population have access to the right facts and sound evidence. On International Women’s Day, the Director of the World Health Organisation for Europe (WHO EURO) released a statement highlighting the need to build back better, with women in the lead,1 with emphasis on diminishing the severe socioeconomic impact of COVID-19 on women, on ensuring their involvement on COVID-19 prevention and control decision-making and on enhancing social support, prevention, detection and treatment for women at risk of domestic abuse. On the same day, EUPHA announced the formation of the Working Group on Gender Equality and on Women’s Empowerment (SDG5 WG) to comprehensively map the needs, the priorities, and the key actioning areas in European and global public health, to achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls to meet Sustainable Development Goal 5 (SDG5) of the United Nations (UN).2 Even though some of the most developed countries in the world are found in the European Region, reports of violence against women show a dramatic increase across Europe, coupled with compromised or disrupted access to services because of the pandemic. The report of the European Institute on Gender Equality on gender-based violence (GBV) reports that, when the pandemic hit, no EU Member-State had a gender-sensitive preparedness plan in place to address a potential surge in terms of violence against women.3 We have seen awareness campaigns across EU Member-States, but the inability to adequately support affected women constitutes a human rights violation, rather than being a private issue.4,5 We have yet to see pan-European and, indeed, globally coordinated efforts to protect women from violence at work and at home, and to allow them unhindered access to the services needed to support them even—particularly—at times of crisis. Less than half of countries in the WHO and UN Global Status Report on Violence Prevention report availability of mental health services to address victims’ needs, with two-thirds of countries in the Region of the Americas and the European Region and only 15% in the African Region. We cannot expect women to lead across communities when their existence is continuously threatened. It is, therefore, essential to ensure the global effort to prioritize access to all necessary services; these should be co-developed with women across communities, researchers and practitioners. The cost of inaction extends well beyond those directly affected posing concrete risks to societal wellbeing and cohesion. Members of our global public health community must unite their voices and lead this effort to change policymaking priorities. Recognizing the messages already coming from many members across our communities, members of EUPHA’s SDG5 WG took the opportunity to raise awareness and broker interdisciplinary dialogue organizing an extended plenary to conclude the activities of the International Festival of Public Health dedicated to Women’s Health. Many speakers highlighted the need for horizontal and vertical measures and the importance of cross-sectoral, interdisciplinary collaboration to re-align policies and political agendas, and to monitor actions and progress with appropriate indicators. The importance of different determinants at interplay and the role of legislative frameworks and the judicial system was mentioned as key to tackling lesser-known public health issues such as structural violence against women, a critical aspect we have to overcome to meet SDG5. Structural violence stemming from social arrangements requires a shift on how we address GBV, including in terms of the social, political and economic organization of our world.6,7 The pandemic has brought to the fore the large gender gaps in the quality of employment, especially for women working in the care sectors. Care Economy is expanding, but care work is characterized by a void of benefits and protections, low-wage or non-compensation agreements,8 and increased exposure to physical, mental and even sexual harm. Pre-pandemic trends, with high concentration of women in jobs with low wages, long working hours, limited opportunities for career advancement, and exposure to occupational health and safety risks, resulted in unprecedented collateral damage during the pandemic.9 These effects have often been compounded by violence and harassment, at work and at home. In a timely effort, the International Labour Organisation (ILO) Violence and Harassment Convention, 2019 (Policy No. 190), entering into force on 25 June 2021, provides a clear and useful framework for tackling violence and harassment in the world of work that ranges from prevention to protection, enforcement and remedies, training and awareness raising.10 The Generation Equality Forum (30 June–2 July 2021) launched a 5-year action journey to achieve irreversible progress towards gender equality. We note the momentum, the unprecedented financial commitments (40 billion USD), and the emphasis on GBV, the Care Economy and climate justice. With the launch of the Compact on Women, Peace and Security and Humanitarian Action, we believe the time to mobilize the global public health community, researchers and practitioners alike, in concerted, concrete and sustainable actioning is now. At the time where women’s solidarity is gaining momentum across the world, we tend to be more focused on celebrating progress. We, however, need to acknowledge the backward effect that will take years to counter and the role political choices make in terms of placing women at risk; our sisters in Afghanistan are at peril not for gender equality, but for survival. We note the complete absence of explicit pledges relating to human rights and the protection of the status of women in the Doha Agreement despite the well documented extensive atrocities against women. This threatens rolling back decades of work on public health, poses a threat to global health security and to any peace process too. Never have there been stronger voices to protect the rights of women and girls to health and education and never had we more opportunities to come together as a global public health community. We need to move to action to demonstrate the criticality of addressing these issues for sustainable development and to ensure resilience and prosperity for all people, communities and societies. On behalf of the EUPHA working group on gender equality and women’s empowerment. The SARS-CoV-2 virus has spurred renewed interest and action globally for the digital transformation of health services and public health. COVID-19 is a watershed moment for digital health: the ways in which digital tools and data have enabled us to follow, adapt and mitigate the effects of the pandemic are unprecedented. COVID-19 has shown us that the future of digital public health is here. And it’s here to stay. The leaps in the real-world application of digital health we have witnessed in recent months would have been unthinkable in pre-pandemic times. Digital tools have brought care to remote and disconnected areas; people have benefited from mental health support, often delivered remotely through digital tools; patients have accessed life-saving medicines digitally, at times making paper prescriptions obsolete; healthcare professionals have been able to review data and treat patients in novel and inclusive ways. These advances, coupled with a well-developed digital infrastructure, high levels of digital literacy and the availability of trusted public health information sources, have saved lives and empowered millions to make informed decisions about their health. It is clear that there is no going back. However, having all populations able to realize this promising future is an elusive, long-term undertaking that is further complicated by entrenched societal inequalities that delay or prevent access to the benefits that digitalization can offer. On one hand, some countries have been able to boast pandemic responses underpinned by prior strategic investments in integrated public health and primary care systems, supported by advanced digital structures and a digitally savvy health workforce. Others have struggled to achieve even rudimentary levels of access to health data, with entire populations—including health workers themselves—lacking basic digital tools and skills, compounded by the absence of data governance. The reasons for these disparities are self-evident: the burden of existing inequalities, coupled with systemic underinvestment in the digital training of health workers and lagging digital transformation in primary care are resulting in millions of people being left behind. That is why we need to work proactively to ensure that the positives of digitalization are distributed equitably within and between countries and that we leverage new innovations to strengthen the resilience of populations to combat health threats of the future. WHO/Europe’s Programme of Work (EPW) is driven by the mission and commitment of leaving no one behind. And progress in digital health is at the heart of this commitment. Firstly, embarking upon the path of digital health transformation requires establishing strong governance for digital health to avoid perpetuating existing socio-economic inequities. Progress is not only about finding and applying new tools; it is also about ensuring that everyone can benefit from them equally. Indeed, empowerment through digital health is a flagship of the EPW focusing on digital health solutions that preserve health equity, gender equality and human rights. The outputs of this flagship initiative aim to strengthen public health and primary care in countries through enhanced surveillance capacity and accelerated action to improve population resilience and mitigate the impact of health security threats. Second, while COVID-19 has removed some of the barriers to digital health adoption, it has shown us the importance of having timely access to health data electronically to ensure an informed, consistent and measured health system response to pandemics. Governments, academia, the private sector and all other key stakeholders need to agree that the open and transparent sharing of information is key to identifying those segments of the population who are most at risk, to create more efficient and responsive health systems, and to achieve better health outcomes for our populations. Clearly, if we are to achieve public health goals and effectively predict and mitigate future threats, we are dependent upon data without borders—data and analytics that can be transferred into action. Third, to ensure accountability and sustainability long-term, we need political commitment: where scientific knowledge is brought into the political forum, protected as a public good and safeguarded to build public trust. Science and politics together offer the right mix of evidence and intuition—the two necessary ingredients of good decision making. People must be empowered to make positive life choices and understand their health impacts, through digital platforms and access to online services, that are evidence-based, ethical and fair, knowing that their interests are foremost. The lives of millions of people hinge on the digital path we choose from here. In less than two years, digital health has gone from being optional to essential. We still have a long way to go in reaping the benefits that the digital transformation of health will bring—beyond COVID-19—and ensuring that those benefits are made available equitably, to all. We can only respond to the many interconnected health challenges we face, now made even more pressing by the pandemic, through a radical rethinking, and action. And that action must be digital. autores: Iryna М. Goncharenko | Nina A. Krakhmalova
instituicoes: Kyiv National University of Technologies and Design
palavras_openalex: ecosystems | social integration of youth | professional adaptation | labor market competition | social pessimism | university graduates | professional partnerships | labor socialization | professional self-development | professional skills development | professional maturity
resumo: This article tackles a wide range of issues related to social and professional adaptation of youth in the context of structural and social transformations. It is observed that currently, the employment and occupation challenges remain are among the most critical objectives to be attained and need to be resolved as soon as possible. It is argued that the objective reality of modern social relations is the constantly changing labor market environment; moreover, the current situation in the employment sector significantly complicates the situation for young people. In particular, it is emphasized that the labor market puts young professionals in the system of fierce competition with professionals who already have work experience. Ultimately, transformations in various fields – social, economic and political system of fierce competition – have caused a decline in the social value of labor for many young people that has resulted in moral degradation and triggered social pessimism – a disbelief that they will be ever able to get an interesting job that is paid fairly which translates into polarization between effort and wages, which in fact often differ. A survey of graduates conducted in the frameworks of the University Hackathon Ecosystem has revealed the quantitative and qualitative characteristics of future professionals and their ability to integrate into the social environment. Processing of research outcomes using the tools of mathematical statistics to obtain values with estimated availability and reliability has demonstrated the validity of the developed favourable organizational and pedagogical environment in the university. In this context, consistent implementation of this organisational and pedagogical paradigm ensures the highest effectiveness of adaptation to professional activities based on education values as well as social integration readiness. The proposed model of promoting professional partnership-based adaptation of students between the university and social institutions and organizations characterizes the pre-working period of educational and professional adaptation. It is assumed that enhancing the students’ adaptation to professional career will help would be professionals find confidence in their abilities and become competitive in the labor market, reinforcing new values of professional self-development and professional development, and facilitate further integration into society. It is argued that the use of traditional labor socialization methods is not always sufficient to attain relevant professional maturity which is associated with different character and motivation to professional activity. The findings verify that some young people are engaged in non-professional activities, some work in the profession but do not seek to develop their professional skills, there are also cases of discrimination against young people by the older generation which refer to professional growth opportunities. An experiment based on the University Hackathon Ecosystem provides argument that the professional socialization of individuals assumes a certain time period to enter the professional environment, gain professional experience, master the standards and values of the professional community, as well as the process of accumulation and active implementation of personal professional experience.

resumo: Digitalization or digitalization (from the English digital) not only of the economy, but also of almost all spheres of our life is happening before our eyes. We have long been familiar with the digitization of data and perfectly use the digital form of any type of information in our work and entertainment: text, image, drawing, sound, video, photos, paper documents and printed publications, paintings. Scanned – received an electronic document, i.e. its digital form. According to statistics, more than 70% of the world's population uses mobile applications worldwide, even in the poorest sector of households. Every day, the number of Internet users is growing exponentially. Half of the world's population has access to the Internet. resumo: Play BallRepresentations of Women on Vintage Baseball Photo Postcards Cathy Leogrande (bio) and Brian Sheehy (bio) Much has been written about the depictions of baseball on various print materials of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. From game programs to early tobacco and trade cards, baseball action and players were depicted in drawings and photographs. Among items produced between 1905 to 1915 were suggestive and comic photo postcards depicting men and women in baseball uniforms posed in romantic scenes with suggestive captions using baseball terminology. These cards were produced at a time when societal norms and gender roles were changing. This article describes some of the themes that emerge from a closer analysis of the postcards given the historical context within which they were produced, sold, and collected. Baseball was becoming a common love for men and women in the early twentieth century. Using baseball in these postcards seemed to diffuse the polarization of changing gender norms through humor. Some of the cards could be viewed as supportive of that change while other cards used humor to mock or demean the ever-changing gender landscape. Baseball provided a common language that could be used metaphorically to illustrate those changes in a gentler and more humorous way. The following descriptions of these items documents the conflicting perceptions of women and the sport itself. Analysis of these littleknown baseball artifacts provides a glimpse into the beginnings of changes in perceptions of men, women, and their relationships at the beginning of the twentieth century. early twentieth century: the new woman looks and acts differently The turn of the century was a time in which society in all aspects of life, both in Europe and America, was changing. The Victorian Age in England had ended with Queen Victoria's death in 1901, and societal norms were evolving. [End Page 163] Everything from clothing styles to acceptable behavior had already begun to shift as the Edwardian age began. The role of women was one of the areas that saw the most radical changes. From traditional demure wives and daughters who remained at home pursuing activities such as gardening and needlework, women were now less interested in marriage and raising a family and more open to education and employment. Three areas of reform provide context for examining the baseball postcards described here. First, women became independent and were able to act as they chose rather than as society expected. Sanctions that previously kept many young women mired in tradition were less effective in maintaining females who were demure and quiet out of fear of scandal. Second, clothing changed dramatically as women began working and taking part in athletic leisure activities. Third, American attitudes toward sex began to change through education and other efforts such as the social hygiene movement. The effects of these three reform movements are all observable in the baseball postcards published in the early twentieth century. While the notion of capitalist femininity emerged from America's promotion of middle-class femininity as the reproductive center of a flourishing economy, the concept of socialist femininity derived from the Soviet Union's construction of working-class women as emancipated labor heroines. Scholars studying the construction of Cold War femininities have tended to focus on how these polarized femininities were propagated by the United States and the Soviet Union as ammunition for national contestation.1 However, the casting of Cold War femininity solely in terms of United States-capitalist women and Soviet Union-communist women overlooks the complex connections between women in different nations in favor of emphasizing the polarization between competing ideologies or affirming the homogeneity within each ideology. Recently, the complexity of women's existence in the Cold War era has been given more nuance in relation to specific national contexts and non-binary identities. This research has touched upon the constructions of femininity [End Page 464] in West Germany and Japan under the co-influences of American and national discourses of femininity,2 the resemblance between the United States and the Soviet Union in their allegations of (dis)loyalty aimed at women in the Cold War era,3 women's political and social activism in the communist nation of Yugoslavia in the early Cold War era,4 and the formation of femininity in Finland under the co-influences of Sovietism and Americanization.5 However, little attention has been paid to how constructions of femininity in China during the Cold War period emerged in relation to those in the United States. This article seeks to address this gap through a comparative analysis of two Cold War plays: Tennessee Williams's A Streetcar Named Desire (1947) and Yang Lüfang's Cuckoo Sings Again (1957). I interrogate the national fantasy of ideal femininities in both America and China, first, by examining how these femininities were constructed to support the socio-economic ideologies of each nation and, thereafter, by suggesting how Williams' and Yang's plays complicate those constructions through "failed" performances that exceed the containment of women's experiences in this period. resumo: Shakespeare: ShakespeareWe're exhausted, dismayed, and angered over the way our lives have gone off track these past 2 years. COVID-19 never seems to end, and the new normal is distinctly abnormal. Leaving aside the minor inconveniences, the effects on society have been ample. To name a few: economic disruption (job losses due to shutdowns, supply chain issues, stock market flip-flops), social disruption (increased murder rates, increased crimes against women and people of Asian descent), political polarization piled on existing political polarization to the detriment of basic public health measures, schools closed and 6-year-olds trapped at home with working parents whose interplay with their co-workers is by Zoom conferences. But more than anything else, a nagging sense that nothing is safe and predictable anymore has led many to live in a permanent state of unease. All of us in the health care professions know the human toll, the lives lost, the exhausted ICU nurses and ED physicians, the noisy ventilators, and the sad family conferences. And all this followed by the long COVID symptoms that we are just beginning to understand and will wrestle with for years. We all have stories we could share, but we are too tired to care anymore. Already 2019 seems like a different era, some facsimile of an old Jetsons Saturday morning children's cartoon, when life was dominated by technologic advances and Mother Nature was just one minor special interest group, recognized but usually ignored by a populace enamored by the latest shiny new gadgets. An era where one could go online and get a ticket to Bangkok or Paris, stand in line at a crowded airport, sit next to someone with a mild cough, fly overseas for 12 hours and think nothing about it. That was BC: Before COVID. In the After Covid (AC) universe, a trip to the local grocery store can seem fraught with hazard. Fly overseas to a medical conference? Forget it. Get on a cruise ship, those floating coronavirus hot boxes? Are you nuts? We no longer have the freedoms we took for granted, and many of the limitations are the self-imposed ones derived as much from our own psyches as from public health departments or the CDC. What's worse, we no longer trust our fellow citizens. Is the woman standing behind me at the checkout line, her homemade cloth mask covering only her chin, vaccinated and boosted? Is her child's cough some mild rhinovirus or the latest highly transmissible variant? Will I get in an argument over mask wearing at my child's school? I never used to worry about someone's flu vaccine status—perhaps foolishly—but now I ask every patient I see in clinic about their COVID shots. And underling everything else, this question: when will it all end? A once-in-a-century pandemic leaves us with few relevant historical comparisons. The last great pandemic was the 1918-1920 Great Influenza, which killed somewhere in the range of 50-100 million people in a world less populated than today. That pandemic came in four waves: a mild one with characteristics of a regular flu season, followed by the major killing fields of late 1918, followed by another significant outbreak that killed tens of thousands in the U.S. in 1919, followed by a 1920 series of localized but lesser outbreaks. So roughly 3 years of fear and deaths, and then back to normal. Of course, that flu never actually went away. It mutated into something less dangerous, its progeny continuing until today. It still kills in the thousands per year, though fewer in the era of COVID: masks work. Perhaps influenza's slide from pandemic to the endemic is our fate with COVID-19. Or perhaps, and this is devoutly to be yearned for, deliverance will come in the form of a universal COVID vaccine, as some have suggested. Either of those two outcomes would be welcome. But history offers other, more dismal scenarios. Imagine, if you will, that you are miraculously transported to Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564. If you attend Holy Trinity church on April 26, you will see the baptism of William Shakespeare. The parish register for that date, probably a few days after his birth, lists him as Gulielmus filius Johannes Shakspere.” But don't linger there. On July 11, the same parish register informs us “Here begins the plague.” After that there is a steady drumbeat of plague-related deaths lasting through the end of the year, including many young children. Shakespeare was lucky. Follow him as he moves to London, sometime in the late 1580s, and the plague is waiting there as well. In 1592, the plague killed roughly one Londoner in twelve. The city authorities had strict rules shutting down the playhouses and other public spectacles once plague deaths reached 30 per week, so young Shakespeare uses his down time to write his poem Venus and Adonis, which earns him the patronage of an Earl of Southampton. The poem includes these lovely lines: “Long may they kiss each other, for this cure/...To drive infection from the dangerous year/That the star-gazers having writ on death/May say, the plague is banish'd by thy breath.” Or, as in the case of COVID, “spread by thy breath.” In 1603, the plague came again in a big way, killing 30,000 people in a city of 200,000, and the playhouses were shut down to prevent spread of the infection. And in 1606 the plague returned, and again Shakespeare and his company faced government-enforced shutdown and loss of income. Shakespeare's company, originally the Lord Chamberlain's Men during Queen Elizabeth's time, then the King's Men (for they were favorites of King James) left London and toured the provinces when the playhouses were shut down. But if one stayed in London, and the Black Death was known to have afflicted a family member, one's house was boarded up for a month and the house's occupants forbidden to leave. In James Shapiro's wonderful book The Year of Lear, subtitled Shakespeare in 1606, the author makes the case that the playwright's landlady may have died of the plague at the age of 40. If so, as in 1564, Pasteurella pestis may have come too close for comfort. Shakespeare mentions the words “plague” and “pestilence” in his plays, though usually not as the centerpiece of the works. Perhaps the memories are too painful for the citizens of London. But the plague is frequently there in the background, as in real life. Take Romeo and Juliet, for instance. When Romeo's friend Mercutio is stabbed and lays dying, he says “a plague a' both your houses.” To modern ears, this is just a witty metaphor, but if you were attending the Globe Theatre then, how would it have sounded? You've seen friends die in days, purulent painful buboes turning lymph nodes into torture chambers. You are scared for your life just thinking about it. Perhaps the phrase would be the equivalent of saying something like, “I hope you both die of cancer.” If you lived through 1603, where 15 percent of the population perished in a matter of months, this was no innocent metaphor. It was a curse. Later in the play, in what will have tragic consequences for the young lovers, a letter is not delivered to Romeo in time. The reason is the plague: “the searchers of the town, /Suspecting that we were both in a house/Where the infectious pestilence did reign, /Sealed up the doors, and would not let us out.” Quarantine is a very old idea, and for Shakespeare's audience, a living presence. The plague would not disappear from London until after 1666, when the Great Fire of London, and the subsequent rebuilding of much of the city in brick rather than in thatched roofs, made it less friendly to the fleas and rats that transmitted the plague. Here's the thing that amazes me: the Black Death first arrived in England in 1348. 1603 was 255 years after that, and the bubonic plague has another half century or more to torment the citizens of England. Two hundred fifty-five years ago was 1767; imagine COVID arriving then and coming back every few years, killing only a few in “good” years and 15 percent in the bad years. And having a half century more to go before disappearing for good. What an intensely depressing thought. But that was the world in which Will Shakespeare lived. If there is any cheer to be derived from the infectious disease history of Shakespeare's times, those long-ago plague years, let it be this: in 1606, when the Globe Theatre shut down for most of a year, Will Shakespeare didn't goof off. Shakespeare scholars believe that he penned Macbeth, Antony and Cleopatra, and King Lear, all within a 12-month period. Has any writer ever had a better year? Or, perhaps, consider late 1665. This is the last time that the plague will visit England, but its spread has temporarily shut down Cambridge University. The students are sent home until things cool down in 1666 and classes resume. One of the students, young Isaac Newton, goes home to Woolsthorpe Manor. In 1726, near the end of a not-too-shabby scientific career, he shares this anecdote with his biographer: “After dinner, the weather being warm, we went into the garden & drank tea under the shade of some apple trees... he told me, he was just in the same situation, as when formerly, the notion of gravitation came into his mind...occasioned by the fall of an apple, as he sat in a contemplative mood.” Somewhere, in some lab, or perhaps in a crowded apartment, some grad student or postdoc, who's life has been put on hold by the pandemic, is sitting in a contemplative mood. Newton's apple, I want to believe, has fallen out of the sky and plunked this smart kid on the head and we just haven't heard about it yet. Perhaps finding the cure for cancer or working out the development of the universal vaccine that will end COVID-19 once and for all, but in any event creating something that will transform the world. There is, after all, precedent; the greatest playwright in human history and the human race's greatest physicist both allow us to hope that something good will come out of all this pain and suffering. resumo: FigureWe live in unprecedented times. The United States is approaching 47 million cases of COVID-19 with more than 750,000 deaths (Johns Hopkins University and Medicine, 2021). The pandemic represents lives and communities changed by loss of life, connection, and contributions of those who have died and for survivors experiencing long-lasting effects. Nursing has experienced enormous change. Increased flexibility and hours of additional work for clinical rotations and nursing student education have occurred. New graduates working in COVID units and ICUs have witnessed more deaths over the past 2 years than many of us have experienced during our entire careers. Vaccine mandates cause growing polarizations in our profession. Shortages continue, with 62% of hospitals reporting a staff vacancy rate above 7.5% (NSI Nursing Solutions, 2021). Higher pay draws travel nurses away from their communities. Strikes for fairer pay and better staffing are taking place. A recent American Association of Critical-Care Nurses (AACN) survey of over 6,000 acute and critical care nurses reported 92% believe the pandemic will lead to shortened careers in nursing. 66% have considered leaving nursing. 76% believe unvaccinated populations threaten nurses' physical and mental well-being (Davis, 2021). Nurses' pain, exhaustion, frustration, and anger are often directed toward healthcare systems and the latest wave of patients who frequently are unvaccinated. “I do not have compassion for these patients. This group of patients is here because of their own choices” is a common response from nurses and others in healthcare. Two realities exist: burnout and compassion fatigue. Burnout typically is associated with “occupational factors, such as workload, autonomy, and rewarding, rather than personal relationships,” whereas compassion fatigue is “an inability to engage, or enter into a caring relationship” (van Mol et al., 2015, p. 3). We need to understand what is at play here. “Empathy requires high-level brain function, but as stress levels rise, brain function that drives empathy tends to shut down. It's a survival mechanism” (Sohn, 2021, para 11). “When healthcare workers feel overwhelmed, trapped, or threatened by patients demanding unproven treatments or by ICUs with more patients than ventilators, they may experience a fight-or-flight response that makes them defensive, frustrated, angry, or uncaring” (Sohn, para 12). Nurses of faith also experience these emotions leading to questions about our purpose and calling. Showing self-compassion is not a selfish act. We cannot give from an empty cup. Reaching out to trusted colleagues for presence and prayer provides physical, emotional, and spiritual support. Seeking professional help can be a step toward healing. Lamenting our pain can deepen our trust in God. Giving voice to our feelings is often the first act of “moving through” the trauma, reducing the shame and stigma of what we often deny or numb in ourselves. In this issue, you'll discover print and online articles discussing our response to the pandemic from a faith-based perspective, information about the COVID-19 vaccines, and resources to support your practice. Please share your stories and reach out for support through our prayer line and nurse groups. Your voice matters here.

resumo: Reviewed by: Radical Sufficiency: Work, Livelihood, and a US Catholic Economic Ethic by Christine Firer Hinze Drenda Butler Radical Sufficiency: Work, Livelihood, and a US Catholic Economic Ethic. By Christine Firer Hinze. Washington, DC: Georgetown University Press, 2021. 360 pp. $39.95. In this timely work, Hinze advocates for what she describes as "radical sufficiency"—the sustainable pursuit of livelihood for all—in response to the manifold economic injustices, such as low wages, unpaid care labor, and systemic disadvantages, people face today. Her development of such a response carefully tends to the historical contours of the U.S. economy and reactions to its limitations. By thoroughly fleshing out this history, Hinze demonstrates that current realities like the private household, class mobility, and rampant consumerism have not always been economic givens but rather emerged in response to historical situations, such as the rise of capitalism, immigration, and political unrest. Hinze thus draws attention to the ways our values have shifted over time, a fact which implicitly fosters optimism that they can shift again—hopefully toward sufficiency, which is needed for economic justice for all. Hinze's treatment of history also shines light on the important role that Catholicism, as expressed [End Page 69] in a figure like Monsignor John A. Ryan, has played in advocating for workers' rights. In detailing the contributions of Ryan and other Catholics in the historical fight for fair wages, Hinze consequently creates continuity between their work and our concerns today. While Hinze's historical overview demonstrates the legacy that Catholics and others have inherited, this is not an uncritical acceptance, for she also emphasizes radical sufficiency's need for intersectional attention to the unequal power dynamics at play in gender, race, class, and environment—a dynamic missing from the historical responses. Such attention will recognize the unequal care labor demanded of women and how this is further demanded of women of color. It will recognize the role of slavery in the construction of the U.S. economy and the lasting impact this has had on people who are not white. It will recognize the ways in which class struggles have been downplayed in relation to these other categories and, on an existential level, how our economic choices and structures impact the very earth on which we live and leave behind for others. Hinze's presentation of these issues is refreshingly nuanced, detailing their interpenetration and diversity in particular instantiations. Weaving personal stories of those within these groups throughout her analytical treatment, Hinze reminds her readers that to speak of economic issues is ultimately to speak of real people, embodied in a variety of ways and circumstances. Thus, Hinze's suggestions for what radical sufficiency might look like practically are as nuanced and open to change as the people and situations to which they respond. While the threads of continuity that such an ethic must necessarily entail are a communal orientation, privileging of persons over markets, and the limiting of consumption, how these might be sought and instantiated, she leaves open for discernment. She stresses, however, that such a pursuit will require cooperation on all levels: the individual and the communal, the private and the public, the secular and the religious, the conservative and the progressive. Overthrowing the entire current system will not do, for she is clear that consumption itself is not the issue so much as a culture of [End Page 70] consumerism, markets are less the problem than their unfettered orientation to endless production. A proper seeking of radical sufficiency, then, will require both personal conversion and systemic change, a much-needed mingling in the face of current political polarization over the responsibility of individuals versus society. Ultimately, Hinze's work will resonate with anyone wishing to reflect more deeply on current economic issues, whether the Fight for $15, the economic impact of COVID-19, or the worker shortage throughout the United States. Her intersectional approach makes her work relevant to studies in gender, race, and similar fields and the religious themes for theological studies, especially economic ethics and Catholic social teaching. resumo: Rapid urbanization has come to be recognized as a major aspect of human development for a decade, when globalization increasingly interefered with city development. The mega-urban regions of Southeast Asia are among the world's fastest growing agglomerations, whose growth dynamics both depend on global influence and local strategies contributing to a permanent polarization of urban society. The focus of this article is on the Philippine National Capital Region (NCR), which is analyzed in terms of city development, migration and rural transformation. Special emphasis was put on (international) economic investment in NCR, which dramatically changed the urban employment structure. The interconnections of migration, internationalized economies and family networks for the uprooting of people seem to prove that megacity development is no longer independent of international influence.
