titulo: Long – Term Distribution of the Job Offer in Romania and Job Polarization
autores: Carmen-Elena Bănescu | Emilia Țițan | Daniela Manea
instituicoes: Bucharest University of Economic Studies
topico_primario: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality
palavras_openalex: job polarization | job vacancies | labor market | digitalization of the economy | Markov chains | vocational education | Romania
resumo: In the case study we aim to analyse the long-term distribution of vacancies on the Romanian labour market. This approach allows us to identify one of the long-term consequences of the digitalization of the economy, namely polarization. Polarization can be viewed from several perspectives, but here we are only referring to the polarization of the job supply. The phenomenon implies a significant reduction in interest in mid-level jobs. Thus, to identify the probability that this phenomenon will already manifest itself in Romania, we carried out an analysis with the help of Markov chains. In this way we will identify the occupations that could be the most numerous in the long run in Romania. Even if Romania does not indicate an obvious polarization of the labour market, in the long run, clues in this regard can be identified. There is a system of vocational training at national level, but it does not cover the prospects of the labour market.

titulo: An “Invitation to Learning”: Mortimer Adler’s How to Read a Book, Everyman’s Library, and the Ideal of a “Common Culture”
instituicoes: Harvard University | University of Oxford
palavras_openalex: Mortimer Adler | common culture | canon debate | John Lubbock | Charles Eliot | reading instruction | liberal arts education | literary canon | self-education | John Guillory | Matthew Arnold | Henry James | Jean-François Lyotard
resumo: Within the so-called “canon debate,” the question of what is really at stake in the study and the teaching of the humanities, nothing has been as controversial as the place of “great books” lists as tools for organizing school curricula and continuing education. Harsh criticism reached the British writer and banker Sir John Lubbock as early as 1886, when he recommended his list of the “Hundred Best Books” to the students of F. D. Maurice’s Working Men’s College, London. Based on a revised version of August Comte’s Positivist Library, Lubbock’s list included standard Greco-Roman works, acclaimed English classics such as Shakespeare, Milton, and Carlyle, the Bible and even the Koran, and was promptly dismissed by critics like Matthew Arnold and Henry James.1 A few decades later, when the President of Harvard University Charles Eliot tried to organize the fruits of a thriving publishing industry with his “five-foot shelf” idea, the result was no different. A 1909 editorial in The Nation attacked Eliot’s notion that the Harvard Classics series could “transform anybody into a man of liberal education” with its affordable pocket-sized editions, protesting that not only did it “turn the whole idea of our colleges into ridicule”; no less, “the five-foot shelf, instead of being vaguely indicated or left to the imagination, is expressly prescribed . . . .”2 For several critics, this feeling of prescription, of being imposed culture from “above,” has always been implicit in the notion of the “finite number” that a select list or series promotes, signifying attainable, yet ready-made culture.3 According to John Guillory, “[t]he fetishized list is one symptom of what Lyotard has described as the ‘postmodern condition of knowledge,’” a world of mass culture consumed by “the nostalgia for totality [...] in the midst of its carnival of cultural diversity, its infinite dispersal and fragmentation of knowledge.”4 More recently, Mary Hammond, quoting Norman Feltes, has noted the ideological influence of Lubbock’s “hundreds” on the twentieth-century phenomenon of the reprint series in similar, negatively loaded terms: the list has “a finality of its own, existing precisely as a fetish which may be owned”;5 without it, “no course of self-instruction can be complete.”6 The act of fetishizing “classics” is a common yet misleading trend in publishing and literary studies. It leads to a simplicist labeling of “great books” collections or programs as conservative, without considering the democratic ambitions that the reformists involved in such initiatives often harbored. Moreover, fetishization effects polarization. As Katha Pollitt argued in a 1991 article for The Nation, reprinted in Lee Morrissey’s anthology Debating the Canon: “In America today the assumption underlying the canon debate is that the books on the list are the only books that are going to be read, and if the list is dropped no books are going to be read.”7 Pollitt points her finger to the divisions that have counterposed radicals and liberals in recent years, especially after the rise of the liberation movements since the second half of the twentieth century. For Morrissey, these polarities, exacerbated by the publication of works such as Harold Bloom’s The Western Canon (1994), still live with us today: “Those who might want to teach Bloom’s ‘baker’s dozen, Homer, Virgil, Dante, Chaucer, Shakespeare, Cervantes, Montaigne, Milton, Goethe, Tolstoy, Ibsen, Kafka, and Proust,’ will also need to consider, thanks to Bloom’s binary, whether they want to be identified by colleagues and students as unsympathetic to historically marginalized voices.”8 Is it possible to think beyond these poles? Can we imagine literature as a universally shared heritage, without aligning such an ideal, by default, with conservative political thought? And is there a way to return to “great books” with a more nuanced understanding of the questions that such books raise? In this paper, I would like not only to answer these questions in the affirmative, but also to illustrate that many mid twentieth-century promoters of “great books” even anticipated some of the issues we are concerned with today. One of these has recently been posed in the form of an open interrogative by Low Ying Ping and Joshua Ang: what is the relationship between the “educational canon” and the “larger canon”?9 Guillory’s answer in 1991 was a simple warning against equating “lists” or “syllabi” with “canon,” where the former merely act as educational tools extracting from an imaginary totality: “Everything that counts as ‘knowledge’ is a selection from a continually expanding aggregate.”10 The process of selection should not mislead us, however. Instead, as Jonathan Rose suggests, it should be treated as an inclination intrinsic to human nature: “Though canons can be changed, canonization is inevitable, given that we must choose among the millions of books available to us.”11 Defending John Lubbock from his detractors, Rose has shown that his list “was conservative only in the sense that it included no living authors”; it radically impacted the minds of nineteenth-century readers, pushing them far beyond the horizons of the “hundred best.”12 It is my purpose to apply a similar thesis to a different historical and cultural period, with the aid of two intertwined case studies. To answer the question of how the educational system and the outer world interact, and to dispel the misconceptions outlined above, I focus on two products of twentieth-century culture: Mortimer Adler’s How to Read a Book: The Art of Getting a Liberal Education (1940); and Everyman’s Library (1906–1956).13 The stakes seem even higher in the twentieth century, for at least two reasons. For once, controversies revolving around the academic curriculum in Anglophone institutions were particularly heated at this time, ranging from anti-canonist disputations such as John Dewey’s “Challenge to Liberal Thought” published in Fortune (1944) to New Criticism’s attempts to teach the art of close reading to a much wider swath of university students. Among such attempts were textbooks and popular anthologies like Cleanth Brooks and Robert Penn Warren’s Understanding Poetry (1938) and Cleanth Brooks’s Understanding Fiction (1943), which account for the increasing importance of the study of literature as central to the educational pathway of American public universities in the 1940s. Perhaps even more crucially, the two world wars, posing the threat of totalitarianism and annihilation, had the inevitable effect of bringing several nations around the globe to reflect on what building a “common” liberal culture might entail, a concern that occupied the public mind in academic and noncollegiate contexts alike. As for my case studies, both Mortimer Adler and the publisher of Everyman’s Library were at the forefront of promoting “great books” for a wider and more socially variegated audience in various ways. A former attendee of John Erskine’s General Honors course at Columbia in 1920, Adler was hired by the University of Chicago in the 1930s and helped reorganize the undergraduate education there. How to Read a Book, his 1940 bestseller, brought together the reflections he matured during his years of teaching, also including an appendix that listed useful books for acquiring a “liberal education.” Everyman’s Library, on the other hand, was a reprint series conceived by a working-class publisher with similar ambitions, a product of the same late-Victorian culture of self-improvement that John Lubbock would have also detected in his audience. titulo: PROBLEMATICS OF SETTLEMENT OF INHERITANCE RIGHTS OF DAUGHTER WITH SIBLINGS IN THE MAHKAMAH SYAR’IYAH BANDA ACEH AND ACEH
instituicoes: Universitas Islam Negeri Ar-Raniry
periodico: Dusturiyah Jurnal Hukum Islam Perundang-undangan dan Pranata Sosial
palavras_openalex: Islamic inheritance law | faraidh | daughters' inheritance rights | Ibn Abbas | judicial decision disparities | inheritance dispute
resumo: This research discusses the Polarization of Judges' Decisions in the Settlement of Sibling Inheritance Rights (Case Study of Decision Number: 193/Pdt.G/2020/MS.Bna AND 21/Pdt.G/2021/MS.Aceh). The formulation of the problem studied is: 1. Why is there a disparity in the judge's decision regarding the position of relatives as heirs in an inheritance dispute at the Religious Court in decision number: 193/Pdt.G/2020/MS.Bna vs. 21/Pdt.G/2021/ MS. Aceh? 2. Has the judge's decision in resolving the dispute over the determination of heirs protected the rights of heirs in accordance with faraidh? This research is normative and practical juridical research, namely library research supported by results in the field in the form of interviews with related functional officials of the Banda Aceh Syar'iyah Court and Aceh Syar'iyah Court. This study concludes that: 1. The disparity in the decisions of the Banda Aceh Syar'iyah Court and the Aceh Syar'iyah Court occurred due to an understanding of the Jumhur Ulama's opinion which stated that a daughter cannot be hindered by a daughter in receiving an inheritance. Jumhur Ulama's definition of "kalalah" is the death of someone who does not have a father or son. This is in line with jurisprudence and the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas, which stipulates that girls can wear the hijab to inherit, but girls cannot wear the hijab inherited from their brothers. 2. The judge's decision at the Banda Aceh Syar'iyah Court in resolving the dispute over the determination of heirs has protected the rights of heirs in accordance with faraidh. This is because the opinion of the jumhur of scholars and the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas are in line with the opinion of the panel of judges. Then the daughter in this case is an adult and has a steady job and income, which is different from the case in jurisprudence.

titulo: What is the nature of the crisis in French unionism?
palavras_openalex: trade union crisis | collective bargaining | peripheral workers | individual employment contracts | employment protection
resumo: The gradual change in the model of production since the 1970s produced a heterogenization and polarization of workers’ terms of employment— between, on the one hand, a segment of workers with stable employment, legal protection and good representation by the unions and on the other hand an increasingly populous segment of peripheral workers who were cut off collective bargaining and whose terms of employment were “negotiated” individually when they were hired. By this analysis, it is not so much the institutionalization of French unionism that lies behind its crisis as the de- institutionalization of the wage relationship, one of the conditions of which seems to be the weakening of the union itself. The unions find themselves in a situation where they alone are opposing an increased riskiness in labour relations that, while distancing them from the peripheral segments of the workforce, is locking them into defensive positions.

titulo: Shifts in the Employment Structure in Korea
topico_primario: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality
palavras_openalex: employment structure | job polarization | deindustrialization | trade expansion | population aging | non-regular workers | labor demand shocks | labor supply shocks
resumo: This study analyzes changes in the employment structure from 2000 to 2021 according to the job-based methodology. The results show that Employment in higher-paid jobs increased between 2000 and 2009. Employment polarization, on the other hand, emerged between 2009 and 2019. This study quantitatively identifies the labor demand and supply shocks using sign restrictions. The results show that the demand for high-income ICT and science and technology experts has increased significantly since 2000 suggesting that technology changes have had a significant impact. Deindustrialization, trade growth, and population aging had a significant impact on employment changes for low- and middle-income jobs. As the population ages rapidly in the 2010s, employment in health and social work services is increasing rapidly. In addition, changes in government policies related to non-regular workers and the expansion of the welfare system affected changes in employment type.

titulo: Job polarization and future of jobs in India
instituicoes: University of Kerala
topico_primario: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality
palavras_openalex: job polarization | future of work | India | middle-skilled workers | wage inequality | occupational classification | retraining | upskilling | technological change | labor market
resumo: World Economic Forum report on future jobs have brought in wave of questions and expectations about the future job market. Even though technological upgradation is not new to the economy, the pace at which current changes are happening is extreme. Its high time that economies must rethink about theoretical occupational classification and make way to coming changes. Current job market must be reskilled and upskilled to attain the benefits of this change. Job polarization is a not a new term to many countries, developed countries have already gone through job polarization and wage inequality. The wages per hour for high and low skilled are much more than middle skilled in developed countries. India has already felt the impact of job polarization, but the percentage of impact is much less than other developed countries. This paper explains the impact of job polarization in India and why India will be one among those countries most effected by job polarization. Since India’s job market is more concentrated on middle skilled employees, with future jobs accelerating its presence in India, it’s time to reskill and upskill the existing middle skilled job force to reap its benefits fully.

titulo: Relações entre a desindustrialização brasileira e a indústria criativa
autores: Filipe da Silva | Gustavo Möller | Leandro Valiati
palavras_openalex: creative industries | deindustrialization | knowledge-intensive production | labor market polarization | industrial employment | service sector employment | Brazil
resumo: O ganho de relevância da indústria criativa nos últimos 30 anos ocorreu em meio a tendências de desindustrialização. Esse processo foi resultante, entre outros fatores, do surgimento de um modelo de produção mais intensivo em conhecimento. Assim, houve uma absorção do emprego industrial pelos setores de serviços e criativos, dando origem a uma polarização do mercado de trabalho. No entanto, observou-se que a polarização brasileira foi distinta daquela dos países desenvolvidos, pois se caracterizou por uma intensidade criativa menor.

titulo: Cadmium and Lead Induced Proinflammatory Cytokine Polarization in Petroleum Products Occupationally Exposed Nigerians
autores: Ehiaghe Alfred Friday | Mba Martins Douglas | Usiosefe Raphael Erhunmwunse | Uwaifo Nicholas Eghosa | Ehiaghe Joy Imuetiyan | Eremwanarue Aibuedefe Osagie | Digban Kester | Emeje Paul Isaac
instituicoes: Benson Idahosa University | Igbinedion University | Kogi State University | Nnamdi Azikiwe University | Novena University | University of Benin
periodico: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
palavras_openalex: cadmium | lead | petroleum products | occupational exposure | inflammatory cytokines | interleukin-1 alpha | IL-4 | heavy metals | zinc | copper | automotive mechanics | granulocyte count | blood cell count | personal protective equipment
resumo: The toxicological effects of petroleum product had been associated with various metabolic defects such as cardio-vascular attacks. But there is limited information about the cytokine responses of individual who are occupationally exposed to petroleum products in Nigeria. The study was aimed at evaluating the cytokine responses to the accumulation of cadmium, lead, zinc and copper in the petroleum products using blood levels of interleukin-1 alpha, interleukin-4, cadmium, lead, zinc and copper in occupationally exposed individuals in Abuja, Nigeria. The case-control study randomly selected sixty-three occupationally exposed (test group) and sixty non exposed individuals (control group). The occupationally exposed subjects, consisting of twenty-four automobile mechanics (AM), eighteen generator mechanics (GM) and twenty-one petrol station attendants (PSA) in filling stations who consented to participate in this study. Cytokine levels were determined by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay method. Heavy metals were analyzed by atomic absorption spectrophotometer method. Full blood count was done using hematology auto-analyzer. All numerical results were analyzed with one-way ANOVA with post hoc multiple comparisons test while student’s t- test was used to compare independent variables. Cadmium levels were significantly higher in AM and PSA (p<0.002) while lead levels were significantly higher in AM and GM (p<0.04) as compared with the control group. Zinc and copper levels were significantly lower in AM and GM as compared with the control group (P<0.002) but within the acceptable levels. Granulocytes count was significantly higher in GM and PSA, whereas, red blood cells count and packed cell volume were significantly lower in GM and PA as compared with control group (p<0.001). IL-1α and IL-4 levels were significantly higher in AM, GM and PSA as compared with the control group (p<0.01; 0.017) respectively. Regardless of profession, prolonged exposure to petroleum products tends to shift the cytokine balance toward a pro-inflammatory pattern. Thus, when handling such materials, personal protective equipment should be worn to avoid the accumulation of cadmium and lead, which might act as mediators.

titulo: James Sweeney and micro‐based attempts to make macro relevant
palavras_openalex: Chinese economic growth | macroeconomic statistics | state-owned banks | bad debts | Ponzi schemes | GDP measurement | Chinese listed companies | investor returns | China–United States comparison
resumo: Westerners have long been impressed by China's remarkable economic growth, by its ability to report the largest, uninterrupted series of increases in GDP during the past 30 years. But as we saw in the last chapter, such growth has failed notably in providing returns for those Western and Chinese investors willing to entrust their savings to listed Chinese companies. And figuring prominently in that story, the gargantuan assets and suspiciously large and consistent reported profits of today's Chinese state-owned banks seem to be telltale signs of a kind of Ponzi scheme—one designed to conceal a still rising mountain of bad debt, continuously rolled over and backed by assets with small and disappearing values (Think of Evergrande's unfinished buildings, and all the others that have been demolished without ever housing tenants.).1 But how could so many presumably smart and interested people, including investors and the regulators appointed to protect them, have fallen for such a scheme? A big part of the answer, as we argue in this chapter, has to do with major limitations of the macro statistics that are routinely compiled and released by government officials everywhere, and received and reported by many business economists (and most of the business press) as holy writ. In a book published by Cornell University Press in 2018 called Unrivalled: Why America Will Remain the World's Sole Superpower, political economist Michael Beckley begins by telling us what any American who's been to China is likely to be aware of—that the United States continues to be “several times wealthier” than China. But more surprising, and counter to the received (certainly pre-Covid) wisdom is Beckley's report of the progressive widening of the wealth gap between the U.S. and China since the onset of the Global Financial Crisis in 2007, a gap that Beckley estimates has been growing by “trillions of dollars every year.”2 has a bigger GDP, a higher investment rate, larger trade flows, and a faster economic growth rate than the United States. How can China outproduce, outinvest, and outtrade the United States—and own nearly $1.2 trillion in U.S. debt—yet still have substantially less wealth? Chinese businesses suffer from chronically high production costs, and China's 1.4 billion people impose substantial welfare and security burdens. The United States, by contrast, is big and efficient. American businesses are among the most productive in the world, and with four times fewer people than China, the United States has much lower welfare and security costs. almost always increases GDP, even if the funds are wasted on boondoggles. In fact, the most common method of calculating GDP is called the “expenditure method” and involves simply adding up all of the spending done by the government, consumers, and businesses in a country in a given time period.3 Hiring workers always increases GDP, even if they spend all day getting drunk in the break room. Boosting production always increases GDP, even if the goods rot on the shelf and tons of toxic waste are released in the process. In fact, a country can increase its GDP by dumping toxic waste in the streets and hiring millions of workers and spending billions of dollars to clean it up. populous countries generate considerable economic activity simply by existing. Even a nation caught in a Malthusian hell, in which all output is immediately devoured and living standards and technological progress are stagnant, will post a large GDP if it has a big population. And since GDP also counts most security costs as output and a “$100 million gulag shows up the same as a $100 million innovation center,” GDP fails to account for the economic costs of ongoing “internal unrest and international conflict.” So, what happens when we try to adjust for these distortions of national income accounting? How productive is China's economy? The answer Beckley comes up with is remarkably consistent with Carl Walter's account in the last chapter: Since 2007, nearly all of China's growth in GDP has come from two sources: hiring workers and spending money. During the same period, however, China's growth in productivity has been “not only unspectacular, but virtually nonexistent.”4 In the United States, by contrast, productivity increases have been estimated to account for roughly 20% of US economic growth in not just the past decade, but most of the past century.5 Even without visiting China, one could conclude from these productivity figures that much of China's GDP is a mirage based on fruitless investment. It is only when one tours China, however, that the sheer volume of waste becomes apparent.6 China has built more than 50 “ghost cities”—entire metropolises composed of empty office buildings, apartment complexes, shopping malls, and, in some cases, airports.7 By failing to take account of such costs, then, GDP and other standard macro measures have long contributed to the widespread impression that China is overtaking the United States. A more realistic picture of the Chinese economy, as provided by Beckley (and Carl Walter), would show a nation that “is barely keeping pace as the burden of propping up loss-making companies and feeding, policing, protecting, and cleaning up after one-fifth of humanity erodes China's stocks of wealth.” But to get such a picture, what might analysts consider using instead of the conventional national income accounts? And what could macro and business economists do to address the clear shortcomings of GDP? if a country cuts down a forest to build a new office park, the value of the forest would show up as a loss on the country's balance sheet. If a country spends $50 billion imposing martial law in one of its regions—or growing food to feed its people or cleaning up toxic waste or hosting the Olympics—then $50 billion would be deducted from its stock of assets. In short, there would be no free lunch. And as Beckley points out, both the World Bank and the UN have begun compiling and publishing rough estimates of countries’ wealth stocks in three main areas: (1) produced capital (man-made items such as machinery, buildings, infrastructure, software); (2) human capital (the population's education, skills, and working life span); and (3) natural capital (water, energy resources, arable land). Alongside the information provided by these two sources, Beckley also sets estimates of over 100 different countries’ private stocks of financial wealth compiled and published annually by the investment bank Credit Suisse.8 The story told by each of these three approaches, each using different data and methods, is reassuringly similar: The United States, as already mentioned, is several times wealthier than China. And far from getting smaller, as the popular press has long been suggesting, the gap between the two nations’ stocks of wealth has not been shrinking but growing “by trillions of dollars each year.” Also, important to keep in mind, this growing divide between the United States and Chinese wealth was taking place well before the onset of the pandemic in 2020. What's more, this division can also be seen clearly in measures that go well beyond the financial, in everything from air quality to employment opportunities for new college graduates. This tells us that the US advantage in virtually all these social dimensions—with the notable exception of opioid and alcohol addiction—was expanding during the years leading up to the outbreak of Covid. Since the pandemic, and without making light of America's own problems, the growth of this inter-country wealth and welfare divide between the United States and China has clearly accelerated, to the point of becoming a source of political tension (Figure 1). We have just finished showing some of the many ways that GDP and other macro statistics can be used to misrepresent national economic performance and, even with the best of intentions, end up misleading policymakers, the press, and the body politic. But the distortions thus far have been those noted, and criticized, in Chinese, not American macro accounts and accounting. But what about US GDP and other macro variables: are they giving us the information we think they are; and could they be reworked, or at least reinterpreted, in a way that tells us more about what we really want to know? In the lead article of the Fall 2020 issue of my JACF, James Sweeney, then Chief Economist of the investment bank Credit Suisse, began by expressing his thought that “the prestige of our National Income Accounts has peaked.” But what did he mean by that, and why could it matter? For one thing, it suggested that the dismal assessments of real US GDP and wage growth we have been hearing from most macro and business economists for the past three or four decades should be taken with not just a grain, but maybe truckloads of salt. Such conventional macro statistics, and the media who breathlessly report them, are invariably wielded by both political parties—Trump's campaign in 2016 no less than Biden's in 2020—as grounds for handwringing over calamitous and irreversible drops in US productivity and standards of living. How can stock markets keep pushing higher when GDP, job growth, and other “fundamentals” are all down and on their backs, and many companies find themselves unable or unwilling to offer guidance? A big part of the answer to this question, as James suggested in his article, has to do with the limitations of conventional macro measures in capturing two critical determinants of both economic growth and stock prices: inflation and productivity. And let's start with inflation: How and what do we really know about how much the prices of a representative basket of goods and services go up in a particular year? To answer this question, James starts with an amusing account of a 1996 Federal Open Market Committee meeting in which Fed Chair Alan Greenspan is pressed by future chair Janet Yellen to define his goal of “price stability.” Greenspan's response: “zero percent inflation, when properly measured.” Then, after Yellen cites the well-known imprecision of the inflation measurement process as grounds for the Fed's continued use of its standard 2% inflation target, Greenspan just shrugs and says, “Okay, let's leave it at that, and move on.” This exchange between these two highly regarded Federal Reserve leaders was consistent with and likely reflected, the findings of studies of inflation like the Boskin Commission's in the mid-1990s. What such studies found was an upward bias of some 100–150 basis points in the annual CPI estimates during the ’80s and ’90s. And it is not just the failure of the CPI to track and reflect things like consumers’ tendency to find cheaper substitutes in response to price hikes. More important—and far more troubling when measuring productivity—is the inability of macro stats to account for changes in the “quality” of goods and services. If the car you bought last year is in most respects twice as effective in meeting your “wants and needs” as the one you bought five years ago for half the price, then its inflation would in fact be roughly the zero percent that Greenspan claimed to be aiming for. But if reliance on national income accounts has likely led for years to a significant overstatement of US inflation, it has almost certainly resulted in a much larger, and more misleading, understatement of US productivity. And the question that productivity measures purport to answer is an especially important one. Indeed, for this book—and for many economists from Adam Smith on—it's likely to be the most important of all, the key to national wealth: To what extent, it asks us to keep finding better ways to figure out, is the value of the goods and services produced by US companies each year rising faster than the cost of the inputs, including investor capital, used to produce such goods? One major limitation of the national income accounts in answering this question is that our estimates of inflation and GDP are based mostly on transactions—and so they reflect mainly just the dollar amounts paid and received. The value of goods or services provided gratis, or at prices significantly below what consumers might or would pay for them, go unrecorded in GDP or inflation. What this suggests, then, is that our measures of nominal GDP and wage growth are giving us reasonably reliable indications of aggregate spending on final goods and services. But in the case of our real measures, the systematic overstatement of US inflation and failure to reflect increases in quality (and gains in “consumer surplus”) have not only exaggerated the extent of slowdowns, but may have prevented us from seeing actual increases in productivity—and, who knows, maybe even in real wages?—in recent decades. All this raises the tantalizing possibility that such under-the-radar productivity increases have a lot to do with the efficiency and stock price gains of US companies during the past four decades. And although James himself cautions against taking this idea too far—after all, he still has his own macro credentials to defend—I like to hold up his own favorite illustration of an increase in the quality of his life. His example is Google's Waze app, whose vast benefits to all and sundry continue to elude the national income accounts. And in what is probably the most telling indicator of our basic problem with our macro measures, James goes on to note that, “In my meetings with CEOs, my suggestions of a productivity slowdown in corporate America almost invariably gets laughed out of the room.” Now, as James will be the first to tell you, none of what you have just been told is news. These shortcomings of the macro data have long been understood, and acknowledged, by serious macro and business economists themselves. Where the problems arise is from the uninformed and uncritical acceptance of macro numbers as providing reliable representations of things most of us care deeply about, like living standards, the cost of living, worker efficiency, technology growth, and general social welfare. All of these concepts and concerns, needless to say, play a major role—but also alas end up getting seriously distorted—in today's policy debates and public assessments of the health of the economy. If the most trusted and widely reported data reinforce the wrong message, the data itself can be a cause of genuine mischief, including misguided public policy as well as distorted private decision-making. titulo: The Effects and Mechanisms of the Digital Economy on Employment: A Review and Prospect
periodico: Journal of Global Economy Business and Finance
palavras_openalex: digital economy | employment | employment structure | job quality | job polarization | income inequality | employment income | working hours | flexible employment | social security | job satisfaction | digital dividend | technological change
resumo: The new wave of technological revolution led by the digital economy has brought new opportunities and challenges to employment. This paper reviews the economic effects of the digital economy and summarizes its impact on employment from three perspectives: employment scale, employment structure, and employment quality. The research findings indicate that the digital economy affects the employment scale through substitution, compensation, and creation effects. In terms of employment structure, the digital economy has accelerated the shift of labor from the agricultural and manufacturing sectors to the service sector. Regarding employment skills, the digital economy may lead to job polarization and income inequality. Regarding employment quality, the digital economy influences wage income and income inequality, manifested in longer working hours, the emergence of new employment forms, and challenges to social security for flexible workers. At the same time, it positively impacts workers' job satisfaction. However, the existing research paradigm and methods on the relationship between the digital economy and employment still have limitations. In the future, it is necessary to refine the definition and measurement of the digital economy, introduce it into employment theory models, delve into the impact and transmission mechanisms of digital economy development on employment, and better unleash the digital dividend.

titulo: Is basic income an alternative to social security?
autores: National Public Law Review | Byeongrok KIM
palavras_openalex: basic income | social security | welfare state | mutual aid | social solidarity | redistribution | economic inequality | socioeconomic polarization | automation and job loss | COVID-19 economic crisis | South Korea
resumo: In the face of the economic crisis caused by the COVID-19 epidemic, discussions on basic income are becoming active again. Basic income theorists say that AI and robots will eliminate jobs and that the introduction of basic income will be inevitable. But the problem is social security. The principle of a 'welfare state' must work in social security. The welfare state is based on mutual aid and social solidarity. It is a system in which citizens put taxes and insurance premiums into the community's piggy bank, and people who need them take them out according to the size they need. The entire nation saves money in piggy banks, but the n received is always a small number. The salary is generous because n is small. I don't take it right away, but I can always go and get help when I'm in danger and a need for social recognition arises. But there are no piggy banks in basic income countries. Everyone shares it as it is. It cannot be more equal than this, but the salary is inevitably low because there are many ns. And there is no social solidarity or mutual aid. The state just plays the role of Robin Hood. The contrast of redistribution varies by income level, and there is no social security or welfare. This is why social security cannot be left to basic income now and in the future. In addition to global economic inequality, socioeconomic polarization is intensifying in Korea, and basic income is drawing attention as an alternative system that can contribute to resolving economic injustice amid concerns over employment loss caused by digital technology innovation.

resumo: Figure: abortion, women's health, Roe v. Wade, pregnancyFigureNo one wants to discuss abortion. The conversation is more complex, polarizing, and fatiguing than COVID or the corporate takeover of health care. But emergency medicine is the profession that trains EPs to brave the conversations that no one wants but needs to have: intimate partner violence, child abuse, end-of-life issues, depression, sexually transmitted infections, homelessness, drug abuse, sex trafficking, social determinants of health, mental health, suicide...the list goes on and on. Why should abortion be any different? It may, in many cases in the ED, even be part of the same discussion. Like COVID, the politicization of scientific information makes objective fact-speaking an arduous skill to peel apart from the polemics embedded in our culture and language. This is as true for physicians and medical staff as it is for patients. Winning your position becomes a personal, moral anger rather than being with someone in distress and accepting a solution with which you may disagree. Many years ago, I remember a reclusive elderly woman having a STEMI who would not agree to go to the cath lab until someone went to feed her cats. “I would rather die than have my cats go hungry,” she said. She meant it literally. I was in utter disbelief. But it wasn't until I accepted her evaluation of her situation that we could begin to solve an issue of life and death for her—and her cats. We ended up sending one of our security guards to her house to feed them. And it was the first thing she spoke about when she woke up from sedation. She taught me a valuable lesson as a younger physician to train myself not to shake my head in disagreement (metaphorically or literally) while someone is telling me something I don't want to hear. Abortion is far more nuanced than a cardiac cath lab and cats, but the approach of suffering with another person with whom you may disagree instead of trying to win your position is a valuable emotional framework upon which to exercise medicine. I will be providing no heroic or feel-good stories about a woman seen in the ED who wants her pregnancy ended nor about one who is pregnant again and not in a physical, social, or mental situation conducive to birthing and rearing a child. These types of anecdotal stories should not be given because a single story, like the woman and her cats, runs the risk of being generalized medically under a topic that is as immeasurably complex and variable as any topic in all of medicine. Binary Thinking and Wisdom How we define terms in the most measurable, objective way possible is the first crucial step in discussing what exactly we are talking about, whether it's sepsis, heart attack, or abortion, and should occur long before we can begin to talk about treatment. The definitions and approaches to the circumstances are subject to wide variance. The circumstances surrounding induced abortion are often multitudinous: Are we talking about a blastocyst or a 10-week fetus completing organogenesis? A previable fetus or a fetus that can be viable outside the womb? A healthy fetus or an anencephalic fetus? A mother whose life is reasonably in physical danger (and how are these odds determined?), a woman pregnant by a criminal act of violence, a woman pregnant by coercion, or a mother (and father) with no economic, mental, or social resources to raise an infant without neglect being likely? An egg fertilized by sperm and kept for embryo transfer, an embryo or a fetus terminated out of family or community shame, or an embryo or a fetus terminated out of an inconvenient time in life due to job demands or aspirations? Or a combination of several of these? This is not just about a woman who can choose to have an abortion. Some women don't get an abortion but don't want to be pregnant and are deeply unhappy and scared about having a baby. Some women get an abortion even though they want to have a child because, in the immediate circumstance they are in, having a baby feels like it will destroy them. The physical and emotional permutations are frankly unimaginable and not necessarily static. Someone on any political side wanting to vote on this topic with a thumbs up or down shows a serious lack of knowledge and perhaps a lack of empathy for human beings on the other side of the argument. Binary thinking destroys every opportunity for wisdom. Neutral Clarity I offer no expertise in approaching the obstetrical, medical, legal, ethical, and social dilemmas of induced abortions, but I would like to explore several aspects of scientific medical definitions and community language surrounding unwanted pregnancy that often lead us away from objectivity and toward the politically polemical. Using COVID again as an analogy, the medical community should be compelled to keep repeating those scientific definitions and facts we know with as much clarity and dispassion as possible in the hope that we can begin to have a discussion of integrity and purpose. Can we agree at least on the same set of scientific language without people just yelling their opinion into existence with half-truths? We need clarity. We need a neutral scientific lexicon surrounding the use of the word “abortion” in medicine. Here is my short list of suggestions surrounding our current medical lexicon of abortion. An Ambiguous Umbrella Reporting off G3P1Ab2 lacks necessary clarity. Abortion is a loaded word, and our medical lexicon needs careful subdivisions of the ambiguous umbrella of abortion. Terms like “spontaneous abortion” or “threatened abortion” should be abandoned for the word “miscarriage” in our speech, dictation, and notation. “Elective abortion” should be abandoned for the term “induced abortion.” The word “elective” is often used in abortion centers around the fulcrum of choice. A miscarriage is not a choice, and termination of pregnancy due to maternal endangerment is an extremely limited choice. A termination of pregnancy from a rape or with a fetus with limited capacity for life is logically not the same unconstrained choice as other abortions. An abortion needed to save the physical life of the mother is not really elective, and could be termed “emergent near-death termination of pregnancy.” And perhaps abortions as a result of rape or fetal abnormalities that are devastating and unlikely to sustain life deserve another term like “termination of pregnancy.” Women deserve this clarity. Ignoring these distinctions under an ill-defined word with “abortion” in it muddles the conversation and may wrongly impugn women that they have chosen a situation in which they may feel they had little choice. Avoid Euphemisms “Pregnancy” should not be used as a euphemism. Pregnancy is a condition of a woman who is pregnant. It is not a condition of the father—he is not pregnant. The fetus is not the pregnancy. We do not look at your pregnancy; we ultrasound your fetus. A woman does not miscarry the pregnancy; she miscarries a fetus. The words “mother” and “baby” in an initial interview should be stated as “the woman who is pregnant” and “the embryo” (less than eight weeks) or “the fetus” (eight-week gestation or longer). “Fetus” will be the most likely terminology for pregnant women in the ED receiving an ultrasound or fetal heart tones. The fetus is not the woman's body. The fetus has its own unique DNA that is not part of the woman's body. The fetus is not a bunch of cells. Anyone who has studied embryology will know that this is unique human tissue that is in the process of being. The word “person” is more problematic because the legal arguments are not about whether the fetus is a human, but whether it has the rights of a “person,” the same rights women and Black people did not have earlier in our history. “Life” is also more problematic for legal reasons because the “termination of a life” could be translated as “killing.” A fetus as a human being or human emergence would be more accurate and less polemical than “part of the woman's body,” “a blob of tissue,” or “the life of the baby.” Abortion is not a reproductive term. The embryo-fetus is produced already. This is not a decision about reproduction. This is a decision about carrying and birthing. Induced abortion would better fall under parturition rights rather than reproductive ones. Women's rights historically have centered around full personhood and citizenship by voting and later cultural power in leadership in the family and society. These good developments in empowering women to have a voice are often placed under a positive umbrella of an individual woman's rights. Complex science deserves an objective and precise lexicon. Medical terms and definitions, like scientific data, need to be created with as little bias as possible as much as possible. Manipulation using polemical phrases should be avoided. The polarization of the topic of abortion in the United States has destroyed even the medical community's ability to create verbiage that doesn't vote for a political side. It is not wrong to have an informed medical opinion about a course of action under unique and particular circumstances, but these discussions cannot be entertained, much less translated for our communities, unless we adopt and speak with a clarity of terms. The topic of abortion deserves better. Those who are pregnant in the emergency department deserve better. Share this article on Twitter and Facebook. Access the links in EMN by reading this on our website: www.EM-News.com. Comments? Write to us at [email protected]. Dr. Mosleyis an emergency physician in Wichita, KS.

titulo: Dylanomics Why Economies ‘Not Busy Being Born’ Are ‘Busy Dying’
instituicoes: Cornell University

resumo: The flowering of what came to be called ‘Development Economics’ in the 1950s and 1960s doubtless brought much good to the world. Thinkers as varied as Simon Kuznets, Anne Krueger, Philippe Aghion, Jean Drèze, Nancy Birdsall, and Jeff Sachs, whom I’ve not had the honor of meeting, through Kaushik Basu, Partha Dasgupta, Ravi Kanbur, Dani Rodrik, Amartya Sen and Joe Stiglitz, whom I have, have done great service to humanity in helping bring hundreds of millions of people out of poverty. I fear there is also one critical error that has come in the train of much modern Development Economics as practiced by some (not all) American and other ‘developed’ world economists, however, though it’s not to be laid at the doors of the folk I’ve just named. That is a tendency — including my own until not all that long ago – to think, thanks to the understandable focus of modern Development Economics on ‘undeveloped’ economies, of development as something one does and is then done with — what I call ‘Development as “Done Deal”’ or ‘One-Off Achievement.’ This tendency, I now think, has led some once ‘developed’ nations, notably the USA, into ongoing decline and stagnation. For it has led some to think that, once we're ‘developed’, there is nothing more for us, as ‘us,’ to do. For this reason, I propose often that we add a new ‘thinker’ — in this case, a poet — to the pantheon of development thinkers noted above. I refer to Robert Zimmerman, a.k.a. Bob Dylan, whose aphorism that ‘he not busy being born is busy dying’ could be a mantra of many economists henceforth. Let me explain why I say this, beginning with a brief bit of history and then pivoting to the present … What I call the ‘Development as “Done Deal”’ fallacy seems to have taken off with the ‘takeoff’ conception of development famously pushed by Walt Rostow some 60 years ago. Rostow, a vigorous Cold Warrior tellingly posted with the predecessors of the US CIA and then National Security Council rather than any development bank or ministry of economics, had a reason to develop and promote ‘takeoff’ theory. His aim was to ensure newly independent ex-colonies wouldn’t be attracted to Soviet or Chinese style communism back when the Cold War was at its coldest — a brief revealed in the subtitle to his best-known book: ‘an Anti-Communist Manifesto.’ When that is your purpose, you perhaps ‘naturally’ look to one milestone — ‘Developed! Done!’ — in seeking the ‘safe zone’ where Khrushchevian or Maoist blandishments grow less attractive. Nations that achieved ‘takeoff’ could join ‘the West,’ staying on our side of the proverbial ‘Iron’ and ‘Bamboo’ ‘Curtains.’ But the ‘takeoff’ conception, along with the classification scheme it encouraged — ‘undeveloped,’ ‘under-developed,’ ‘lesser developed’ and ‘developed’ nations — also introduced an insidious complacency. Already ‘developed’ countries, having achieved ‘takeoff’ decades if not centuries earlier, were encouraged to think there was no more for their public sectors to do where ‘national development’ was concerned. Markets in these states were by now established; private sector entities could accordingly ‘take it from here.’ That was a costly mistake, as we’ve now seen ‘developing’ for at least several decades. For ‘developed’ countries are deindustrializing, their middle classes disappearing along with their industries. That has brought ever more wealth polarization along with productive decline, and that has in turn brought us populist and racialist backlashes throughout the ever-less developed ‘developed’ world. And so here is the first of three lessons we must now re-learn since the Cold War is over, and the reason for my citing Dylan as someone economists can learn from. Development is forever. It’s never finished, never a done deal. Development, like life, is perpetual. It’s a continuous process of inventing, then producing and seamlessly disseminating, new techniques and technologies economy-wide. And this requires as much in the way of carefully coordinated collective agency — continuously exercised such agency — as does ‘takeoff’ itself. But developmentalists who think of development as a done deal or one-off achievement don't see or do this. They miss the need, hence they miss the fulfillment. There are, of course, some notable exceptions at this point. Daron Acemoglu’s and Simon Johnson’s magisterial new Power and Progress (2023), for example, is an excellent case in point, as are earlier works by both authors. (Full disclosure: Professor Johnson is a long-term friend and former IMF colleague.) Much the same can be said of Acemoglu's work with James Robinson, in particular The Narrow Corridor (2019) and Why Nations Fail (2013). And of course no one can fail to know Mariana Mazzucato's (another dear friend) The Entrepreneurial State (2015), which now seems in effect to have inaugurated an era. The problem, however, is that even a decade after the earliest among the aforementioned works, these authors remain more or less outliers, even if distinguished outliers. And I fear that development economics at least as practiced in the ‘developed’ world will not be living up its fullest potential until that's no longer the case — indeed, until multiple economists in the mold of those just mentioned are regular appointees or consultants to ‘developed’ nations' governments. It is crucial to recognize here, I think, that the problem isn’t that private sector entities in the developed economies are all corrupt or sociopathic, however true that might be of some such. Nor is the problem a matter of ‘perverse incentives’. It is, rather, that normal incentives among individual persons and firms in market economies pertain to behaviors within those economies, not to behaviors ‘about’ such economies. Individual persons and firms, that is to say, simply don’t have capacity for — or, therefore, interest in — doing the coordinating that ongoing development entails. We can appreciate this more fully if we remember two further lessons about true development in addition to its perpetuality … The first additional lesson grows directly out of the ‘dissemination’ observation just made. It is that development is synergistic. It’s multi-sectoral and multi-regional, and hence it must be coordinated in cross-cutting ways. It must coherently combine the best efforts of all private sector industries and all public sector levels of government across both productive and geographical space. And by ‘best efforts’ I mean here all segments doing precisely — and only — what they do best. As I’ve written previously, an electronic vehicle (EV) industry, by way of one salient example, can’t grow absent a battery industry and regional networks of charging stations. And yet private sector industries can no more push one another profitably to move first or zone for charging stations than can public sector actors efficiently produce EVs or batteries. All sectors and industries must work together, in coordinated and facilitated, not merely chaotic or dictated, fashion. Similarly, as I have also noted before, a new chip factory in a given location will hardly make sense in the absence of reliable sources of water, power, neighborhood housing, schooling, and transportation for growing workforces and shipment — as President Roosevelt’s WWII planning team well understood in connection with earlier national production challenges when old industries had to be quickly grown and new industries had to be jump-started. Nor will a wind farm or geothermal dig for energy in one site of production be efficient if there is already a solar array or hydropower station underway nearby in a neighboring place. Inefficient overlaps, in other words, are as much to be avoided as are debilitating gaps. Yet no single firm or US state has the resources or authority to ensure all needed parts of the whole that is chip, battery, or EV manufacturing are available. Hence, again, the need of public and private sector coordination and financing at all levels. For private sector industry, then, ‘best efforts’ means doing much of the inventing, the producing, and the distributing. For public sector agencies, it means spotting and addressing all holes and overlaps — all regional disparities, redundancies, financing shortfalls and other ‘market failures’ — that private sector firms lack the means, the authority, or the rational incentives to correct. And it means doing so in ways that ensure all of our states, regions, industries and citizens take part in and contribute to our nation’s great never-ending productive project. The second additional lesson we now must re-learn in addition to development’s perpetuality is that ‘national development’ is, well, national. As I’ve argued before, early economists like Adam Smith and James Steuart, and statesmen who learned from them like the US’s first Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton and Germany’s early developmentalist Friedrich List, were admirably clear about this. They spoke of ‘The Wealth of Nations, not ‘the wealth of the world.’ The discipline of ‘Political Economy’ that they initiated and then acted upon explicitly addressed itself to the leaders of distinct polities (hence ‘political’ economy), not one non-existent or would-be ‘world polity’ or ‘global society’ (not that there’d need be anything wrong with such a thing were it actually to exist as one unified democratically governed entity). Many later economists in the developed world, unfortunately, as their models grew ever more general than those of the early political-economists, abstracted away from such things as sovereign nations, separate societies, and their people. They knew not ‘citizens,’ but ‘representative agents’. They spoke not of states or of nations, but of ‘the market’ considered as one abstract or global thing rather than many concrete national things — as if the whole world were one single economy for which ‘national’ policymakers somehow were or could be held responsible. The penchant for abstraction that led modern economists to part ways with early political-economists was not entirely without value. It brought great gains in logical rigor and theoretical understanding, as do 'most ‘general’ theories and models. But too many modern policy-makers informed by the latterday economists, unlike earlier generations of Hamiltonian and Listian policy-makers informed by earlier political-economists, have purchased their rigor and theoretical understanding at the expense of empirical relevance and practical wisdom. In a world of nation-states, for as long as we inhabit it, policy-makers can control only, and hence must focus mainly on, that for which they are actually responsible. Those are their ‘domestic’ economies made up of their national citizenries, not a nationally uncontrollable and barely existent ‘global economy.’ And any national economy, to be strong and creative and prosperous through time, had to be a productively ‘diversified’ economy — diversified within the national boundaries that policy-makers could actually ‘affect’. It had to have robust agricultural, industrial, commercial, and financial sectors. I hasten to add here two things I am not saying, lest there be any confusion about the two things that I have said. First, though I urge restoration and facilitation of national productive development as a perpetual and well-coordinated national project, I do not mean to suggest that world markets or other nations — especially allies — and their interests are to be disregarded. I mean simply that they are not to be depended upon. The ‘outsourcing’ of ‘developed’ nation's primary industries (and jobs!), and the over-reliance on ‘global supply chains,’ that we began in the 1990s have been catastrophic. Those developments must be reversed and our sovereignty restored even as we respect other nations and their sovereignties. Second, though I urge coordination and facilitation of ongoing national development as a perpetual project, I do not mean to suggest ‘central planning’ or public encroachment on private terrain, any more than we mean to suggest private corruption of public offices. I mean simply that our public and private sectors have their own special functions and must be fully utilized in those functions. Private sector firms have control over microeconomic matters but do not have control or authority over macroeconomic matters. They cannot coordinate efforts across industrial sectors or across all of our nation's States and regions — nor, usually, can they finance such efforts efficiently. Public sector instrumentalities for their part cannot generally invent, develop, market or disseminate new products, techniques, or productive technologies. They can only facilitate and smoothen the processes through which private sector persons and entities do that. Are there any proposals or proposers on the horizon who ‘get’ all of this? Thankfully, yes. US Congressman Ro Khanna and Senator Marco Rubio have recently proposed bipartisan, bicameral legislation that I drafted, which erects the first two of four pillars I put in a draft bill I first floated in 2020 — a permanent Cabinet-level National Development Council like our National Security Council charged with developing and regularly updating a National Development Strategy, and a repurposed Federal Financing Bank within Treasury to finance the execution of that Strategy. Both legislators also have articulated sophisticated new developmentalist visions — the Congressman in a growing series of books, OpEd pieces, and major articles in respected policy journals, and the Senator in multiple white papers. It is to be hoped, then, that more legislators will quickly be joining Congressman Khanna and Senator Rubio in their visionary proposals and legislation. Until then, we must push for rapid passage of their legislation by both the present and the next US Congress. And we must remember and never forget that Development is Forever, in order that our society might be, to channel another Bob Dylan number, ‘Forever Young’.

instituicoes: UiT The Arctic University of Norway
palavras_openalex: light-sheet microscopy | SOLIS | electron microscopy | X-ray microscopy | X-ray free-electron laser | X-ray phase contrast imaging | X-ray absorption spectroscopy | X-ray diffraction tomography | X-ray phase-contrast tomography
resumo: The editors of Microscopy Today congratulate the winners of the 14th Microscopy Today Innovation Awards competition. The ten innovations described below advance microscopy in the areas of light microscopy, electron microscopy, and X-ray microscopy. These innovations will make microscopy more powerful, more productive, and easier to accomplish. Arctic University of Norway Developer: Florian Ströhl SOLIS is a new type of light-sheet fluorescence microscopy method that allows imaging of entire volumes of samples at high resolution without the background haze common with other types of fluorescence microscopy. The acronym SOLIS stands for scanned oblique light-sheet instant-volume sectioning, and, as this name suggests, the method uses an angled light-sheet that sweeps through the sample volume. At each instant in time, a multifocus imager is used to linearize the illuminated plane onto a single row on a camera sensor. Once a full sweep is completed, the entire volume is mapped onto the plane of the camera. There are two cases for the camera's read-out mode. In the first case, the camera's shutter is open for the full duration of the sweep. The recorded image planes are indistinguishable from image planes taken under widefield illumination, and it is therefore corrupted by background haze. In the second case, each sensor line is read individually and synchronously with the light-sheet sweep. A light-sheet swept at an oblique angle thus results in an image with a filled missing-frequency cone, which increases axial resolution. The SOLIS method offers several advantages over other types of fluorescence microscopy. In addition to high-resolution imaging of entire volumes of samples without the background haze, it keeps the ease of use of confocal microscopy (only a single objective near the sample) while exceeding the speed of light-sheet microscopy at light-exposure levels comparable to spinning disk microscopy. It also provides axial superresolution as the light-sheet is swept at an oblique angle and thus provides access to additional axial spatial frequency information akin to 3D structured-illumination microscopy. The ability of SOLIS to quickly and accurately image large volumes could have a significant impact on such fields as neuroscience, developmental biology, and cell biology. Furthermore, the ability to generate 3D recordings at high speed could lead to a fruitful symbiosis of light-sheet and fluorescence-fluctuation-based superresolution microscopy, which requires large amounts of raw data to generate sub-diffraction-resolution images. Potential applications include study of the development and function of organs and tissues, interactions between cells and their environment, and the mechanisms underlying diseases. DECTRIS AG Developers: Luca Piazza, Daniel Stroppa, Christoph Hoermann, Pietro Zambon, Vittorio Boccone, Markus Vitins, Sergio Bottinelli, and Matthias Meffert The DECTRIS ARINA® is a retractable, electron-counting detector specifically de­veloped for four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D STEM). It combines a speed of up to 120,000 frames per second with a high dynamic range and noise-free readout, thus enabling high-quality data acquisition at the native speed of a conventional STEM. The ARINA detector uses hybrid-pixel technology, connecting a thick layer of semiconducting sensor material to an application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) pixel-by-pixel using bump-bonding. This approach allows users to select the sensor material best suited for a specific electron energy range: silicon (Si) for 30–200 keV or a high-Z material for 300 keV. Furthermore, it is a radiation-hard detector that does not require a beam-stop. The detector employs a mixed-mode CMOS electron-counting ASIC with 100 µm pixels in a 192 × 192 matrix and high-speed readout electronics capable of reaching 120,000 frames per second. A DECTRIS-patented instant retrigger mechanism permits a non-paralyzable counting mode of up to 108 electrons per second per pixel. As a result, the detector provides noise-free readout, high dynamic range, and single-electron sensitivity, making possible dwell times below 10 µs. It has a compact design and an active area of 20 mm by 20 mm (or 192 pixels by 192 pixels). The ARINA detector is compatible with a wide range of high-end scanning transmission electron microscopes. Neither hybrid-pixel technology nor 4D STEM are new to electron microscopy. Yet this detector can reach high speed without compromising sensitivity and dynamic range. To make 4D STEM experiments as viable as conventional STEM image acquisition requires the recording of diffraction patterns with a pixelated detector at fast frame rates and with sufficient sensitivity to capture single electron hits over a high dynamic range. Until now, no detector technology could satisfy all of the requirements of a 4D STEM experiment. This fast hybrid-pixel detector provides a more inclusive recording of the scattering information from the specimen for the same electron dose compared to a conventional detector. This is an ideal tool for the most challenging 4D STEM applications, such as crystalline phase mapping, orientation mapping, and ptychography. Applications include strain mapping and differential phase-contrast imaging. Gatan, Inc. Developers: Paul Mooney, Cory Czarnik, Ben Miller, Tom Sha, and Brian Lee The Metro counting camera is a large-format direct-detection camera designed to work between 60 and 200 keV. It detects and identifies individual electron events at high speed, enabling low-noise imaging at low electron dose rates. While the sensor is fast, outputting 1,477 frames per second at full 2k × 2k resolution, the camera does not dump terabytes of sparse data or heavily compressed data. Instead, it produces final images with good contrast in the well-known *dm.4 format from Gatan, with optional live drift correction, just like the popular Gatan OneView camera. In addition, each Metro camera is equipped for in situ acquisition. The Metro camera also has a dedicated diffraction mode, which enables higher intensities to be quantified, and is optimized to keep the background dark. The resulting counted diffraction patterns exhibit excellent sharpness and signal-to-noise. Metro has a higher detective quantum efficiency (DQE) at 80 kV than previous direct-detection counting cameras from Gatan, which were optimized for higher kVs. The Metro is instead optimized to operate in a lower range (60–200 kV) for applications such as in situ experiments, diffraction, and 4D STEM. Ease of use was a key objective in Metro development, and unlike the K3 IS, the other direct detection camera for materials science from Gatan, the user interface was designed to feel like the Rio and OneView cameras from Gatan. Building upon the technical and commercial success of K3, Metro enables exceptional imaging and diffraction performance, especially at low electron dose rates. This performance should enable even older microscopes to obtain data from beam-sensitive samples that previously would have been excluded from high-resolution imaging. The Metro camera is designed to support a variety of TEM techniques, including low-dose imaging, in situ imaging, diffraction, and 4D STEM. Metro is the first Gatan direct detector that isn’t a life science camera first and material science camera second. The camera will be especially useful for materials requiring either low-kV or low-dose illumination, but it can be used for any material. Since every Metro camera is a Gatan in situ camera, it synchronizes image data with metadata provided by the microscope and by in situ holders from partner specimen holder manufacturers. NanoElectronic Imaging Developers: William A. Hubbard and B. C. Regan NEI’s STEM EBIC system enables straightforward imaging of electronic and thermal features that are otherwise difficult, if not impossible, to visualize in the TEM. Electron beam-induced current (EBIC) is a measure of the current generated in a sample as it is raster-­scanned by a focused electron beam. Associating the measured EBIC with the beam position produces an EBIC image. First implemented in the 1960s, EBIC imaging is usually performed in a scanning electron microscope (SEM) to map electric fields in microelectronic devices. For instance, the built-in electric field of a p-n junction separates electron-hole pairs generated by the beam, producing a strong EBIC signal. Recently, thousand-fold improvements in current measurement sensitivity have led to practical EBIC imaging in scanning transmission electron microscopes (STEMs). This improved sensitivity reveals previously undetectable EBICs. In particular, the EBIC generated by secondary electron emission (SEEBIC) can now be routinely visualized. Standard TEM-based techniques excel at determining the physical structure of a sample—the atomic locations and elemental identities—but they struggle to distinguish a metal from an insulator, or a warm interconnect from a cold one. In microelectronic devices, such electronic and thermal structure is generally of greater interest than the physical structure. STEM SEEBIC-based imaging of micro- and nano-electronic devices reveals these signals at high resolution. It can, for instance, quantitatively map conductivity, electric field, temperature, SE yield, active dopant concentration, and work function. NEI’s STEM EBIC system is a turn-key solution for measuring extremely small EBICs. Low-noise STEM EBIC images of sub-pA signals, including SEEBIC, can be acquired in under two minutes. Extrinsic noise (for example, line noise) is nearly undetectable, so image filtering and post-processing are not necessary. The system—featuring a sample holder, custom substrates, and electronics optimized for EBIC in the TEM—is equipped with two independent EBIC amplifier channels for acquiring EBIC from different electrodes simultaneously. Two-channel EBIC can definitively separate SEEBIC from standard EBIC in situations where both are present, which greatly facilitates analysis and interpretation. NEI’s STEM EBIC system is designed to work with other in situ techniques, including heating and biasing on either custom-fabricated test devices or FIB-extracted cross-­sectional samples. Protochips, Inc. Developers: Stamp Walden, Alan Franks, John Damiano, Mark Uebel, Kate Marusak, Nelson Marthe, Mike Coy, and David Nackashi AXON Dose™ calibrates TEM beam current, calculates the dose at each specimen area, and manages dose measurements through changes in spot size and magnification. This device consists of a dedicated Faraday cup TEM holder, a picoammeter for measuring current, and a machine-vision-based software module for controlling the microscope and registering the beam current. The TEM holder has two regions, a Faraday Cup for measuring current and a transparent region for measuring beam area. The AXON Dose software automatically controls the TEM during calibration, moving the holder between the two areas, measuring both the beam current and the beam area. Calibration can be done for either TEM or STEM. After calibration, the user may place the sample into the instrument using whatever holder they choose, and AXON Dose will record dose rate and total accumulated dose as metadata for every image. This dose information is used to create visualizations of accumulated dose, and, based on exposed dose and dose rate, provide a reference to quantify beam effects where exposure has already occurred. AXON Dose is a major advancement over previous methods for the following reasons: (1) AXON Dose records the total accumulated dose on a pixel-by-pixel basis, even while the user is moving the beam or goniometer. A complete historical record of beam location and dose rate is recorded as metadata. This is an advance over existing dose-measurement technologies that only account for what is happening in the current frame. (2) AXON Dose uses a well-known Faraday cup method to calibrate the dose rate directly at the sample location. Using machine vision software, the system automatically calibrates beam current against beam area across many different microscope settings with minimal user intervention. The system also accounts for effects related to cold FEG guns and electrostatic beam blanking shutters. The quantification of dose recorded as metadata gives scientists the ability to organize, share, and repeat experimental results, particularly when electron dose is a contributing factor in the analysis. Applications include studies of zeolites, metal-organic frameworks, and polymers. Dose management is essential for in situ TEM work involving corrosion, batteries, and synthesis, where beam effects can alter the experiment. Sigray, Inc. Developers: Wenbing Yun and Benjamin Stripe The Sigray AttoMap-310 microXRF system provides highly sensitive, non-destructive microanalytical quantification of low atomic number (low-Z) elements. The system is a micro X-ray fluorescence (microXRF) analytical tool, in which X-ray illumination generates characteristic X-rays from spot sizes on the sample down to 3–5 µm. By measuring the flux and energy of the X-rays emitted from the illuminated spot on the sample with an energy-dispersive silicon drift detector, concentrations of a large number of elements can be determined simultaneously. Rastering the sample with respect to the illumination spot produces micron-scale elemental images. The angle of X-ray acquisition can be varied from 0 to 70 degrees for sample sizes up to 100 × 100 mm. AttoMap-310 innovations include a patented X-ray source that can operate at five customizable X-ray energies. This tunability allows users to select the appropriate illumination energy to increase sensitivity by orders of magnitude and enables sub-parts-per-million (sub-ppm) sensitivities to be achieved for a wide range of elements. Furthermore, Sigray has developed several specialized X-ray source target materials, such as SiC and Ca, which enable the AttoMap to deliver high sensitivity for elements such as C, O, N, F, Cl, and Na. Compared to SEM EDS, sensitivity can be several hundred times better. Paired with the X-ray source are proprietary X-ray optics that deliver spot sizes down to 3–5 µm. To further maximize the system’s sensitivity to low atomic number elements, AttoMap-310 uses theta-two-theta geometry wavelength-dispersive optics. This allows incidence angles that range from normal incidence (highest spectral resolution) to grazing incidence (highest sensitivity for low-Z elements). Elemental range is from B to U. The capabilities of the AttoMap-310 have already enabled new research applications in semiconductor processing, mineralogy for geological research, metal-containing biomolecules, and the characterization of new materials. Non-destructive sub-ppm sensitivity at micron-scale spatial resolution is typically only achieved using synchrotron microXRF systems, where researchers must apply for beam time and travel many miles, slowing research work. In addition, industrial applications (for example, semiconductor and pharmaceutical) often need synchrotron-like analysis capabilities for proprietary samples. Applications include imaging trace nutrients in mutant plant species, monitoring dopants in next-generation transistors, and identifying trace-level contaminants in batteries. Spectrolight, Inc. Developer: Wilson Yang The Spectrolight Tunable Laser System (TLS) employs TwinFilm™ technology to provide accurate wavelength tuning for pico-second pulsed supercontinuum lasers. The TwinFilm technique combines two angle-dependent tunable bandpass filters that enable specific wavelength selection by using independent angle rotation of each filter. This means the transmitted light's center wavelength and bandwidth are both fully adjustable. In addition, a compensation glass plate is simultaneously rotated to offset any slight walk-off in the beam path, which enables exceptional pointing stability with minimal deviation. In this way, the center wavelength can be selected to be at any wavelength between 410 nm to 1650 nm, and the bandwidth can be adjusted anywhere between 3 nm to 15 nm in real time via software control. The Tunable Laser System employing TwinFilm technology provides high throughput with over 75% transmission. It provides reliable pointing stability, fast tuning speeds (20–200 ms), and center wavelength tuning up to the short-wavelength infrared range.
