resumo: Abstract Taking bus and subway into account, an asymmetric polycentric urban system equilibrium model is constructed to explore the impacts of rail transit on the distribution of residents and labor force in a linear polycentric urban system. By comparing the urban system equilibria before and after the introduction of rail transit, the influence of rail transit on urban performance is analyzed. The results show that the introduction of rail transit makes the advantaged center more attractive for the labor force, and further widens the economic level gap between the two business centers. Specifically, larger distance between the two commercial centers and the higher subway travel cost would strengthen the polarization effect caused by rail transit investment. Since the improvement of transportation makes it easier for residents to accept long-distance commuting and they are more willing to choose the jobs in the advanced center.

titulo: Blackstone vs BlackRock
instituicoes: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique | Centre de recherche sur les Inégalités Sociales | Institut d'Etudes Politiques de Paris
palavras_openalex: infrastructure funds | real estate investment funds | asset management | BlackRock | Blackstone | Thames Water | privatization | institutional investors | pension funds | investment funds | capitalism | public services | financialization | 2024 floods | England | Thatcherism | private equity | hedge funds | mutual funds
resumo: Heavy rains in the first half of 2024 fueled not only Britain's rivers, but also public outrage over the poor quality of England's sewage system. Charming little streams in the English countryside overflowing with untreated human feces made headlines across the Channel. Critics argued that Thames Water's ownership was to blame for the poor quality of this public service, its chronic under-capacity and decades of under-investment. Indeed, after its privatization during the Thatcher era, the company changed hands several times and was often owned by large investment funds run by firms such as Macquarie, one of the largest infrastructure funds. Brett Christophers' book, Our Lives in Their Portfolios, is timely in exposing the capitalist mechanisms behind the British sewage scandal. This book focuses on infrastructure and real estate funds. Behind a sophisticated and sometimes esoteric vocabulary, these funds are simple capitalist devices through which asset managers invest their clients' wealth in various types of assets. As explained in detail in chapter one, this type of contract differs from traditional investment schemes such as stocks or bonds. The investment fund managed by an asset manager is a secretive and opaque vehicle, open only to a very select group of institutional players, such as pension funds, insurance companies and banks, foundations, who accept, in return for the promise of a regular cash flow, to lock up their money for a certain period of time and leave it to the asset manager to decide its fate. Asset management is not a new phenomenon and has been studied by various social scientists who have focused, for example, through rich ethnography on everyday investment practices or on workplace discrimination that maintains an upper-class white male hegemony (Neely, 2022; Ortiz, 2021). Chrisophers' book remains discreet about its methodology, probably because it is aimed at a broader audience than the social science academic public. Nevertheless, the academic reader will quickly notice that, unlike most social studies of finance research, Our Lives does not rely on first-hand observations and interviews or on statistical analysis, but rather on a vast amount of secondary material, including an impressive collection of excerpts from the financial press and financial reports. Nevertheless, this extensive material allows him to paint a comprehensive picture of asset management over the last few decades and to highlight the worrying evolution of some of its sectors. Asset management has evolved rapidly since the 1970s, directing investments toward a variety of targets, such as listed companies (mutual funds and hedge funds), unlisted companies (private equity), or emerging companies (capital risk). In the last decade, a new type of fund has boomed: infrastructure and real estate funds. Water, energy, communications, transportation (parking lots, highways), social services (especially day care and retirement facilities), farmland, housing—all of these assets of our daily lives are the new fields in which these asset funds are flourishing. While these funds sometimes buy listed or unlisted operators in these sectors, they generally prefer to acquire infrastructure assets such as wind farms, water pipes, parking lots, housing, on which various actors (operators, states, households) depend and for which they have to pay regular fees. This emergence, described in Chapter 2, stands in contrast to other financial innovations. Indeed, the United States has been more of a follower than a leader in developing this niche. In fact, infrastructure emerged on the other side of the world in Australia in the 1990s, bolstered by the privatization of energy assets by the state of Victoria. In the 2000s, this business developed further in Europe (and especially in the United Kingdom) and the United States: low interest rates, the lack of profit prospects in traditional financial markets due to the global financial crisis, and the fall in real estate prices made this asset class particularly attractive: cheap infrastructure and real estate assets that generate regular income. By 2020, this niche activity, once small and barely visible, had gained some importance in the world's wealth, with key players such as Blackstone, Brookfield or Macquarie, described in detail in the last part of Chapter 3. Compiling various financial reports, Christophers estimates their importance at $4 trillion in 2020, including $1 trillion in housing and $3 trillion in infrastructure (p. 8). Moreover, its growth is impressive when compared to the $1 trillion in assets under management in 2009 (p. 94). Thus, real estate and infrastructure assets now account for 4% of the $100 trillion in assets under management and almost 1% of global net worth—$535 trillion (Chancel et al., 2022). Still, one might wonder why we should care about this class of assets, since its importance in asset management is still limited. Moreover, it is not new that important assets of everyday life, such as one's house, farm, or field, are owned by someone else, whether present or “absentee landlord”. Chapters 4 (“The costs”) and 5 (“Who gains”) detail the pernicious aspects of this assetization of real estate and infrastructure. In fact, infrastructure and real estate funds, more than individual owners, pursue a systematic strategy of maximizing returns. Far from their image of long-term investors, they prioritize assets that generate short-term, predictable, regular income, such as regular monthly fees and rents for occupying an apartment, farming land, or using water pipes. Thus, those funds systematically underinvest. They do not hold on to their assets for long. After a few years, they transfer them to a new owner before the costs of chronic underinvestment become visible. When contracting with the state to take over some assets, the inclusion of “revenue guarantees” to protect against insufficient fees is also a common “de-risking” strategy (p. 171). In short, the key to these funds' success lies in the intelligent use of “natural monopolies” (p. 206). By controlling assets on which many parties (users, cities, states) depend, they gain power over them and intensively exploit contractual incompleteness: raise fees, underinvest, or reduce quality. These pernicious effects are probably at their greatest when asset managers invest in public-private partnerships (PPPs). They take advantage of the willingness of state entities to limit their current debt by offering a “market” solution that ultimately farms out these entities' future revenues. While these asset funds are costly for asset users, especially for state actors and ultimately for citizens, one might wonder who benefits from their development. Could it be the “teachers, nurses and firefighters” who benefit through their pension funds investing in this new asset class to fund their future pensions (p. 233)? The book quickly debunks this heroic hypothesis. First, these investment funds are mostly open only to a very select elite. Second, even if pension funds could invest in these vehicles, they are not as profitable as one might think. While they reward asset managers with hefty profits and bonuses, the picture for investors is not so rosy. In fact, like hedge funds, these opaque vehicles opt for a 2/20 fee structure. Asset managers earn both 20% of the fund's profits and a 2% annual fee on the amounts invested. While the 20% serves as an incentive and ideological justification, asset managers often make huge profits solely on the 2% fee, without adding any significant value to their clients. Finally, investment funds are companies that are particularly involved in “fiscal extractivism”. Not only do they register their funds in tax havens to take advantage of the opacity and lack of taxes on corporate income, but they also pay profits as “carried interest,” which is undertaxed in many countries, such as the United States. Overall, then, the book paints a broad, insightful, and disturbing picture of the development of infrastructure and real estate funds. It does an excellent job of warning a wide public audience about the social costs and risks of this new activity. At times, academic readers may wish the book was more specific about the precise mechanisms that underlie the power of this industry. While the examples are generally striking, even outrageous, one wishes for better explanations to completely exclude the alternative neoliberal/market efficiency narrative. A link to neoinstitutional economics (à la Williamson) and economic sociology would have been helpful to characterize market power and asymmetry. Moreover, one might wonder whether the mechanisms identified by the author are entirely specific to this activity. In fact, short-termism, de-risking, monopoly power, contractual incompleteness, fiscal extractivism, etc. are mechanisms that are widely found in capitalist (and even pre-capitalist) economies. What may be specific to asset management, however, is that this activity not only bundles assets but also these extractive mechanisms to an unprecedented degree. Christophers also introduces a new concept that deserves some discussion. The growing influence of asset managers over the key assets of everyday life should lead us to consider the emergence of a pernicious “asset-manager society” which differs from the “asset-manager capitalism” described by Braun (2022). Indeed, the latter refers to the fact that large asset management firms such as BlackRock, Vanguard or State Street have paradoxically become key players in contemporary capitalism. Specializing in low-cost passive index management that replicates major stock indexes, they now own a significant share of the economy (up to 20% of the S&P 500 for the big three) and, if they were a little less “passive,” could play the role of “universal owners” interested in maximizing the returns of the economy as a whole, rather than acting as individual shareholders maximizing the profits of the companies they control one by one. In contrast, infrastructure and real estate asset managers such as Blackstone actively manage the assets they control and do not hesitate, for example, to evict tenants in order to maximize profit on each specific asset. How can we reconcile this polarization between “asset-manager capitalism” and “asset-manager society,” between Blackstone and its offspring BlackRock, and even between different divisions of BlackRock itself (since it also has a secondary involvement in infrastructure funds)? One way is to think of finance as a field (à la Bourdieu), with conventional, listed, passive finance facing alternative, unlisted, active finance. Thinking of it as a field helps to better understand how asset management works and its recent polarizing political impact (Benquet & Bourgeron, 2022).

resumo: Job polarisation is the growth of high- and low-skilled employment relative to middle-skilled employment, typically in developed countries. Based on Khazanah Research Institute’s (KRI) descriptive study in 2017, Malaysia’s workforce experienced job polarisation over the last two decades. This study uses a different approach, i.e. multinomial logistic regression, to measure the probability of employment choice by different job categories to validate the presence of job polarisation in Malaysia. Unlike past research that used headcounts based on wage quantiles, this paper considers the individual and sectoral effects. This study confirms the job polarisation finding of KRI (2017) by comparing Malaysia’s employment structure between 2011 and 2017. Technology changes the methods and skills required to perform the same tasks. Besides, the adoption of technology depends on the firm’s or industry’s foresight of how technology may change the productivity of the worker. If the investment cost of a technology is greater than the training cost, firms may not adopt the technology. If an industry has the foresight of how technology may change the performance of tasks, and recruit workers in tandem with upskilling programmes, the phenomenon of job polarisation will fade out eventually.

resumo: INTRODUCTION The necessity for dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) in flow diverters (FDs) limits its application in the treatment of intracranial aneurysms due to haemorrhagic risks. Surface-coated FDs aim to reduce thrombogenicity, potentially allowing patients to be on single antiplatelet (SAPT) posttreatment.[1,2] The p64 movable wire hydrophilic polymer-coated flow diverter (p64 MW HPC FD) (Phenox, Bochum, Germany) is a hydrophilic polymer-coated stent that inhibits platelet plug.[3] Several case series investigating its safety and efficacy were reported from Europe.[1,4,5,6] This retrospective case series examines the efficacy and safety of p64 MW HPC FD in a single centre in Asia. METHODS We performed a retrospective study of consecutive patients treated with p64 MW HPC FD between April 2021 and October 2021 in a single tertiary referral centre in Singapore at National Neuroscience Institute. Asymptomatic patients with unruptured intracranial aneurysms were selected for FD deployment if they fulfilled the following criteria: (a) intradural aneurysm or intradural component along the internal carotid artery (ICA), (b) wide-neck aneurysm size ≥5 mm with interval growth or irregular surface with daughter sac, and (c) consensus at multidisciplinary meetings with the neurosurgical team before treatment. The study was approved by the SingHealth Centralised Institutional Review Board (CRIB reference: 2022/2298), and patients’ consent was waived. Patients received 5 days of DAPT before the procedure. All patients received aspirin and a second antiplatelet, that is, either clopidogrel or ticagrelor. For patients with suboptimal platelet inhibition with clopidogrel on Multiplate Analyzer (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany), or CYP2C19 poor to moderate metaboliser, the second antiplatelet of choice was ticagrelor. After FD placement, patients were continued on DAPT for 3 months, followed by lifelong aspirin. The duration of DAPT may be extended in patients with potentially higher thromboembolic risk. Preprocedural catheter angiogram was performed in all patients. The FDs were sized by the arterial diameter and distance between the proximal and distal landing zones. All procedures were performed under general anaesthesia and via femoral access. Intraprocedural systemic heparinisation was adjusted based on body weight and activated clotting time to achieve 2–2.5 times of baseline value. Deployment of FD was performed via ‘0.021-inch microcatheter with 0.088-inch or 0.096-inch long sheath positioned at the distal cervical ICA. Intermediate catheters were used in some cases for additional support. Patients’ demographics, clinical and radiological data were collected. All patients were reviewed at discharge and at 3–6 months and 1-year postprocedure. Radiological follow-up was scheduled at 3–6 months with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the intracranial arteries, and at 1 year with either catheter angiogram or MRI of the brain with MRA. Aneurysm occlusion was assessed with O’Kelly–Marotta grading scale.[7] Outcomes were classified as radiological and clinical. Radiological outcomes included aneurysm occlusion, stent patency and in-stent stenosis (ISS). Clinical outcomes included postprocedural new neurological deficit, change in functional status (modified Rankin Scale) and mortality. RESULTS Eight patients were included in the study, of whom four (50%) were males. The mean age of patients was 58 (range 45–70) years. A total of nine unruptured saccular aneurysms along the ICA were treated. Of these, eight aneurysms were at the paraophthalmic segment distal to the ophthalmic artery and one aneurysm was at the distal cavernous segment with its superior aspect likely intradural. Mean aneurysmal width, heights and neck dimensions were 5.8 (range 3.1–9.6) mm, 4.2 (range 3.0–6.8) mm and 3.7 (range 3.0–5.5) mm, respectively. Mean aspect ratio (height : neck) was 1.2 (range 0.7–1.3). Adjunct coiling was performed in one patient with aneurysm width of 9.6 mm. Two adjacent aneurysms in another patient were treated with a single FD. Two (25%) patients had intraprocedural complications. The first patient had focal twisting at the proximal FD during deployment, requiring balloon angioplasty to adequately open the FD [Figure 1]. The FD deployed was 4.5 × 24 mm. The patient was placed on 6 months DAPT postprocedure. The second patient had FD foreshortening shortly after deployment despite initial satisfactory position. The FD was left alone due to satisfactory coverage across the aneurysm neck.Figure 1: Digital subtraction angiography images show (a) suboptimal expansion of flow diverter (4.5 × 24 mm) with focal twisting at the proximal aspect of the stent (arrow); (b) balloon angioplasty that was performed across the focal twisting of the flow diverter, and (c) improvement of the focal twisting of the stent with adequate wall apposition (arrow).Angiographic outcomes Table 1 provides a summary of the angiographic outcomes in our patients. Immediately after FD deployment, eight (89%) out of nine aneurysms showed persistent total filling of the aneurysm (O’Kelly–Marotta [OKM] grade A), while the remaining patient had subtotal filling (OKM grade B).Table 1: Radiographic outcomes in patients with unruptured internal carotid artery aneurysms treated with p64 MW HPC FD.At 3–6 months, MRA was performed in seven out of eight patients to assess intra-aneurysmal flow. Among the eight aneurysms assessed, four (50%) showed absent flow, three (38%) showed minimal flow and one (12%) had persistent flow. No infarct was detected. At 1 year, catheter angiogram was performed in seven patients. Among the eight aneurysms assessed, seven (88%) showed complete occlusion (OKM grade D), whereas one (12%) had subtotal filling (OKM grade B3). The last patient who opted for MRI follow-up at 1 year showed absent intra-aneurysmal flow. All stent positions were unchanged. The patient who had focal twisting during FD deployment had excellent stent-wall apposition on catheter angiogram. Two (25%) FDs exhibited mild ISS [Figure 2], but the patients were asymptomatic and did not require angioplasty. Postprocedure, no patient had new neurological deficit or deterioriation in the modified Rankin Scale, and no mortality was reported.Figure 2: (a) Angiography 3D reconstruction image, (b) cone-beam CT image and (c) angiography image at deployment of flow diverter show good stent-wall apposition. (d & e) Follow-up angiography images at 1 year show in-stent stenosis at the proximal (long arrow, d) and distal (short arrow, d) aspects of the flow diverter, along with complete aneurysm occlusion.DISCUSSION We reviewed the outcomes of eight patients with nine anterior circulation saccular unruptured aneurysms who underwent p64 MW HPC FD placement. At 1-year follow-up, the complete occlusion rate was 88%. There was no new neurological deficit, deterioration or mortality reported in our cohort. Our aneurysm occlusion rate at 1 year is comparable to the rates in other institutions, which ranged between 65% and 85% at 6–9 months post-FD placement.[1,4,5,6,8] This demonstrates the efficacy and reproducibility in outcomes of p64 MW HPC FD across centres and interventionalists. In our study, four out of the eight treated aneurysms that showed absent intra-aneurysmal flow signal at the 3–6 months follow-up MRA had OKM grade D occlusion on 1-year angiogram. The remaining four aneurysms with minimal or persistent intra-aneurysmal flow on MRA had either complete occlusion or incomplete filling at the 1-year angiogram. Therefore, the absence of intra-aneurysmal flow signal in the initial MRI at 3–6 months appears predictive of the eventual aneurysm occlusion. This correlation between early MRA findings and late angiographic results may allow MRA to be a surrogate for invasive angiogram procedures and guide follow-up management. No postprocedural clinical adverse events or mortality was observed in our patients. Hellstern et al.[1] reported a case of delayed parenchymal haemorrhage 2 months after the procedure, which was treated conservatively with subsequent good recovery. Similarly, there is no mortality reported across the published case series using p64 MW HPC FD, even in patients with acute aneurysm rupture.[1,4,5,6,8] The intraprocedural complications in our study were focal twisting and foreshortening of FD, which were also observed in other studies not limited to p64 MW HPC FD.[1,4,5,9] Risk factors for FD twisting include longer stent, large aneurysms and recurrent aneurysms.[10] Indeed, the stent used in our case of FD twisting was the longest in our cohort, and this could have led to microcatheter rotation during deployment after anchoring of the distal stent.[10] Therefore, early recognition of stent twisting is important when deploying longer stents. In contrast, foreshortening of FD is due to suboptimal wall apposition and excessive stent compaction. Hence, appropriate sizing and optimal FD placement are paramount in reducing its occurrence.[11] Our case of intra-procedural FD foreshortening may be related to undersizing and over-compaction of the stent. A clinical concern for FDs is ISS by intimal hyperplasia. Two patients in our cohort demonstrated mild ISS. One of them reported non-compliance to the antiplatelet regime. In both cases, the stents appeared to have intimal thickening at its ends. The deployment of the concerned stents was uneventful without excessive manipulation or use of adjuncts such as angioplasty balloon. The stent-wall appositions were also satisfactory on follow-up angiograms. In clinical studies investigating p64 MW HPC FD, ISS is not routinely reported. Among the studies that reported ISS, the overall incidence ranged from 8% to 25%.[1,4,5] For instance, Hellstern et al.[1] reported an ISS rate of 8% at 2 months and 19% at 4 months in their patient cohort with SAPT. All patients in their cohort were asymptomatic, although one patient underwent balloon angioplasty due to inadequate collateral vessels. No patient with ISS had long-term clinical deficit.[1,4,5] In clinical studies, the rate of ISS in uncoated p64 FD was reported at 29% while the rate in coated HPC was 8%–25%.[1,4,5,12,13] In our centre, we conventionally use DAPT for 3 months after FD deployment, followed by lifelong SAPT. Previous reports showed the feasibility of surface-coated FD using SAPT with comparable safety profile.[14] With the lack of large-scale randomised controlled trial at this juncture, we believe that patients treated with surface-coated FD should still receive DAPT. However, surface-coated FD should be considered in patients who may require early termination of the second antiplatelet, such as those who require additional operations or have high rebleeding risks. We recognise in this initial experience that the treated aneurysms have low rupture risk without specific anatomical or technical challenges, which may introduce bias leading to favourable outcomes. The clinical application of p64 HPC MW FD in large aneurysms or challenging anatomy would require further investigation. The limitations of this study are its retrospective nature, small patient cohort and the lack of a control group to compare p64 HPC MW FD to other FDs. The safety of surface-coated FD under SAPT compared to uncoated FD under DAPT would need to be investigated in randomised controlled trials, such as the COATING study.[15] In conclusion, based on our initial experience, p64 MW HPC FD is effective in the treatment of intracranial aneurysms, with a satisfactory occlusion rate and no clinical complications. Imaging observations of mild ISS, stent foreshortening and reversible focal twisting have also been reported with other FDs. Further studies with larger aneurysms, challenging vascular anatomy and the use of SAPT may be considered to further assess the safety and clinical applicability of p64 MW HPC FD. titulo: Scrutinising Polarisation: Patterns and Consequences of Occupational Transformation in the Swedish Labour Market
instituicoes: National Taiwan University

palavras_openalex: labor market polarization | occupational structure | high-skilled jobs | low-skilled jobs | digitalization | neoliberalism | deregulation | Fordism | post-industrial economy | labor market segmentation | temporary employment contracts | precarious employment | occupational prestige | female-dominated professions | trade unions | collective bargaining | Sweden | labour market flexibility | social polarization | inequality
resumo: Since the 1990s, changes within the labour market in Sweden have taken place with a clear trend towards polarization resulting in a significant alteration in the structure of occupations and organization of work, etc. The book presents an in-depth understanding of how the impact of digital technologies and neoliberal policies have contributed to developing patterns of employment and the escalation of social polarization. As noted, the demand for high-skilled occupations has seemingly increased alongside the demand for lower skilled occupations; likewise, there is a declining increase in work opportunities associated with medium-skilled occupations. The book also provides a clear framing of polarization by differentiating it from inequality, while also examining and re-examining the parameters from the predominantly Fordist economic model of the twentieth century to the current neoliberal or deregulated markets model of development. The book provides an examination of the transformation and polarization that has occurred in the Swedish labour market since the 1990s, considering the effects of occupations and the structuring of occupations on some social groups and organizations. The book also sees the impact of digital technology, and changes prompted by neoliberal policies that are observed in employment structures in developed industrialized nations to incite ‘social polarization’. This has seen demand for high-skilled occupations and low-skilled occupations, yet the growing availability of demand for medium-skilled occupations has diminished. The book also provides a framing of polarization and distinctly separates it from inequality noting that polarization is characterized as homogeneous within social groups, like the skilled occupations and the unskilled occupation and heterogeneous across social groups. This phenomenon may occur even in societies where inequality is relatively low. The book reviews the historical changes in the labour market, identifying a shift from Fordist production models that supported the middle class to a post-Industrial era characterized by neoliberalism and deregulated markets. The research underscores the significance of intellectual, cognitive, emotional and interpersonal skills in contemporary work, particularly in female-dominated professions, where these factors may profoundly influence individuals' perceptions of occupational prestige. In this publication, the rising flexibility and segmentation of the labour market are thoroughly investigated. It elucidates how corporate HR strategies and policy developments have embraced the increasing use of temporary contracts and precarious employment. The role of digitalization is foregrounded, showing that advances in technology improve efficiency, which can increase the demand for labour, particularly for non-traditional work from both highly skilled and low-skilled workers. The text also addresses the significant challenges unions face in regard to mobilizing and engaging in collective bargaining, in part because the thinking about retaliation, such as losing or not renewing contracts is a significant issue here. The research highlights the crucial role of unions in defending workers' rights, particularly those who work in precarious jobs. Labour sociology often looks at how social institutions, such as unions, can coordinate and leverage management power to defend wages, job security and working conditions. Nonetheless, the diminishing union membership, especially among blue-collar workers, greatly inhibits worker solidarity and strength. The book discusses the interplay between precarious employment and managerial control, accentuating how short-term contracts exacerbate workers' vulnerabilities to exploitation and retaliation. Labour sociology examines how these employment conditions deepen social inequality, particularly affecting marginalized groups with lower educational attainment and income. Although the book does not delve deeply into it, labour sociology frequently studies the impacts of digitalization and neoliberalism on the labour market, suggesting that these forces may contribute to employment polarization, increasing the proportion of high-skilled and low-skilled jobs, while medium-skilled positions gradually disappear, ultimately exacerbating social stratification and economic inequality. From a perspective of social security, this book particularly emphasizes the safety and health risks present in the workplace. A survey conducted by the transportation workers' union indicates that many couriers encounter violence at work, including personal attacks and threats involving firearms. The growing peril of violence is increasingly recognized as an important problem in social security, threatening not only the health and safety of workers but also their mental wellness and job satisfaction. The authority of the Swedish Work Environment Authority, particularly their use of fines for unreported events, demonstrates the vital function regulators can serve in improving safety standards and regulatory compliance. The success of regulators in improving conditions is vital to social security, as it indicates that businesses are therefore responsible for both workers' health and safety. Viewed through the lens of social security, strengthening social insurance to compensate for workers' sick leave and work-related injuries is especially important in alleviating the economic burdens faced by individuals and society as a whole. Additionally, the influence of labour market policies suggests that transitioning towards a work-oriented welfare model, prioritizing employment over welfare provision may compel individuals to engage in unsafe or low-paying jobs. This further impacts social security, undermining workers' bargaining power and increasing their vulnerability. It highlights the necessity of formulating policies that balance employment incentives with adequate safety and welfare protections. In summary, by integrating perspectives from labour sociology and social security, discussions surrounding changes in the labour market should extend beyond economic and technological factors to consider the impacts of social policies and labour organizations. A comprehensive understanding of the multifaceted effects of these changes on various social groups will facilitate the development of a more equitable, inclusive and resilient labour market structure.

resumo: This special issue of California History commemorates the centennial of the Border Patrol and the Immigration Act of 1924. While a series of public commemorative events are being held across the country, we decided to publish new research that critically examines the troubled origins and history of the U.S. Border Patrol and the restrictive immigration legislation that created it. We are proud to feature one Leading Edge article, three Research articles, and a Public History piece that offer new directions in the fields of immigration and borderlands history.Ramón Gutiérrez’s Leading Edge contribution frames the essays in this special issue. Drawing from key secondary sources and a wide range of primary sources, including government records and memoirs, Gutiérrez presents a sweeping historical overview of immigration policing along the nation’s southern international border. He states: “My goal here is to explain how the policing of the U.S.–Mexico border developed to implement the legislative goals of successive presidential administrations regarding the country’s changing labor needs,” while simultaneously pointing out how business cycles and public opinion shaped labor recruitment or expulsion efforts. Readers will find Gutiérrez’s article intriguing for its “broad historical overview based primarily on my teaching of American and Mexican immigration to the U.S. over the last four decades, rather than as a deeply researched essay steeped in primary research.” His synthesis of secondary and primary sources shows how immigration control shifted from state control after the Civil War to federal authority and then to a resurgence of state-based immigration control measures since the 1980s. A major strength of this piece is the numerical data tracing the growth in immigration resources to surveil and curb unsanctioned entry as well as the number of undocumented immigrants detained and deported. Gutiérrez traces the evolution of the Border Patrol, from mounted inspectors seeking to capture illicit Chinese immigrants to the birth of the Border Patrol in 1924 and its early professional footing, to the expansion of its duties during Prohibition, the massive coercive expulsions of ethnic Mexicans during the Great Depression, through the Bracero Program (1942–1964) and Operation Wetback in 1954. The essay proceeds with the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, which ended national immigration quotas; continues with the 1970s War on Crime, massive amnesty, and enforcement with the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986; and concludes with a discussion of the current conflict between federal and state immigration control. We expect this essay to inspire future research on the U.S. Border Patrol as it evolves alongside immigration policy and a changing economy. Much uncertainty remains due to the upcoming 2024 presidential election and the candidates’ sharply contrasting views about immigration. One thing is certain, however: the Border Patrol’s embrace of new technology and artificial intelligence will mark a new era for border enforcement but will also raise new questions about transparency, oversight, and human rights.Drawing from meticulous research in the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services History Office and Library, Erica Toffoli’s pathbreaking essay analyzes a range of primary sources, principally photograph albums, to show how the Border Patrol relied increasingly on electronics technology in the 1950s to surveil the international line. Influenced by histories of optics and photography, Toffoli traces the government’s propaganda that trumpeted the success of border control while at the same time admitting its failure to halt the rising mass of undocumented immigrants. The Border Patrol’s reliance on optical electronic surveillance in the form of mechanized sensors (“electric eyes”) to augment human sight “allowed the agency to articulate its own self-image and that of its chief enemy: the Mexican ‘illegal alien.’” In addition to evaluating photographs of Border Patrol agents doing their duties, Toffoli includes a section on border control photojournalism in the 1940s and ’50s. The author argues that “the Border Patrol crafted an institutional iconography that showcased its prescient, scientific oversight even as it displayed the U.S.–Mexico boundary’s persistent insecurity.” The Immigration and Naturalization Service’s archival material reveals the agency’s contradictory messaging—it includes celebratory vignettes of dedicated personnel and the statistics of illicit captures, yet the organization could not possibly stop the entry of millions of the unsanctioned entrants, a paradox that Toffoli deems a “dedicated effort and assured failure.” Put another way, “[p]aradoxically, this visual culture lauded technological innovation and foreshadowed its failure.”The significance of Toffoli’s essay is its contribution to the history of technology in border policing. A close analysis of the photo-books in the Border Patrol archives shows how the border wardens sought technological assistance to prevent or capture illegal entry from Mexico. By reading written and visual sources across the grain, Toffoli is able to spotlight the inconsistencies in the government’s propaganda as well as its reliance on optical electronic technology to supplement, and frequently replace, human surveillance. Toffoli asserts that “the visual archive confirms the Border Patrol’s obsessive commitment to surveillance technologies, even as it allows the agency’s darker history of xenophobic violence to surface with disturbing clarity.” Scholars have parsed the Border Patrol’s official documents and reports and mined congressional testimony, yet this essay opens a new source of material to show how the agency’s propaganda and photographs claimed the border was “besieged by racialized migrants who were barely human,” contributing to racist portrayals of Mexicans (and other Latinos) flooding into the country in the public’s mind. Policing the U.S.–Mexico border was not only a visual project but also a nativist and racial project that deployed a series of surveillance technologies (e.g., night-vision goggles, ground sensors, etc.) in the name of modernization, sovereignty, and national security. Overall, Toffoli’s innovative investigation uncovers the U.S. Border Patrol’s long history of using visual technologies to police the nation’s borders and in so doing to vilify the Mexican migrant as the quintessential “racial Other.”This article will inspire future research into new border surveillance mechanisms such as drones, robots, and automated towers equipped with artificial intelligence that can be used against migrant border crossers, but also against U.S. citizens. Since the U.S. Border Patrol is allowed to travel up to one hundred miles away from the border, whether inland or offshore, citizens will be constantly monitored under this new surveillance network. Toffoli’s article raises new questions about the use of technology by federal governments, with little regulation and protection of vulnerable populations displaced by war, economic instability, and climate change. Unbridled surveillance of the U.S. Border Patrol raises concerns about the Fourth Amendment rights that protect people from unreasonable searches and seizures by the government.Sonia Hernández contributes new scholarship on “anarcho-motherhood,” or labor activism centered on maternal labor’s interest against capitalists and the U.S. and Mexican governments. Through the biographies of two radical Mexican labor organizers, Caritina Piña and Felipa Velásquez, who were active in northern Mexico during the 1920s and ’30s, Hernández contends that “[w]ithout ever stepping outside of their native country, with little acknowledgment of the importance of their work at the time, both women challenged the unchecked, ever-growing power of the United States, whose business interests profited from low-wage labor on both sides of the border. In this way, labor organizers like those discussed here directly influenced state efforts to regulate immigration and control geopolitical boundaries.” This archival-based article offers a fascinating example of radical working women’s ideologies and resistance activities against the state’s policing and repression.Anarcho-motherhood rejected women’s suffrage and cooperation with the state. With women making up half of Mexico’s industrial labor source, Piña and Velásquez searingly criticize the fact that women earned half of what a man was paid for the same job. Hernández writes, “There was an activism that kept conversations about labor inequalities moving forward and, unlike many labor activists of the era, they spoke insistently of the specific concerns of women.” Her scholarship is significant because both activists defied the Mexican and U.S. governments in support of maternal labor activism. Both were anarcho-syndicalists, adherents to a philosophy that opposed the authority and power of the state and the Catholic Church and instead champions workers’ rights and freedoms. The maternal strain of anarcho-syndicalism, which Hernández terms “anarcho-motherhood,” elevated women to the center of labor organizing, as the mothers and reproducers of the working class: “motherhood that did not bow to state interests nor political parties but served women themselves and their communities.”Caritina Piña operated in Tamaulipas, where, as the secretary of the influential labor union Confederación General de Trabajadores (CGT)—an anarcho-syndicalist organization—she carried on communication with unions, published articles on labor activism in labor newspapers, wrote petitions to leaders on both sides of the border to free political prisoners, and became involved in oil strikes. Hernández concludes that the “anti-U.S. capitalist critique would not have been possible without women like Piña, who oversaw” the union’s daily operations. Piña’s contemporary, Felipa Velásquez—the single mother of eight children—was a schoolteacher in the Mexicali Valley of Baja California, across the border from the Imperial Valley. As a member of the CGT, she wrote and published articles in anarcho-syndicalist newspapers criticizing worker repression, and she was a virulent critic of the Catholic Church. She also engaged in two major agrarian land seizure efforts and was imprisoned for her activities. Velásquez’s writings critical of the Church offer insight into Mexico’s 1920s anticlerical movement. In the end, both these women “point to a radical labor activism that challenged state discourse, directly affecting state efforts to control immigration, transborder migration, and pro-labor movements.”This article raises new questions about the anarchist movement typically understood as male dominated, and contributes toward a greater understanding of the anarchist roots of transnational feminism and international labor movements in the U.S.–Mexico borderlands. Also, this study of Mexican women who became transborder labor organizers and challenged U.S. and Mexican state governments points to new directions in the field of borderlands history. Hernández masterfully weaves together primary and secondary sources from both sides of the U.S.–Mexico border that will inspire new research on borderlands feminism and radical labor movements.Douglas Sackman’s research article wields the medium of visual art to add to our knowledge of border control protest by examining the creative works of painters Judy Baca and Ana Teresa Fernández. Sackman’s captivating analysis of murals by California artists engages issues of settler colonialism, immigration, border walls, and environmental justice. When the Army Corps of Engineers invited Los Angeles visual artist Judy Baca to create a mural on the concrete walls encasing the Los Angeles River, she envisioned something much larger, by engaging her hometown community to help paint hidden histories of Los Angeles. While most are familiar with the Great Wall of Los Angeles, declared in 2017 as a National Historic Site by the U.S. Department of Interior, few know about Baca’s murals on immigration and the U.S.–Mexico border wall. The La Memoria de Nuestra Tierra, California mural depicts the violence of the border wall on the land and its people, and the forthcoming “Immigration Wall” design shows the immigrant rights movement and family separation during the Trump era. Ana Teresa Fernández, a San Francisco visual artist, risked arrest by Border Patrol agents when she attempted to “erase” the border wall by painting it with the same colors as the sky and natural terrain. Like Baca, Fernández recruited a group of volunteer painters to protest the U.S.–Mexico border wall.Although each artist engages with the wall in different ways, Sackman believes they both invoke a utopian vision of bringing people together across borders. According to Sackman, Baca “has brought repressed or erased history and people to light, and she explicitly envisions the border wall as unnatural.” Meanwhile, Fernández symbolically erased the border wall between San Diego and Tijuana. Through painting, “Baca represents what has been erased, while Fernández erased what has been represented,” offering a stunning visual of art in opposition to border control. While scholars have long examined artistic protest, Sackman’s essay shows how painters use the medium to “affirm inclusion, empathy, and human and ecological connections across the border between Alta and Baja California.”Beginning in 1976, Baca and others from the Social and Public Art Resource Center, which she cofounded, painted an epic mural called the Great Wall of Los Angeles on the concretized Los Angeles River to highlight the history that had been erased. She and over 400 young compatriots spent 15 years painting more than 600 faces, mostly of people of color, to visually place people back into the history of Los Angeles. Baca later painted another epic mural “representing the border fence as stakes driven into the body of people and the land.” Thirty-five years later, Fernández first reimagined an erased border, swishing blue paint on the border wall as a symbol of the sky. Over the years she staged similar artistic border control protests. She turned the optic of erasure on its head by symbolically erasing the border wall to remember that once a wall didn’t exist and people moved across the landscape unhindered. After Donald Trump was elected U.S. president in 2016, Fernández returned to the same spot where she painted the wall in 2011, and with the help of volunteers, she painted the wall sky blue, pronouncing: “We have to fight to create spaces where people can come back together.”This essay is significant, for it shows how non-elites demonstrate power in opposition to hegemony through nonviolent public acts. Sackman’s biting critique of migration control through the work of the artists Judy Baca and Ana Teresa Fernández (and other protesters) is important because the artwork opposes the unnatural—a physical wall across the landscape—“to reenvision human movement across it as natural.” Baca’s Great Wall of Los Angeles is the largest and longest mural on Earth. Sackman argues that through the act of painting murals and de-murals, these artists use “opposite techniques to reach similar ends” by wielding “a brush loaded with history…to make present those who have been erased” from memory. Meanwhile, Fernández’s wall erasure art demonstrates the unrelenting efforts by activists and artists to oppose border control efforts. In 2016, Sackman and colleagues from the University of Puget Sound toured the border from El Paso to San Diego. He uses an eyewitness ethnographical approach to discuss the places he visited and anti-border wall activists he met along his journey. Sackman follows in the footsteps of border correspondents and writers who have documented the impact of border control on the everyday lives of the residents along the international line. He argues the border artists and activists “are attempting to re-naturalize the border and dissolve the Make-America-Great-Again-Wall, an inhuman and unnatural monument.” Sackman’s contribution raises new questions about the power of art and how it can be used as a tool of resistance against discriminatory immigration policies and the border wall that separates families and loved ones. His article will inspire future research on transborder art activism and cultural production about the border wall and immigration issues.In interviews held at the University of Texas at El Paso Institute of Oral History, Yolanda Chávez Leyva and Kimberly Sumano Ortega lay out a fascinatingly intimate Public History essay on the U.S. Border Patrol through the voices of agents and the immigrants who encountered the border policing agency. Their article showcases the largest collection of border oral histories in the United States. The Institute of Oral History has been collecting and preserving oral history interviews for almost fifty years, focusing on the Mexican Revolution, the Bracero Program, the Border Patrol, and immigrants and refugees. More recently, the institute introduced a new oral history project on refugees and asylum seekers from Central and South America. This new project will inspire future research on the Migration Protection Protocols, also known as the “Remain in Mexico” policy, that forces asylum seekers to risk kidnapping, extortion, rape, and other forms of violence as they wait in Mexico for their court hearing. Amid the political polarization that surrounds border issues and immigration, it is important that researchers and policymakers turn to the Institute of Oral History collections to learn from the voices and memories of people living on la frontera. resumo: There was what seemed to be bad news for science teachers in a pair of survey reports on the American public’s attitudes toward science issued in 2023. According to the Pew Research Center’s report, “the share of Americans who say science has had a mostly positive effect on society has fallen and there’s been a continued decline in public trust in scientists,” while according to the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research’s report, “after remaining steady over the past two decades, overall confidence in the scientific community fell in 2022.”These results might suggest that science teachers have not been performing effectively, given that their job includes instructing students about science and its effects on society. Likewise, these results might suggest that science teachers will find their jobs more difficult in the future, particularly in localities infected by a lack of confidence in the scientific community. Biology teachers, who frequently address socially controversial topics such as evolution, climate change, vaccination, genetically modified organisms, and sex and gender, are no exception.But not so fast. A study by Jon D. Miller and his colleagues published in Science and Public Policy in 2024 offers a more nuanced view. That is partly because the surveys included in the study assessed trust in scientific expertise not with a single abstract question but with a composite index of concrete questions. Respondents were asked, with regard to the scientific topic they identified as of most interest to them, how much they would trust information on that specific topic from a variety of sources, including reliable sources such as the National Academy of Sciences and the National Institutes of Health.The Miller study found a recent sharp decline in respondents with a moderate level of trust in scientific expertise—from 74 percent in 2016 to 42 percent in 2020. A substantial body of work in survey research suggests that moderate responses to rating scale questions often reflect indifference. Accordingly, the study attributed the decline to the COVID-19 pandemic, which in effect forced respondents who might have been previously indifferent about trusting science to take a stand. The majority sided with science: the proportion of respondents with a high or very high level of trust increased by 20 percentage points.By the same token, the declines reported by Pew and AP-NORC may reflect, rather than a decrease in public trust in scientific expertise, a rebound to normal levels of public interest in science, understandable in light of the successful development and deployment of effective public health measures, including vaccinations, against the novel coronavirus. In both surveys, increases were noted primarily in preferences for a middle option (such as “a fair amount” or “equal[ly] positive and negative”), which, again, may often reflect indifference, not distrust of the scientific community.However, even in light of these considerations, not all is rosy. All three reports detected signs of polarization along political lines. Between 2016 and 2020, according to Miller and his colleagues, the proportion of respondents with a very low or low level of trust in scientific expertise increased by only 0.9 percentage points among liberal Democrats, by 10.8 percentage points among the general public, but by 19.7 percentage points among conservative Republicans. Such polarization is persisting after the official end of the COVID-19 pandemic in May 2023, judging from Pew’s report.Political polarization is not a challenge that science teachers are typically equipped to overcome. But Miller and his colleagues identified a factor that, they say, “is a better single indicator of trust in scientific expertise than ideological partisanship”: civic scientific literacy, the basic understanding of science necessary to comprehend scientific information aimed at the general public. Unsurprisingly, respondents with a high level of civic scientific literacy tended to have a higher level of trust in scientific expertise. And helping students to develop their civic scientific literacy is squarely within the science educator’s wheelhouse.So these results suggest that simply by teaching science properly, science educators are already helping to instill trust in the scientific community in their students. But focusing specifically on helping students to understand why reliable sources of scientific information are trustworthy—and similarly on helping them to understand why unreliable sources are not—promises to be even more effective. A swelling chorus of voices (including that of John Rudolph in his October 2023 American Biology Teacher commentary) is indeed arguing for instilling trust in science to be regarded as a primary goal of science education.In the meantime, the National Center for Science Education recently concluded the data acquisition phase of a nationally representative survey of public middle and high school educators that included questions about their attitudes and practices with regard to the nature of science and trust in science. A first-of-its-kind effort, the survey is intended to provide science education policymakers with the evidence they need to launch the project of making activities aimed at instilling trust in science a staple of the science classroom. The result will surely be good news for science teachers.

titulo: Quantitative Analysis of the Future of the Sharing Economy, Housing, White-Collar Labor Markets, and Problems in Big Cities
palavras_openalex: sharing economy | housing affordability | short-term rental platforms | Airbnb | gig economy | remote work | coworking spaces | urban inequality | housing prices | labor market polarization | platform regulation | large cities | New York | London | Istanbul
resumo: This research project explores the future of the sharing economy and its profound effects on housing markets, white-collar labor dynamics, and socio-economic challenges in large metropolitan areas. Using quantitative economics and econometric techniques, the study evaluates how platforms such as Airbnb, Uber, and coworking spaces are reshaping urban life, exacerbating housing affordability issues, and altering labor market structures. By analyzing housing market data, labor statistics, and platform economy data from major cities like New York, London, and Istanbul, this research provides empirical insights into how the sharing economy influences urban economic landscapes. The study employs difference-in-differences (DiD) and multivariate regression models to assess causal relationships, particularly in terms of housing market disruptions caused by short-term rental platforms and labor market fragmentation driven by the rise of gig and remote work. Spatial econometric techniques are also used to explore geographic disparities in housing and employment impacts across urban districts. Preliminary findings indicate that the proliferation of sharing economy platforms has contributed to housing shortages and increased prices in central urban areas, while labor markets experience growing polarization, with high-skilled workers benefiting from remote work opportunities and low-skilled gig workers facing economic precarity. This research offers valuable policy insights into the regulation of short-term rentals and the protection of gig economy workers, highlighting the need for regulatory frameworks that address urban inequality and labor market shifts. By integrating data from multiple sources, this study contributes to the academic discourse on urban economics and provides a framework for understanding the long-term socio-economic implications of the sharing economy in big cities.

titulo: Job Polarization with Advent of Technology: A Changing Landscape of Employment explored through Bibliometric Analysis
instituicoes: Punjabi University
periodico: International Journal of Diplomacy and Economy
topico_primario: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality
palavras_openalex: job polarization | employment trends | technological change | labor market | research trends
resumo: Employment trends have been changing over the decades. A phenomenon in employment has been observed recently which is termed job polarisation. Technology has been considered the main reason for this phenomenon. This study aims to trace the advancement of literature concerning job polarisation from the year 1990 to 2023. A total of 175 research studies are extracted from the Scopus database. After applying the inclusion criteria, 144 studies are considered for analysis through bibliometric and network visualisation techniques. The research work of 291 authors is considered to underline the most eminent authors, journals, countries and organisations in this field of research. The bibliometric maps, networks and tables have been made and examined using bibliometric tools, such as VOSviewer and Biblioshiny. This study also uncovers the major themes that have been focused on in the literature. The future research areas that require the attention of researchers are also highlighted in this study.

titulo: Forever Chemicals, Endless Testing? Expert Advice to Be Prepared for Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances
autores: Frederick G. Strathmann | Susan Burden | Jenna Hua | Andrew Patterson | Robert A. Middleberg
instituicoes: Berkeley City College | Environmental Protection Agency | Eurofins (United States)

resumo: Public awareness of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) has risen exponentially in recent years. They are commonly known as “forever chemicals,” though the term is not entirely accurate given such a broad class of chemicals. These chemicals are challenging given that the long history of use of these compounds make them uniquitous around the globe. PFAS are a group of synthetic chemicals that have been widely used in various industrial and consumer products due to their unique water- and grease-resistant properties. These compounds are found in everyday items like nonstick cookware, food packaging, and water-repellent clothing. However, their stability, which makes them so useful, also means they persist in the environment and in the human body. In recent years, PFAS have raised significant concerns in both environmental and clinical contexts. Environmentally, they contaminate water sources, soil, and even the air, leading to widespread human exposure. Clinically, the accumulation of PFAS in the body has been associated with a range of adverse health effects, including altered liver function, thyroid disease, immune system disruptions, and potential links to certain cancers. Understanding the impact of PFAS is crucial for laboratory medicine professionals and physicians, as these compounds may influence both environmental health and patient outcomes, particularly in vulnerable populations. In addition, laboratory testing for all types of PFAS is set to play a prominent role in helping to characterize, mitigate, and address the impact of their ubiquitous use and consequent mass, ongoing exposure. The evolving role of the laboratory, along with the inevitable consequences of public attention on the scale that has been given to PFAS, can leave individuals within clinical laboratory testing scrambling to provide accurate and helpful responses to questions received. This Q&A presents viewpoints on regulatory aspects, patient care impacts, environmental monitoring, and consumer health. Insights on test design, technology requirements, and how to address potential questions about a PFAS result from a patient or clinician are provided. What significant advances in our understanding of PFAS have been made and what further advances are required to fully address the impacts of PFAS? Susan Burden: We are beginning to learn more about the toxicity of PFAS beyond perfluorooctanoic acid and perfluorooctane sulfonate. However, most PFAS continue to have little to no available toxicity data. Given the size of the PFAS chemical class, it is impractical to conduct traditional, animal-based toxicity testing on all specific PFAS. In 2019, scientists in the US Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Office of Research and Development (ORD) initiated a project designed to test a set of structurally diverse PFAS using new approach methods (NAMs). NAMs include any technology, methodology, approach, or combination that can provide information on chemical hazard and risk assessment to avoid the use of animal testing. To date, ORD has tested a set of approximately 150 structurally diverse PFAS using a variety of NAMs, including NAMs that screen for general toxicity, immunotoxicity, thyroid effects, and developmental neurotoxicity. Additional screening efforts, however, are needed to better understand the range of potential hazards across the class of chemicals and prioritize PFAS for further study. Building a better understanding of potential hazards across the chemical class is also expected to help us break the large, structurally diverse class of PFAS into smaller categories based on similar chemical, physical, and toxicological properties. Such categories could then be used to further hazard assessment and inform hazard- or risk-based decisions, potentially accelerating efforts to protect human health and the environment. Robert Middleberg: Information on exposure in social media and the lay press is ahead of actual understanding of the health impacts of PFAS. It is clear that additional toxicological and epidemiological work has to be done to see if knowledge about the effects of PFAS can move past “suggests,” “associated with,” “putative,” etc. As such, I think one could reasonably state that our toxicological knowledge remains in its infancy. Certainly, while there is a substantial body of literature regarding PFAS, especially perfluorooctanoic acid and perfluorooctane sulfonate exposure and potential links to diseases or cancers within endocrine, cardiovascular, reproductive, hepatic, renal, and other physiological systems, questions still remain as to the strength of any association or causal link. As with most serious adverse effects of chemicals, often one needs to wait many years to see true outcomes, and studies need to be designed appropriately and without cognitive bias. This will be the only way to fully address the holistic impacts of PFAS. Multiple signals and other confounding factors also complicate our understanding of PFAS. For example, what else was someone exposed to during the same time they were exposed to PFAS? As a specific example, while PFAS are well-known to be present in the protective gear of firefighters, this population is also routinely exposed to an almost infinite number of chemicals while fighting fires; distinguishing signal from noise in such populations is very difficult. If this is overlayed with hobbies and environmental factors (e.g., well-water, etc.), the toxicological dilemma of multiple exposures and multiple endpoints becomes a true concern. Even so, well-designed cohort and case-controlled studies may add clarity to the issue moving into the future. Jenna Hua: Recent advances in our understanding of PFAS have significantly enhanced our ability to assess their ecological and human health risks. Research has elucidated the mechanisms of PFAS bioaccumulation and biomagnification in aquatic ecosystems, providing critical insights into their environmental persistence and potential for long-term ecological impact. The EPA has implemented robust methods for detecting and measuring PFAS in various environmental media, which are essential for evaluating the effectiveness of remediation technologies and informing regulatory actions. Furthermore, the establishment of legally enforceable drinking water standards for several PFAS by the Biden-Harris administration marks a pivotal step in mitigating human exposure and protecting public health. Despite these advances, several critical areas require further development to fully address the impacts of PFAS. Enhanced report-back mechanisms and educational initiatives are necessary to empower individuals and clinicians with actionable steps to mitigate PFAS exposure. Currently, clinicians lack formal training in environmental health, which is crucial given that the exposome—encompassing all environmental exposures—accounts for up to 70% of disease risk, compared to 30% attributed to genetic factors. Integrating environmental health into medical education and practice is imperative to improve patient outcomes and community health. Systematic testing of consumer products for PFAS contamination is also essential. This includes screening food packaging and other materials for PFAS and investigating safer, biodegradable alternatives that do not pose health risks. Cleaning up the supply chain involves identifying and mitigating sources of PFAS exposure, educating manufacturers, and developing safe disposal methods for PFAS-containing materials. These efforts, combined with ongoing research and policy advances, are critical to reducing the pervasive impact of PFAS on human health and the environment. Andrew Patterson: Fully characterizing linear and branched isomers with high-resolution ion mobility while simultaneously looking for indicator compounds, or compounds that might be obscured by coelution, will be key to understanding PFAS. If unique PFAS tracers are uncovered by high-resolution ion mobility, the focus can shift to looking for those unique features in an array of complex matrices. Additionally, the fate and transport of environmental precursors that are transformed into commonly regulated PFAS target analytes are poorly understood and therefore incompletely addressed in policy, regulation, and decision-making intended to protect human health. Improved methods for assessing and understanding the impact of precursors are needed. Since precursors can serve as a reservoir for legacy PFAS, increased awareness of precursor fate is a critical aspect of PFAS knowledge. titulo: Comparative Study on the Alignment of IB PYP with National Curriculum in China and South Korea
periodico: Asia Pacific Journal of Educational Research
palavras_openalex: International Baccalaureate | Primary Years Programme | curriculum alignment | national curriculum | China | South Korea | Education 4.0 | Fourth Industrial Revolution | competency-based curriculum | subject-centered curriculum | globalization of education | neoliberalism in education | multiculturalism | global citizenship
resumo: This study explores the impact of the Fourth Industrial Revolution on education, focusing on the expansion of International Baccalaureate (IB) programs in China and South Korea. As technology reshapes industries, there is a need to develop students’ innovative and technological skills for future employment. Drawing from the World Economic Forum’s “Schools of the Future” report, the research emphasizes Education 4.0, which uses technology to enhance innovation, technical skills, communication, and global citizenship. In addition, Korea’s shift from a subject-centered curriculum to a competency-based curriculum under the influence of social polarization, population decline, and technological advancement is described. The IB system is seen as a comprehensive response, promoting holistic development and readiness for modern challenges. However, it also highlights contradictions in the IB framework, balancing neoliberal values with global equity and multiculturalism. By analyzing the IB Primary Years Programme (PYP) integration with national curricula in China and South Korea, the study provides insights to enhance the PYP and improve national systems. The findings aim to guide the localization of the IB PYP and foster synergy between international and national frameworks, preparing students for a globalized future and evolving job market demands.

resumo: OP-BST-01 DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY OF THE WHO CLASSIFICATION FOR FINE-NEEDLE ASPIRATION CYTOLOGY OF SOFT TISSUE TUMORS: A RETROSPECTIVE STUDY S Bishnoi, A A Khan, S Ahuja, C Ahluwalia, S Ranga; Department of Pathology, Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, New Delhi, India Introduction: Soft tissue tumors present diagnostic challenges due to their histopathological diversity. Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) is a minimally invasive technique for initial evaluation, but interpreting these cytological samples is complex. The World Health Organization (WHO) has proposed a new classification system to standardize soft tissue cytopathology. Materials and Methods: A retrospective observational study was conducted on 203 soft tissue FNA samples collected from January 2022 to June 2023. Samples were stained with Papanicolaou and Giemsa, and reviewed by two pathologists. Histopathological correlation was performed on 117 cases. Samples were categorized according to the WHO classification: Nondiagnostic (ND), Benign, Atypical, Soft Tissue Neoplasm of Uncertain Malignant Potential (STNUMP), Suspicious for Malignancy (SFM), and Malignant. Results: The distribution of cases was: ND (3.4%), Benign (62.5%), Atypical (4.9%), STNUMP (5.4%), SFM (13.8%), and Malignant (9.9%). The risk of malignancy (ROM) was 33.3% for ND, 1.2% for Benign, 40% for Atypical, 25% for STNUMP, 80% for SFM, and 100% for Malignant. Sensitivity and specificity were highest when SFM and Malignant categories were considered positive for malignancy. Sensitivity was 77.27%, specificity was 97.83%, and diagnostic accuracy was 93.86%. The interobserver agreement was moderate (Cohen’s kappa = 0.454). Discussion: The WHO classification system provides a reliable framework for diagnosing soft tissue tumors with high sensitivity, specificity, and diagnostic accuracy. The system’s structured categories help standardize reporting and improve clinical decision-making. Discrepancies in ROM values between studies highlight the need for further research to refine the system. Conclusion: The WHO classification for soft tissue cytopathology significantly enhances diagnostic accuracy and standardization in reporting FNA samples. Our study supports the system’s reliability and effectiveness, advocating for its continued development and implementation in clinical practice. OP-BST-02 INVESTIGATING NERVE PATHOLOGY IN LEPROSY: A CYTOLOGICAL STUDY Bhavna Langan1, Sonal Sharma1, Preeti Diwaker1, Chander Grover2; 1Department of Pathology, UCMS and GTB Hospital, Delhi, India, 2Department of Dermatology, UCMS and GTB Hospital, Delhi, India Introduction: Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous disease which primarily involves the peripheral nerves and is characterised by hypoesthetic skin lesions, thickened peripheral nerves with the presence of Mycobacterium leprae. It occurs in a spectrum ranging from most severe (lepromatous) to least severe form (tuberculoid). In cases with only nerve involvement, confirmation is done with nerve biopsy, which is an invasive and time-consuming procedure and can lead to nerve damage. Hence, a safer option is needed. Fine needle aspiration (FNA) has emerged as a valuable diagnostic tool in detecting nerve involvement in leprosy. Due to limited literature documenting cytological findings of peripheral nerves in leprosy, we conducted this study to fill the gap regarding the same. Aim and Objectives: To study the role of FNAC in the evaluation of peripheral nerve involvement and to compare cytomorphological features with skin cytology as well as histopathological findings of cutaneous nerves in leprosy. Materials and Methods: Clinically diagnosed and skin biopsy proven consenting adults having thickened nerve were taken. After clinical examination, FNAC from peripheral nerves and skin lesions was performed. The smears were stained with May Grunwald Giemsa (MGG) and Fite stains. Haematoxylin & Eosin stained skin biopsy slides were retrieved from the archives and reviewed. Observation and Results: The MGG and Fite stained slides from thickened nerves and skin lesions showed evidence of necrosis, granuloma, macrophages, giant cells, neutrophils and lymphocytes. Conclusion: The cytomorphological findings in peripheral nerves of patients with leprosy were consistent with the findings of skin cytology as well as histopathology.
