palavras_openalex: labor market | digitalization | digital economy | labor market polarization | industrial transformation | job loss | role of the state | employment
resumo: В статье рассмотрено воздействие цифровизации на рынок труда. Отмечено, что рынок труда поляризован, происходит отраслевая деформация, обусловленная активным развитием IT-сферы и сокращением рабочих мест в других отраслях. Это неизбежно ухудшает материальное положение высвобождаемых работников. Обоснованы социально-экономические последствия цифровизации, проявляющиеся на различных уровнях и оказывающие влияние на всех участников рынка труда. Подчеркнута роль государства как института, определяющего вектор развития цифровой экономики с соблюдением интересов государства, бизнеса и общества.

titulo: Digital Economy and Common Prosperity: Theoretical Logic, Practical Challenges and Practical Paths
instituicoes: Yan'an University
periodico: International Journal of Frontiers in Sociology
palavras_openalex: digital economy | common prosperity | digital dividend | platform economy | platform monopolization | antimonopoly regulation | digital labor | digital divide | wealth polarization | capital accumulation | urban-rural coordinated development | human-centered values
resumo: The development and expansion of digital economy has laid a solid material foundation for realizing common prosperity. However, the digital economy is also facing many challenges, such as accelerated monopolistic competition in the platform economy under the logic of capital, the paradox of subjectivity and unequal production relations in the process of digital labor, the digital divide that prevents the disadvantaged groups from sharing the digital dividend, and the increasing polarization effect in the distribution of wealth. Therefore, to give full play to the digital dividend, it is necessary to increase the anti-monopoly governance of the platform economy to prevent the uncontrolled expansion of capital; to build a people-oriented digital economy value; to promote the coordinated development of urban and rural areas and regions, so that the people can share the dividend of digital development; and to release the digital dividend through the organic combination of the government and the market.

titulo: When Eurovision Came Out: LGBTQ+ Visibility and the Eurovision Song Contest in the “Queer 1990s”
periodico: QED A Journal in GLBTQ Worldmaking
palavras_openalex: Eurovision Song Contest | LGBTQ visibility | queer politics | European integration | European Court of Human Rights | Amsterdam Treaty | sexual orientation discrimination | European Broadcasting Union | gay and lesbian rights | sexual equality | public service broadcasting | transgender rights
resumo: Europe's “queer 1990s,” at least for those who put their faith in liberal activism and legal reforms, represented a distinctive, post-Cold-War turning-point, when the European integration project still attracted widespread optimism for future prosperity and social progress.1 Indeed, the very symbolic meanings of “Europe” within that liberal project shifted to encompass sexual equality in these 1990s through cumulative legislative and judicial moves by the European Union (EU) and the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR). After much lobbying by Western European NGOs connected through the International Lesbian and Gay Association (ILGA), formalized as “ILGA-Europe” in 1996, activists harnessing the EU's ambition to become a “community of values” persuaded it to incorporate sexual orientation in the new antidiscrimination clause of the 1997 Treaty of Amsterdam.2 Significant ECHR judgements on trans people's identity documents, equalized ages of sexual consent, and gay and lesbian rights to military service showed that judges were recognizing changing attitudes and treating sexual equality within the European human rights regime in the 1990s even though that regime's creators in the 1950s had excluded it.3 In these “queer 1990s,” the Eurovision Song Contest witnessed its first openly queer performers, Iceland's Páll Óskar in 1997 and Israel's Dana International in 1998.4 Although the contest had long had an active gay following, it was in 1997–98 that LGBTQ+ politics at Eurovision entered what I elsewhere call its “visibility phase.”5Eurovision, as frequently associated with European integration as it is, is not a direct instrument of any European political institutions. It is produced by an entirely separate organization, the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), an association of public service broadcasters which formed for the purposes of technical cooperation in 1950 and staged the first annual Eurovision Song Contest in 1956.6 From its Swiss base in Geneva, the historian Dean Vuletic argues, the EBU always distanced itself from the integratory supranationalism of the future EU, even though it allowed the European Commission to sponsor some “postcard” films and interval acts in 1987, 1988, and 1990.7 Eurovision's “map” of Europe has always been wider than the European political union, from Switzerland's founding participation, through Mediterranean and eastward enlargements that reached further than any EU ambitions, to Australia's incorporation in 2015. Nevertheless, even if only as a “historical fiction,” the ideas of Eurovision and European integration have overpowered archival realities and become interwoven in numerous popular imaginations of the contest.8 Moreover, both projects did emerge in a shared historical context, the political, economic, and cultural climate of early 1950s Western Europe.Eurovision had already gained a queer audience well before the Dublin 1997 and Birmingham 1998 contests, especially among gay men. By the 1970s, gay viewers in many Northern and Western European countries were already recognizing each other as fans. According to interviews with gay fans in Ireland, however, this was still “largely in terms of the closet,” that is, “a shared, open secret with other gay spectators” unseen by the heteronormative world.9 Until the mid-1990s, the contest itself continued to be “presented . . . as hugely respectable” by the standards of mid-twentieth-century European “high culture,” with a live classical orchestra, a black-tie dress code for audience members, and a peripatetic home in prestigious national theatrical/orchestral venues of each host country.10 Queer readings of camp and excess in Eurovision remained “a private affair, embedded in . . . subcultural systems” such as Eurovision parties in private homes or gay pubs/bars, or the activities of the international fan club OGAE, founded with a “largely gay” membership in 1984.11 Even before 1997–98, however, understandings that Eurovision had special meanings for gay fans were beginning to cross into wider public discourse about the contest in the 1990s. This may have been particularly so in Ireland, where Ireland's unprecedented four Eurovision wins in one decade (1992–96) coincided with the 1993 implementation of the 1988 ECHR ruling that Ireland must decriminalize sex between men.12 This sense of simultaneity might also have manifested in other national contexts, including the UK, where the gay press frequently covered activists’ strategy of pursuing legal reforms through the ECHR.Before 1997, Eurovision had known closeted queer performers, including 1961’s winner Jean-Claude Pascal, who represented Luxembourg with the romantic chanson “Nous les amoureux” (“We, the lovers”): its non-gender-specific portrayal of a couple defying community hostility to assert God is on their side has only very recently been reinserted into Eurovision's queer history.13 Óskar, however, was the first openly queer contestant, marking his performance equally as queer to any viewer who knew about his queerness through media coverage, broadcasters’ live commentary, or fandom word of mouth. Óskar's seductive performance of “Minn hinsti dans” (“My final dance”) typified the 1990s’ seeping of queer aesthetics into mainstream fashion and popular culture, and broke the mold of Eurovision performance to prefigure the contemporary contest in numerous ways. His electronic backing track was still a rarity at Eurovision; his sensual interactions with his female dancers, who wore fishnet tights and “kinky” black bodices, gloves, and boots, referenced BDSM aesthetics more daringly than any previous entry had attempted in this respectable, “family”-oriented show; his radio mic might have evoked Madonna's stage outfits; he transgressed masculine gender norms by visibly wearing make-up; his use of props, including a large white leather sofa and multiple television screens on the stage floor, was on greater scale than any previous entry; his sound resembled current chart pop music much more closely than Eurovision entries by the 1990s typically did; and from the five countries where Eurovision was piloting telephone voting (Austria, Germany, Sweden, Switzerland, and the UK), it won notably more points than from the professional juries who traditionally awarded Eurovision scores.Viewed intertextually within transnational popular music culture, Óskar's image, sound, and performance might have evoked particular comparisons with George Michael, a star whose transforming public image became a major popular-cultural narrative in the queer 1990s. Michael's star image since 1990 had shifted from his early music videos’ “explicit heterosexuality” (albeit with potential alternative queer readings) towards the “sexual ambiguity” that had become central to his star “metanarrative” by 1996–97.14 It would be another year before Michael's arrest for public sex in Los Angeles first forced him to declare his sexual orientation on CNN and then inspired him to reclaim the stigma in his 1998 video “Outside,” which directly referenced the arrest, yet in queer culture he was already an object of fascination, desire, and sometimes frustration. His transnational star persona might therefore have made Óskar's more legible as queer. “Minn hinsti dans” has particular commonalities with Michael's 1996 hit, “Fastlove.” Both performances’ characters appear as bored playboys who cannot even be excited by conspicuous sexual excess; in the “Fastlove” video and in Oskar's performance, dancers wear BDSM-inspired clothing, the performer addresses the camera from a sofa, and the space is scattered with TV screens. Eurovision's first openly queer performer, employing queer popular-cultural aesthetics on stage, was thus representing Iceland less than a year after Iceland had become only the fourth European country to introduce registered partnerships for same-gender couples.15A further dimension of queer aesthetics, culture and experience—drag culture and trans femininity—gained visibility at Eurovision when Israeli television selected Dana International for Eurovision 1998. Her participation simultaneously represented a further landmark in Eurovision's queer history, perhaps even in European trans history writ large, but also a knot of contentions that force understandings of Eurovision's “queer 1990s” to confront the widely critiqued politics of “LGBTQ+-friendly” messaging in Israeli public diplomacy.16 The 1990s in Israel were a transitional phase between repression and visibility for LGBTQ+ people: same-gender sex had been legalized in 1988; certain equalities for lesbians, gays, and bisexuals had been introduced in the early 1990s, including the right to serve openly in Israel's all-important military; Israel's first Pride happened in Tel Aviv in 1993; and drag troupes were gaining crossover appeal in mainstream popular culture.17 Dana herself had broken through from Tel Aviv's drag scene into an original recording artist who had released three hit albums, replete with musical and linguistic border-crossing (her songs employed both Western dance and Middle Eastern musical elements, and shifted between Hebrew, English, and Arabic), by the time the Israeli Broadcasting Authority (IBA) selected her for Eurovision in November 1997.18Within Israel, Dana's participation was denounced by ultra-Orthodox rabbis, including the deputy health minister Shlomo Benizri who branded her an “aberration.”19 Media coverage once she was in Birmingham for Eurovision dwelled far more on her gender confirmation surgery than her creative achievements, her deadname was routinely given even in sympathetic articles, and UK newspaper columns mocking the contest were peppered with transphobic remarks. Yet “Diva,” her winning entry, marked her triumph “as a woman singing about women,” linking her own embodiment of glamorous femininity to the myths of Aphrodite, Victoria, and Cleopatra, all mentioned in the song.20 For her winner's reprise, she changed into a feathered outfit by the gay designer Jean-Paul Gaultier, whose career-defining fascination with the homoerotic mariner had earned him appreciation in 1980s and 1990s queer culture.21The “diva” figure, evoked through the nexus of image, lyrics, choreography, couture, and metanarrative in Dana's performance, had of course already enjoyed decades of “iconic” status in transnational queer culture. One of the more serious UK newspaper articles about her before the contest, in The Guardian, remarked she was “said to represent two nations—Israel and gays.”22 Her metanarrative of triumph over prejudice exemplified the “duality of stage/screen and life” that must exist for audiences to invest in diva figures with authenticity, against the background of 1990s LGBTQ+ activism.23 As such, she epitomized the kind of “underdog story” which arguably contributes to Eurovision's queer appeal: The underdog story—the person who battles against obscurity or oppression to triumph against the odds—is a classic gay narrative, through which spectators can read their own stories of fighting through bias and prejudice towards fully realised, proud gay identities. Eurovision is a treasure trove of underdog stories to be sought out and identified with or queered if necessary, year after year.24Her meanings to gay male fans in Israel, as retold to the scholar Dafna Lemish several years later, seemed to map this narrative on to late 1990s Israeli circumstances. Lemish's interviewees frequently aligned themselves with a transnational queer passion for camp, which they eagerly read into extravagant performances at Eurovision, and some perceived that Eurovision's camp let them take pleasure in “the extroverted expression of femininity,” which mainstream Israeli cultures of masculinity would heavily stigmatize.25 Connecting with the imagined “European” space of Eurovision reminded some of past travel to Western European cities where they had seen same-gender couples expressing affection more openly than they could then have done in Israel, and Dana winning Eurovision in the first year of predominantly public telephone voting (following 1997’s successful experiment) could even feel like a show of support from the gay community all over Europe.26 Hundreds of gay fans rushed to central Tel Aviv with rainbow flags, mingling with straight revelers waving the national flag and even football fans celebrating a championship win. “The community as a whole came out of the closet that night,” Lemish observes, and her example illustrates Peter Rehberg's 2007 description of Eurovision as “a rare occasion for simultaneously celebrating both queerness and national identity.”27Even before Eurovision, scholars of Israeli popular culture were recognizing Dana as a singular figure embodying fundamental religious, cultural, ethnic, political, and sexual tensions in Israeli society.28 Yet to talk of her national or international meanings today requires acknowledging how Israeli state organizations since then have instrumentalized a narrative of Israel as a uniquely LGBTQ+-friendly nation in the Middle East to win international public sympathy for the state's actions towards Palestinians, a strategy that critical scholars term “pinkwashing.”29 The scale of its repression and military violence in the occupied Palestinian territories amount, in the eyes of Palestinian activists and their supporters, to “apartheid.”30 In 1998, and when Israel hosted Eurovision 1999 in Jerusalem, the Oslo Accords peace process was still underway, the Second Intifada had not yet occurred, and Israeli forces had not yet launched the devastating operations that led Palestinian civil society to found the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement in 2005. It can be argued that this was a very different historical moment from that surrounding Israel's next, controversial Eurovision victory in 2018.31 Yet Dana's historic Eurovision victory remained a resource for Israeli public diplomacy in this later context.32 A statement by Israel's ambassador to the United States in 2012 citing it as proof that Israel was an LGBTQ+ rights “pioneer,” for instance, directly illustrates for Aeyal Gross “homonationalist discourse and ‘pinkwashing’” in Israel's diplomatic strategy.33 All this must be held together with the immediate meanings Dana's victory had inside Israel, and its revelatory impact for numerous trans people in Europe who had only ever been shown freakish or abject representations of trans femininity in mass media before.34 The politics of her domestic reception in 1997–98 do, however, suggest that LGBTQ+ equality in Israel was won much more contingently in the 1990s than the future tone of Israeli public diplomacy would imply.These two queer “firsts” in Eurovision performance, Páll Óskar in 1997 and Dana International in 1998, show that in the late 1990s queer aesthetics openly came to Eurovision for the first time, in the name of nations that were experiencing dramatic sociolegal changes around LGBTQ+ rights. Yet, performances aside, the organization of Eurovision contests themselves was also changing in the late 1990s in ways that grew Eurovision's queer audience, as a live crowd and as a fandom.  this titulo: Review of periodical literature for 2023: (iv) 1700–1850
instituicoes: University of Oxford
palavras_openalex: Industrial Revolution | industrial development | induced innovation hypothesis | mechanical skills | informal networks | Freemasonry | friendly societies | patents | wool industry | coal industry | coal transportation | canals | Indian cotton textiles | mechanization | court testimony | time use | living standards
resumo: The topic of industrial revolution and industrial development attracted particular attention in 2023. Using econometric analysis Kelly et al. analysed growth pattern across English counties between 1760s and 1830s using male employment patterns to compare the contrasting explanations of the industrial revolution. They focused on textiles and iron industries and found that mechanical and related skills were crucial. Overall, Kelly et al. found that industrialization occurred in areas with low wages and high mechanical skills, whereas factors such as literacy, banks, and proximity to coal had little explanatory power. The work of Otojanov et al. on the other hand supported the ‘induced innovation’ hypothesis as the driving force of the industrial revolution, as cheap energy and capital induced adoption of labour-saving technologies. However, they also found that until the 1820s labour saving was modest. Galofré-Vilà explored the role of informal networks in spurring innovative activity. The author found that counties with a large number of informal networks such as Freemasonry, friendly societies, libraries, and booksellers were more innovative and produced more patents and exhibits for the 1851 Crystal Palace World's Fair. Several articles focused on industrial development. Sugden et al. explored the role of geographical factors, especially proximity to coal, for the location of woollens industry in the West Riding. They found that the key factors that facilitated the concentration in this region were coal, low cost of living, and running water. Allen studied the coal industry and transport. He found that coal markets were highly integrated, and productivity of coal shipments grew between 1695 and 1824, while the geographical pattern of production remained practically the same. Allen found that among the main reasons for the unchanging geographical pattern was the power of the Northeast coal producers that blocked the building of midland canals that would open up the market. Raman explored the role of the spinner's skill and dexterity for determining the final quality of cotton cloth. She argued that the trajectory of the British cotton industry was shaped by the pursuit of matching the quality of Indian cotton textiles and, unable to match the skills of the Indian artisans, British entrepreneurs turned to mechanization. Research on labour and living standards was also strongly represented. Sheng explored the limitations of the method of inferring time-use from court testimony. The author used Old Bailey records to study women's working time in London in 1750–1830. Sheng found that, unlike previous research that concluded that men worked longer in paid employment, women in his sample spent only slightly more time in paid work in the 1830s than in the 1750s. Sheng further argued that another limitation of the simulated time-use recall method for generating aggregate data on times worked in paid work also lies in the fact that sectoral distribution of subjects in the dataset may be biased. Paker et al. explored hiring and employment histories of over 1000 labourers employed in the rebuilding of St Paul's Cathedral between 1672 and 1748. They found that over the studied period the hiring strategies shifted towards labour retention and giving priority to core labourers. In this way, the employment strategies at the Cathedral were in stark contrast to the volatility that characterized pre-industrial labour demand. They also found that day wage rates remained flat over the period, but core workers had access to higher earnings, as they were given more days to work through retention and rehiring, and access to more lucrative watchman shifts. Several articles explored living standards and poor relief. Horrell relied on expenditure patterns of ordinary households between 1260 and 1869 to construct a chained-Laspeyres price index. The author used estimates of consumption of food; articles such as fuel and candles, clothing, etc.; housing costs; and durables such as furniture to reconstruct family expenditures in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Horrell’s work shows a switch away from dairy with industrialization, the responsiveness of meat and poultry consumption to economic conditions, and the shift from beer consumption to beverages such as tea from the mid-eighteenth century. The author argued that, although the results are similar to ‘bare bones’ and the ‘respectability basket’, until the eighteenth century the chained-Laspeyres price index is superior in capturing price levels over industrialization. This is because the shift towards spending on imported groceries and manufactured goods introduced a new dynamic that the chained-Laspeyres price index better captures. Bujokova and Desportes explored Scottish poor relief. They presented two case studies of poor relief in Scotland – Lowland and Highland – between c.1720 and 1790. They showed that towards the end of the eighteenth century the system of poor relief transitioned from one based on a community approach rooted in parish and kirk structures to one based on legalism and the concept of rights based social provision. They also highlighted the role of Scottish political economists’ ideas emphasizing progress and economic growth for this shift. Melander and Miotto examined the 1834 New Poor Law reform and its relationship to criminality. They found that the cut to welfare provision imposed by the reform led to increases in criminal activity with a 17.2 per cent increase in non-violent crime as compared with pre-reform yearly levels. Building a dataset of over 250 000 individual criminal charges between 1828 and 1840, they found that welfare cuts were related to a rise in non-violent property crimes, and these crimes occurred more in times of seasonal unemployment. Broadberry et al. presented a new chronology of business cycles for the period 1700–2010. They found that eighteenth-century business cycles had a shorter duration of 3.4 years and amplitude of 3.2 per cent than those in the post-1945 period, which were on average 16 years with an amplitude of 51.9 per cent. They found that the leading cause of economic fluctuations in the eighteenth century were shocks to agricultural production. The most important of these shocks was the Great Frost of 1709–10, which reduced GDP by 20 per cent. Eighteenth-century recessions were also caused by wars and financial crises. In the nineteenth century the importance of sectoral shocks, such as agricultural shocks, somewhat declined, whilst financial crises continued to be an important factor. The importance of wars declined only after the major economic shock brought by the Napoleonic wars. In the nineteenth century, increasing trade and capital liberalization saw shocks to commodity prices and international trade emerge as causes of recessions. In financial history, the focus was on the Bank of England and also on insurance. O'Brien and Palma, using recalibrated financial data, found that the Bank of England, even though it was a private institution, fulfilled a public role over the eighteenth century, well before the emergence of the Bagehot doctrine. The authors argue that, by providing financial intermediation, the Bank contributed to the development of the fiscal-naval state. Importantly, the Bank provided the state with credit, particularly at times when private credit was unavailable. Yet, the Bank had autonomy from the state and was able to deny the provision of funds when such a step undermined its financial safety. Milevsky focused on eighteenth-century debates surrounding choice architecture – how to design investment options in a retirement plan – and on default options and auto-enrolment into insurance schemes. The author studied the case of Adam Smith, who joined the annuity scheme Scottish Ministers’ Widows’ Fund when he was elected professor at the University of Glasgow. Very strongly represented was research on slavery. Absell studied the effects of slave emancipation in the British Empire on the sugar industry in Brazil. The author found that emancipation and subsequent trade liberalization led to increased demand for Brazilian sugar. Brazil thus saw an expansion of exports and its share of the world sugar market grew. Mishler explored enslaved people's engagement with the legal system in cases of legal activism in the British Empire. Roberts used slave ship drug invoices to relate the slave trade and captivity and drugs. Schwarz studied attitudes of important members of the Royal family towards the slave trade and abolition. The author shows the high level of polarization within the national debate on the issue of abolition by emphasizing that even within the Royal family there was a distinct division of opinion, with the Duke of Clarence, later William IV, favouring the slave trade. Radburn studied firms that supplied gunpowder to the slave trade and the stimulus that the trade gave to the explosives industry in Britain. The author emphasized that, as merchants from Bristol and Liverpool supplanted London slave merchants, new powder works opened in the areas focused on satisfying the specific demands from slave trading. However, as Radburn pointed out, only about 12 per cent of the British production of gunpowder was exported to Africa, so although the African market was essential to the firms connected to slave traders in the provinces, this did not apply to the industry as a whole. These firms were highly specialized, and the quality of the product they made precluded, for example, supplying the British state, and so even after abolition the firms continued to supply African markets. Business history was represented by articles on profit, trade, trading, and merchant networks and also had strong links to slavery. O'Sullivan explored the notion and the understanding of profit in the eighteenth century. To do so, the author studied revolts of Cornish copper miners in the late eighteenth century. O'Sullivan underlined that these revolts were not driven by luddism but were instead a protest against stoppages in mining activity undertaken by the owners who sought to decrease the supply of copper in efforts to increase prices and expand their profits whilst threatening the livelihood of the miners. She concluded that profit needs to be studied in a broader framework and in association with power. Ruderman and van Waijenburg examined the Royal African Company's behaviour in its post-monopoly period using letters to slave ship captains between 1685 and 1706. They emphasized the Company's organizational flexibility epitomized in better safeguarding of ships, more efficient management of slave voyages, and better monitoring of agents in Africa whose opportunities for cheating expanded with the opening of the slave trade. Sweet focused on the economic and social history of a British trading family involved principally in the slave trade – the family of Ambrose Lace. The author argues that, unlike some other British families and corporations whose business activities implicated them in slavery, the Laces focused on slavery as their main enterprise. Sweet links Ambrose Lace with the Calabar massacre and retells the subterfuge that Lace and his firm used to dissuade suspicion and to uphold their business reputation. Buckles presented a case study of John Pinney, a Bristol merchant with a plantation in Nevis, and his social network. The author modified historical social network analysis to better accommodate change over time by incorporating a 2-year moving memory total. Buckles used the methodology to study the business network of Pinney, the experience of enslaved people connected to the network, and the role of Pinney's wife Jane in the commercial network. Research on the economic role of women and their experience in the labour market was very strongly represented. Shepard emphasized that distinction between ‘productive’ and ‘reproductive’ work is a concept that originated in the nineteenth century and would make little sense to early modern women, as care work was often a commercial endeavour. Phillips examined the ways London theatre companies dealt with temporary absences of actresses due to childbearing in the late eighteenth century. The author found that about 20 per cent of actresses under contract with Covent Garden gave birth in the season 1784–5. Phillips found that actresses in major theatres received 1 or 2 months of maternity leave from at least 1770 onwards, and a range of accommodations were available for pregnant actresses. Furthermore, theatre managers also adapted the day-to-day business such as premieres, rehearsals, etc., to accommodate for actresses’ absence. Wakelam argued that the increasing marriage rates and the declining rates of women incarcerated due to indebtedness over the eighteenth century imply that women's economic independence declined. This finding is in contrast to the scholarship that emphasized the continued economic agency of women after marriage. Brock studied the ways in which women shaped private trade of the East India Company. The author reviewed over 1300 petitions addressed to the Company by women between 1600 and 1757 focusing on the various relationships and roles women had. Brock found that about 15 per cent of the petitions sent by women related to private trade in which women were involved and emphasized that women in merchant families had a degree of autonomy and that a woman's credit and trust was often separate from her husband's. Whitehead explored the role letter writing performed in establishing the political authority of elite women and the ways in which letters were used to negotiate patronage. Bolissian used popular health texts to challenge the masculinization hypothesis and claims that women bodies after menopause were perceived by early modern medicine as becoming increasingly masculine. Several papers explored institutions from varied perspectives. Grajzl and Murrell studied caselaw development around land, inheritance, and families, and its impact on economic development. They found that developments in caselaw related to families and inheritance shaped real-income growth. The authors argue that changes in caselaw allowed for new ways of distributing family property and thus enabled new commercial activities to take place. Dimitruk argued that the Glorious Revolution of 1688 expanded access to estate bills to gentry families. Most of the estate bills focused on removing entails and restrictions on the sale of land. The author argued that these acts facilitated Smithian growth in land and credit markets. However, Dimitruk emphasized that passing individual acts was second best to a wholesale reform of the inheritance institutions, as it created opportunities for rent-seeking on the part of members of parliament (MPs) and brokers who prepared the bills for gentry families. Taylor studied tolls on grain – payments made by merchants to market owners for the privilege to sell the grain on their market. The author found that over the eighteenth century tolls became increasingly criticized for obstructing trade, and some markets started to abolish the practice. Skjönsberg used the writings of a Quaker merchant Richard Champion to explore the role of ‘ordinary men’ in shaping eighteenth-century politics. Halliday emphasized English law's capacity for mutation. Lidwell-Durnin explored the role of scientific authority in dispelling public fear in the case of the 1782 London caterpillar outbreak – an invasion of brown-tail moth caterpillars, which prompted fears of famine and plague. Camoglu explored the experience of plague in 1722 London as depicted by Daniel Defoe in a novel A Journal of the Plague Year. The author emphasized the collectively shared experience of the disease against the physical experience of isolation that was an outcome of disease prevention protocols. Maritime history was represented by articles on risk and on institutional frameworks governing shipping. A series of papers on risk and uncertainty in the early modern world were published in the International Journal of Maritime History. Wade et al. argued for the need to reassess the ways that actors in the maritime economy dealt with risk and challenges brought by the natural environment as well as by political and social challenges. They show how this provides new insights into globalization and economic development in the early modern world. Reid explored risk mitigation strategies of British merchant ships and points towards small alterations in the construction of merchant ships that followed the specific demands of the shipyards’ clients connected to cargo capacity, structural integrity, and salaries of sailors. Reid thus empathized that sailing ship technologies remained static as previous research has argued but developed alongside the needs of its clients and with a view of natural hazards and commercial risks that sailing entailed. Dyble and Iodice introduced the AveTransRisk database that captures routes, cargo, weather conditions, ships, seafarers, and transaction costs of maritime trade. Instead, the author argued that, even though some elements of democracy were present, fragmentation between the notions of seventeenth-century buccaneers and privateers and eighteenth-century pirates existed, and this undermines the view that there was a universally shared ‘discipline’ observed by all. titulo: Padrões de intensidade tecnológica e a polarização do emprego na indústria de transformação do brasil
autores: Gabriella Rodrigues Rocha | Tatiana Massaroli de Melo
instituicoes: Universidade Estadual Paulista (Unesp)
topico_primario: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality
palavras_openalex: technological intensity | job polarization | manufacturing industry | technological standardization | innovation intensity | value added | Brazilian manufacturing sector
resumo: Este artigo tem como objetivo analisar o efeito da intensidade tecnológica sobre a intensidade da polarização do emprego na indústria de transformação do Brasil. Para isso pretende realizar uma análise em nível setorial de dois dígitos, utilizando a metodologia de padronização tecnológica proposta por Galindo-Rueda e Verger (2016), em que o agrupamento de dados se deu por meio do algoritmo de Fisher-Jenks. Para identificar a polarização do emprego, a metodologia adotada é o Índice de Intensidade de Tarefas Rotineiras (RTI) proposto por Autor e Dorn (2013). Observou-se, assim como na maioria da literatura, um padrão de concentração da produção em setores de mais baixo grau de inovação, em relação ao valor adicionado. Os resultados do RTI apontam que os empregos nos setores da indústria encontram-se polarizados, porém, a intensificação foi baixa. Em que, a hipótese de que quanto maior a intensidade tecnológica maior a polarização do emprego, apresenta inconsistência em alguns setores.

titulo: Yellow vests: who were they?
palavras_openalex: labor market transformation | materialism | political positioning | Emmanuel Macron
resumo: The “yellow vest” protests that happened in France during the period from the late 2018 to the first half of 2019 became one of the key events of E. Macron's first presidential term. The largest protest movement since 1968 was caused by a complex of socio-economic and political problems including the polarization of employment, the erosion of the middle class, the democratic deficit, and the expansion of forms of civic and political participation. The purpose of the article, which examines the socio-value portrait of the yellow vests consists of several aspects. First, the author demonstrates which socio-professional and age groups formed the core of the protest, and what were the reasons behind the protest. The issue of low representation of French youth among protesters is touched upon. Author traces the correlation between the involvement in the protest and the income level, place of living and key aspects of the perception of the economic and political situation in the country. The article shows the relationship between the emergence of the movement and long-term changes in the labor market, the polarization of the middle class and the increasing divergence between its lower and upper strata. The author of article analyzes the value portrait of the yellow vests and the correlation in the motivation of the protesters of materialistic and post-materialistic values. The analysis of the values of the “yellow vests” is based on a wide range of social surveys and data from the World Values Survey. Author shows how the request for “vests” combined materialistic demands and consumer desires with a request for visibility and the opportunity to have more influence on the socio-economic policy of the state. Finally, the study of the political positioning of the yellow vests allows us to look at the causes and meaning of the movement in a broader context.

titulo: Quels freins à la transition écologique du vignoble ?: Enseignements de l’économie comportementale

instituicoes: Bordeaux Sciences Économiques | Environnement, territoires en transition, infrastructures, sociétés | Instituto Nacional de Investigação Agrária e Veterinária | Université de Bordeaux | École Nationale Supérieure des Sciences Agronomiques de Bordeaux-Aquitaine

palavras_openalex: wine grape production | pesticide reduction | behavioral barriers | consumer inertia | risk perception | nudging | agroecological transition | certification | product claims | public policy | innovation adoption
resumo: Reducing the use of pesticides in winegrowing requires the development of innovations (substitute products, machinery, plant equipment, digital technology, etc.) However, many of these innovations, whether technical or organizational, are in fact already widely available today. The question therefore arises as to whether the key lies in the identification of an ever-increasing number of innovations, or in their attractiveness, and therefore in the incentive system that underpins them. Could it be that the underlying trend in favor of the environment is in fact being slowed down by a number of obstacles linked to corporate routines, the reluctance of marketers and even consumers, or a biased assessment of risks and performance? In addition to monetary incentives - some innovations are currently too costly or too risky to be implemented by most producers - this article argues that the obstacles to the ecological transition of vineyards are also behavioral in nature. Behavioral economics provides a better understanding of these obstacles, both for producers, who are victims of behavioral “locks”, and for consumers who, when it comes to food consumption, often only change their habits incrementally. This scientific discipline highlights the fact that each actor has his or her own objectives, constraints, networks, inertia and, ultimately, rationality. Our experimental tests, recently carried out in France, Spain and Portugal, reveal and analyze these phenomena. They also enable us to identify original avenues for public policies (such as “informational nudges”) or corporate strategies (product claims and certification) in favor of agro-ecological transition.

titulo: THE IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ON EMPLOYEE SOCIAL MOBILITY
palavras_openalex: employee mobility | artificial intelligence | generative AI | internal mobility | labor market transformation | COVID-19 pandemic | talent retention | skill development | hybrid work | employee well-being | labor productivity | workforce competitiveness
resumo: The article examines the transformative impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on employee mobility in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, geopolitical polarization, and the rapid evolution of new technologies. It highlights how structural changes in the labor market, catalyzed by the pandemic, have driven increases in various forms of mobility. Trends in corporate mobility management policies aimed at retaining valuable talent are analyzed, along with job growth as a key factor in enhancing global mobility and unlocking labor potential. The role of targeted training programs in promoting internal mobility is explored, particularly through innovative skill development initiatives and technology training, fostering long-term collaboration between employees and companies. The article argues for the critical role of internal mobility in creating an effective work environment conducive to higher labor productivity. It reveals the connection between hybrid employment models and mobility processes, emphasizing the integration of generative AI as a tool to amplify these dynamics. The evolution of job roles due to the widespread adoption of generative AI is analyzed in detail, underscoring the importance of mobility in adapting to new professional demands. The study demonstrates the positive effect of AI adoption on increasing productivity and identifies short-term mobility as a key driver of efficiency. Generational differences in mobility are examined, with a focus on the paradox of limited mobility among youth despite their adaptability to advanced technologies. Additionally, the article connects mobility to enhanced employee well-being, satisfaction, and socio-economic sustainability. It advocates for a human-centered approach to managing mobility and stresses the importance of international organizational involvement in facilitating effective implementation. Concluding, the article underscores the interaction between AI and employee mobility as a foundational element for maintaining and enhancing workforce competitiveness in the global talent market.

titulo: The rise of AI in health care: transforming the future
autores: Vijay Yanamadala | Virgílio Bento | Steven Paul Cohen
instituicoes: Northwestern University | Quinnipiac University | Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences | Walter Reed National Military Medical Center
periodico: Journal of the International Society of Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine
topico_primario: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
palavras_openalex: artificial intelligence in healthcare | health care delivery transformation | health workforce shortage | clinician burnout | administrative burden | appointment scheduling | health equity | health care access | AI-assisted diagnosis | clinical decision support | clinician-AI collaboration | health system sustainability | AI adoption barriers
resumo: As with every technological revolution in health care, the advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has been met with a mix of enthusiasm and fear. Central to these concerns is the extent to which medical decisions are being transferred to a technology operating on incompletely understood logic and the perceived loss of connection between health care practitioners and patients. However, when viewed from the perspective of potential rather than hazard, AI can catalyze a much-needed transformation in medical care. Particularly in the current landscape, where health care systems are facing critical shortages, compromising system sustainability and equity, the urgent need for a technological revolution is paramount. In the United States, 52% of a clinician’s time is dedicated to documentation tasks, increasing disillusionment and burnout.1 In addition, delays in accessing care stem from escalating demands for health care services amidst worsening provider shortages, leading to waiting lists for appointments, treatments, or procedures, as well as screening, diagnosis, and preventive care. With the advent of AI, a field of computer science focused on developing systems capable of performing tasks that normally require human intelligence, the paradigm is likely to change. Many types of AI, such as generative AI, machine learning, and other specialized forms, such as natural language processing and computer vision, have been successfully applied in health care. AI systems can efficiently allocate resources and schedule appointments by analyzing patient data and predicting care demand, including the likelihood of “no-shows.” In surgical care, AI technologies are starting to revolutionize orthopedic surgical planning and navigational accuracy toward more precise, safe, and efficient settings.2 In postsurgical, AI can be used to predict compilations (eg, lumbar spine fusion).3 These are just a few examples where AI applications can have profound rippling effects across health systems. Taking AI more deeply into clinical care, though, can prove more challenging. Here, we firmly believe that clinicians and engineers need to work hand-in-hand to identify points of stress and/or failure and deploy AI to solve them. We argue that many improvements can be done at the operational or administrative level, with profound second-order and third-order effects that result from downstream choices about how to use the efficiencies gained. AI can also significantly promote health equity by, first and foremost, enhancing health care accessibility, especially in underserved areas and populations. In a direct testimonial to this potential are AI-powered care systems that remotely allow for musculoskeletal rehabilitation4 as well as addressing other health domains such as the prevention of vision loss and blindness (Lions Outback Vision), dental assessment (Pearlii), and high-risk pregnancy detection.5 AI can ease consultation, diagnosis, and definition of treatment plans, without geographical or scheduling constraints, making high-quality care accessible to all. Although biased AI models may exacerbate existing disparities, when their design follows “human-in-the-loop” approaches and recommended development best practices, fair and ethical AI can be attained.6 These best practices should include the use of large, representative real-world samples for data acquisition, integration of bias-mitigation techniques during model development (such as constraints, regularization terms, and fair representation learning), provision of explainability techniques to clarify decision-making processes, and model surveillance after algorithm deployment.6 In addition, AI analytical power outpaces traditional analyses,7 being able to uncover patterns or underlying mechanisms that contribute to health care access disparities or low-value care interventions, which are more prevalent among marginalized populations.8 Leveraging health records and claims, AI systems can predict individuals at risk of chronic conditions or unnecessary surgeries.9 Technology has the power to enable early interventions, preventing care escalation and improving clinical outcomes while reducing costs for patients and health care systems. Including social determinants of health data in AI systems has proven to remarkably increase model performance.10 All of the above demonstrates that the power of AI can be harnessed toward health equity. Perhaps more controversial is the potential of AI to humanize health care via stronger therapeutic alliances between patients and their providers and patient-centered approaches. AI should be designed to complement, rather than replace, the clinician’s critical reasoning and emotional intelligence, ensuring that automation preserves the human connection and empathy central to the clinician-patient relationship—elements vital for effective diagnosis and care. While it’s common to argue that technology dehumanizes health care, AI actually offers a true opportunity to do the opposite, especially since the massification of modern computing. Past experiences have shown that the effect of a given technology is dependent on the right use case. For instance, while smartphones have been accused of creating social isolation, they actually allow individuals to better communicate with their loved ones. Similarly, AI humanizing potential can be explored through 2 concurring aspects, as illustrated below. AI algorithms can help streamline administrative tasks such as documentation, scheduling, and billing in musculoskeletal management (eg, MetaDoc.AI), allowing clinicians to free up time to focus on patients.8 AI systems can also rapidly interpret vast amounts of complex medical data for clinical decision support, enhancing triage and diagnostic accuracy (eg, RevelAI Health). Eliminating routine clerical tasks and enabling faster, more accurate decision-making can enhance care delivery efficiency and quality. It also encourages human-centered care, allowing clinicians to build trust, communicate effectively, and show empathy—key to achieving treatment compliance and patient satisfaction. This is where another aspect comes into play. With the inception of generative AI, communication in the clinical setting has also started to undergo a transformation. Humanization of interactions through AI can be embedded within clinical workflows to enable remote care delivery and reduce clinicians’ documentation burden. In stressful or emotional situations, AI can guide clinicians to use empathetic language, fostering compassionate interactions. In postoperative or postpartum situations, for example, remote human-like conversations have proven effective in promptly responding to a patient’s queries and providing reassurance from the comfort of their home.2 We believe it is only a matter of time until more evidence on this subject amounts. A third aspect in which AI may improve care and reduce costs involves patient selection for expensive or risky therapies. For example, whereas 50% of a large patient population may improve with a pain-relieving procedure like decompression surgery or arthroplasty, this success rate is actually composed of patients extremely likely to benefit (eg, those with an acute, progressive MRI-confirmed radiculopathy with no psychosocial issues, opioid use, or secondary gain) and those unlikely to benefit (eg, patients with central sensitization, degenerative noncompressive etiology, psychosocial issues, work-related disability, opioid use), alongside those who “could” benefit. There are dozens of clinical and demographic variables that may affect outcomes, and in the future, AI may be able to synthesize them to precisely estimate the benefits (eg, 69% + 9% or 18% + 4%) instead of a generic 50% “coin flip” estimate. Although the above examples may seem obvious, there are several known challenges and unknown obstacles along the way. However, we strongly believe that this potential needs to be embraced, as the stakes were never higher. Executing it will, however, require a nondogmatic discussion about the role of AI within health care. If anything, the rise of AI should lead us to question the evidence and doctrine behind current practices, their true need, and the efficiency of their delivery. During this process, we must not fall into the trap of examining only the care that is being provided, but also—and especially—the care that is not. By adopting an overly cautious position that hinders AI exploration, we risk missing out on AI’s transformative benefits. When built with an emphasis on ethical considerations and within safety boundaries, AI risks can be effectively mitigated. Health care needs change, and AI offers just the venue to do this. As health care providers and administrators dedicated to improving the lives of patients, we must grasp this opportunity as it arises, as it can be done right. The author reviews some of the megatrends related to the economic and social aspects of artificial intelligence from the demand side of the labor market, based on recent macroeconomic data sources, empirical research and forecasts. The trends under review directly affect the employees of the present day and are currently prominent in companies’ recruitment processes, i.e. they should be seen as an intensely present pattern on the demand side of the labor market. Some dangerous labor market and economic sociological megatrends are also reviewed in the paper. The author also draws attention to some of the striking trends that are expected in connection with the transformation of occupational structures and labor market polarization. The article reviews – from the demand side of the labor market – the skills and competences that are expected to increase and to which career guidance practitioners should pay particular attention in the coming years.

resumo: This special issue was designed as a response to several events that have brought the idea of safety, or lack thereof, to the forefront of academic, political, social, and cultural debates.When it was first proposed to Open Cultural Studies, Europe was in upheaval, still grappling with the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February of 2022 and the images of millions of people, especially women and children, rapidly fleeing the country to seek protection and assistance elsewhere.This scenario, along with the recurring news about the refugee and migrant crisis and the waves of people desperately trying to cross European borders to find asylum, compelled us to reflect on their condition as being "out of place" (Cresswell, 1996).We wanted to consider what kind of safe zones they encounter when crossing borders, when they are not allowed to cross them, or even when they decide to stay.By using (in)voluntary mobility and the hope of a new start as our departing point, we were interested in thinking about circumstances in which the idea of (un)safety is at play.Three contexts came to our minds immediately: First, the COVID-19 pandemic and how it forced people, on the one hand, to isolate and avoid the spreading of the potentially deadly virus under the slogan "stay home, stay safe," on the other hand, to incorporate into their daily routines several practices of social distancing and personal hygiene to mitigate the health crisis and save lives.Second, the technological revolution and how it has drastically changed how people relate to each other communicate, as well as how information is stored and exchanged.A by-product of technological advances and the consequent digitalization of life is, of course, the misuse of technology, which elevates risk for users (sharing personal or sensitive data, identity fraud, hacking activities, corporate espionage, cyberbullying, internet addiction, etc.).Furthermore, emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and their dual use as both a threat and an ally also appeared as relevant topics of discussion.AI may bring on several other risks: job losses, bias, data leak and theft, or the application of systems such as facial recognition to normalize mass surveillance and track and monitor minority groups.Simultaneously, it can be used to enhance safety by reducing human error, identifying anomalies and potential hazards, or offering predictive insights, among others.Overall, technology can facilitate life and access to information and entertainment.Cinema, literature, and resumo: Education forms the foundation of social development, improves quality of life, and supports the creation of sustainable communities. It does so by delivering essential services, fostering territorial cohesion and social integration, developing human and social capital, stimulating economic growth, and laying the groundwork for higher income and better employment opportunities. Additionally, it boosts competitiveness and productivity. Ensuring access to quality primary education at the place of residence, along with equitable opportunities for vocational training and higher education, is critical for the sustainable development of the Arctic territories. This study contributes to the scientific discourse on the development of human resources and educational infrastructure in the Russian Arctic, continuing the author’s publication series on the social infrastructure of the Arctic. The article aims to examine changes in human resources and infrastructure within the education system of the Russian Arctic over the past two decades and to propose directions for its further development. The research employs methods such as content analysis, logical reasoning, and comparative analysis. Findings indicate that, in recent years, the education sector in the Russian Arctic has undergone optimization through mergers and closures of institutions and reductions in personnel, leading to increased polarization in the sector. Addressing these challenges requires policy improvements to ensure access to quality primary education not only in urban centers but also in sparsely populated Arctic areas. There is also a need to expand vocational training opportunities directly within Arctic regions, codify existing initiatives, and integrate them with new educational projects and programs. The practical significance of this research lies in its potential application in public administration for advancing the education system in the Russian Arctic. Future research in this area should focus on in-depth analyses of international practices, studies of wages and the private education sector, and evaluations of the quality of educational programs.

resumo: Introduction: Inhalation of asbestos fibers can lead to a range of diseases, including asbestosis, pleural plaques, lung cancer, and malignant mesothelioma. Despite regulatory efforts, asbestos-related diseases remain a significant public health issue. Objectives: This study aimed to assess the characteristics and prevalence of asbestos-related diseases among exposed workers. Methods: We conducted a descriptive cohort study with underground workers in Buenos Aires, Argentina, from March 2018 to March 2023. A comprehensive screening and surveillance program, including medical examinations, was implemented to identify exposure-related signs and symptoms. Histological sections from paraffin-embedded tissue blocks were analyzed using light and polarization microscopy for lung cancer cases. Results: A total of 2,690 participants were included, of whom 2.8% (n = 77) had asbestos-related diseases and 0.22% (n = 6) had lung cancer. Occupational exposure exceeding 20 years was significantly associated with an elevated risk of asbestos-related diseases (odd ratio: 3.02; 95%CI 1.7-5.3). Conclusions: The prevalence of occupational diseases among underground workers was consistent with findings from other surveillance programs for asbestos-exposed workers. Occupational exposure exceeding 20 years emerged as a significant risk factor, markedly increasing the likelihood of asbestos-related diseases.

resumo: This article summarizes problems of ethnic relationships among Bratislava (former Pressburg or Pozsony) residents during the 20th century. The lives of the citizens in this period were repeatedly significantly influenced by political twists changing the society. They affected also their personal integrity (and ethnic identity). The analysis is based on documents drawn from ethnological research and data from the archives and period newspapers. During the twentieth century the ethnic phenomenon now and again played a decisive role in shaping the town structure. lt seems that the presence of several ethnic groups softened the ideological polarization of the residents and enabled them more often to express tolerance in solving conflictual situations. On the contrary, when as a result of social processes one ethnic group gained hegemony due to the government pressure (on the verge of 19th and 20th centuries it was the Hungarian ethnicity, after 1938 Slovak population), the position of members of different nationalities deteriorated and intolerance increased. The tendency of the development was clear: the plural society (also due to forced migration) was changing (at least in the wiev of statistics) to ethnically homogenous one. From the middle of the 19th century Bratislava was an important centre of state institutions. It resulted not only in the increase of population, but also in expansion of administrative, industry and ideology. Bratislava became the destination of newcomers drawn by new job openings and cultural opportunities, but many of them were attracted by the vision of power and functions. Satisfying the demands of loyal supporters of each new system was inevitably cletrimental to the "former" ones, who had to leave their posts, gained mostly not so long ago (under the previous regime). Therefore, within each change, the representatives of the newly gained power perceived the often ethnically defined groups of Bratislava residents as their enemies. Their posts, flats, and properties were offered to those who were expected to support the new regime. Such lures and sanctions enforced not only the real movement of the population, bul also a "migration in the place", that is a declarative assimilation to ethnic, social or other politically preferred identity of the actually protected status. Ethnological research shows that such shifts were not rare. The multicultural character of Bratislava survived until World War II, although its ethnic character, at least statistically, has greatly changed. There were two main elements in forming the structure of Bratislava: natural attraction of the administralive, political and industrial centre and the pressure of governments, including principles of social engineering. All regimes and state forms, which followed until 1989, used such pressure (not with the same force). The arrival of members of certain ethnic groups , after 1948 social groups, were motivated by promises of privilege and their loyalty was expected. On the other hand, those, who were seen by the new power as its potential threat, left the town "wilingly" or more often by force. Such contrary movements were permanent, however, their intensity grew since the end of 1938, when on our territory totalitarian political culture was established with all its malpractice, only its types and manners changed. The climax of social engineering was in 1938-1953, during the fascist regime and outbreak of communist totality. We can speak about exchange of population. During one and half decade a forced departure of Czechs, deportation of Jews, expulsion of Germans, drift of a part of Hungarian population took place. Members of "bourgeoisie" had to leave the town because of so-called "Action B11". In the first place, they were representatives of town creating urban middle classes. As a natural result, all official statistical data since the beginning of the fifties have confirmed the domination of Slovak population. It might be useful to define this borderline also in terminology and from this date to distinguish between the pluralistic Pressburg and monoethnic Bratislava). According to all censuses conducted after World War II, over 90 % of the population declared Slovak nationality. In spite of this, in ethnically (seemingly) homogenous environment after the 1989 Velvet Revolution ethnic tensions increased again (especially against Romani people and Jews, to a lesser extent against Czechs).

resumo: This paper reports attitudes and behaviors regarding the 2024 national election in Bangladesh as described by Dinajpur Sadar voters, using a mixed-methods approach with quantitative and qualitative data. A representative sample of 120 respondents-including a variety of professions and relatively fair gender representation-offers insight into electoral engagement, trust in political institutions, and their principal concerns. Local economic issues in job creation and stability of income appear as critical in shaping political preferences. While 58.33% of those surveyed would still trust political parties to represent public interests, a notable percentage of 41.67% can be seen as skeptical, reflecting political polarization. Youth disengagement is a clear concern: over half show low enthusiasm for participation. Misinformation has remained an issue: up to 23.3% reported seeing misleading election-related information online. Moderate confidence in election officials contrasts with a pervasive sense of uncertainty about electoral fairness, with 55-60% suspecting potential corruption. According to the findings, the economic issue, facilitation of transparency, and particular programs for the youth and women should be implemented to inspire more civic engagements. The findings pave the way towards strategies to build trust, combat misinformation, and strengthen democratic engagement in Dinajpur Sadar.

periodico: Journal of Indian Academy of Oral Medicine and Radiology

resumo: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into various domains has sparked transformative changes, particularly in health care, education, and publishing. Among the most innovative advancements is generative AI, a subset of AI capable of producing content that mimics human cognition and creativity. Its emergence in academic and research publishing is reshaping traditional practices, introducing efficiencies while also raising critical ethical and operational questions. Generative AI models, such as GPT-4, Bard, and others, have exhibited extraordinary capabilities, including text generation, summarization, and data interpretation. These tools are redefining key research processes, notably in literature review summarization, manuscript drafting, language editing, and data visualization. For instance, generative AI can process extensive research literature to synthesize core trends, saving researchers significant time and effort.[1] Similarly, it can assist in the structural development of manuscripts, particularly during the preliminary stages, enhancing overall productivity. These applications extend to supporting non-native English-speaking researchers through translation and editing tools, fostering inclusivity and collaboration on a global scale.[2] The advantages of generative AI in research are manifold. It significantly expedites time-intensive tasks, such as citation formatting and image creation for data visualization. By automating routine aspects of academic writing, it allows researchers to focus on higher-order analytical tasks.[3] Furthermore, the accessibility of generative AI tools facilitates collaboration by enabling seamless interaction through cloud-based platforms. By providing alternative phrasing and perspectives, AI enhances creativity in academic work. Institutions with limited resources can also benefit from the cost-effective solutions that AI tools offer, acting as substitutes for traditional editorial services.[4] However, the adoption of generative AI in research publishing is not without its challenges. Ethical dilemmas emerge, particularly concerning authorship and plagiarism. The incorporation of AI-generated content in scholarly work blurs the lines of intellectual contribution, raising questions about accountability. Additionally, AI’s dependence on training datasets, which may contain biases or inaccuracies, can compromise the reliability of outputs.[5] This is particularly concerning in disciplines, like medicine and science, where precision is paramount. The lack of critical thinking and nuanced understanding inherent to AI systems further underscores the need for human oversight to maintain the rigor of academic work. Despite these challenges, generative AI continues to demonstrate its transformative potential through diverse applications. For instance, a study by Wang et al.[1] revealed that using GPT-3 for manuscript drafting reduced writing time by 40%, improving coherence and readability. Journals are likely to incorporate AI for initial manuscript screenings, accelerating the submission review process.[4] Real-time collaboration platforms powered by AI could offer iterative feedback to researchers, facilitating continuous improvement in their work. Personalized recommendations for citations and references could enrich the scope and depth of research. Nonetheless, the development of robust ethical guidelines will be essential to ensure the responsible use of AI, safeguarding transparency and accountability in academic publishing. Numerous AI tools exemplify the ways in which generative AI is revolutionizing the research landscape. Platforms, like ChatDoc, Explainpaper, and Humata, streamline the process of analyzing dense academic material by extracting key insights and offering plain-language explanations. Tools, such as Elicit and Paper Digest, simplify the literature review process, identifying knowledge gaps and summarizing critical findings. Advanced writing assistants, like Wordtune Read, Quillbot, and Spinbot, refine academic prose while minimizing redundancy and avoiding plagiarism. Models, like GPT-Minus1, challenge researchers to critically evaluate their hypotheses by generating counterarguments, fostering intellectual depth. Furthermore, AI-powered tools, like SciScore, are now being used in peer-review processes to identify methodological flaws and ensure compliance with journal standards.[5] In conclusion, generative AI is poised to act as a collaborative partner for researchers, enhancing creativity, efficiency, and inclusivity in academic publishing. However, its integration demands a balanced approach that considers ethical implications alongside technological advancements. By embracing generative AI responsibly, researchers, educators, and policymakers can unlock unprecedented possibilities for innovation and progress in the field of scholarly communication.

resumo: Background Formerly incarcerated individuals (FIIs) encounter difficulties with covering the cost of dental and medical care, adhering to medication regimens, and receiving fair treatment from health care providers. Yet, no published research has examined modifiable pathways to increase FIIs' health literacy (HL), which is essential for addressing the health needs of this vulnerable population. Objective The aim of this article is to examine neighborhood characteristics (neighborhood deprivation, racial and economic polarization, and residential segregation) and public assistance program enrollment as structural determinants of limited health literacy (LHL) among FIIs. Methods Using a socioecological framework, we analyzed a subsample of 578 FIIs from the 2023 Survey of Racism and Public Health, an online cross-sectional survey spanning U.S. Department of Health & Human Services Regions 1, 2, and 3. HL was assessed using the Brief Health Literacy Screen. Logistic regression models estimated unadjusted and adjusted associations of LHL with neighborhood characteristics and public assistance program enrollment. Adjusted models controlled for age, race and ethnicity, gender identity, educational attainment, marital and employment status, number of children, chronic health conditions, and incarceration length. Key Results The 578 FIIs had an average age of 46, with 42% having LHL. We observed a statistically significant association between public assistance program enrollment and LHL (unadjusted odds ratio [OR] = 2.72, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.87, 4.01; adjusted OR = 2.50, 95% CI: 1.62, 3.88). We found no statistically significant associations of LHL with neighborhood deprivation, racial and economic polarization, and residential segregation. Conclusions Our findings suggest that there may be an opportunity to develop tailored interventions for increasing HL among FIIs through public assistance programs. Dissemination of HL resources among this marginalized group can improve their self-management of chronic diseases. This is of paramount importance because FIIs must simultaneously navigate other challenges after incarceration (e.g., unstable housing). autores: Barbara Alba | Gwen Mancuso | Kerry Hensler | Devon Nicholas
instituicoes: NewYork–Presbyterian Hospital
