resumo: 矽肺是一种由长期吸入二氧化硅颗粒引起的慢性肺部疾病，目前仍是最主要的职业病之一。矽肺的发病机制较为复杂，了解矽肺的发病机制对发掘诊断矽肺的有效生物标志物及研发治疗矽肺的药物至关重要。病程开始时，可吸入肺泡的二氧化硅被肺泡巨噬细胞吞噬，并释放一系列炎性细胞因子，这些因子招募其他免疫细胞到损伤部位。同时，像活性氧的产生和肺泡内的脂多糖等加剧了炎症反应和细胞损伤。随着时间的推移，持续的炎症反应激活成纤维细胞，促进细胞外基质成分的沉积，导致矽肺特征性的纤维化进程。近期研究还揭示了自噬、凋亡和焦亡等细胞死亡机制在矽肺发展中起了重要作用。本文综述了矽肺的热门发病机制，重点讨论了炎症因子的释放，氧化应激、内质网应激、巨噬细胞极化、细胞程序性死亡及热门信号通路等机制，并探讨了新兴的矽肺治疗策略。Silicosis is a chronic lung disease caused by the prolonged inhalation of silica particles, and it remains one of the most prevalent occupational diseases. The pathogenesis of silicosis is complex, and understanding it is crucial for discovering effective biomarkers for diagnosis and developing therapeutic drugs. In the early stages of the disease, inhaled silica particles are engulfed by alveolar macrophages, which release a series of inflammatory cytokines, such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6. These cytokines recruit other immune cells to the site of injury. Meanwhile, the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and the presence of lipopolysaccharides in the alveoli exacerbate the inflammatory response and cellular damage. Over time, persistent inflammation activates fibroblasts and promotes the deposition of extracellular matrix components, leading to the characteristic fibrosis in silicosis. Recent studies have also highlighted the roles of autophagy, apoptosis, and pyroptosis in the progression of silicosis. This review summarizes the current understanding of the pathogenesis of silicosis, focusing on mechanisms such as the release of inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum stress, macrophage polarization, programmed cell death, and key signaling pathways. It also explores emerging therapeutic strategies for silicosis.

resumo: Abstract This work reports the design and performance analysis of two multiple quantum well (MQW) blue LEDs, focusing on their optical characteristics. The first LED incorporates a conventional InGaN/GaN type-I band alignment quantum well, while the second features a (InGaN-ZnGeN2-InGaN)/GaN type-II quantum well. Their optical output power and efficiency droop are systematically compared to evaluate performance enhancements. Using well-calibrated APSYS simulation program we obtain energy band diagram, electroluminescence spectra, carrier concentration and radiative recombination rate. The employment of InGaN-ZnGeN2-InGaN QWs reduces the polarization field effect which causes increasing overlapping between electron and hole wave functions thereby leading to enhanced radiative recombination events. In addition a large valence band offset in type II band alignment increases concentration of holes alongside their better confinement in the MQW active region. Using numerical analysis our proposed type II LED is found to exhibit 225.7% improvement in output power and only 2% efficiency droop in contrast to 49% in type I LED at a current of 120 mA.

The author, based on the Global Risks Report 2024 from the World Economic Forum, notes that eight of the thirty-four risks in the next two years will have social consequences: societal polarization, lack of economic opportunity, involuntary migration, erosion of human rights, insufficient infrastructure and services, infectious diseases, chronic diseases and health conditions, unemployment.The analysis of the International Labor Organization (ILO) Report “World Employment and Social Outlook: Trends 2023” allowed the author to identify the challenges of the global labor market that should be taken into account when shaping trends in the development of national education systems, including: a shortage of decent work, a global slowdown in employment growth, an urgent need to increase labor productivity in countries with high rates of population aging, accelerating changes in the requirements of enterprises in the global labor market for employee skills, the persistence of inequality in access to higher education in different regions of the world, an increase in the need to implement policies, the involvement of women and marginalized groups in the labor market, including ensuring state support in host countries for access to education for large-scale flows of refugees and asylum seekers, and a reduction in sources of education funding.In the conclusion, the author summarizes a list of the latest trends in the development of national education systems in the world, which are formed in response to the above challenges, namely: globalization and internationalization of higher education, development of flexible forms of lifelong learning, reforming education for refugees and asylum seekers, digitalization and implementation of revolutionary technological innovations in the education sector, large-scale expansion (massification) of higher education in the countries of the Global South.

titulo: ANALYSIS OF THE DIRECTIVITY CHARACTERISTICS OF PHASED ARRAY ANTENNAS WITH AXIAL SYMMETRY WITH HARMONIC AND NON-HARMONIC EXCITATION
autores: Антон Федорович Шевченко | С.М. Піскунов | O. Kryhin | V. Nazarov | S. Prokhorenko

resumo: The advantages of utilising antenna arrays with axial symmetry in radar systems are considered in this paper. It is noted that the employment of such antennas, in conjunction with modern technologies for space-time spectrum management, such as Multiple- Input-Multiple-Output and Frequency Diversity Array, has the potential to enhance the performance of spatially coherent radar systems, particularly in the context of fire control radars and short-range and very short-range air defence systems. The paper presents a mathematical model of antenna arrays with axial symmetry in the form of a circular array consisting of elementary, non-interacting, electrically small electric dipoles. This model enables the evaluation of the directivity characteristics for emitting (receiving) the harmonic and non-harmonic waves. The presented model enables consideration of polarization and diffraction phenomena in designing antennas for spatially coherent radars. The chosen form of representation of the basic expressions of the mathematical model facilitates the estimation of the directivity characteristics at both uniform and non-uniform distributions of antenna array elements in both far-field and Fresnel regions for different types of array design. The diffraction phenomena on the conducted surface of the antenna array are considered by the image theory. The numerical analysis of the dependence of the directivity characteristics of circular antenna arrays on different types of amplitude-phase distributions and the values of the design parameters of the antenna system under harmonic and non-harmonic excitations is presented. It is shown that when choosing the amplitude-phase distribution at the middle frequency of the spectrum for sharply directed radiation (reception) of non- monochromatic narrowband signals in a ring antenna array with large electrical dimensions and parameters typical of FDA and MIMO radars, changes in the directivity and the level of side lobes are insignificant. The compromise choice between placing the array elements in free space or above the conductive surface requires a detailed evaluation of the mutual coupling.

titulo: AI and the Future of Work: Navigating the Third Wave of Technological Disruption
instituicoes: University of San Francisco
periodico: International Journal of Advances in Engineering and Management
topico_primario: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality
palavras_openalex: artificial intelligence | future of work | large language models | technological disruption | labor market transformation | job displacement | skill development | curriculum reform | labor market polarization | wealth concentration | productivity | institutional arrangements
resumo: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, particularly recent developments in large language models, has sparked debates about the role of humans in the workplace. While apocalyptic narratives suggest wholesale worker replacement, reality reveals a complex economic and social transformation process. This article explores technological disruption through historical context, comparing the current AI revolution with previous industrial and software waves. It analyzes the distinctive characteristics of the AI revolution—unprecedented development pace, cross-industry impact, and complementary rather than purely substitutive effects. Strategic responses are proposed at individual (skill development), institutional (curriculum reform), policy (workforce transition programs), and community levels (grassroots initiatives). Economic implications are considered through productivity enhancement potential, labor market polarization risks, and wealth concentration concerns. The evidence suggests AI will transform rather than eliminate employment, with outcomes significantly influenced by institutional arrangements and policy choices rather than technological determinism alone.

resumo: Abstract This paper aims to understand China’s uneven regional development in recent years on the basis of on political economics theories. We summarizes two theories from the political economics on uneven regional development—framework of production and framework of exchange—and unifies them by theories of labor value and capital circulation. It means to show that uneven regional development will be explained with value production, value realization and capital accumulation, and their interactions as well. This framework can not only explain regional disparities in a static sense, but also presents dynamically developments of regional disparities—first rising and then falling. Empirical research finds China’s regional disparities result mainly from the value production gap. During the period of analysis, China went through a capital accumulation biased towards less developed regions, jointly shaped by market logic and government behavior. It made the effect of reducing regional disparities stronger than the “polarization effect” around 2007, producing a narrowing of disparities across regional development.

titulo: The Impact of Digital Economy Development on Labor Employment Transformation
palavras_openalex: digital economy | skill polarization | industrial upgrading | tertiary sector employment | human capital accumulation | urbanization | regional economic development | digital infrastructure | China
resumo: The rapid development of the digital economy has profoundly reshaped the landscape of labor employment markets. Based on Chinese provincial panel data, this study investigates the mechanisms and empirical impacts of digital economy on labor transformation from skill structure and industrial dimensions. The research reveals three key findings: First, digital technologies have significantly increased demand for high-skilled labor through a “polarization effect,” while reducing the proportion of medium- to low-skilled jobs. Second, the digital economy has driven industrial upgrading toward service-oriented and high-end sectors, with the tertiary industry’s employment share continuously rising. Third, regional economic development levels, human capital accumulation, and urbanization processes play regulatory roles in digital-economy-driven employment transitions. Policy implications include strengthening digital infrastructure construction, improving multi-level education systems to cultivate new talent, and accelerating the digital transformation of traditional industries. This study provides theoretical foundations and practical pathways for implementing an employment-prioritizing strategy in the digital economy era.

Through the descriptive analysis approach and the econometric approach based on the Engel and Granger methodology and Granger causality, it was found that entrepreneurship and innovation have a positive role in enhancing employment opportunities and reducing unemployment rates, especially youth unemployment, theoretically and in previous studies. Using the joint integration model through the Engel-Granger methodology, which showed the absence of an integration relationship between the study variables. titulo: A Paradigm Shift in Health Surveillance: Preparing for the Future of Longevity
autores: Vivek Jason Jayaraj | Diane Woei-Quan Chong | Mohd Ismail | Nur Aisyah Abdul Rahim | Karthikeyanathan Ramoo
instituicoes: Ministry of Health | National Institutes of Health | University of Malaya
palavras_openalex: health surveillance | healthy longevity | population aging | Internet of Things | real-time health monitoring | smartwatches | artificial intelligence | big data analytics | predictive modeling | human-machine interaction | social determinants of health | genomic data | digital health infrastructure | health system adaptation | privacy and security
resumo: As lifespans lengthen, societies face the challenge of ensuring people live these additional years in good health [1]. The World Health Organization's (WHO) Global Roadmap for Healthy Longevity envisions "years of good health approaching the biological life span, with physical, cognitive, and social functioning enabling well-being" [1,2]. But as people age, their health problems become more complex, so we need to transform public health surveillance.Traditional surveillance has depended on periodic surveys, hospital discharge data, and mortality statistics, which provide retrospective insights rather than data we can act on in real-time. In a digital era marked by personal computing, the internet, and mobile healthcare, surveillance must become proactive, continuous, and data-driven. We must proactively monitor and address the health concerns of our growing population of elderly citizens, harness technology to effectively address the complexities of ageing populations, and use big data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) to enable predictive modelling, real-time insights, and personalised interventions. To future-proof our health systems we recommend leveraging technologies, big data analytics, and AI to create an adaptive surveillance ecosystem—one that evolves to integrate emerging technologies and novel data streams [1,3]. In this essay, we explore two interlocking paradigm shifts: the first is a shift in foundational infrastructure, to centralised lifetime health records, ubiquitous IoT devices, and AI-driven analytics; the second is a shift in how we use advanced human–machine interfaces and responsive AI solutions to harness these real-time data streams for immediate interventions. The first shift will transform surveillance systems within a decade to address the health challenges of an ageing population. This shift depends on three components: centralised health records, ubiquitous IoT sensing for real-time monitoring, and AI-driven analytics for targeted interventions. Centralised lifetime health records (LHR) will become the primary repository for health data from birth to death, integrating electronic health records, genomic profiles, and social determinants of health [1,4]. IoT sensing will collect and transmit health data in real-time to interconnected devices, such as smartwatches. Today, smartwatches can monitor heart rate, activity levels, sleep patterns, and even electrocardiograms; future iterations are likely to capture richer, more nuanced data about an individual's health. A network of these sensors will overlay the LHR, continuously capturing real-time health data at individual and population levels [1]. IoT-infused LHR, alongside other non-traditional data from our environments and social media, will stream information to AIs and machine learning tools that will analyse data in real-time, identify patterns, predict outcomes, and detect emerging issues that might escape human observation [1]. This triad will facilitate precise interventions at population, community, and individual levels so we can prevent chronic conditions and personalise health strategies [1,4,5] extending health and life.In alignment with the consequentialist paradigm of surveillance, the second shift will translate personalised surveillance data into immediate action via technologies like human-machine interfaces (HMIs) and AI [6]. An early example of an HMI is Neuralink, a chip that interfaces with the brain to assist individuals with neurological disorders. AIs of the future may be superintelligent agents that will constantly be available to us. In this scenario, advanced AIs will translate surveillance inputs from real-time IoT data and data developed in Phase 1 into real-time interventions implemented via HMIs, bypassing traditional intermediaries and improving the responsiveness of the public health system [7–9]. Imagine an older adult’s typical morning routine in this scenario. Upon waking, their AI companion reminds them to take their medication, having analysed their sleep patterns, vitals, and schedule for optimal timing and dosage. As they prepare for a bus ride, the AI detects subtle gait changes via sensors in their clothing and living space, advising them to slow down via a brain interface, and calculates an increased fall risk based on their current state. The AI guides them to a rest station to recuperate. Chemical and vitals sensors track their heart rate and blood sugar levels. As their vitals normalise and their gait improves, the system updates their status in real-time. Meanwhile, their AI/HMI assistant notifies emergency services to be on a yellow alert based on their location and health status. Anti-fall devices, like smart clothing, are primed for deployment if needed. While the first paradigm shift lays the groundwork, the second opens a new frontier in health surveillance and intervention, requiring health systems to be more modular and agile in adapting to evolving technologies and unforeseen challenges [1,9,10].As we venture into this new era of health surveillance, we must navigate complex ethical challenges. Safeguarding against a "Big Brother" scenario is paramount, so data management systems must be robust and decentralised to prevent misuse of sensitive information [1,5]. Participation in health surveillance should remain voluntary, based on informed consent. We must also ensure access to these technologies is equitable. We risk exacerbating health disparities if we fail to democratise access to devices and digital infrastructure [1,2]. The digital divide extends beyond affordability, encompassing issues of connectivity, user-friendly design, and digital literacy. We must answer questions about data ownership, consent, and the right to be forgotten in lifelong health tracking. Our path forward demands technological innovation, moral imagination, and a sound ethical grounding, so health surveillance advancements serve the greater good without compromising fundamental rights [1]. We must also acknowledge and address the limitations of AI, such as biases embedded in algorithms, opaque decision-making processes, and the challenge of ensuring model accuracy across diverse populations. Government agencies must lead healthcare providers, technology companies, and academic institutions in collaborating to develop standards, protocols, and ethical frameworks for data collection and analysis. Public health professionals will need skills in data science, AI, and digital health to use these advanced surveillance systems [1,5,7,10].The future of health surveillance lies in the convergence of big data, IoT, AI, and advanced human-machine interfaces. By embracing these technologies and shifting our approach from reactive to proactive monitoring, we can better assure healthy longevity in an ageing world. As we navigate this transformation, we must remain committed to ethical principles and ensure the benefits of advanced health surveillance are distributed equitably across all segments of society. Only then can we truly realise the vision of a future where people of all ages can thrive, enjoy ‘ageing in place,’ and reap the benefits of longer, healthier lives.

titulo: Research of the Social and Human Capital Structure of the Population Employed in Agriculture

resumo: Providing competitive advantage in international markets, encouraging innovation, increasing productivity and supporting sustainable growth constitute the long-term goals of countries. In order to gain competitive advantage in changing market conditions, it is not enough to limit natural resources, capital, labor and production factors; the existence of social networks and information is also needed. To increase competitiveness in agriculture, which stands out as the primary sector for rural areas in country economies; there is a necessity to use technology, value-added production, effective use of resources, provide employment opportunities, employ qualified human resources and develop strong collaborations. In accordance with these needs, it is necessary to adapt the concepts of social and human capital to the agricultural sector and develop strategies for the current situation that are concretized with data. Within the scope of this study, a micro-scale study was carried out to analyze the social and human capital structure of the agricultural employment market in Konya. Face-to-face interviews were conducted via a survey with a total of 268 agricultural operators, 96 unpaid family laborers, 294 agricultural workers and 30 agricultural intermediaries. In employment areas where data were collected using social and human capital scales, problems such as social exclusion, feeling insecure due to working conditions, polarization between local and foreign labor, and low levels of bridging social capital were encountered. Policy recommendations have been developed to solve these problems and also policy recommendations have been made for community building and successful employment management in agriculture.

titulo: Risks of Human Capital Development in the Context of the Utilization of Artificial Intelligence
palavras_openalex: human capital development | artificial intelligence | digital inequality | labor market polarization | algorithmic discrimination | retraining | digital transformation | digital inclusion | continuing education | staff adaptation | ethical risks of AI
resumo: The article is devoted to the study of risks and challenges arising in the process of human capital development in the context of the rapid introduction of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, such as the automation of professions, deepening digital inequality, obsolescence of educational systems, polarization of the labor market and increased algorithmic discrimination. The relevance of the study is due to the fact that AI radically transforms the labor market, educational systems and social structures, which necessitates a revision of approaches to human capital management. The novelty of the work lies in a comprehensive analysis of the impact of AI on the development of human capital through the prism of economic, social and ethical aspects. The study used methods of analysis and synthesis of scientific literature, a systems approach, case analysis of examples of the impact of automation on professional trajectories, as well as comparative analysis of countries with different levels of access to advanced technologies. In the course of the work, key risks were identified: automation of routine professions, growing digital inequality, obsolescence of traditional educational models, polarization of the labor market and increased algorithmic discrimination. The results of the study testify that if it does not introduce staff updating programs immediately, the ill effects of automation will trigger additional social disparities and degradation of the competitive skills of staff. The study results bear witness that the need emerges of making efforts toward staff updating policies and bringing the system of education in line with the stable development of the economy and the society. The performed analysis of the example has also found a correlation between the intensity of the digitalization processes and staff adaptation and the adaptation efficiency itself and showed the need of updating the programs of education and additional adaptation of staff with the highest urgency. The discussion of the research results has showed that risk minimization strategies could include continuous education development, implementation of retraining programs, and support for creative and interdisciplinary skills. The article emphasizes the need for a comprehensive and systemic approach to adapting human capital to the challenges of digital transformation. Prospects for further research are related to the study of the long-term social consequences of automation, sustainable educational models development, and the creation of mechanisms that ensure digital inclusion and equal access to the opportunities of modern technologies.

titulo: The relationship of fairness-related perceptions with college entrance system and the employment system
autores: Jaewon Royce Choi | Minhee Jang | Shimwook Choi | Taeyun Jung
palavras_openalex: fairness judgments | perceived inequality | college entrance examination | blind recruitment | personnel selection | educational inequality | income inequality | Korean higher education
resumo: This study examines the relationship between fairness judgment criteria, perceptions of inequality, and evaluations of two college entrance exam policies: the expansion of regular admissions and the expansion of social consideration and equal opportunity screening. It also investigates perceptions of two personnel recruitment policies: the open blind recruitment system and the in-house recommendation system. A survey was conducted on 265 Korean adults (119 males, 146 females). Results showed that individuals favoring equity-based fairness preferred regular admissions expansion, while those prioritizing equal or necessary opportunity favored equal opportunity allocation. Similarly, those attributing inequality to social factors preferred equal opportunity policies, whereas those linking it to personal factors favored regular admissions. However, fairness judgment criteria and perceptions of inequality showed little correlation with hiring policy preferences. An ANOVA analysis on three subgroups (equal/social cause, equity/social cause, equity/individual cause) found a significant interaction between these variables regarding support for entrance policies and their perceived role in addressing educational polarization. Participants generally preferred open recruitment over the recommendation system, considering it more effective in reducing income disparity. These findings are discussed concerning existing research.

titulo: Maximizing the potential of digital technologies for shared decision-making in cardiovascular care
autores: Dion Candelaria | Trond Røed Pettersen | Mei Sin Chong | Linda G Park
instituicoes: Haukeland University Hospital | National University of Singapore | San Francisco VA Medical Center | The University of Sydney | University of California, San Francisco
palavras_openalex: shared decision-making | digital technologies | cardiovascular care | nurses | electronic health records | interoperability | clinical integration | clinician training | artificial intelligence | personalized decision support | patient engagement | teach-back | health literacy | reimbursement policy | implementation strategies | patient-centered care | shared decision-making tools | patient values and preferences | risk communication | long-term evaluation | clinician-patient communication
resumo: This invited commentary refers to ‘How is digital technology used to facilitate shared decision-making between healthcare professionals and patients in cardiovascular care? A scoping review’, by D. Leysen et al. https://doi-org/10.1093/eurjcn/zvaf029. Digital technologies (DTs) have the potential to facilitate shared decision-making (SDM) in cardiovascular care.1 These tools enhance patient engagement, improve two-way clinician–patient communication, and support informed patient decision-making.2 However, DTs on their own do not guarantee positive outcomes. To maximize their effectiveness, these DTs must be designed, implemented, and integrated thoughtfully into clinical practice.3 The scoping review by Leysen et al.4 takes the first step in characterizing the DTs that are available to facilitate SDM and examine conceptualization of SDM. The review highlights both the promise and the challenges of using DTs for SDM, emphasizing the need for structured implementation strategies.4 This commentary explores how nurses and other clinicians could apply DTs for SDM in cardiovascular care, focusing on clinical integration, clinician training, patient accessibility, artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled personalization, and long-term evaluation. For DTs to be widely adopted, they must be seamlessly integrated into existing healthcare systems, particularly electronic health records (EHRs). Currently, many DTs function as stand-alone applications, requiring additional effort from nurses and other clinicians to incorporate them into their workflow. Enhancing interoperability between DTs and EHRs would enable clinicians to access decision-support tools directly within patient records, facilitating real-time, data-driven discussions during consultations and clinical care. Beyond technical integration, the successful implementation of digital SDM tools in routine practice requires organizational support. Healthcare institutions should establish policies that encourage the use of DTs, provide adequate training for clinicians, and allocate sufficient time within consultations and clinical care for SDM. Additionally, reimbursement policies that recognize the value of SDM could further incentivise adoption and sustainability. Nurses play a crucial role in ensuring that DTs are effectively utilized, as they are often the primary point of contact for patients. As frontline providers, nurses are essential in promoting engagement by guiding patients in using DTs and ensuring they understand the information presented for SDM. Employing strategies such as the teach-back method can further support comprehension and improve health literacy, ultimately strengthening the SDM process.5 The success of DTs depends on whether nurses can use them effectively to facilitate meaningful discussions. Effective communication skills remain paramount, as nurses must help patients interpret risk information, address concerns, and guide them towards decisions that align with their values and preferences. However, many nurses and clinicians may not receive the prerequisite and ongoing training in SDM and digital health tools,6 which can hinder adoption. Incorporating digital SDM training into health curricula, as well as offering ongoing professional development opportunities, can enhance clinician competency. Structured training programs can support clinicians in integrating digital SDM tools into their practice without compromising the quality of patient interactions, allowing nurses to serve as advocates for person-centred technology use. A key consideration in implementing digital SDM tools is patients’ eHealth literacy, defined as ‘the individual’s ability to seek, find, understand, and appraise health information from electronic sources and apply the knowledge gained to address or solve a health problem’.7 While DTs are designed to empower patients, effective use requires an acceptable level of digital proficiency. Vulnerable groups, such as older adults, individuals with lower socioeconomic status, and those with limited education, may struggle with complex digital interfaces or prefer not to use DTs for a variety of personal reasons. Therefore, ensuring accessibility and inclusivity in design is crucial, and co-designing these tools with end-users can help tailor them to meet diverse needs.8 Accessibility resources such as large text subtitles, voice-over functions, content delivered in plain language, and information presented through video9 can enhance usability, making digital SDM tools more appealing to a wider range of patients. Nurses can help bridge gaps in eHealth literacy and can assess a patient’s comfort level with digital tools and provide alternative formats, such as printed decision aids or guided discussions, when needed.10 Beyond accessibility, usability plays a significant role in determining whether digital SDM tools will be widely adopted by both patients and nurses. User-friendly interfaces, intuitive navigation, accessible language, and socio-cultural appropriateness are essential to enhancing engagement.11 Multimedia elements, such as videos and infographics, can further improve patient comprehension, while multilingual support and culturally tailored content can help address disparities in eHealth literacy. Additionally, well-designed digital SDM tools should integrate personalized risk assessments, interactive decision aids, and adaptive educational resources to foster a more individualized approach to decision-making. Standardizing these usability features across platforms will not only enhance patient engagement but also ensure that all users receive consistent and high-quality decision support, regardless of the tool they use. By incorporating nurses’ feedback into the design and evaluation of digital SDM tools, developers can ensure that these technologies align with real-world clinical workflows and effectively support person-centred care. Artificial intelligence-driven decision-support systems are rapidly advancing, and hold promise in enhancing the personalization, predictive capabilities, and automation of SDM processes. Through the analysis of vast amounts of patient data, AI can generate tailored treatment recommendations, allowing for a more individualized approach to decision-making.12 Furthermore, machine learning algorithms can enhance SDM by predicting patient-specific risks and treatment outcomes based on historical health data. Artificial intelligence-powered chatbots and virtual assistants further aid by providing real-time information and guidance to patients, supporting them before and after consultations. Additionally, natural language processing can improve communication between patients and clinicians by simplifying complex medical information into easily understandable insights. Despite these advancements, integrating AI into SDM presents challenges, including data privacy concerns, the need for regulatory oversight, and the potential risk of algorithmic bias.12 To harness AI effectively, healthcare institutions must ensure that AI-driven tools are transparent, ethically developed, and continuously validated against clinical evidence. Future research should explore how AI can complement existing digital SDM tools, rather than replace human decision-making, to enhance both efficiency and person-centred care. A dedicated focus on AI and next-generation DTs in SDM would provide valuable insights into the future of digital SDM. As AI continues to evolve, its role in SDM should be closely monitored, ensuring that it aligns with ethical and clinical best practices while maximizing its potential to improve cardiovascular care. Many studies evaluating digital SDM tools focus on short-term outcomes, such as improved patient knowledge and reduced decisional conflict.13 While these are important indicators of success, long-term impact on treatment adherence, lifestyle changes, and clinical outcomes remains underexplored. To fully understand the value of DTs in SDM, more longitudinal studies and real-world implementation research are needed. Healthcare systems should invest in large-scale, multicentre randomized controlled trials to assess the effectiveness of digital SDM tools over time. Key metrics should include patient adherence to treatment plans, sustained engagement with digital tools, and overall improvements in cardiovascular health outcomes. Additionally, qualitative research exploring patient and clinician experiences with DTs can provide valuable insights into barriers and facilitators of adoption. Digital technologies can enhance SDM in cardiovascular care, but their effectiveness depends on thoughtful implementation. To use DTs well for SDM, they must be designed with end-users, integrated into clinical workflows, and supported by clinician training programs. Addressing disparities in eHealth literacy and ensuring accessibility for all patients will be critical for equitable adoption. Additionally, AI and emerging technologies should be leveraged responsibly to enhance personalization, predictive analytics, and decision support. Finally, long-term evaluation is needed to measure sustained impact on patient outcomes. By prioritizing these strategies, healthcare systems can maximise the full potential of digital tools for SDM, ultimately improving person-centred cardiovascular care. resumo: Abstract The aim of this paper is to estimate the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on the wage polarization in Italy, combining individual characteristics with their task content in terms of physical proximity within the workplace. We use an innovative dataset which combines data from two sample surveys, the Italian Labor Force Survey and Italian Survey of Professions, which provides information on nature and content of the tasks. First, by employing a non-parametric method (the Relative Distribution) we detect a general increasing wage polarization in the sub-period 2020–2019, driven by lowest deciles, after a reduction in the previous one (2019–10). Different groups have been also isolated. Workers with low education, high proximity to customers job, such as the immigrant, younger and female ones are the categories that more suffered the general downgrading of the Italian wages happened during the COVID-19 crisis.

titulo: Feminist legal education and teaching competition law
instituicoes: University College Dublin
periodico: Journal of European Competition Law & Practice
palavras_openalex: feminist legal education | gender injustice | gender bias in law | law school curriculum | intellectual property law | land law | property law | women lawyers
resumo: The paper considers the place of gender in overall legal education Beyond competition law, the paper offers general guidance from feminist teachers in law modules (such as intellectual property law and land law), which are not overtly orientated to addressing equality/discrimination It serves to encourage competition law teachers specifically to identify competition law’s potential to uncover gender injustice and considers how to assess gender dimension in competition law modules In 2018, Auchmuty claimed that law teaching for too long, has proceeded on the basis that there are no gender perspectives in the curriculum.1 Competition law is not routinely taught through a gender lens. The relevance of gender to competition law is relatively underappreciated and scholarly research on gender and competition law published in peer reviewed academic outputs is at a comparatively fledgling stage.2 An even more specific gap in the literature is academic reflection on the place of gender in a competition law classroom. This article hopes to encourage competition law teachers to open the eyes of our students—the future competition lawyers (academics, enforcers, practitioners)—to gender issues which are generally overlooked in the competition law curriculum.3 In this author’s view, law subject areas, like competition law, which are taught without due regard to gender, in practice, risk perpetuating existing gender injustice. This article starts with a reflection on the place of and space offered to gender in legal education. This entails considering why gender matters and, then, highlighting some distinctive aspects of feminist legal education. The challenging question of how to introduce gender perspectives to students who are not enrolled in standalone gender modules is next addressed. Drawing on the experience of teachers of Land Law, Property Law, and Intellectual Property Law (fields which are not explicitly directed at redressing injustice), it offers guidance on teaching and assessing gender in a competition law module. That the gender bias of law was first exposed by feminists explains why legal education and legal scholarship relating to gender is called feminist.4 Feminism and its perspectives are various.5 Therefore, before exploring the place of gender in legal education, it is essential to set out this article’s understanding of gender. Gender is approached in this article in the way articulated by Auchmuty and Conaghan as described next. Gender is regarded by Auchmuty in terms of ‘the relationship between men and women which, throughout Western history, has been one not simply of inequality but of power—with men in the dominant position and women subordinate. Gender as a category of study emerged as a result of feminist struggle against this subordination.’6 For Conaghan, gender should be understood ‘as relational, that is, an expression of (often oppressive) social relations rather than social identity…. as a category of social ordering and can therefore be deployed as an analytical tool to interrogate particular social relational configurations and their effects.’7 She, further asserts that feminist (and queer) scholarship use of a gender lens ‘is not committing itself to a position that gender is always and necessarily a category of legal significance; rather it proceeds on the hypothesis that it is likely to be to see what insights this may produce.’8 These conceptions of gender along with Conaghan’s hypothesis shape this article’s quest to seek possible insights from applying a gender lens when teaching competition law so that students’ attention is intentionally directed to identifying any potential effects of competition law’s substantive provisions and/or its institutional (in the broadest sense) architecture on social relations between genders (and, indeed, among other classifications of persons). A common belief among feminists, albeit to varying strengths, is that law plays ‘some part in consolidating, expressing, underpinning and supporting existing power relations in societies.’9 Feminist praxis involves asking ‘the rigour question, and to consider what a School without feminism is saying about itself.’10 Legal education11 which ignores the possibility of a gender dimension is consonant with the ‘jurisprudential imagination’ in which ‘law occupies a self-consciously artificial and gender devoid world in which the individual legal subject is presumed to be without gender, although as feminist analysis has shown, “he” is generally male by default.’12 Androcentrism generally connotes a belief in the superiority of males and it espouses ‘a definition of males and male experience as a neutral standard or normal and females and female experience as a sex-specific deviation from that norm.’13 Being aware of androcentric inclinations encourages one to question, by adopting a female standpoint, the prevalence of presumptions of objectivity and neutrality. Essentially, applying a gender lens entails querying ‘assumptions, working and outcomes of laws that are otherwise presented as neutral, universal and objective.’14 Querying neutrality, universality, and objectivity renders gender enquiry highly sensitive to the possibility of gendered impact [which is where one gender may be more negatively impacted than another gender by a measure]. Feminist examination of International Law principles, contends that they may affect men and women differently.15 Appraising the objectivity of laws entails, as Manji puts it, ‘digging deeper’ by, for example, by going ‘behind the judicial language of balance, fairness and efficiency.’16 Indeed, detecting ‘the silences within a discipline is a familiar feminist method that questions the objectivity of a discipline, as well as the ways in which law distinguishes certain issues as irrelevant, or of little significance.’17 The above feminist strands are next drawn together to shine a spotlight on feminist analyses of Intellectual Property Law (IP).18 IP was chosen because it is a legal subject area which competition law teachers might find sufficiently proximate to offer inspiration. Notwithstanding their formally neutral drafting, training a gender lens on IP regime reveals its potential to worsen the relative socio/economic relations between genders. Easton contends that ‘the wider framework surrounding the substantively neutral law has developed to exacerbate existing socio-economic divisions and to increase marginalisation of certain groups.’19 In support, she points to the unequally experienced burden of increasing regulatory mechanisms (such as charges for registration and costs of legal professional to police IP protections).20 She notes particular areas of IP where the protection of ‘predominantly female creativity’ has been relatively marginalized.’21 Easton concludes that while ‘copyright law may operate under a substantive guise of neutrality it is its wider application, particularly in relation to commercialisation, that leads to an unequal enjoyment of the wealth created by the legal framework.’22 Feminist pedagogies entail ways of re-imagining legal education with a view to fostering ‘a critical approach to law and how it shapes and is shaped by issues of gender.’23 Treating gender as a category analysis of power relations within social and/or market relations (as opposed to identity) reveals the value of pursuing gender enquiry in legal subject areas which are typically taught on the basis of being gender neutral. Deploying gender perspectives when teaching competition law develops students’ capacity to cast a critical eye over traditional approaches to its substantive concepts and its institutional operation. Being sensitive to gender issues nudges competition law students to reflect on the claimed objectivity of this field. A key benefit, according to Hunter, is that ‘[F]eminist law teachers crucially expose the notion of legal objectivity as a myth and enable students to understand how it can function to obscure the reality of inequality and to insulate such inequality from questioning.’24 Thus, feminist teaching of competition law draws students’ attention to exploring the possible existence of gender injustice associated with apparently neutral provisions. Black and Dunne cited a common thread among the contributions to their edited collection as ‘the problem of ostensibly gender-neutral laws, which perpetuate gender injustice.’25 Another benefit of feminist legal pedagogy for competition law is its capacity to ‘open the mind’ of competition law students to new perspectives, at a time when society is evolving and becoming ever more diverse.26 The above provides a rationale for teaching competition law students by drawing on feminist techniques to uncover gender issues which would otherwise remain covert. The next matter to be addressed is where and how gender may be taught to law students. This entails considering, firstly, the design of law programmes. The design of legal education programmes varies considerably across the globe. Contrast, for example, jurisdictions (such as the USA) where law school is attended by graduates with those jurisdictions where high school leavers enter directly into law schools. Within the latter category, the length of undergraduate study of law ranges from three years in academe to five or more years. Naturally, the variation in the duration of legal education directly affects the scope of content of the degree programme. Added to this, is variation in teaching methods. The socratic method has generated discussion on its differential advantages and challenges for various cohorts of students (including cohorts grouped by gender). Another relevant variability in the teaching context is the ratio within a programme of legal practitioners who teach in relation to those who consider themselves to be ‘legal academics who research and undertake research-led teaching.’27 This article confines itself to considering competition law teaching to undergraduate students in an academic (rather than professional training) setting. Yet, even in the academe setting, one must acknowledge the (at least indirect) influence of legal professional regulators on what is taught on academic legal education programmes. These variables in legal education programmes affect the extent to which law students may be exposed to gender perspectives. Some law students may have the opportunity of undertaking a module/course which is devoted to studying gender aspects of law. However, unless the module is compulsory it is unrealistic to expect every student to register to a stand-alone module which is dedicated to studying gender issues in law. The explanations for this reality are varied. There are, of course, students who choose not to register for a module dedicated to studying gender and law. Their reasons may include the belief that future employers (especially in commercial law firms) esteem expertise acquired in other modules. Indeed, Thornton highlights students’ resistance to modules whose title includes feminist due to fears of a negative effect on their future employability.28 Other students who might like to choose a gender module are precluded, in practice, by the design of their law programme. Undergraduate law programmes, in recent years, tend towards offering a more abundant range of optional modules than that available to earlier generations of law students. This leads to a very generous menu from which only a limited selection may be made. Their selection is capped at a specified number (often expressed in credits) and is further limited by the requirement to complete core foundation modules/courses. Obviously, there is even less space to choose optional law modules in law undergraduate programmes which contain a prescribed interdisciplinary or transdisciplinary component or those which confer dual legal qualifications where students must acquire competency in two legal systems and, often, in two different languages. These are some of the reasons which throw light on why some undergraduate law students are unable, in practice, to fit a module on gender into their selection. Feminist law teachers are clear that there is a need to reflect on and try to understand ‘the assumptions about gender relations that are often at play in legal practice and legal doctrine, which are often obscured when gender is not explicitly addressed in the mainstream legal curriculum.’29 If one accepts the value of gender perspectives for law students the most challenging question is how to offer gender insights to undergraduate law students who are not those enrolled in modules dedicated to gender and law.30 Feminist scholarship’s insistence that law be studied in its political and economic context means that it has ‘opened up gender and law as a subject of enquiry, and brought it in from the margins of the LLB curriculum.’31 Some feminists wish not just that every Law School offers feminist modules course(s), but that feminist legal education be ‘spread throughout the curriculum and normalised’.32 The authors of the eighteen chapters in the edited collection Great Debates in Gender and Law would ‘like all law students to emerge from university recognising the importance of gender in everything they study, seeing it not as an optional add-on for a few people who are interested in “that sort of thing” but integral to law making and the legal process…’33 Its chapters consider gender debates in each of seven core foundation modules (contract, tort, public law, criminal law, land law, equity and trusts, and EU law) and some optional modules (including International Law and Human Rights; Company Law and Corporate Governance; Legal History; Law and Literature/Literary Jurisprudence).34 Notably, the collection does not include competition law. It was this omission that first prompted this author to reflect on the potential contribution of gender to teaching competition law.35 In some law schools, what have been described as ‘strong willed core module leaders’ introduced additional context into the curriculum of core modules so that students must critique the rules’ substance instead of just ‘learning what they are and how to apply them.’36 That Land Law, a law curriculum subject which is most ‘often presented as gender neutral, devoid of power, highly technical and fundamentally apolitical’ is taught using feminist techniques supports this article’s contention that competition law may be taught by drawing on feminist legal pedagogy.37 That competition law is infrequently a core module offers some opportunity. There is a view that optional modules ‘provide more space for idiosyncratic approaches, lenses and content and the pairing of like minded teachers coming together out of choice to teach an elective together.’38 Newcomers to feminist legal education can learn much from the reflections and guidance offered by Auchmuty who has deep and lengthy experience of teaching core law modules and optional law modules. It is to her credit that she is so transparent about some ‘push back’ she has received from students’ feedback appraisals. She remarks on how many law students ‘think feminism is a private matter, like religion, sexuality, or party politics: any mention of these is regarded as proselytising, out of place in the objective lecture theatre.’39 She, having reflected extensively on how to incorporate gender into the Property Law curriculum, offers the piercing advice of letting ‘the subject matter speak for itself’ so students study the primary sources rather than relying on textbooks summaries and lecture handouts.40 In her experience, it is essential for the law teacher to choose a topic ‘that lends itself to feminist analysis’ and most importantly to employ a methodology ‘that requires students to read cases in full and so come to see for themselves where the inequalities and injustices have lain.’41 This advice should guide competition law teachers when deciding on suitable topics for gender analysis. Topics such as defining the relevant market clearly lend themselves to feminist approach, especially in relation to gendered products such as personal care items (for example deodorants) for males being marketed differently than ones for women.42 Assistance is available from publications by some leading competition law teachers who have applied a gender lens to topics including market definition and institutional design.43 It is crucial, in Auchmuty’s experience, that the entire exercise occupies a central rather than a marginal place in the module and, for that reason, her chosen assessment is by means of writing an alternative judgment- a feminist judgment. autores: Kimin Kim | Jung-Woo Kim | Seong-Jae Cho

palavras_openalex: technological change | globalization | employment by occupation | skill-biased technological change | routine-biased technological change | automation | R&D intensity | export orientation | labor cost reduction | business expansion | manufacturing employment | managers and professionals | clerks | low-skilled workers | personnel policy | Korea
resumo: This study examined the impact of technological change and globalization on employment volume and employment composition by occupation, targeting manufacturing businesses with 30 or more employees extracted from the Korea Labor Institute's Workplace Panel Survey 2017-2021(7th to 9th waves). It was estimated mainly through panel fixed effects. According to the analyses, the increase in R&D intensity increased the proportion of managers and professionals and reduced the employment volume and proportion of production workers, supporting the hypothesis of skill-biased technological change. In addition, workplaces with an automation level of 80% or more reduced the number and proportion of clerks and increased the number of unskilled workers, proving the hypothesis of routine-biased technological change. While controlling these technological effects, an increase in the proportion of exports was found to increase the employment proportion of clerks and actually reduce the employment volume and proportion of managers and professionals. In addition, when the purpose of going out into the world was divided into labor cost reduction and business expansion, the business expansion type did not have a statistically significant effect on employment by occupation, while labor cost reduction type of overseas expansion was found to reduce the employment volume and proportion of managers and professionals. This can be interpreted as a focus on short-term cost reduction rather than innovation. These results imply that a differentiated approach is needed by factor and occupation in human resources policy aiming manufacturing industry.

resumo: Abstract Based on recent evidence from Europe, the paper shows that polarisation and upgrading are not mutually exclusive trends, but rather, simultaneously defined recent structural changes in employment. The results show that (a) the occupational structure shows a general shift towards high-skill jobs, (b) the prevailing upgrading patterns are often accompanied by job polarisation, as the share of middle-skill jobs declines in most cases, and (c) while low-skill employment often outperforms middle-skill jobs, it has tended to decline. In addition to analysing trends for EU-27 countries with different levels of development for the latest available time periods, the article also shows that occupational upgrading patterns are rather intertwined with job polarisation and are compatible with both the Skill-Biased Technical Change (SBTC) and Routine-Biased Technical Change (RBTC) hypotheses. The employment dynamics of low-skill workers are uncertain, as they are not fully compatible with any theoretical model, thus pointing to the need for a finer understanding of changes in occupational structure, and the extent to which both polarisation and upgrading are shaping the evolution of the labour force structure under the impact of (ongoing) technological change.

resumo: The article analyzes current challenges and prospects for human development in Ukraine in the context of war and post-war reconstruction. The main attention is paid to the concept of human development as an integral characteristic of social progress based on four key components: productivity, equality, sustainability and empowerment. The author examines the state and trends of human development in Ukraine in the context of uncertainty caused not only by low living standards, problems in the field of decent work, demographic crisis, imperfect pension system, poor quality of educational and medical services, growing polarization in society, inflation, but also by new challenges of war. The authors examine the impact of war on the demographic situation, labor market, education system, social inequality and living standards of the population. The necessity of optimizing the processes of prevention and risk management in the context of a long-term war is substantiated. It is determined that the formation of the institutional framework for human development should be guided by the strategic framework of the EU social policy. The main guidelines of such a policy should be: inclusiveness of social development; accessibility and high quality of social services; high quality of life, including labor; decent work; competitive conditions for development; healthy longevity and social justice. At the same time, it emphasizes the importance of creating favorable conditions for the comprehensive development of the individual, in particular by improving access to healthcare and education services, social integration of internally displaced persons and reducing inequality. The restoration of human capital and the introduction of European standards in all spheres of life are seen as key priorities for restoring the living environment and ensuring sustainable development of Ukraine in the post-war period.

resumo: The primary purpose of this qualitative study is to examine and understand the lived experiences of school administrators as they navigate the integration of artificial intelligence technologies in educational management. To ensure a comprehensive understanding of AI-powered management systems, eight (8) school administrators was selected using purposive sampling, a technique that allows the deliberate selection of participants based on their experience, expertise, and direct involvement in AI implementation. AI is poised to redefine school leadership by automating routine tasks, freeing administrators to focus on instructional quality and stakeholder engagement, but this shift demands leaders who are fluent in technology, data science, and ethics. Effective adoption must be holistic—addressing technical infrastructure, sustainable funding, regulatory frameworks, and robust change‑management strategies that involve and upskill staff to view AI as a supportive partner rather than a threat. At the same time, leaders must champion transparent, bias‑aware, and privacy‑conscious AI systems developed collaboratively with vendors and stakeholders to uphold educational values. When these elements align, AI equips administrators with real‑time, granular insights into student performance, enrollment, staffing, and operations, enabling more proactive, equitable, and evidence‑based decision‑making across the school system. Keywords: Leading Through the Lens, Technological Change, School Administrators' Experiences, Artificial Intelligence (Ai), Integration in Educational Management

titulo: INTEGRATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE INTO RECRUITMENT: POTENTIAL AND CHALLENGES FOR THE IT SECTOR OF UKRAINE
palavras_openalex: artificial intelligence in recruitment | IT industry | Ukraine | predictive analytics | candidate evaluation | digital footprint | text analysis | psychological profiling | algorithmic bias | discrimination risk | transparency in decision-making | trust in employer | legal and ethical issues | human resource management | talent competition
resumo: The article examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into recruitment processes in the IT sector of Ukraine, taking into account the criteria of reliability, loyalty and honesty of candidates, which are increasingly being assessed automatically in the context of the digitalization of the labor market. The author substantiates the relevance of introducing intelligent systems in recruitment in order to increase the efficiency, objectivity and accuracy of personnel decision-making, especially in the context of high competition for talent, personnel changes caused by the war, and the need for rapid business adaptation to the challenges of an unstable environment. A structured analysis of the four stages of AI evolution in the field of recruitment is carried out: from automation of routine operations and algorithmic screening to the use of machine learning and predictive analytics methods to predict the professional potential of candidates. The author identifies the intelligent methods used to assess candidates' compliance with corporate values, soft skills and trustworthiness, in particular, based on digital footprints, text analysis, sociometric indicators and psychological profiling. Modern recruiting tools that integrate AI to optimize the processes of search, selection, and performance analytics are detailed. The author outlines the main risks associated with the use of AI in HR practices: algorithmic bias, limited representativeness of training samples, lack of transparency of decision-making models, risk of discrimination, reduced trust on the part of candidates, and potential reputational losses for the employer. Both the advantages of AI – increasing speed, reducing costs, minimizing subjective influence – and ethical, legal and social challenges are presented in a balanced manner. The article proves the prospects for further development of intelligent systems in the field of human resource management. The results of the study can become a practical basis for the implementation of technologically sound solutions in the HR strategies of Ukrainian IT companies, contributing to strengthening their competitiveness in the post-crisis economic transformation.

titulo: How Gender and Work Status Shape Political Ideology: Evidence from Homemakers in Spain
instituicoes: Istanbul Technical University | University of Duisburg-Essen

resumo: This article analyzes the role of women's engagement in paid versus unpaid work in determining gender and intra-gender polarization in political ideology. Modern gender gaps in political ideology, where women place to the left of men, have replaced traditional gaps in Western democracies since the 1990s. Southern Europe, with low rates of women's labor force participation, lagged behind this transformation. This study examines the case of Spain for 1993–2019, to explore the long-run evolution of political ideology at the intersection of gender and work status. Homemaking status is a strong driver of conservative political positioning. Instrumenting homemaking status with regional-level labor force participation to alleviate endogeneity issues confirms a causal chain: macro trends in women's labor force participation rate predict the probability of homemaking occupation at the individual level, which in turn impact political ideology. The article argues that intra-gender occupational gaps are crucial in determining contemporary political cleavages.HIGHLIGHTS The interaction between gender and paid and unpaid work status drives political ideology.Homemaking status is identified as a strong driver of conservative political positioning in Spain, similar to findings for Italy and Turkey.Macroeconomic trends in women's labor force participation predict women's greater support of left-wing political parties.Macroeconomic growth patterns that exclude women from jobs may trigger a political tendency toward authoritarian conservative regimes.

titulo: Artificial Intelligence Reshaping the Labor Market: Structural Unemployment and Skill Reconfiguration
instituicoes: Henan University
topico_primario: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality
palavras_openalex: artificial intelligence | labor market | structural unemployment | skill polarization | job displacement | job creation | technology substitution | industrial robotics | automation | education policy | skill inequality | embodied robotics | China
resumo: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into economic systems has triggered profound transformations in labor markets, characterized by structural unemployment and the urgent need for skill reconfiguration. This paper examines the dual impact of AI—job displacement and creation—through the lens of technological substitution and innovation. Drawing on empirical evidence from China's industrial robotics adoption and global trends, we argue that AI-driven automation exacerbates skill polarization while simultaneously generating demand for high-skilled roles. Policy frameworks must prioritize adaptive education systems, equitable skill redistribution, and institutional safeguards to mitigate inequality. Emerging solutions such as AI workforce management platforms and embodied intelligent robotics ecosystems exemplify the dual role of technology in reshaping labor dynamics. Our analysis underscores the necessity of interdisciplinary collaboration to address the socio-economic challenges posed by AI.

resumo: Against the backdrop of artificial intelligence reshaping the income distribution pattern of enterprises, the widening gap between labor and capital income shares has raised concerns about social equity. This article empirically tests the impact of artificial intelligence applications on the income share gap between labor and capital based on data from Chinese A-share listed companies from 2010 to 2022. Research has found that the application of artificial intelligence significantly widens the income gap between labor and capital, with the core mechanisms being the capital labor substitution theory and the theory of technological progress bias; Heterogeneity analysis shows that this effect is particularly prominent in non-state-owned enterprises (expanding by 0.35%) and labor-intensive industries (expanding by 0.28%), while state-owned enterprises do not show significant expansion due to policy constraints (salary control, job stability responsibilities) and technology intensive industries due to skill technology complementarity. This article suggests alleviating distribution polarization by strengthening worker skills training and designing profit sharing mechanisms, providing policy insights for coordinating technical efficiency and income equity.

titulo: THE ROLE OF INDUSTRIAL INNOVATIONS IN THE TRANSFORMATION OF THE INVESTMENT STRATEGY OF TRANSNATIONAL CORPORATIONS UNDER CONDITIONS OF DIGITAL GLOBALIZATION
palavras_openalex: multinational corporations | industrial innovation | investment strategy | digital globalization | R&D investment | spatial concentration of innovation | regional innovation clusters | international division of labor | strategic autonomy | high-tech industry | biotechnology | investment risk assessment
resumo: This study focuses on the changing role of industrial innovation in shaping the investment strategies of transnational corporations within the context of the digital transformation of the global economy. The relevance of the topic stems from the growing influence of the innovation factor on the competitive positions of corporations in a global environment where technological breakthroughs have become a permanent condition. In today’s setting, the ability to rapidly adapt investment policy to external shifts determines both the resilience and the scale of TNCs’ involvement in the transformation of market systems. The purpose of this article is to identify the key sectoral and spatial vectors of TNCs’ innovation-driven investment activity and to analyse the mechanisms that define the substantive content of their strategic priorities. The methodological framework combines a structural-comparative approach, systems analysis, and methods of economic and statistical interpretation of dynamic trends. The study covers shifts in the sectoral distribution of capitalization, the spatial concentration of R&D expenditures, and the identification of external factors shaping the logic of innovation-oriented investment decisions. Particular attention is given to the formation of technological zones of influence in which TNCs accumulate innovation capital to reinforce their positioning within the global division of labor. Based on the systematization of empirical data, the study reveals an intensification of innovation space oligopolization, primarily concentrated in digital and biotechnological domains. It is shown that the emergence of regional innovation clusters is accompanied by a strategic polarization of TNCs in accordance with their sectoral priorities. The research finds that the shift in investment focus toward high-tech sectors reflects not only market-driven adaptation but also the long-term pursuit of strategic autonomy under conditions of global uncertainty. The practical value of the study lies in identifying structural dominants of innovation-based investment strategies of TNCs, which may serve as a foundation for the development of analytical tools to assess investment risks and forecast innovation positioning in a transformed global landscape.

titulo: The employment of double-adjuvant nanoparticle to enhance immune responses for neoantigen vaccine
autores: Liang Xiao | Yue Wu | Yukun Dai | Yanping Sun | Shuqing Chen
palavras_openalex: neoantigen vaccines | nanoparticle vaccine | CpG oligodeoxynucleotides | R848 | KRAS G12V | multi-epitope peptide | dendritic cell maturation | M1 macrophage polarization | CD8+ T cell responses | tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes | melanoma | personalized cancer immunotherapy | nanoparticle self-assembly
resumo: Cancer immunotherapy faces challenges in achieving durable antitumor immunity due to poor immunogenicity of tumor antigens and inadequate immune activation. In this study, we developed a self-assembling neoantigen nanoparticle vaccine (Neo-NV) integrating charge-modified KRAS G12V-derived multi-epitope peptides with dual adjuvants—hydrophilic CpG oligonucleotides (ODNs) and hydrophobic R848. Neo-NV demonstrated enhanced antigen uptake by dendritic cells (DCs) in vitro, promoting DC maturation and M1 macrophage polarization, while stimulating robust neoantigen-specific CD8⁺ T cell responses. Additionally, Neo-NV enhanced the activation of antigen-specific T cells from human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and their proliferation in immunodeficient NSG mice. Moreover, it significantly increased CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cell proliferation in the spleen and PBMCs of mice, while promoting the activation and aggregation of CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells in the draining lymph nodes. In murine KRAS G12V melanoma models, Neo-NV significantly suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival without systemic toxicity, as evidenced by stable body weight and normal hepatic/renal biomarkers. Mechanistically, Neo-NV enhanced tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) activation and memory precursor T cell formation. This study establishes Neo-NV as a modular platform for personalized immunotherapy, highlighting the synergy of dual adjuvants and self-assembled nanoparticle in overcoming neoantigen immunogenicity barriers.

resumo: This study investigates the impact of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, on labor market dynamics, focusing on knowledge-intensive services and clerical sectors where AI adoption is accelerating.The study pursues two main objectives: (1) to identify institutional and sectoral mechanisms driving these transformations, and (2) to assess policy tools capable of mitigating their disruptive effects.Adopting an evolutionary institutional perspective, the article bridges fragmented literatures on AI and labor, proposing a meso-level framework that captures both historical continuities and sector-specific transitions.Unlike studies focusing narrowly on task automation or macroeconomic job shifts, it highlights how governance, skills regimes, and organizational routines shape AI's labor outcomes.AI's effects mirror past techno-economic shifts, bringing efficiency gains alongside social risks like job polarization and deskilling.Departing from deterministic narratives, this article draws on evolutionary theory (Nelson & Winter, 1982; Dosi, 1988), integrating insights from labor sociology (Casilli, 2019), innovation studies (Torres-Cierpe et al., 2022), and critical perspectives on automation (Suchman, 2007; Zuboff, 2019; Brey, 2000).These interdisciplinary insights align with the broader AI & Society discourse.The findings suggest AI's labor impact is more about task redistribution than job displacement, highlighting the need for adaptive industrial policies, inclusive digital upskilling, and social dialogue mechanisms to manage transitions in these sectors.The conclusion emphasizes that the future of work will depend more on governance choices than AI's intrinsic capabilities.

titulo: Nostalgisk autokratisering: korleis kan vi forstå Tyrkia under Erdoğan?
instituicoes: Oslo Nye Høyskole

resumo: Tyrkia har under Recep Tayyip Erdoğans leiarskap gradvis vorte meir autoritært. Parallelt med dette har regjeringa hans stadig oftare tatt i bruk historiske referansar og symbolikk, særleg frå Det osmanske riket. Basert på oppdaterte forskingsfunn og data analyserer eg korleis polarisering, personalisering og populisme har fremja autokratisering i Tyrkia. Eg set denne forskingslitteraturen opp mot dei forenklande framstillingane som ofte dominerer i det offentlege ordskiftet, og argumenterer for at nostalgien er eit populistisk verkemiddel som regimet bruker for å halde oppe ein opposisjonell identitet sjølv når ein har etablert full kontroll over statsapparatet. Dei historiske referansane handlar om å framstille Tyrkia og Erdoğan-regimet som ein underdog som kjempar mot ytre og indre truslar. Gjennom denne retorikken forsøker Erdoğan å appellere til brei folkeleg støtte samstundes som han undergrev demokratiske institusjonar. Nostalgien vert såleis brukt med to mål for auge: som eit forsøk på å legitimere og dekke over autoritære ambisjonar og for å halde oppe eit populistisk ideal om å representere folket. Abstract in English:Nostalgic Autocratization: How to Understand Erdoğan’s TurkeyUnder Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's regime, Turkey has gradually become more authoritarian. Parallel to this development, his government has increasingly made use of historical references and symbolism, particularly from the Ottoman Empire. In this article, I survey the most recent research on democratic erosion and analyze how polarization, personalization, and populism have promoted autocratization in Turkey. I contrast this body of research with the simplified representations that often dominate public discourse. Recent research has also noted how nostalgia often serves as a populist tool employed by the regime to maintain an oppositional identity – even after having established full control over the state apparatus. Through the employment of this rhetoric, Erdoğan seeks to appeal to broad popular support while simultaneously undermining democratic institutions. Nostalgia is thus used with two main purposes: as an attempt to legitimize and conceal authoritarian ambitions, and to uphold a populist ideal of representing 'the people'.
